- No test asserts the number or placement of `synchronizeSearchIndexPrefix()` calls, so nothing pins the structure being replaced. That is good news: the safety net is entirely behavioral.

**Write this test first.** There is no new failing test, and an implementation agent should not invent one. I searched every mutating member of `LogicalLineStore` against every call site in `Terminal.swift` and found no reachable path today that mutates record ownership and then reads search without a refresh: `admit` is always followed by `enforceScrollbackBudget` in all three of its callers (`resizeHeight` shrinking arm, `resizeWidth` tail, `scrollRegionRows` pushing arm), `setWidth` is inside `resizeWidth` which ends in `enforceScrollbackBudget` with no search read in between, and the row-0 `repairClearedSpacer` does not change record ownership. So the trap is latent, not live, and this is a pure structural refactor. The characterization test is `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalSearchTests.swift#retainedIndexMatchesOracleAcrossStoreMutations` ("the retained index agrees with the oracle across store boundary mutations"): it already walks output, both resize directions, wrap-claim sever and restore, ED 3, eviction, and a forced split, asserting the ordered result against an independent oracle after each. Run it before the change, keep it green through it, and do not weaken it. If the agent wants one genuinely new behavioral test, the honest one is the finding's own suggestion: assert that `searchStatus` and `activeSearchMatchRange` both still resolve after `resizeWidth` alone (no budget pass), which pins the `setWidth` funnel call that today has no sync of its own -- but expect it to pass before the change too, because the trailing `enforceScrollbackBudget` covers it.

**Blockers and surprises.** Five things the finding does not admit. (1) The `private`-does-not-bind correction above: this is a new-file refactor, not a new-method refactor. (2) The read surface is large -- about 45 non-mutating `history.` reads in Terminal.swift -- so the wrapper needs a cheap read path (`var store: LogicalLineStore { get }`) or the diff explodes; the finding's effort estimate assumes only the seven write sites. (3) Copy-on-write is a genuine hazard, not a formality: `Search.Context` already holds `let history: LogicalLineStore`, and TerminalSearch.swift cites research/31/F13 for a measured copy caused by a second live reference to the store. `withMutation` must hand out `inout` on the stored property with no intermediate copy. Note that today's `synchronizeSearchIndexPrefix` deliberately makes a local `let retainedHistory = history` to avoid overlapping access -- the funnel has to solve the same problem, and it must solve it by ordering (mutate, release the inout, then refresh) rather than by copying. (4) Three tests bound `Instrument.searchIndexMaintenance` counts, one of them at `<= 2`; a per-row funnel breaks them. (5) `withUnlimitedScrollbackForTesting` assigns a whole store (`copy.history = history.rebased(...)`), which is neither a read nor a mutation and needs its own door on the wrapper. On the easier side: no design doc constrains where the store lives (docs/design/2026-08-06-swift-terminal-engine.md#E1 and #G9 constrain projection and invalidation semantics, not ownership), and `TerminalDamageAccumulator`-style internals are not involved. Sequencing per the audit's X1: land this before FIND-1 and PARSE-6, and shape the exit callback as an inspection-level API so those two change what it does rather than where it is called from.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The stated ideal is right, with the audit's own Correction folded in: the funnel must live in a separate file so `private` actually binds, otherwise the by-construction claim is false and this is just a tidier version of the pushed obligation. One refinement the finding does not name: the refresh should be per funnel body, not per store mutation. `severScrollbackWrapClaim` performs two mutations that are one logical change, and `appendToScrollback` performs one per admitted row; refreshing per mutation would multiply the search-maintenance instrument counts that three existing tests bound.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

<a id="interact-2"></a>

##### INTERACT-2. Carry the normalized `TerminalViewportCell` into `TerminalPointerEvent` and decide link cancellation inside the policy

`api-shape` &middot; impact 3, confidence 4 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionVocabulary.swift#TerminalPointerEvent`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#isViewportPosition`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#cancelTerminalLinkInteraction`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#forwardPointerDown`

**Problem.** `terminalCell(at:...)` produces a `TerminalViewportCell` that answers whether the point was actually on the grid -- its own doc says a caller "reads it here instead of re-deriving the grid extents with its own math". Then the view destructures the cell into `column`/`row`/`offsetX` and drops `isInsideGrid`, because `TerminalPointerEvent` has no field for it. The insideness is smuggled back in as a *second*, separately ordered call to `cancelTerminalLinkInteraction()`, whose correctness depends on hand-written ordering comments ("the press is delivered before the cancellation", "the cancellation runs before the release"). Meanwhile the policy re-derives insideness with `isViewportPosition(column:row:terminal:)` against the terminal's geometry -- but the coordinates it tests were already clamped into range by `terminalCell`, so that guard can never reject an off-grid pointer. The out-of-band cancel is the only thing preventing an off-grid Cmd-press from arming a link at the clamped edge cell.

**Evidence.** `terminalCell` returns `TerminalViewportCell(column: clampedColumn, row: min(max(Int(row),0), rows-1), offsetX:, isInsideGrid:)`; `TerminalPointerEvent.down/.up/.move` take only `column: Int, row: Int, offsetX: Double, modifiers:`. `forwardPointerDown` sends `.down(button, column: cell.column, row: cell.row, ...)` and then, separately, `if cell.isInsideGrid == false { controller.cancelLinkInteraction() }`; `forwardPointerUp` runs the cancel *before* the send; `deliverPointerMove` runs it after. `isViewportPosition` checks `(0..<terminal.geometry.columns).contains(column) && terminal.geometry.rows.indices.contains(row)` on already-clamped values.

**Ideal fix.** Change `TerminalPointerEvent` to carry the `TerminalViewportCell` itself (`case down(TerminalMouseButton, cell: TerminalViewportCell, modifiers:, clickCount:)`, and the same for `up`/`move`). `decideTerminalPointer` then reads `cell.isInsideGrid` where it currently calls `isViewportPosition`, and returns the hover/arm clears for an off-grid event as part of the one decision. Delete the separate `cancelLinkInteraction` forwarding path and the ordering comments with it; keep `cancelTerminalLinkInteraction` only for the genuine mouse-exit-with-no-event case.

**By construction.** "A pointer event whose coordinates were clamped from an off-grid point but which claims to be on the grid" becomes unrepresentable, and so does "the cancel was sent in the wrong order relative to the event" -- there is no second message left to order.

**Cheaper fallback.** Add an `isInsideGrid` parameter to each event case and keep the separate cancel call for the exit path only. Cheaper, but it leaves the value split across a bool and a coordinate pair that a caller can still contradict.

**Verification.** Behavioral test in `TerminalInteractionPolicyTests`: Cmd-press at a point below the last row (an off-grid cell whose clamped row holds a link) and assert the decision arms nothing and opens nothing on release, with no separate cancellation call. Existing link-activation tests must keep passing. `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalCore --filter InteractionPolicy`.

**Risk.** Every pointer call site and the recording/replay layer (`NeutralTerminalRecording`, `TerminalPTYHost`) must be updated together; recorded tapes that encode the old event shape need regenerating, which the project permits (no backwards-compatibility constraint).

**Vetted.** Every quote is real: `terminalCell` returns a clamped column/row plus `isInsideGrid` computed from the raw point; `TerminalPointerEvent` carries only `column`/`row`/`offsetX`; `forwardPointerDown` sends the event then cancels, `forwardPointerUp` cancels then sends, `deliverPointerMove` sends then cancels, each with the ordering comment quoted. The ordering is pinned by a real test -- `tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTests.swift` "an off-grid press or release cannot open a link" -- whose own preamble says the reverse order silently opens a link. So the hazard is real and currently held together by ordering plus one UI test.

**Correction.** The claim that `isViewportPosition` "can never reject an off-grid pointer" is false, and deleting it would be a regression. The live AppKit view is not the only producer: `NeutralTerminalRecording#neutralPointerEvent` mints events straight from recorded `column`/`row`, so a tape replayed into a terminal with a different geometry supplies genuinely out-of-range coordinates, and `TerminalWezTermAdaptedTests#characterDragSnapsWideCellsAndClampsOutOfBounds` states in its preamble that the link arm relies on `isViewportPosition` while the selection arm relies on clamping, and that an unclamped row would be an out-of-bounds index rather than a wrong answer. Worse, `TerminalViewportCell.isInsideGrid` defaults to `true`, so a cell minted by a replay producer would assert insideness it never measured. Corrected ideal: carry the `TerminalViewportCell` in the event so the point's insideness travels with the coordinates and the off-grid clears become part of the one decision (deleting the second message and its ordering comments), but keep `isViewportPosition` as the range check against the *current* geometry and treat an event as off-grid when either test fails. The two facts are different -- "the point was on the grid the view measured" and "these coordinates address this terminal" -- and the policy needs both.

**Sharper ideal.** Carry the cell AND keep the geometry range test; the off-grid decision is then one message with two inputs, rather than one message that trusts a producer-supplied bool.

<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 20 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `TerminalViewportCell` in `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionVocabulary.swift` carries `column`, `row`, `offsetX`, and `isInsideGrid`, with `init(column:row:offsetX:isInsideGrid:)` defaulting `offsetX` to 0 and `isInsideGrid` to `true`. `terminalCell(at:cellSize:columns:rows:) -> TerminalViewportCell?` in the same file returns a clamped column/row plus insideness computed from the raw point (a range test, deliberately not a read-back of the clamp). In the same file, `TerminalPointerEvent` has three cases carrying loose scalars: `.down(TerminalMouseButton, column:row:offsetX:modifiers:clickCount:)`, `.up(TerminalMouseButton, column:row:modifiers:)`, `.move(column:row:offsetX:modifiers:)`. `decideTerminalPointer(_:terminal:state:)` in `TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift` destructures those scalars and re-derives insideness via `private func isViewportPosition(column:row:terminal:)`, which range-tests against `terminal.geometry`. `cancelTerminalLinkInteraction(state:)` is a separate public entry point returning `TerminalLinkCancellation(hoverMutation: .clear, armMutation: .clear)`. This shape landed four commits ago in `fb05e7b2 refactor(pane): read pointer insideness off the normalized cell`, implementing `plans/impl/2026-08-18-1059-cell-insideness-and-swapchain-inputs.md`, whose invariant I2 states the ordering rule this finding proposes to delete.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift -- link release rejects a same-target run recreated after pointer down

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift -- point normalization floors clamps and rejects degenerate geometry
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalWezTermAdaptedTests.swift -- a character drag names whole cells and survives ends outside the viewport
- tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTests.swift -- a grid that shrinks under a parked pointer drops the hover chrome (pins that insideness is re-derived at ask time, never stored -- invariant I1 of the landed plan)

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift -- Cmd moves set hover while release exit and out-of-bounds transitions clear it -- it drives `.move(column: -1, row: 0, modifiers: [.command])`, i.e. an out-of-range coordinate with no cell behind it, and asserts the clears. Under the new shape you must decide what cell a column of -1 becomes; this test is the one that forces the decision and it must keep asserting the same clears. It also asserts `cancelTerminalLinkInteraction(state:) == TerminalLinkCancellation(hoverMutation: .clear, armMutation: .clear)` directly, which stays valid since the function survives.
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift -- a drag leaving the grid selects out to the edge it left through -- THE ambush. It builds a genuinely off-grid cell via `terminalCell(at: .init(x: 97, y: 1), ...)` on a 4-column grid, then drops `isInsideGrid` when constructing the `.move`. Once the cell travels, that move arrives with `isInsideGrid == false` and the test asserts the selection STILL extends to the edge. So off-grid handling must be scoped to the link arms only; a general 'off-grid means clear everything' reading of the finding breaks this test and would be a real behavior regression.
- tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTests.swift -- an off-grid press or release cannot open a link -- its preamble is written entirely about the delivery ordering this finding deletes ('the cancellation and the pointer report have to run in the order that produces this outcome ... and the reverse order silently opens a link on either path'). The scenario and both assertions stay exactly right; the Why-it-exists paragraph must be rewritten to say the outcome now falls out of one decision instead of two ordered messages. Do not delete this test -- it is the only end-to-end proof of the outcome.
- tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTests.swift -- the cell-naming test that destructures `.down(_, column, row, _, _, _)` -- compile break, trivial rewrite.
- tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTestShim.swift -- three `case let` patterns in `sendPointer` -- compile break.
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- `private extension TerminalPointerEvent { var neutralEvent }` -- compile break.
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPaneSessionTests/TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests.swift -- ~27 literals -- compile break.
- Any checked-in tape fixture that encodes mouse events, if `NeutralTerminalMouseEvent` gains a field. Check `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/Fixtures` and `DanTermRecordingFixtureTests.swift` before choosing the field option.

**Write this test first.** Suite `TerminalInteractionPolicyTests` in `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift`. Name: "a Cmd press whose point fell outside the grid arms no link". Scenario: a 16x2 terminal fed `https://a.co` so row 0 holds an activatable link; build the press cell with `terminalCell(at: .init(x: 20, y: 200), cellSize: .init(width: 10, height: 16), columns: 16, rows: 2)`, which clamps to column 2, row 1 -- wait, use a point below the last row so the clamped row is the LINK row: `.init(x: 20, y: -5)` clamps to row 0, column 2, with `isInsideGrid == false`. Feed `.down(.left, cell: thatCell, modifiers: [.command])` to `decideTerminalPointer` and assert `decision.armMutation == nil` (nothing armed) and `decision.consumption != .link`; then feed an on-grid `.up(.left, cell: inGridCell, modifiers: [.command])` and assert `decision.openLink == nil`. Why it fails today: the event shape has no way to carry the insideness, so the press arrives as plain `(column: 2, row: 0)`, `isViewportPosition` accepts it (the coordinates were clamped into range), `terminal.activatableLink(at:)` finds the link, and the decision arms it -- so `armMutation` is `.set(link)` and the assertion fails. Today's production only avoids this because `forwardPointerDown` sends a second, separately ordered `cancelLinkInteraction` message that the policy-level test cannot see. This test is exactly the hazard the UI-level ordering test guards, moved down into the layer that should own it.

**Blockers and surprises.** Four. (1) A very recent plan constrains this: `plans/impl/2026-08-18-1059-cell-insideness-and-swapchain-inputs.md` invariant I2 states the exact ordering rule this finding deletes, and it landed four commits ago as `fb05e7b2`. The finding supersedes it rather than contradicting it -- I2 is the correct rule for a two-message design, and this finding removes the second message -- but the plan should be cited and the supersession stated, not silently reversed. Invariant I1 from that plan (insideness is always read at ask time, never stored from an earlier event) must survive: the cell travels inside one event, which is not the same as storing a bit. (2) The audit's Correction is right and must be honoured: `isViewportPosition` stays. Deleting it, as the finding's Ideal-fix paragraph literally says, is a regression against `NeutralTerminalRecording` replays at a different geometry, and `TerminalWezTermAdaptedTests#characterDragSnapsWideCellsAndClampsOutOfBounds` says in its preamble that an unclamped row there is an out-of-bounds index, not a wrong answer. (3) The off-grid clears must be scoped to the LINK arms only, or `offGridDragSelectsToTheEdgeItLeftThrough` fails and a real selection behavior breaks. (4) The diff is large and almost entirely mechanical: ~116 event literals in one test file, plus ~27 in another, plus two independent copies of the event-to-neutral mapping. That is the whole reason this is 'medium' and not 'small'. One thing that is easier than it looks: the UI harness compiles the real vocabulary file, so there is no fake `TerminalPointerEvent` to keep in sync -- `scripts/tests/test-ui-harness_test.sh` actively forbids re-declaring it in `tests-ui/`.

**Readiness: needs-decision.** One decision a human should make first: what `isInsideGrid` a replay-minted cell gets in `NeutralTerminalRecording#neutralPointerEvent`. Either `NeutralTerminalMouseEvent` gains an `isInsideGrid` field (tapes then record what the view measured, and old tapes decode to the `true` default exactly as `offsetX` decodes to 0) or replays mint `true` and lean on `isViewportPosition` alone. The first is more honest and costs a tape-format change, which the project explicitly permits; the second is smaller and leaves a value that claims a measurement it never made. Everything else is ready.

<a id="interact-3"></a>

##### INTERACT-3. Delete `TerminalDamageAccumulator`'s copy of the shift-composition rule and let it hold a `TerminalDamage`

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamageAccumulator`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamage`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#drainDamage`

**Problem.** The scroll-shift composition rule -- same region sums, `abs(combined) >= region.count` collapses to region rows, a region mismatch escalates to full -- is implemented twice, once in `TerminalDamage.applyShift` and once in `TerminalDamageAccumulator.recordShift`. The two structs are otherwise the same three fields (`isFull`, `shift`, `bits`) with two copies of `==` as well. Production only ever runs the accumulator's copy (`Terminal` stores `damage: TerminalDamageAccumulator` and calls `damage.recordShift`), while `TerminalShiftDamageTests` exercises only the `TerminalDamage` copy. So the rule that ships is the untested one, and they have already drifted: the value type preconditions `region` inside `0..<bits.rowCount`, the accumulator only documents the requirement in a comment, and an out-of-range region there reaches `TerminalDamageRowBits.translate`, which indexes `words[index]` without bounds checking.

**Evidence.** `TerminalDamage.applyShift` and `TerminalDamageAccumulator.recordShift` contain the same `combined`/`bits.translate(region:by:)`/`if abs(combined) >= region.count { shift = nil; bits.fill(region) }` sequence. `TerminalDamage.recordShift` adds `precondition(region.lowerBound >= 0 && region.upperBound <= bits.rowCount, ...)`; the accumulator's version only says "The caller guarantees `0 < abs(delta) < region.count` and `region` within the grid". `Terminal.swift` uses `damage.recordShift(region: range, delta: signedAmount)` on the accumulator; every `recordShift` call in `TerminalShiftDamageTests` is on a `TerminalDamage`.

**Ideal fix.** Make the accumulator a thin wrapper that stores one `TerminalDamage` and forwards `record`/`recordShift`/`recordFull` to it, with `drain()` returning the value and resetting to `.none` at the current row count -- or drop the accumulator entirely and give `TerminalDamage` the `reset(rowCount:isFull:)`, `coversViewport(rowCount:)` and change-reporting the terminal needs. One copy of the rule, and the shift tests then cover the code the terminal runs.

**By construction.** "The tested shift rule and the shipped shift rule disagree" becomes unrepresentable, because there is only one rule; and the accumulator can no longer accept a region the value type would have rejected.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep both types but move the composition body into one shared `TerminalDamageRowBits`-level helper both call, and add the missing region precondition to the accumulator. Cheaper, still leaves two `==`, two `isFull`/`shift` pairs, and two drain-time state machines.

**Verification.** Point the existing `TerminalShiftDamageTests` composition cases at whatever `Terminal.drainDamage()` returns after real scrolls (feed a scroll region, drain, assert `shift` and `rowIndices`), so the assertions run through the production path. `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalCore --filter ShiftDamage`, plus the throughput benchmark to confirm drain-time allocation did not regress.

**Risk.** The accumulator exists partly to reuse its word storage across drains; today `drain()` already hands the array to the returned value and then calls `removeAll()`, which copies on write anyway, so the reuse is mostly notional -- but confirm with the scrollback-stream benchmark rather than by argument.

**Vetted.** The duplication is real: `TerminalDamage#applyShift` and `TerminalDamageAccumulator#recordShift` carry the same sum/translate/collapse/escalate sequence, the two structs hold the same three fields, and each has its own `==`. `TerminalDamage#recordShift` does have the region precondition the accumulator lacks, and `TerminalDamageRowBits#translate` writes `words[index]` over `lowerWord...upperWord` derived from the region, so an out-of-grid region there would index out of bounds.

**Correction.** Two load-bearing evidence claims are wrong. First, `TerminalDamage.applyShift` is not test-only: `formUnion` calls it, and `formUnion` runs in production on every publish (`TerminalFrameSwapchain` composes stale damage per buffer, `TerminalPaneSession.consume` does `pendingDamage.formUnion(frameState.damage)`). Second, the accumulator's copy is not untested: `TerminalShiftDamageTests` contains `TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests`, which drives real scrolls and asserts on `terminal.drainDamage()` -- below-budget and at-budget one-line scrolls, `scrollsComposeAcrossOneDrain` (the pending-shift sum branch), a DECSTBM region scroll, reverse index, alternate screen, and the selection fallbacks. That is behavioral coverage of the accumulator's composition through the production path, which is also exactly what the finding's **Verification** section proposes adding. So "the rule that ships is the untested one" should be dropped; what remains is ordinary duplication (two composition bodies, two `==`, two state machines) plus a missing precondition on the accumulator, which is why the impact drops. The collapse branch (`abs(combined) >= region.count`) on the accumulator does appear uncovered by the scroll tests -- that is the one genuine coverage gap and it is the argument for the merge.

**Conflicts with.** [FRAME-3](#frame-3), [FRAME-4](#frame-4)

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 8 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift` holds three types. `public struct TerminalDamage` has `isFull`, `shift: TerminalDamageShift?`, and `private var bits: TerminalDamageRowBits`, a hand-written `==` comparing `isFull`/`shift`/`bits.sameRows(as:)`, a `private mutating func applyShift(region:delta:) -> Bool` carrying the sum/translate/collapse/escalate rule, `public mutating func recordShift(region:delta:)` which preconditions the region against `bits.rowCount` before delegating to `applyShift`, and `public mutating func formUnion(_:)` which also routes through `applyShift`. `struct TerminalDamageAccumulator` (internal) has the same three stored fields, its own `==`, and its own `recordShift(region:delta:) -> Bool` that re-implements the identical sequence with no region precondition, plus `hasDamage`, `coversViewport(rowCount:)` (which reaches into `bits.words` directly), `recordFull() -> Bool`, `record(row:) -> Bool`, `record(rows:) -> Bool`, `reset(rowCount:isFull:)`, and `drain() -> TerminalDamage`. `Terminal` stores `private var damage: TerminalDamageAccumulator` and touches it at exactly eight places: `hasPendingConsumerWork`, `drainDamage()`, `recordPresentationFullDamage`, `recordPresentationDamage(row:)`, `recordPresentationDamage(rows:)`, one `TerminalDamageAccumulator(rowCount:isFull:)` construction in init, one `damage.reset(rowCount:isFull:)`, and `recordScrollDamage`, which calls `damage.coversViewport(rowCount:)` and `damage.recordShift(region:delta:)`. Nothing has moved since `5f7a377f perf(terminal): record scroll damage as a shift and translate planner reuse (33/T9+T20)`.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamageAccumulator` -- Deleted, or reduced to a thin wrapper holding one `TerminalDamage`. The whole-deletion form is the better ideal and is what makes the `==` and state-machine duplication go away.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamage` -- Gains the producer surface: `mutating func reset(rowCount:isFull:)`, `func coversViewport(rowCount:) -> Bool`, `var hasDamage: Bool`, `mutating func drain() -> TerminalDamage`, and change-reporting `Bool` returns on `recordFull`/`record(row:)`/`record(rows:)`. These can be `internal` (only `Terminal` calls them), which keeps the `lib/` public surface unchanged -- except `coversViewport`, which FRAME-3 wants public. Note `recordShift` currently returns Void on the value and Bool on the accumulator; the merged one must return the Bool, since `Terminal#recordScrollDamage` gates `pendingConsumerWork.noteDamageChanged()` on it.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamage.applyShift` -- Becomes the one composition body. Two behavioral differences between the copies must be reconciled deliberately: on a region mismatch the value does `self = .full` while the accumulator does `return recordFull()` (same outcome, but the accumulator's also reports 'changed'); and the accumulator's no-pending arm omits the `shift = nil` that is a no-op there. The region precondition the value has and the accumulator lacks is the missing guard the finding calls out -- adopting it is the point.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalDamage.swift#TerminalDamageRowBits.words` -- `coversViewport` reads `bits.words` directly. Once it lives on `TerminalDamage`, that access is still in-file and still legal, but FRAME-3's Correction notes it is really a rewrite against `TerminalDamageRowBits`'s API rather than a move. Consider giving the bitset a `coversRows(_:)` so the word poking is in one place.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#damage (stored property)` -- Type becomes `TerminalDamage`. The init at the `TerminalDamageAccumulator(rowCount: rows, isFull: true)` site needs a `TerminalDamage(rowCount:isFull:)` equivalent.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#drainDamage` -- `damage.drain()` must still reset the producer to empty AT THE CURRENT ROW COUNT. This is the one real design wrinkle: `TerminalDamage.none` and `.full` are statics whose `bits` have `rowCount == 0`, so a naive `let out = damage; damage = .none` loses the grid height and the next `record(row:)` silently refuses every row (`TerminalDamageRowBits.insert` guards `row < rowCount`). `drain()` has to keep the row count, exactly as the accumulator's `bits.removeAll()` does today.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#recordScrollDamage` -- `damage.coversViewport(rowCount:)` and `damage.recordShift(region:delta:)` call the merged members. Read the surrounding guard: this caller already returns early when `amount >= range.count`, so the collapse branch is unreachable from a single scroll and only reachable through the pending-sum path -- which is the coverage gap the merge closes.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#recordPresentationFullDamage / #recordPresentationDamage(row:) / #recordPresentationDamage(rows:) / #hasPendingConsumerWork / the hard-reset `damage.reset(rowCount:isFull:)` site` -- Signature-only; each keeps its `if changed { pendingConsumerWork.noteDamageChanged() }` shape.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- a one-line scroll below the history budget drains a shift plus O(1) rows
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- a scroll at the history budget drains the same shift-carrying value
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- two scrolls in one drain compose into one summed shift (the pending-sum branch; the single most important guard on the accumulator's copy of the rule)
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- a DECSTBM region scroll translates only the region
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- reverse index at the top records a downward shift

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- an active selection forces a non-pushing scroll back to region rows
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift -- TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests -- an active selection rides a whole-viewport push scroll as a shift

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalDamageTests.swift -- consumer-work generation covers every pending category and re-arms after drain (pins the `Bool` change-report contract that `recordFull`/`record` must keep)
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalDamageTests.swift -- fresh damage drains once and repeated drains stay empty (pins the drain-and-reset behavior, including the row-count survival wrinkle above)
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalDamageTests.swift -- row damage crosses storage word boundaries without changing public indexes

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalDamageTests.swift -- consumer-work generation covers every pending category and re-arms after drain -- its comment names `TerminalDamageAccumulator.record(row:)` by type. The assertions are behavioral and stay; only the comment needs the new name.
- Nothing else. I grepped `TerminalDamageAccumulator` repo-wide: it appears only in TerminalDamage.swift, in Terminal.swift's stored property and construction, and in that one test comment. No test constructs one, and no test reaches into `bits` or `words`.
- Worth knowing: `tests-ui/SwiftTerminalSessionViewTestShim.swift` declares its OWN fake `TerminalDamage` (a `Set<Int>`-backed stand-in), so the UI harness is completely insulated from this change. `lib/TerminalPTY` and `app/` consume only the public value surface (`isFull`, `isEmpty`, `formUnion`, `rowIndices`, `maximalContiguousSpans`, `withGlyphHalo`, `expandingShift`), none of which changes.

**Write this test first.** This is a pure refactor with one genuine coverage gap, so the right first step is a characterization test for the gap, not a test that fails for a structural reason. Suite `TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests` in `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalShiftDamageTests.swift`. Name: "scrolls that sum to the region height collapse to region rows in one drain". Scenario: a terminal with a DECSTBM region of N rows; feed enough scrolling output to record N same-region one-line shifts WITHOUT an intervening drain, then call `terminal.drainDamage()` and assert `damage.shift == nil` and `damage.rowIndices == Array(region)`. This is the accumulator's `abs(combined) >= region.count` collapse branch, which the existing `scrollsComposeAcrossOneDrain` stops short of: `Terminal#recordScrollDamage` returns early when a single `amount >= range.count`, so the branch is reachable only by summing. Against today's tree this test should PASS -- the accumulator implements the branch -- which is the honest situation: write it, watch it pass, and it becomes the characterization test that proves the merged single rule did not change behavior. If it fails today, you have found a real drift between the two copies and the finding's impact was underrated; say so. Do not write a test that asserts there is one struct instead of two -- that is structure, and AGENTS.md forbids it. The audit's own Verification section, which proposes pointing the composition cases at `drainDamage()`, is already satisfied: `TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests` does exactly that today. Say so rather than duplicating it.

**Blockers and surprises.** Three, none fatal. (1) The row-count-across-drain wrinkle described under `drainDamage` above: `TerminalDamage.none`/`.full` carry `rowCount == 0`, and `TerminalDamageRowBits.insert` silently refuses rows past `rowCount`, so a merged `drain()` that resets to `.none` would make the terminal stop recording damage entirely -- and it would fail loudly in `TerminalDamageTests`, but only if you look. Design `drain()` to keep the row count from the start. (2) The finding's Risk about word-storage reuse: `drain()` today hands `bits` to the returned value and then calls `bits.removeAll()`, which copies on write anyway, so the reuse really is notional -- but agent-docs/measurement-discipline.md applies, and the honest move is to run the `scrollback-stream` benchmark before and after rather than argue it. (3) Sequencing: FRAME-3 and FRAME-4 both explicitly say 'do after INTERACT-3', and FRAME-3's Correction says half of it arrives free once this lands (it wants `coversViewport(rowCount:)` on the public value, which this puts there). So land this first and check whether `coversViewport` should be `public` rather than `internal` at that moment, to save FRAME-3 a second pass. On the easier side: no design doc constrains the type split -- the file's own header comment cites research/33 T20 and T9 for the word-backed representation and the shift contract, and both survive the merge unchanged -- and no consumer outside `Terminal` touches the accumulator.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The finding offers two ideals -- 'thin wrapper holding a TerminalDamage' or 'drop the accumulator entirely'. Only the second is the ideal by the AGENTS.md bar: a thin wrapper leaves two types, two names, and a second place a future member can be added to, so 'the tested rule and the shipped rule disagree' is still representable. Drop the accumulator. Also, one premise in the finding's Problem section is wrong and the audit's own Correction already retracts it: `TerminalDamage.applyShift` is not test-only (`formUnion` calls it, and `formUnion` runs on every publish through `TerminalFrameSwapchain` and `TerminalPaneSession.consume`), and the accumulator's copy is not untested (`TerminalScrollShiftDamageTests` drives real scrolls through `drainDamage()`). What actually justifies the work is plain duplication -- two composition bodies, two `==`, two state machines -- plus the missing region precondition and the uncovered collapse branch. Write the plan against that, not against 'the rule that ships is untested'.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

<a id="interact-4"></a>

##### INTERACT-4. Put the selection granularity inside `TerminalSelectionMutation.set` instead of beside it

`api-shape` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#TerminalSelectionMutation`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#TerminalPointerDecision`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#extensionDecision`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPaneSession/TerminalPTYHost.swift`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCoreRecording/NeutralTerminalRecording.swift`

**Problem.** A pointer decision reports its selection as two parallel optionals -- `selectionMutation: TerminalSelectionMutation?` and `selectionGranularity: TerminalSelectionGranularity?` -- that must agree. Nothing enforces the pairing, so producers compute the same condition twice and consumers guess. Both consumers apply `decision.selectionGranularity ?? .character`, which silently converts "the policy forgot the granularity" into "this was a character selection" -- and a wrong settled granularity is not cosmetic: it is what a later Shift-click extension inherits, so the next extension would extend by the wrong unit.

**Evidence.** `extensionDecision` ends with `selectionMutation: fixed == moving ? .clear : .set(orderedRange(fixed, moving)), selectionGranularity: fixed == moving ? nil : granularity` -- the same predicate spelled twice. `pointerDownDecision` does the same with `granularity == .character ? .clear : .set(anchor)` / `granularity == .character ? nil : granularity`. `TerminalPTYHost.swift` and `NeutralTerminalRecording.swift` both contain `granularity: decision.selectionGranularity ?? .character`.

**Ideal fix.** `enum TerminalSelectionMutation { case clear; case set(TerminalTextRange, granularity: TerminalSelectionGranularity) }`, and drop `selectionGranularity` from `TerminalPointerDecision`. Producers state the pair once; both consumers switch on the mutation and pass the granularity straight to `terminal.setSelection(_:granularity:)` with no `??` default left to write.

**By construction.** "A set-selection with no granularity" and "a clear carrying a granularity" become unrepresentable, and with them the `?? .character` default that would otherwise settle the wrong extension unit.

**Cheaper fallback.** None -- the ideal fix is small; it is one enum payload and two consumer switches.

**Verification.** Existing `TerminalInteractionPolicyTests` and `TerminalSelectionTests` assertions on `selectionMutation` / `terminal.selectionGranularity` re-express against the new payload and must keep passing; add one test that double-clicks (token granularity), then Shift-clicks further right, and asserts the extension stays token-granular through the host seam. `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalCore` and `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalPTY`.

**Risk.** Purely mechanical; the only exposure is the number of test call sites that pattern-match `.set(range)` and need the new payload.

**Vetted.** Verified verbatim: `extensionDecision` ends with `selectionMutation: fixed == moving ? .clear : .set(orderedRange(fixed, moving)), selectionGranularity: fixed == moving ? nil : granularity`; `pointerDownDecision` spells the same predicate twice with `granularity == .character`; and both consumers apply the default -- `TerminalPTYHost.swift` line ~1352 and `NeutralTerminalRecording.swift` line ~600 each read `granularity: decision.selectionGranularity ?? .character`. The settled granularity is what a later Shift-click inherits (`pointerDownDecision` reads `terminal.selectionGranularity` to build the extending drag), so a wrong default really would extend by the wrong unit. Every producer of `.set` today does pair a granularity, so this is a latent representable state rather than a live bug -- which is what keeps impact at 3 rather than 4.

##### INTERACT-5. Parameterize the one cell-to-search-unit scan by position type instead of writing it twice

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 3 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 5 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift#scanClosedRecordSearchUnits`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift#forEachSearchUnit`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/NeedleWindow.swift#NeedleWindow`

**Problem.** Search scans the same content twice with two copies of the same algorithm, differing only in which coordinate type they emit: `scanClosedRecordSearchUnits` walks closed records and emits `RecordTextPosition` units, `forEachSearchUnit` walks the projection and emits `TextAnchor` units. Both make the identical decisions -- `narrow`/`wideHead` fold to a grapheme key, `padding` becomes `.scalar(0x20)`, `wideTail`/`spacerHead` emit nothing, a non-forced-split boundary emits `.scalar(0x0A)` spanning to the next row's column 0 -- and `NeedleWindow<Position>` is already generic precisely so one matcher can serve both. Because the closed prefix and the mutable suffix of a single query are scanned by different copies, any drift between them shows up as a match that appears or disappears as rows retire from the live grid into closed history, which is exactly the transition a user cannot reproduce on demand. The copies have already diverged in detail: the record scan clamps a wide cell's end with `min(scan.cellCount, cellOffset + width)`, the projection scan does not clamp at all.

**Evidence.** `scanClosedRecordSearchUnits` has `switch kind { case .narrow, .wideHead: key = Self.searchGraphemeKey(for: scalars); case .padding: key = .scalar(0x20); case .wideTail, .spacerHead: key = nil }` plus a `.scalar(0x0A)` unit when `previous.isForcedSplit == false`. `forEachSearchUnit` has the same switch over `cell.kind` and the same `.scalar(0x0A)` unit when `absoluteRow < lastContentRow, row.isSoftWrapped == false`. Both then feed `matcher.record(NeedleWindow.Unit(key:start:end:))`.

**Ideal fix.** Extract one generic unit emitter -- a function over a cell-kind/scalars/boundary source that yields `(SearchGraphemeKey, Position, Position)` triples, with the two sources supplying only how a position is minted and how a line boundary is detected. Both scans then differ by a position factory and a row source, and the fold/skip/boundary rules exist once.

**By construction.** "The closed-history scan and the live-projection scan classify the same cell differently" becomes unrepresentable, so a match can no longer change existence purely because its row moved from the live grid into closed history.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep both scans but pin them together with a property-style test that feeds the same content through the record path and the projection path and asserts identical key sequences. That catches drift instead of preventing it, and it needs maintaining alongside the two copies.

**Verification.** Behavioral test: search for a needle straddling the history/live seam, then feed enough output to push the whole match into closed history, asserting `searchStatus` total and `activeSearchMatchRange` are unchanged at every step -- including a needle containing a wide character, a padding cell, and a hard line break. The existing `scannedSearchMatchRanges` oracle gives a second comparison point. `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalCore --filter Search`.

**Risk.** This is the hot scan path; `forEachSearchUnit`'s comment says it avoids constructing selection units and avoids allocating for the single-scalar cell. The generic version must stay non-allocating and inlinable, so it needs the `scrollback-stream` / search benchmarks before and after.

**Vetted.** Both scans exist and both contain the cell-kind switch quoted, and the clamp asymmetry is real (`min(scan.cellCount, cellOffset + width)` in the record scan, no clamp in `forEachSearchUnit`). But the two loops are not one algorithm in two coordinate systems. `scanClosedRecordSearchUnits` iterates *records* (logical lines) through `history.forEachClosedRecordCell` and emits a boundary unit when `previous.isForcedSplit == false`; `forEachSearchUnit` iterates *display rows* through `ProjectionRows.forEachRow` and emits one when `row.isSoftWrapped == false`. Different iteration domain, different cell accessor, different boundary source. What they actually share is the kind-to-key classification, and both already call the same `Self.searchGraphemeKey(for:)` on the same `TerminalScalars` type.

**Correction.** The proposed generic emitter would have to take the row source, the position factory, and the boundary predicate as parameters, which re-introduces everything that differs and leaves only the switch shared -- so it is a large change for a small deduplication. The real ideal is a single `searchUnitKey(kind:scalars:) -> SearchGraphemeKey?` classifier both loops call, which is where the only genuinely duplicated rule lives, plus adding the missing end clamp to the projection scan. Note also that the matcher half was already unified deliberately (commit 4f9d4701 "unify search scans on one matcher"), and that `scannedSearchMatchRanges` already exists as a cross-implementation oracle -- the index built from the record scan is compared against a direct projection scan in tests -- so the drift the finding fears is partly instrumented today. Impact drops accordingly.

**Sharper ideal.** Extract the shared cell-kind classifier only; leave the two traversals as the different things they are, and clamp the projection scan's wide-cell end.

**Conflicts with.** [FIND-3](#find-3)

<a id="interact-6"></a>

##### INTERACT-6. Key pointer-owner and wheel-remainder storage by their enums instead of by hand-written slots

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#TerminalInteractionState`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInteractionPolicy.swift#wheelRemainder`

**Problem.** `TerminalInteractionState` stores one owner per mouse button as a three-element array literal indexed by `button.rawValue`, and one wheel remainder per route as three named fields reached through three hand-written switch functions. Both are per-case storage enumerated by hand. `TerminalMouseButton` is a plain `Int`-raw enum with no `CaseIterable`, so adding a fourth button (back/forward, which AppKit does deliver) makes `state.pointerOwners[button.rawValue]` a fatal index-out-of-range at the first press rather than a compile error; adding a wheel route means remembering to extend three separate switches.

**Evidence.** `fileprivate var pointerOwners: [TerminalPointerConsumption?] = [nil, nil, nil]`, read and written throughout `decideTerminalPointer` as `state.pointerOwners[button.rawValue]`. `TerminalMouseButton` is declared `public enum TerminalMouseButton: Int` with `left = 0`, `middle = 1`, `right = 2` and no `CaseIterable`. The wheel side has `localWheel`/`reportWheel`/`alternateWheel` plus `wheelRemainder(for:state:)`, `setWheelRemainder(_:for:state:)` and `resetWheelRemainder(for:state:)`, each a three-case switch over `TerminalWheelRoute`.

**Ideal fix.** Make both enums `CaseIterable` and hold the per-case values in one small keyed value (a dictionary keyed by the enum, or a fixed-size store built from `allCases`) with a subscript. `state.owners[button]` and `state.wheel[route]` then have no index arithmetic and no per-case accessor functions, and a new case gets storage automatically.

**By construction.** "A button with no slot in the owner array" and "a wheel route wired into some of its accessors but not all" become unrepresentable: storage is derived from the case list rather than restated next to it.

**Cheaper fallback.** Leave the storage shape and add `CaseIterable` plus a `precondition(button.rawValue < pointerOwners.count)`. That converts a crash into a louder crash and keeps the three wheel switches.

**Verification.** Behavioral test: drive a full press/drag/release gesture on each button and each wheel route through `decideTerminalPointer` / `decideTerminalWheel` and assert ownership latching and fractional accumulation are unchanged; the existing `TerminalInteractionPolicyTests` wheel-remainder and owner tests cover most of this already. `swift test --package-path lib/TerminalCore --filter InteractionPolicy`.

**Risk.** `TerminalInteractionState` is `Equatable` and copied per event; a dictionary makes it refcounted, which matters if this value is copied on a hot path. Prefer a fixed-size inline store over a `Dictionary` if the pointer path shows up in a profile.

**Vetted.** `fileprivate var pointerOwners: [TerminalPointerConsumption?] = [nil, nil, nil]` indexed by `button.rawValue` is real, `TerminalMouseButton` is a plain `Int`-raw enum with no `CaseIterable`, and `wheelRemainder`/`setWheelRemainder`/`resetWheelRemainder` are three switches over `TerminalWheelRoute` beside three named fields.

**Correction.** The wheel half of the problem does not exist as stated. All three wheel accessors are exhaustive `switch` statements over a non-frozen-in-module enum, so adding a `TerminalWheelRoute` case is a compile error in each of them -- the compiler already enforces what the finding says a developer must remember. Only the pointer-owner array is a genuine hazard, and only a latent one: a fourth `TerminalMouseButton` case would make `state.pointerOwners[button.rawValue]` a runtime index-out-of-range instead of a compile error. So the finding shrinks to "give `pointerOwners` storage derived from the case list", which is a few lines, and the wheel-storage rework should be dropped rather than done. Keep the finding's own risk note: prefer a fixed-size inline store over a `Dictionary`, since `TerminalInteractionState` is `Equatable` and copied per event.

**Write this test first.** There is no new failing test, and none should be written. The finding is a pure refactor: with only three `TerminalMouseButton` cases, `pointerOwners[button.rawValue]` is in bounds for every value the type can hold, so no input reaches the hazard and no observable behavior changes. A test that added a fourth case to prove the point would be asserting the storage's structure, which AGENTS.md forbids. The characterization test is `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalInteractionPolicyTests.swift#linkArmPrecedesReportMotion`: it is the only test that holds two different owners for two different buttons in one state at the same time (right latched to report, left latched to link, then a move that link wins), so it is the one test that would fail if the new keyed store mixed up its keys. Run it, then `pointerOwnershipLatch` and `selectionGestureCompletionOwnership`, before and after the change; the whole `--filter InteractionPolicy` suite is the wider net.

**Blockers and surprises.** Nothing blocks this, and it is smaller than it reads. Three things worth knowing. First, `TerminalMouseButton` lives in `TerminalInputEncoding.swift`, not in the policy file or the vocabulary file the finding names, so the change spans two source files. Second, `rawValue` carries protocol meaning beyond array indexing: `encodeTerminalMouse` uses `button.rawValue` as the mouse-report button code and as the `1 << rawValue` held-button mask, and `NeutralTerminalRecording` reconstructs a button with `TerminalMouseButton(rawValue: $0 - 1)`.
