They call `driver.reconcile(...)` and read `.appliedProjection` / `.unappliedTabIds` / `.unappliedGroupIds` by name, so adding a field is source-compatible; changing `applySidebarOps`'s tuple is not visible to them because only the driver calls it. Check before assuming zero UI churn.

**Write this test first.** Suite `SidebarItemStoreTests`, name "a single-group identity change rebuilds the outline instead of dropping every op". Scenario: build model A with one group G1 holding tab t1 and model B with one group G2 holding tab t2 -- both single-group mode, different group ids, disjoint tabs, which is the shape a coalesced create-group-plus-delete-group sweep produces. Seed a store from A with `seedSidebarStore(A)` (the existing file-private helper), then apply `computeSidebarRowOps(old: desiredSidebar(in: A), new: desiredSidebar(in: B))` through `store.apply(_:projection:)` with B's projection. Assert `store.displayedTabItem(t2) != nil` and `store.displayedTabItem(t1) == nil`. Why it fails today: `computeSidebarRowOps` sees `old.isSingleGroupMode == new.isSingleGroupMode`, so it does not emit `.reloadAll`. It then emits `.insertGroup(G2, 0)` and `.removeGroup(0)` from the group-level `sidebarSequenceOps`, and emits no tab-level ops at all, because the level-2 loop skips any new group with no matching old group. The store rejects both group ops (`guard !projection.isSingleGroupMode`), so nothing at all happens: t1's row stays mounted and t2's row is never inserted. Two notes for the implementer. First, this test must be written against `SidebarItemStore`, not against the `applySidebarRowOps` / `checkRowOps` model-apply harness in ReconcileTests -- that harness happily applies group inserts and removes in single-group mode, so it would pass on the current tree and prove nothing. The gap between that harness and the real store is itself part of the finding. Second, `.rejected` alone does not make this test pass: with `.rejected` wired to a driver-level reloadAll the pure store test still sees no repair, because the escalation lives in app/. So the store test drives the `computeSidebarRowOps` half of the fix, and the `.rejected` half needs its own (smaller) test asserting that a refused op returns `.rejected` rather than `.none`.

**Blockers and surprises.** The finding's original damage claim does not reproduce, and the Vetted paragraph says so: the cache the diff runs against only ever rolls back group and tab attribute fields, never row identity or order, so the store's structure and the cached projection cannot drift through the normal path. Do not start by trying to write the test the original Verification describes (seed the store from a stale state with one row missing) -- the Correction rejects it explicitly as a state the pipeline cannot produce. Three further things. (1) The finding's Ideal fix -- stop validating indices and derive row positions from the projection -- is not the ideal here and I would not pursue it. `app/SidebarView.swift#applyRowOp` hands the store's index straight to `NSOutlineView.insertItems(at:inParent:)` / `removeItems(at:inParent:)`, and those calls must receive the same index the store used, so the mutation keeps carrying it either way; deriving it from the projection changes where the index comes from without removing the possibility of disagreement, because the store's mounted rows and the projection are still two structures. The structural fix that actually removes the class is the narrow one the Correction names: make the diff and the store agree about when a group row exists (the `isSingleGroupMode` gate), and make disagreement loud everywhere else (`.rejected` plus escalation). (2) The escalation needs a decision that the finding does not make: on rejection, does the driver keep the old projection and let the NEXT sweep repair, or does the current sweep run a reloadAll immediately? Keeping the old projection is simpler but leaves the outline visibly wrong until something else triggers a sweep, and coalesced sweeps can be up to 75ms apart or absent entirely if nothing else changes. Same-sweep reloadAll is the correct behavior and is more code. (3) `SidebarOutlineMutation` is not `Equatable` (it carries `SidebarItem`, a class), so the store tests match it with file-private `requireX` / `isX` helpers rather than `==`; a new `.rejected` case needs its own helper in that style, not an equality assertion.

**Readiness: needs-decision.** One choice belongs to a human before this starts: on a rejected row op, does the sweep escalate to a full reloadAll immediately (correct, more code in app/SidebarView.swift and the driver) or does the driver simply refuse to advance its cache so the next sweep repairs (smaller, but the outline stays wrong for an unbounded interval since nothing guarantees a next sweep)? The computeSidebarRowOps half of the fix -- the isSingleGroupMode gate plus the group-identity reloadAll -- has no such question and is ready to start on its own; it is also the half that carries the failing test. A reasonable slice is to land that first and take the .rejected escalation as a second commit once the escalation policy is chosen.

</details>

##### MODEL-3. Collapse ContainerShape to layout plus zoomedLeaf; derive the structural fingerprint

`simplification` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 1 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/ModelOperations.swift#ContainerShape`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/ModelOperations.swift#containerShape`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#computeContainerOps`

**Problem.** `ContainerShape` stores three facts of which two are derived. `tree` is exactly `layout` with the ratios dropped, and `isZoomed` is exactly `zoomedLeaf != nil`. Both duplicates participate in `Equatable`, and `isZoomed` is read by nothing at all -- it can only produce a spurious shape difference. The initializer also takes `tree` and `layout` independently, so a value whose structural fingerprint disagrees with its own layout tree is representable.

**Evidence.** `ContainerShape` declares `let tree: ContainerShapeNode; let layout: ContainerLayoutNode; let isZoomed: Bool; let zoomedLeaf: PaneId?`, with an initializer defaulting `layout` to `defaultContainerLayoutNode(tree)` -- a fabricated 0.5-ratio tree. `containerShapeNode` and `containerLayoutNode` are the same walk, the second keeping `ratio`. `containerShape(of:)` always builds them consistently (`isZoomed: tab.paneTree.isZoomed, zoomedLeaf: tab.paneTree.isZoomed ? tab.paneTree.focusedPaneId : nil`). `computeContainerOps` reads only `oldShape.tree != shape.tree`, `oldShape.layout != shape.layout`, and `oldShape.zoomedLeaf != shape.zoomedLeaf`; grepping `isZoomed` across app/ and lib/ finds no read of `ContainerShape.isZoomed` outside its own declaration and test fixtures.

**Ideal fix.** Reduce `ContainerShape` to `let layout: ContainerLayoutNode` and `let zoomedLeaf: PaneId?`, with `var structure: ContainerShapeNode` computed by dropping ratios from `layout`. Delete `isZoomed`, `containerShapeNode(_:)` over `SplitNodeModel`, and `defaultContainerLayoutNode`; `computeContainerOps` then compares `structure` for `.setTree` and `layout` for `.setLayout` off one stored value.

**By construction.** A container shape whose structural fingerprint contradicts its own layout tree, and a shape claiming zoom with no zoomed leaf (or a zoomed leaf with zoom off), stop existing as values.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is smaller than what it replaces.

**Verification.** The existing container-op model-apply tests must keep passing: build old/new shapes from real `TabModel`s via `containerShape(of:)`, apply `computeContainerOps` to a presence/visibility map, and assert it equals the new key set and visibility. Add one case asserting a ratio-only edit yields `.setLayout` and never `.setTree`.

**Risk.** Test fixtures construct `ContainerShape(tree:isZoomed:zoomedLeaf:)` directly and must be rewritten to build a layout node; no production caller does.

**Vetted.** Read `ModelOperations.swift#ContainerShape`, `#containerShapeNode`, `#containerLayoutNode`, `#defaultContainerLayoutNode`, `#containerShape(of:)` and `Projections.swift#computeContainerOps`. Every claim holds: `tree` is `layout` with ratios dropped, `isZoomed` is `zoomedLeaf != nil` at the only production construction site, the initializer takes both independently with a fabricated 0.5-ratio default, and `computeContainerOps` reads `tree`, `layout` and `zoomedLeaf` but never `isZoomed`. Grepping `isZoomed` across app/ and lib/ finds only `PaneTree.isZoomed` plus one test fixture (`ReconcileTests.swift`) and IPC reply keys -- no production read of `ContainerShape.isZoomed`.

**Sharper ideal.** Do not add a computed `var structure: ContainerShapeNode` that rebuilds a tree from `layout`: reading it in the diff would allocate two indirect-enum trees per comparison, which is worse than the mirror it replaces. Store `layout` and `zoomedLeaf` only, delete `ContainerShapeNode`, `containerShapeNode(_:)` and `defaultContainerLayoutNode`, and give `computeContainerOps` a recursive `structurallyEqual(_:_:)` over two `ContainerLayoutNode`s that compares ids and directions and skips ratios. That is the version the RECON-2 addendum prices, and it needs the same two behavioral tests: a ratio-only edit must emit `.setLayout` and never `.setTree`, and a split or close must emit `.setTree`.

**Conflicts with.** [RECON-1](#recon-1)

There is no scenario where the current code produces a wrong op, so an implementer who insists on a red test will end up asserting structure, which the AGENTS.md test rule forbids. The correct framing: the pair of tests that guards this refactor already exists and both must keep passing -- "a ratio-only container change requests layout without a tree edit" (which is the .setLayout direction, present today) and this new split/close case (the .setTree direction, which is only covered incidentally today inside computeContainerOpsUsesFullBuildOnlyForAbsentTab, using synthetic cShape fixtures rather than real TabModels). So write the new test first as a characterization test built from real TabModels via containerShape(of:), confirm it is green, and only then delete the mirror. Both directions are named in the RECON-2 addendum as the precondition for deleting the second mirror, and they are exactly the two ways a wrongly-written structurallyEqual fails: misreading a ratio change as structural tears the container down and loses pane view state, misreading a real tree change as ratio-only leaves the panes unmounted.

**Blockers and surprises.** Nothing hard, and the change is smaller than it reads. Four things worth knowing. (1) The `isZoomed` deletion is safe but load-bearing for one existing assertion: `containerShapeStructuralChangeUnequal` asserts a zoom toggle changes the shape, and today both `isZoomed` and `zoomedLeaf` differ. (2) `defaultContainerLayoutNode` exists purely to serve the two test fixtures' `layout: nil` path; deleting it is what forces the fixture rewrite, and that rewrite is the entire compile-break surface. The honest report is "the shape-builder frames are present or absent under reconcileContainers", read from `just benchmark-trace scrollback-stream template="Time Profiler" seconds=30`. Landing MODEL-3 first is the stated order and the right one: RECON-1 then adds its field to a two-field struct instead of a four-field one. Do not merge them -- RECON-1 changes behavior (ops stop firing) and MODEL-3 does not, and mixing a behavior change into a pure refactor destroys the characterization argument above.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The finding's Ideal-fix paragraph proposes a computed `var structure: ContainerShapeNode` derived from `layout`. That is worse than the current code for the one thing this change is about: `computeContainerOps` reads it once per tab per sweep, and each read would rebuild an indirect-enum tree, heap-allocating a box per node -- the exact allocation the mirror was costing. The audit's own Sharper-ideal paragraph already retracts it in favour of a recursive `structurallyEqual(_:_:)` over two `ContainerLayoutNode`s. Follow the Sharper ideal, not the Ideal fix. Also note the deeper lift RECON-2 raises and MODEL-3 does not: `SplitNodeModel` stores a whole `PaneModel` in its leaves, which is the only reason a projection mirror has to exist at all. Leaves holding a bare `PaneId` with panes in a side table would make `tab.paneTree.root` itself the container shape and the projection a copy rather than a rebuild -- but that directly contradicts the tree-owns-panes invariant stated in Model.swift's pane-access section header ("A pane exists iff a tree leaf owns it") and pinned by TreeOwnsPanesTests, so it is not on the table without a much larger decision. Say so in the plan and leave it there.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

**Added by the cost pass (RECON-2).** The performance pass prices this mirror per sweep rather than per reader. `desiredContainerShapes` rebuilds both indirect enums for every tab in the model on every reconcile sweep, and an indirect enum boxes each node, so a tab with P panes heap-allocates 2 x (2P-1) boxes per sweep -- and sweeps run inline for every non-coalescing Msg and at up to 1/0.075s for coalesced ones. Dropping the `tree` mirror and comparing the layout tree with a ratio-skipping structural walk halves that allocation count and removes the one reason the projection needs a second traversal. No calibrated workload can decide it, because every workload on the ladder runs one tab and one pane: the honest instrument is `just benchmark-trace scrollback-stream template="Time Profiler" seconds=30`, reading the combined main-thread share of the shape-node builders and `swift_allocObject` under `reconcileContainers`, and the honest report at one tab is "the frame is present or absent", not a speedup. The regression risk is that structural equality and layout equality stop being two separately stored values that can be compared field by field: if the ratio-skipping walk is written wrong, a pure ratio change is misread as a tree change and the container is torn down and rebuilt (losing pane view state), or a genuine tree change is misread as ratio-only and the panes never remount. Both directions need a behavioral test over the diff -- a ratio-only edit must emit `.setLayout` and never `.setTree`, and a split or close must emit `.setTree` -- before the second mirror is deleted.

##### MODEL-4. Group the sidebar group row's reload attributes into one Equatable value

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#SidebarGroupProjection`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#computeSidebarRowOps`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#advanceSidebarCache`

**Problem.** Which fields of `SidebarGroupProjection` count as "reload attributes" is written out by hand in two places that must agree: the diff that decides whether to emit `.reloadGroup`, and the cache-retention helper that rolls a suppressed group row back. Adding an attribute and forgetting either list is silent -- forget the diff and the row never repaints; forget the retention and the cache claims an unapplied attribute was painted. The tab row has no such hazard because it is compared and retained as a whole value.

**Evidence.** `computeSidebarRowOps` compares a hand-built tuple: `if (oldGroup.name, oldGroup.unreadAlertCount, oldGroup.tabCount, oldGroup.isFirst) != (newGroup.name, newGroup.unreadAlertCount, newGroup.tabCount, newGroup.isFirst) { ops.append(.reloadGroup(id: newGroup.id)) }`. `advanceSidebarCache#retainGroupReloadAttrs` re-lists the same four: `merged.groups[gi].name = oldGroup.name; merged.groups[gi].unreadAlertCount = oldGroup.unreadAlertCount; merged.groups[gi].tabCount = oldGroup.tabCount; merged.groups[gi].isFirst = oldGroup.isFirst`. The contrasting tab path is one whole-value compare (`if let oldTab = oldTabById[newTab.id], oldTab != newTab`) and one whole-value assignment in `retainTabProjection`.

**Ideal fix.** Nest the four fields in a `SidebarGroupProjection.Attributes: Equatable` value (`name`, `unreadAlertCount`, `tabCount`, `isFirst`), leaving `id`, `isCollapsed`, and `tabs` as the structural fields. The diff becomes `oldGroup.attributes != newGroup.attributes` and the retention becomes `merged.groups[gi].attributes = oldGroup.attributes`, so both sides name one value and a new attribute joins both automatically.

**By construction.** An attribute that drives a group-row repaint but is absent from the suppression rollback (or the reverse) cannot be written: there is one value, not two enumerations of one.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- this is a pure regrouping of existing fields.

**Verification.** Existing sidebar row-op model-apply test, plus one behavioral test: with a group row under inline rename, change a group attribute, assert no `.reloadGroup` is applied to that row, and assert the change is re-emitted on the next sweep after the rename ends.

**Risk.** `SidebarGroupProjection` is built in `desiredSidebar` and read by `app/SidebarView.swift`'s group-cell configuration; both need the extra `.attributes` hop.

**Vetted.** Read `Projections.swift#SidebarGroupProjection`, `#computeSidebarRowOps` and `#advanceSidebarCache`. The four-field tuple compare and the four-line `retainGroupReloadAttrs` assignment are exact, and the contrasting tab path really is one whole-value compare plus one whole-value assignment. The same four fields are enumerated a third time in the doc comment on `SidebarGroupProjection` ("name/bell/tabCount/isFirst"), so the hazard is three lists, not two. Scored down because no live bug follows: the surface is one row's attributes, the failure mode needs a future field addition, and the damage is a group row that repaints late or a cache that claims a repaint it did not get -- both self-correcting on the next reloadAll.

**Conflicts with.** [RECON-4](#recon-4)

<a id="model-5"></a>

##### MODEL-5. Move per-pane search and notification-throttle state into PaneModel so pane teardown prunes them

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 4 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#AppModel`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#PaneModel`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/ModelOperations.swift#clearPaneSideTables`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#desiredSearchOverlays`

**Problem.** `AppModel` keeps two dictionaries keyed by `PaneId` whose entire lifetime is the pane's -- `searchState` and `lastNotificationTime` -- outside the tree that owns panes. Pruning them is a convention: every pane-destroying path must remember to call `clearPaneSideTables`, and there are five such call sites. This is the same dual-ownership drift the model already eliminated for panes themselves.

**Evidence.** `AppModel` declares `var lastNotificationTime: [PaneId: [AlertKind: Date]] = [:]` and `var searchState: [PaneId: SearchModel] = [:]`, while the pane-access section header states the principle they violate: "Panes live only in the split-tree leaves ... NO stored index is kept (that would reintroduce the drift this refactor removes)", and `SplitNodeModel.leaf` states "A pane exists iff a tree leaf owns it (no separate `AppModel.panes` dict), so the old dual-write drift between dict and tree is structurally impossible." `clearPaneSideTables` exists only to re-establish by hand what leaf ownership would give for free, and Update.swift calls it from five separate teardown paths. `desiredSearchOverlays` iterates `model.searchState` rather than live panes, so a missed prune projects an overlay for a pane that no longer exists.

**Ideal fix.** Put `var search: SearchModel?` and `var lastNotification: [AlertKind: Date]` on `PaneModel`. Removing the leaf removes them, so no teardown path can forget. `desiredSearchOverlays` becomes a walk over live panes keyed by `pane.search != nil`, and `clearPaneSideTables` shrinks to the alert feed alone -- `alerts` is a global ordered list, so it legitimately stays a separate prune.

**By construction.** "A destroyed pane's search overlay or notification throttle survives it" stops being expressible, because that state has no storage independent of the leaf that owns the pane.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the dictionaries but derive the prune instead of pushing it: one `reconcilePaneSideTables(&model)` at the end of `update()` filtering both dictionaries to `Set(model.allPaneIds)`. Cheaper, and it removes the five-call-site convention, but a stale entry can still exist for the duration of one message.

**Verification.** Behavioral test: open a search on a pane in a split tab, close that pane, and assert `desiredSearchOverlays(in: model)` holds no key for it and a newly created pane starts with no overlay. A second test closes a pane with a recorded bell time and asserts the next bell on a fresh pane is not throttled.

**Risk.** `PaneModel` is `Equatable` and feeds `desiredPaneToolbar` and container shape comparisons; adding live search state to it means a keystroke in the find field now changes the pane value. Confirm the projections that key off `PaneModel` do not gain spurious diffs -- container shapes drop pane payload already, but toolbar equality should be re-checked.

**Vetted.** Read `Model.swift#AppModel` (both dictionaries and the pane-access section header), `ModelOperations.swift#clearPaneSideTables`, `Projections.swift#desiredSearchOverlays`, and all five `clearPaneSideTables` call sites in Update.swift (lines in `.closeTab`, `.closePane`, delete-group, `closePaneBody`, and the group-teardown path). All quotes check out. Scored down for one reason the finding names but does not price: `clearPaneSideTables` also prunes `model.alerts`, which is a global ordered list that cannot move onto `PaneModel`, so the function and all five call sites survive the change. The by-construction win therefore covers two of three side tables, and a teardown path that forgets the call still leaks the pane's alerts -- the convention the finding is trying to delete is not deleted.

**Sharper ideal.** Same move, but say plainly that it is partial: search and notification throttle stop being forgettable, alerts do not. If the goal is to retire the convention outright, the ideal is to make the alert feed derivable too -- alerts stored per pane and flattened into the global ordered list by a projection -- at which point `clearPaneSideTables` and its five call sites disappear entirely.

**Conflicts with.** [LOOKUP-1](#lookup-1)

**Write this test first.** There is no new failing test: this is a pure refactor. Every pane-destroying path already calls `clearPaneSideTables`, so no user-reachable sequence leaves a stale search overlay or throttle entry behind today, and a test written to fail would have to assert storage location rather than behavior. The two behavior narrowings the change does produce are unreachable from the product (`.searchStarted` for a PaneId that is in no tree, and the defensive `.sessionCreationFailed` fallback for a pane already gone), so neither earns a test. **Blockers and surprises.** Three things worth knowing. (1) LOOKUP-1 is the real tension, not the toolbar equality the finding worries about. Today the light-checkpoint scheduler compares `LightCheckpointProjection(snapshot: toSnapshot(model))` -- a field-by-field snapshot -- so live search state inside `PaneModel` cannot leak into it, and `Persistence.swift#toPaneSnapshot` enumerates fields explicitly, so no persistence change is required. LOOKUP-1 proposes replacing that with a value compare of a `PersistedModel` holding `groups`, at which point every keystroke in the find field mutates the persisted subtree and defeats the O(1) compare. Doing MODEL-5 first is fine; doing LOOKUP-1 afterwards then needs an answer (split `PaneModel` into persisted and live halves, or keep going through `toSnapshot`). (2) The finding's stated `PaneModel`-equality risk mostly evaporates on reading: `containerShapeNode` and `containerLayoutNode` reduce a leaf to `pane.id`, and `desiredPaneToolbar` builds its render from named fields, so neither gains a spurious diff. `app/AppRuntime.swift#notePrimaryHistoryMutation` is message-driven, not model-diff driven. Confirm only the `desiredSearchOverlays` and `desiredPaneFocus` readers. (3) The audit's own vetting is right that this is a partial win: `clearPaneSideTables` and all five call sites survive for the global `alerts` list, so the convention is narrowed, not deleted. If the goal is to retire it, that is a second, larger change (per-pane alerts flattened by a projection) and should be named as out of scope rather than half-done. No hidden non-core reader exists: grep across `app/` and `ios/` finds only one comment in `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift` mentioning searchState; the views read projections only. Note also that `swapPaneModels` and the move-pane paths carry the whole `PaneModel` payload, so search follows its pane exactly as it does today.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The stated ideal is right, but the finding's risk section points at the wrong hazard. `PaneModel` equality is not consumed anywhere that would gain a spurious diff (container shapes and layout nodes drop the payload to `pane.id`; the toolbar render is built from named fields). The hazard that actually exists is the LOOKUP-1 interaction described in blockers. Also worth stating plainly in the plan, per the audit's own vetting: this move retires two of three side tables, and `clearPaneSideTables` plus its five call sites remain for the global alert feed.

**Readiness: needs-decision.** One call for the user: whether live, per-keystroke search state may live inside the pane tree given LOOKUP-1's plan to make `groups` the persisted value compared for checkpoint scheduling. If the answer is yes, MODEL-5 is otherwise ready to start immediately (nothing else blocks it, and the safety net exists). A second, smaller call: whether to keep `clearPaneSideTables` as a one-line alert prune at five call sites or inline `removeAlertsForPane` there.

<a id="model-6"></a>

##### MODEL-6. Drop the submission-to-request reverse index and derive it from the pending requests

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 1 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#AppModel`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#PendingInputRequest`

**Problem.** The in-flight IPC input bookkeeping is stored twice: `pendingInputRequests[requestId].remaining` holds the submission ids a request waits on, and `pendingInputSubmissions` holds the same edges reversed. Nothing ties them together, so every mutation updates both by hand and a disagreeing pair is representable -- a submission mapped to a request that no longer lists it would be resolved a second time, and a submission in `remaining` with no reverse entry would block its request's reply forever.

**Evidence.** `AppModel` declares `var pendingInputRequests: [UUID: PendingInputRequest] = [:]` and `var pendingInputSubmissions: [InputSubmissionId: UUID] = [:]`; `PendingInputRequest` is `var remaining: Set<InputSubmissionId>`. Four sites must keep them in step: `IpcDispatch.swift#dispatch` writes `model.pendingInputRequests[reqId] = PendingInputRequest(remaining: Set(submissionIds))` then loops `model.pendingInputSubmissions[submissionId] = reqId`; the shutdown arm calls `removeAll()` on both; and `.inputSubmissionCompleted` removes from the reverse map, removes from `remaining`, and on rejection loops `for pendingId in request.remaining { model.pendingInputSubmissions.removeValue(forKey: pendingId) }`.

**Ideal fix.** Keep only `pendingInputSubmissions: [InputSubmissionId: UUID]` and delete `pendingInputRequests` and `PendingInputRequest`. A request is outstanding while any entry maps to it; "the last submission completed" is `model.pendingInputSubmissions.values.contains(requestId) == false` after the removal, and a rejection is `model.pendingInputSubmissions = model.pendingInputSubmissions.filter { $0.value != requestId }`. In-flight counts are single digits, so the scan costs nothing.

**By construction.** A submission whose owning request has already replied, and a request waiting on a submission that no longer maps back to it, both become unrepresentable -- one edge set instead of two that must mirror each other.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep both dictionaries but move every mutation behind two methods on `AppModel` (`beginInputRequest`, `completeInputSubmission`) so no caller can touch one map without the other. This preserves the invalid states as values; it only reduces the number of places that can create them.

**Verification.** Behavioral test through the IPC reducer: issue a multi-item pane-input request, complete the submissions out of order, and assert exactly one reply is emitted after the last; repeat with a mid-way rejection and assert exactly one error is emitted and no later completion produces a second reply.

**Risk.** The shutdown arm builds its error list from `pendingInputRequests.keys`; after the change it must build a de-duplicated set of request ids from the values, or it will emit one error per submission.

**Vetted.** Read `Model.swift#PendingInputRequest` and the two `AppModel` dictionaries, `IpcDispatch.swift` (the write of both maps at the dispatch site), and the `.runtimeWillShutdown` and `.inputSubmissionCompleted` arms in Update.swift. Every quoted line is exact, and the derivation the ideal fix proposes works: `.delivered` becomes "no value still maps to this request id", rejection becomes one filter, shutdown becomes `Set(values)`. Scored down because the surface is one IPC method with four consistent mutation sites, no live bug, and single-digit in-flight counts. One detail the finding misses: the shutdown arm currently emits errors in `pendingInputRequests.keys` order; deriving them from a `Set` of values leaves the error order unspecified, so any test that pins the emitted command order must key on ids, not position.

**Sharper ideal.** Write it as `pendingInputSubmissions: [InputSubmissionId: PendingInputSubmission]` where the value carries the request id and (per REDUCE-6) the owning pane id. That is still one edge set with no reverse index, and it absorbs REDUCE-6 instead of being undone by it.

**Do after.** [REDUCE-6](#reduce-6)

**Conflicts with.** [REDUCE-6](#reduce-6)

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 6 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `AppModel` holds the two mirrored maps `var pendingInputRequests: [UUID: PendingInputRequest] = [:]` and `var pendingInputSubmissions: [InputSubmissionId: UUID] = [:]`, with `struct PendingInputRequest: Equatable { var remaining: Set<InputSubmissionId> }` in `Model.swift`. `InputSubmissionId` is `TypedId<InputSubmissionTag>`; `InputSubmissionResult` is `.delivered` / `.rejected`. Both maps are written in exactly one place, the `case .paneInput(let paneId, let input)` arm of `IpcDispatch.swift#dispatch`, which mints one `InputSubmissionId` per item, emits `.sendText` / `.sendInputText` / `.sendInputKey` / `.sendInputWheel` carrying it, then does `model.pendingInputRequests[reqId] = PendingInputRequest(remaining: Set(submissionIds))` followed by a loop filling the reverse map. They are read in two `Update.swift` arms: `case .runtimeWillShutdown` (maps `pendingInputRequests.keys` to `-32603` errors, then `removeAll()` on both) and `case .inputSubmissionCompleted(let submissionId, let result)` (removes from the reverse map, removes from `remaining`, replies on the last delivery, or on rejection removes the request and loops the leftover ids out of the reverse map). Nothing in `app/` or `ios/` touches either map.

Rewrite it to seed through a real `pane.input` dispatch rather than reaching into the model.

The hits are exactly: the two `AppModel` fields and the struct in Model.swift, one `Msg` case, four `Command` cases carrying an optional submission id, the `IpcDispatch` write site, the two `Update.swift` arms, and two test files. The `PaneInputSubmissionId` hits in `lib/TerminalPTY` are a different, unrelated type on the PTY side. I consider the list complete._

Every reachable outcome -- one reply after the last delivery, one error on the first rejection, silence for a late completion, one error per request at shutdown -- is already pinned. <a id="model-7"></a>

##### MODEL-7. Make PaneTree.remove non-mutating and return an outcome that cannot be misread as a live tree

`api-shape` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#PaneTree`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/ModelOperations.swift#removeLeaf`

**Problem.** `PaneTree.remove` mutates in place and reports emptiness through a boolean on its result. In the emptied case it leaves `root` and `focusedPaneId` untouched -- the tree still contains the pane the call just reported as removed -- so the returned value and the mutated tree disagree, and correctness rests on every caller reading `emptiedTree` before writing the tree back. A call site that writes `tab.paneTree = sourcePaneTree` without checking silently resurrects the pane it just moved elsewhere, duplicating a pane id across two tabs.

**Evidence.** `remove` does `guard let newRoot else { return Removal(pane: removedPane, emptiedTree: true, focusMoved: focusMoved) }` -- returning before `root = newRoot`. The callers branch by hand: `Update.swift#movePaneToTab` writes `if !removal.emptiedTree { updateTab(...) { $0.paneTree = sourcePaneTree } } else { removeTab(...) }`, and `movePaneToNewTab` guards with `guard let removal = sourcePaneTree.remove(paneId), !removal.emptiedTree else { return [] }`. `Removal` documents the hazard -- "Describes a removal without permitting an empty `PaneTree` value" -- while still handing back a tree that contradicts its own report.

**Ideal fix.** Replace the mutating method with a non-mutating `func removing(_ paneId: PaneId) -> RemovalOutcome`, where `RemovalOutcome` is `.notFound`, `.emptied(PaneModel)`, or `.remaining(PaneTree, pane: PaneModel, focusMoved: Bool)`. The surviving tree then exists only inside the case that has one.

**By construction.** "A pane tree that reported its last pane removed, still holding it" stops being obtainable: the emptied case carries no tree to write back.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the mutating signature but have callers pre-test `if case .leaf(let p) = tree.root, p.id == paneId`, which is what `movePaneToNewTab` already does for its single-pane path. This spreads the shape test back out to call sites and is strictly worse.

**Verification.** Behavioral test: move the only pane of a two-tab window's first tab into the second tab, then assert the model has exactly one tab and the moved pane id appears exactly once in `model.allPaneIds`. A second test moves a pane out of a split tab and asserts the source tab survives with its remaining pane focused.

**Risk.** Three call sites in Update.swift change shape; each already branches on `emptiedTree`, so the rewrite is mechanical, but the focus-move assertions in PaneTreeTests exercise the mutating form and need updating.

**Vetted.** Read `Model.swift#PaneTree.remove` and `#Removal`, and all three callers (`Update.swift` `.movePaneToTab`, `.movePaneToNewTab` path B, and `closePaneBody`). The early `return` before `root = newRoot` is exactly as quoted, so in the emptied case the local tree still holds the pane the call reported removed; `.movePaneToTab` adopts that pane into the target tab and only the `!removal.emptiedTree` branch stops the source tab from keeping its copy, so an unchecked write-back really would duplicate a pane id across two tabs. Scored down to 2: all three callers branch correctly today, every one already copies the tree into a local `var` first, and the change is API hardening with no live defect behind it.

**Sharper ideal.** The proposed `RemovalOutcome` is right. Note that `PaneTreeTests` exercises the mutating form for the focus-move assertions and must be rewritten with it; that is most of the diff.

#### Area: IPC protocol, dispatch, CLI (`IPC`)

_Scope: IPC surface: wire protocol, dispatch, and the CLI client (lib/DanTermProtocol, IpcDispatch/IpcEntityEncoder, lib/DanTermClient, app/IpcServer.swift, cli/main.swift, integrations/danterm/SKILL.md)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** The wire layer is in good shape: framing is one shared `IpcLineFramer` used by both ends, the CLI can only build a request through the typed `IpcRequest` catalog, and `IpcRequestTests.everyCLIRequestRoundTripsThroughCatalog` pins encode/decode against each other for every method, so the two mirrored switches in `IpcRequest` cannot drift silently. The weak spots are the projections that were written as a *third* copy of the same facts with a `default:` escape (the audit descriptor), and the human-facing surface (help text, per-parser usage strings, SKILL.md) which is admitted in a comment to be hand-synced with no check. I did not audit the tape/snapshot record formats, the audit log writer itself, or the transports' socket mechanics beyond their error vocabulary.

<a id="ipc-1"></a>

##### IPC-1. Derive the IPC audit descriptor from the request's encoded params, not a third hand-written switch

`correctness` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 2 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditDescriptor`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#params`, `app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch`

**Problem.** `IpcRequest.auditDescriptor` re-describes what a request carries in a switch that falls back to `default:`, and it misses `group.new`. `group.new` accepts a full `LaunchSpec` (`--cmd`, `--cwd`), it is remote-callable (`requiresLocalCaller` is true only for `quit`), and it produces an audit record -- but the record it produces has `command: nil` and `cwd: nil`. The audit log is the only durable trace of authority an admitted tailnet peer exercised, and a command launched through `group new --cmd '...'` leaves no trace of what ran.

**Evidence.** In IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditDescriptor: `switch self { case .tabNew(_, let value, _), .paneSplit(_, _, let value, _): launch = value; default: launch = nil }`. The catalog case is `case groupNew(name: String, launch: LaunchSpec?, background: Bool)` (IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequest) and the CLI builds it with a launch spec in CLIParser.swift#parseGroupNewCommand (`--cmd`, `--cwd`, defaulted to the caller's cwd). `IpcRequestMethod.producesAuditRecord` returns true for `.groupNew`, and app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch writes `.requestStarted(caller:request: typedRequest.auditDescriptor)` before serving a remote request, so the descriptor is the whole record. The declared intent is in the field doc: "Retains a launch command because it is authority exercised by the caller." IpcAuditDescriptorTests#launchAuthorityIsRetained covers only `.tabNew` and `.paneSplit`.

**Ideal fix.** Stop writing the audit projection as an independent enumeration. Build the descriptor from `IpcRequest.params` -- the one encoding already pinned by the round-trip test -- keeping the target keys named by `targetParameterKeys` plus the launch keys, and replacing content-bearing keys (`text`, `input`) with the existing `IpcAuditInputAccounting` counts. Then a method that carries a launch spec on the wire is audited for it because the wire form is the source, and there is nothing per-method left to forget.

**By construction.** A request that carries launch authority (or a target) on the wire but is invisible in the audit log becomes unrepresentable: the descriptor is a redaction of the sent params rather than a parallel description of them, so there is no arm in which a field can be omitted by falling through.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the hand-written switch but delete both `default:` arms so every case is listed; adding a catalog case then fails to compile until its launch and input accounting are decided. This keeps three descriptions of the same facts, so they can still disagree about a key's spelling.

**Verification.** Add to IpcAuditDescriptorTests: `IpcRequest.groupNew(name: "g", launch: LaunchSpec(cmd: "ssh server", cwd: "/tmp/work", title: nil), background: false).auditDescriptor` has `command == "ssh server"` and `cwd == "/tmp/work"`. Broaden it to a loop over `representativeCLICommands()` asserting that every request whose params contain a `launch` object reports a non-nil `command`/`cwd`, and that no descriptor's encoded form contains pane text. Run `swift test --package-path lib/DanTermProtocol --filter IpcAuditDescriptor`.

**Risk.** Deriving from params means new fields land in the audit log by default, so the redaction list must be a denylist-free design: encode only keys the descriptor names (target keys, launch keys, accounting), never "everything except". Getting that backwards would put pane text in a durable log.

**Vetted.** Read IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditDescriptor whole. The quoted `switch self { case .tabNew(_, let value, _), .paneSplit(_, _, let value, _): launch = value; default: launch = nil }` is there verbatim, and `auditTarget` puts `.groupNew` in the empty-target arm alongside `.ping`. IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequest line 282 is `case groupNew(name: String, launch: LaunchSpec?, background: Bool)`, `producesAuditRecord` returns true for `.groupNew`, `requiresLocalCaller` returns true only for `.quit`, and app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch writes `.requestStarted(caller:request: typedRequest.auditDescriptor)` before serving. IpcAuditDescriptorTests#launchAuthorityIsRetained covers only `.tabNew` and `.paneSplit`. The gap is real: an admitted tailnet peer can run `group new --cmd 'anything'` and the durable record carries `command: nil`.

**Correction.** One qualifier the finding omits: `IpcServer.dispatch` writes the `requestStarted` record only when `state.holdsRemoteSlot` is true, so the blind spot is remote callers only -- which is also the only case the audit log exists for, so it does not weaken the finding.

**Sharper ideal.** The stated recipe -- "keeping the target keys named by `targetParameterKeys` plus the launch keys" -- is wrong in two concrete ways, and C1's resolution paragraph repeats it. First, `auditTarget` today emits `todoId` for the five todo-mutation methods, and `targetParameterKeys` deliberately does not name it (its contract is "the keys whose removal must make decode fail", pinned by IpcRequestTests#everyTargetingCatalogMethodRejectsAbsentTarget, whose error-message assertion depends on that set staying at pane/tab). Filtering params by `targetParameterKeys` therefore silently drops the todo id from the durable log. Second, `params` spells ids with `idValue` -> `uuidString` (uppercase) while `auditTarget` uses `auditId` -> `.lowercased()`, so a naive derivation changes every id's spelling in the log. The ideal is one per-request target-key map (including `todoId`) that both the audit projection and the decode-required-target proof read, with the lowercasing applied once in the redaction step.

**Do after.** [IPC-3](#ipc-3), [IPC-4](#ipc-4)

<a id="ipc-2"></a>

##### IPC-2. Generate the CLI help text and SKILL.md synopsis from one command table instead of hand-syncing three copies

`structural` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 5 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `cli/main.swift#DanTermCLI`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/CLIParser.swift#parseCLI`, `integrations/danterm/SKILL.md`

**Problem.** The command grammar is written out three times: `usageText` in the CLI, ~48 per-parser `usage:` strings inside `parseCLI` and its helpers, and the synopsis block in SKILL.md. Nothing checks them against each other or against the parser, so a new flag, a renamed subcommand, or a changed default can be true in one copy and false in the other two -- and SKILL.md is what agents read as the contract.

**Evidence.** cli/main.swift#DanTermCLI states it outright: "Top-level help text. Kept in sync by hand with `parseCLI` ... there is no automated check, so any change to either touches this string too." The same grammar appears a second time as a literal inside the parser (CLIParser.swift#parseTabNewCommand: `let usage = "usage: danterm tab new (--group <group-id> | --after-tab <tab-id>) [--cmd <s>] ..."`) and a third time at integrations/danterm/SKILL.md lines 37-68, whose own header says "Keep this section synced with `danterm help` and the parser". The only automated SKILL.md check in the tree (scripts/tests/danterm-cli_test.sh) merely `cmp`s the bundled copy against the repo file -- it never compares it to the parser or to the help text.

**Ideal fix.** Declare each command once in `DanTermProtocol` as a table entry: verb path, synopsis line, one-line description, and the parsing closure. `parseCLI` dispatches through the table (so an unknown verb and a per-command usage error both come from the entry), `usageText` renders from the table, and a test asserts the SKILL.md synopsis block equals the rendered synopsis. A command with no help entry, and a help entry with no command, both stop existing.

**By construction.** A documented command that the parser does not accept -- and an accepted command that neither `danterm help` nor SKILL.md mentions -- becomes unrepresentable, because the help text and the synopsis are projections of the same table the dispatcher reads.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the parser as-is but move every `usage:` literal into the table and add one test that asserts SKILL.md's fenced synopsis block is byte-equal to the generated help synopsis. This removes the two worst copies and leaves the parser's structure alone.

**Verification.** A test in DanTermProtocolTests that, for every table entry, `parseCLI` accepts the synopsis's example form and that the rendered help contains exactly the table's verbs; plus a test comparing the generated synopsis to the block in integrations/danterm/SKILL.md. Behaviorally: `danterm help` output and the SKILL.md block stay equal after adding a command without touching either string.

**Risk.** The table must not flatten genuinely different error wording (for example `pane tape`'s multi-line explanations), so entries need a free-form usage body rather than a generated one-liner; over-normalizing would degrade today's error messages.

**Vetted.** All three copies exist. cli/main.swift line 24 carries the quoted admission ("Kept in sync by hand with `parseCLI` ... there is no automated check"); CLIParser.swift holds 41 `usage: danterm ...` literals (the finding's "~48" is close enough); integrations/danterm/SKILL.md lines 37-68 hold the synopsis under its own "Keep this section synced" header. scripts/tests/danterm-cli_test.sh does only `cmp` the bundled SKILL.md against the repo file. The synopsis lines are already byte-equal to the parser usage strings minus the `usage: ` prefix for most commands, so extracting them into a table is mechanical.

**Correction.** The check situation is worse than the finding says, which strengthens it. `danterm-cli_test.sh` is not in the gate at all (justfile `test-cli` only, GUI-required), and it is currently rotted: line 136 asserts `grep -qF 'danterm [--socket <path>] <command> [args]'` while cli/main.swift line 31 spells it `danterm [--socket <path> | --tcp <host:port>] <command> [args]`, and under `set -Eeuo pipefail` that aborts the script. plans/impl/2026-08-12-1748-danterm-group-command.md records the same class of pre-existing break. So the verification for this finding must land as a Swift test in DanTermProtocolTests (in the gate), not as another assertion in that shell script.

**Conflicts with.** [BUILD-2](#build-2)

<a id="ipc-3"></a>

##### IPC-3. Give the todo state change one catalog case so three unreachable `preconditionFailure` arms disappear

`api-shape` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 1 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/IpcDispatch.swift#dispatchIpc`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#decode`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/CLIParser.swift#parseTodoIdCommand`

**Problem.** `todo.done` and `todo.open` differ only by a boolean, and `todo.done`/`open`/`delete` share one argument grammar. Because they are separate catalog cases with identical payloads, three places group them and then re-switch to recover which one they had, each ending in a `preconditionFailure`/`default` arm that the compiler cannot prove unreachable. A future case added to one of those groupings crashes the daemon or the CLI at runtime instead of failing to build.

**Evidence.** IpcDispatch.swift#dispatchIpc: `case .todoDone(let owner, let todoId), .todoOpen(let owner, let todoId):` then `switch request { case .todoDone: shouldBeDone = true; case .todoOpen: shouldBeDone = false; default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo state request") }`. IpcRequest.swift#decode: `case .todoDone, .todoOpen, .todoDelete:` then an inner `switch method` ending in `default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo method switch")`. CLIParser.swift#parseTodoIdCommand takes `method: IpcRequestMethod` purely as a selector and ends in `default: preconditionFailure("todo id parser requires a todo mutation method")`.

**Ideal fix.** Collapse the pair into `case todoSetDone(owner: TodoOwner, todoId: TodoId, isDone: Bool)` while keeping the two distinct wire methods (`todo.done` decodes with `isDone: true`, `todo.open` with `false`), and change `parseTodoIdCommand` to take the request constructor `(TodoOwner, TodoId) -> IpcRequest` instead of a method enum. All three re-switches and all three `preconditionFailure`s go away, and `dispatchIpc` reads the boolean straight out of the payload.

**By construction.** "A todo request reached a branch that cannot name its own variant" stops being expressible: the variant is a value in the payload, and the parser is handed the constructor rather than a tag it must translate back.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the two cases but replace each grouped arm with separate arms that duplicate two lines of body. No `preconditionFailure` remains, at the cost of a little repetition.

**Verification.** Existing behavior tests must keep passing: `IpcRequestTests.everyCLIRequestRoundTripsThroughCatalog` (which requires every wire method to still round trip, so `todo.done` and `todo.open` must stay distinct on the wire) plus the core dispatch tests that `todo done` marks an item done and `todo open` reopens it. `swift test --package-path lib/DanTermProtocol` and `swift test --package-path lib/DanTermCore`.

**Risk.** The wire methods must stay two, not one -- collapsing them on the wire would be an external CLI-surface change and would break the round-trip test's method-coverage assertion. The refactor must keep `IpcRequestMethod` unchanged.

**Vetted.** All three quotes are exact. IpcDispatch.swift lines 472-481 group `.todoDone`/`.todoOpen` and then re-switch to a `default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo state request")`. IpcRequest.swift line 645 groups `.todoDone, .todoOpen, .todoDelete` in `decode` with an inner `switch method` ending at line 654 in `default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo method switch")`. CLIParser.swift#parseTodoIdCommand takes `method: IpcRequestMethod` as a selector and ends at line 884 in `default: preconditionFailure("todo id parser requires a todo mutation method")`. Merging to `todoSetDone(owner:todoId:isDone:)` keeps `method` derivable as `isDone ? .todoDone : .todoOpen`, so the two wire methods survive and the round-trip test still passes.

**Sharper ideal.** The claim that "all three preconditionFailures go away" is true only with one extra step the finding does not name: `decode`'s arm groups `.todoDelete` with the two state methods, so after the case merge the inner `switch method` still needs to separate delete from set-done and Swift will still demand a `default` over the full `IpcRequestMethod`. Ungroup that arm -- a `todoTarget(object:) -> (TodoOwner, TodoId)` helper called from three separate `case` arms -- and the third precondition disappears with the other two.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 9 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** The catalog is `public enum IpcRequest: Equatable, Sendable` in lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift, with three separate arms `case todoDone(owner: TodoOwner, todoId: TodoId)`, `case todoOpen(owner: TodoOwner, todoId: TodoId)`, `case todoDelete(owner: TodoOwner, todoId: TodoId)`, and the wire vocabulary `public enum IpcRequestMethod: String, CaseIterable, Sendable` holding `todo.done` / `todo.open` / `todo.delete`. Three places group those cases and then re-switch to recover the variant, each ending in an unreachable arm: `IpcDispatch.swift#dispatchIpc` groups `.todoDone`/`.todoOpen` and re-switches on `request` with `default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo state request")`; `IpcRequest.swift#decode` (signature `public static func decode(method rawMethod: String, params: JSONValue) throws -> IpcRequest`) groups all three and re-switches on `method` with `default: preconditionFailure("exhaustive todo method switch")`; and `CLIParser.swift#parseTodoIdCommand` has signature `private func parseTodoIdCommand(method: IpcRequestMethod, args: [String], usage: String) throws -> CLICommand` and ends in `default: preconditionFailure("todo id parser requires a todo mutation method")`. The code has not moved since the finding was written; every quoted line is still exactly where the vetting pass found it.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequest` -- Replace the two cases `todoDone(owner:todoId:)` and `todoOpen(owner:todoId:)` with one `case todoSetDone(owner: TodoOwner, todoId: TodoId, isDone: Bool)`. Leave `todoDelete` alone and leave `IpcRequestMethod` completely unchanged -- the two wire methods must survive.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#method` -- The `var method: IpcRequestMethod` projection currently has `case .todoDone: return .todoDone` and `case .todoOpen: return .todoOpen`. It becomes one arm that reads the payload: `case .todoSetDone(_, _, let isDone): return isDone ? .todoDone : .todoOpen`. This is what keeps `CLICommand.method` (which is `request.method.rawValue`) producing both wire names.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#targetParameterKeys` -- The arm `case .todoList, .todoAdd, .todoEdit, .todoDone, .todoOpen, .todoDelete, .todoClearCompleted: return ["pane", "tab"]` needs `.todoDone, .todoOpen` swapped for `.todoSetDone`. Pattern-only, no payload read.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#params` -- The arm `case .todoDone(let owner, let todoId), .todoOpen(let owner, let todoId), .todoDelete(let owner, let todoId):` must split, because the merged case now binds three values while `.todoDelete` binds two. Both arms return the same `ownerParams(owner).merging(["todoId": idValue(todoId)])` body; `isDone` is deliberately NOT written into params -- the wire method already carries it, and adding a key would change the CLI surface.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#decode` -- Ungroup `case .todoDone, .todoOpen, .todoDelete:` into three separate `case` arms sharing a small `todoTarget(object) throws -> (TodoOwner, TodoId)` helper (owner via the existing `todoOwner(object)`, then the `todoId` string plus `UUID(uuidString:)` guard that throws `invalid("invalid todo")`). `.todoDone` returns `.todoSetDone(..., isDone: true)`, `.todoOpen` `isDone: false`, `.todoDelete` returns `.todoDelete`. The inner `switch method` and its `preconditionFailure` both go away. This ungrouping is the step the finding's stated ideal omits -- without it Swift still demands a `default` over the full `IpcRequestMethod`.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditTarget` -- The arm `case .todoEdit(let owner, let todoId, _), .todoDone(let owner, let todoId), .todoOpen(let owner, let todoId), .todoDelete(let owner, let todoId):` must be regrouped: `.todoSetDone` binds three values, so it needs its own arm (or joins `.todoEdit` with a `_` for the third binding) returning the same `auditOwner(owner).merging(["todoId": auditId(todoId)])`. The finding does not name this file; it is a compile break.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/CLIParser.swift#parseTodoIdCommand` -- Change the signature from `method: IpcRequestMethod` to `make: (TodoOwner, TodoId) -> IpcRequest`, drop the `let request: IpcRequest` switch and its `preconditionFailure`, and return `CLICommand(request: make(owner, todoId), outputMode: .none)`.
- `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/CLIParser.swift#parseTodo` -- The three call sites (`case "done"`, `case "open"`, `case "delete"`) pass closures instead of method tags: `{ .todoSetDone(owner: $0, todoId: $1, isDone: true) }`, `... isDone: false`, and `{ .todoDelete(owner: $0, todoId: $1) }`. The usage strings are unchanged.
- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/IpcDispatch.swift#dispatchIpc` -- Replace `case .todoDone(let owner, let todoId), .todoOpen(let owner, let todoId):` plus its `let shouldBeDone: Bool` re-switch with `case .todoSetDone(let owner, let todoId, let isDone):`, passing `isDone` straight into `update(&model, .setTodoDone(owner:todoId:isDone:), env:)`. `Msg.setTodoDone` already carries the boolean, so nothing in Msg or Update changes.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/DanTermProtocol/Tests/DanTermProtocolTests/IpcRequestTests.swift -- everyCLIRequestRoundTripsThroughCatalog -- that `Set(commands.map(\.method)) == Set(IpcRequestMethod.allCases.map(\.rawValue))`, so `todo.done` and `todo.open` must both still be produced by `IpcRequest.method`, and that decoding each command's params reproduces the same typed request
- lib/DanTermProtocol/Tests/DanTermProtocolTests/IpcRequestTests.swift -- everyTargetingCatalogMethodRejectsAbsentTarget -- that stripping both `pane` and `tab` from a todo request's params yields the message "pane or tab required"
- lib/DanTermProtocol/Tests/DanTermProtocolTests/CLIParserTests.swift -- todoStateMutationsParseExplicitPanes -- parameterized over ("done", todoDone), ("open", todoOpen), ("delete", todoDelete): the parsed command's `method` and its `pane`/`todoId` params
- lib/DanTermProtocol/Tests/DanTermProtocolTests/CLIParserTests.swift -- todoStateMutationsParseTabs -- the same three verbs against a `--tab` owner
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoCommandFamilyUsesContextPane -- the full lifecycle: add, edit, done sets isDone true and the reply says so, open sets it back to false, list, delete, clear-completed
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoCommandsWithExplicitPaneTargetThatPaneRegardless -- explicit pane wins over the context pane for done/open/delete
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoCommandFamilyEditsTabOwner -- the tab-owner path for the same verbs
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoCommandsMalformedOrUnknownExplicitPaneNoFallback -- done/open/delete with a bad explicit pane do not fall back to context
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoCommandsWithoutPaneAndContextFail -- refusal before mutation
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- todoDeleteRejectsUnknownId -- -32602 for an unknown todo id
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/UpdateIpcTests.swift -- everyTargetingMethodRejectsAbsentTarget -- includes todo.done/open/delete rows driven by raw method strings

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- (none) -- every test above addresses the todo verbs through `IpcRequestMethod.<case>.rawValue` strings or through `parseCLI([...])`, never by constructing `IpcRequest.todoDone(...)` or `.todoOpen(...)` directly. I grepped `todoDone|todoOpen|todoDelete|todoSetDone` across app, cli, ios, lib, app-tests, cli-tests, client-tests and tests-ui: the only hits in test code are the eleven suites listed above, all of them string-driven. Nothing should stop compiling.

**Write this test first.** There is none, and none should be invented. This is a pure refactor: the wire methods, the params, the audit record, the CLI usage strings and every reply are byte-identical before and after, and the three arms being deleted are provably unreachable today, so no test can distinguish the trees. Write no new test that asserts the enum's shape. The characterization tests are `IpcRequestTests.everyCLIRequestRoundTripsThroughCatalog` (holds the wire surface fixed -- it is the one that would catch a collapse of `todo.done` and `todo.open` into a single method) and `UpdateIpcTests.todoCommandFamilyUsesContextPane` (holds the done/open semantics fixed end to end through dispatch). Run both before touching production code so their green state is the baseline.

**Blockers and surprises.** Four things worth knowing. (1) The finding's claim that "all three preconditionFailures go away" needs the extra step the audit's own Sharper ideal names: `decode`'s arm groups `.todoDelete` with the two state methods, so the case merge alone leaves a `switch method` that Swift still requires a `default` on. Ungroup that arm into three case arms with a shared target helper. (2) `IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditTarget` is a fourth site the finding does not list, and it is a hard compile break: its grouped arm binds two values per case and the merged case binds three. (3) `IpcRequest.params` has the same grouping problem and must split the same way -- and `isDone` must NOT be added to the params object; the wire method is what distinguishes the two, and adding a key would change the external CLI surface and break `everyCLIRequestRoundTripsThroughCatalog`. (4) `CLICommand.method` is `request.method.rawValue`, so the `method` projection must derive the tag from `isDone`; get that wrong and the round-trip test's method-coverage assertion fails immediately, which is a good early signal. Nothing else: integrations/danterm/SKILL.md is unaffected (no verb, flag, usage string or output shape changes), the iOS sources build no todo requests at all (grep for `todo` in ios/*/Sources returns nothing), and app/IpcServer.swift, app/AppRuntime.swift and cli/main.swift only handle `IpcRequest` generically.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

##### IPC-4. Return one traits value from a single exhaustive switch instead of six parallel per-method enumerations

`simplification` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 2 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequestMethod`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#targetParameterKeys`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditTarget`

**Problem.** Adding one request method means writing its name into six hand-maintained lists: the four attribute switches on `IpcRequestMethod` (`terminatesInstance`, `isTargeting`, `requiresLocalCaller`, `producesAuditRecord`), `IpcRequest.targetParameterKeys`, and `IpcRequest.auditTarget`. Each is exhaustive, so the compiler catches an omission -- but the same 33-case list is spelled out six times, and the two target projections can disagree about a key's spelling without any compiler complaint (`targetParameterKeys` says `afterTabId`; `auditTarget` independently repeats it).

**Evidence.** IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequestMethod contains four switches whose non-default arm lists all of `.ping, .doctorPermissions, .ls, .focusInfo, .roster, .groupNew, ... .todoClearCompleted` verbatim. IpcRequest.swift#targetParameterKeys and IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditTarget then group the same cases a fifth and sixth time -- `case .tabNew(let target, _, _): switch target { case .group: return ["group"]; case .afterTab: return ["afterTabId"] }` appears in both files with the key strings typed out twice.

**Ideal fix.** Declare one `IpcRequestMethod.traits` returning a small struct (`terminatesInstance`, `isTargeting`, `requiresLocalCaller`, `producesAuditRecord`) from a single exhaustive switch, with the four properties as one-line projections of it. Take the target keys from one place too: `auditTarget` becomes `params` filtered by `targetParameterKeys` (see the audit-descriptor finding), so the key spellings exist once.

**By construction.** The four attributes can no longer disagree about which cases exist, and the target key vocabulary exists once rather than twice, so an audit record naming a key the wire never used stops being expressible.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the four properties but express three of them as the small exceptional set (`terminatesInstance` is `self == .quit`) and leave only `producesAuditRecord` exhaustive. Fewer copies, but a new method silently inherits the majority answer -- which is exactly what the current comments say they are preventing, so this trade is a real loss.

**Verification.** The existing behavior tests already pin the answers and must stay green: `IpcRequestTests.quitIsTheOnlyInstanceEndingMethod`, `quitIsTheOnlyLocalCallerMethod`, `everyTargetingCatalogMethodRejectsAbsentTarget`, and the audit descriptor's target assertions. Add one test asserting that for every `representativeCLICommands()` entry, `auditDescriptor.target`'s keys equal `request.targetParameterKeys` restricted to the keys actually present in `request.params`.

**Risk.** The traits struct must keep the switch exhaustive (no defaulted initializer), or a new method would inherit defaults silently -- which is worse than today's six lists.

**Vetted.** Read all six lists. IpcRequest.swift#IpcRequestMethod holds `terminatesInstance` (line 97), `isTargeting` (114), `requiresLocalCaller` (130), `producesAuditRecord` (152), each spelling the same 33-case list in its non-exceptional arm. `targetParameterKeys` (387) and IpcAuditDescriptor.swift#auditTarget group the cases a fifth and sixth time, and both independently type the string `"afterTabId"` for `.tabNew(.afterTab)`. The traits half of the finding is correct and its risk note (no defaulted initializer) is the right constraint.

**Correction.** The traits half is sound; the target half of the stated ideal fix is not, and must be rewritten. `auditTarget` and `targetParameterKeys` are not two spellings of one vocabulary: `auditTarget` emits `todoId` for the five todo mutations, and `targetParameterKeys` deliberately excludes it because its contract is "the keys whose absence decode must reject" -- IpcRequestTests#everyTargetingCatalogMethodRejectsAbsentTarget strips exactly those keys and asserts the message is `"pane or tab required"`, which breaks if `todoId` joins the list. Making `auditTarget` "`params` filtered by `targetParameterKeys`" therefore drops the todo id out of the durable audit log, and also flips id spelling from lowercase (`auditId`) to uppercase (`idValue`). The correct single owner is one per-request map of target key to typed id, from which `targetParameterKeys` is the entity-target subset and `auditTarget` is the whole map lowercased. Likewise the proposed new test ("`auditDescriptor.target`'s keys equal `targetParameterKeys` restricted to keys present in `params`") fails today for every todo request and must not be written as stated.

**Do after.** [IPC-3](#ipc-3)

<a id="ipc-5"></a>

##### IPC-5. Make IpcRequest.decode typed-throws so IpcServer cannot need two decode-failure paths

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/IpcRequest.swift#decode`

**Problem.** `IpcRequest.decode` throws only `IpcRequestDecodeError`, but its signature says `throws`, so the server writes two near-identical 12-line failure blocks -- one for the real error, one for an "impossible" error that maps to `.internalError`. The dead branch is untestable and any future edit has to be made twice.

**Evidence.** app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch has `catch let error as IpcRequestDecodeError { ... dispatchToRuntime(.ipcRequestDecodeFailed(reqId: reqId, error: error), ...) }` immediately followed by `catch { ... dispatchToRuntime(.ipcRequestDecodeFailed(reqId: reqId, error: .internalError), ...) }` with identical audit-append and `rememberRequest` lines. Every throw site inside IpcRequest.swift#decode and its private helpers produces `IpcRequestDecodeError` -- `invalid(...)`, `.methodNotFound`, and the `LaunchSpecParseError`/`KeyModsDecodeError`/`PaneTapeSyncPolicyError` cases are all caught and rethrown as `invalid(...)`.

**Ideal fix.** Declare `public static func decode(method:params:) throws(IpcRequestDecodeError) -> IpcRequest`. The second catch block stops compiling and is deleted; the server has exactly one decode-failure path.

**By construction.** "A decode failure the server classified as an internal error" becomes unrepresentable: the type system states that decoding fails only with the client-facing vocabulary, so there is no second outcome to handle.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** Existing server behavior must hold: a request with an unknown method still answers JSON-RPC -32601 and a bad-shape request -32602, with a `requestDecodeFailed` audit record in both cases. Covered by the decode tests in `swift test --package-path lib/DanTermProtocol --filter IpcRequest` plus the CLI end-to-end script scripts/tests/danterm-cli_test.sh.

**Risk.** `throws(E)` propagates: any helper called from `decode` that gains a differently-typed error must convert it explicitly. That is the point, but it makes future edits in that file slightly more deliberate.

**Vetted.** app/IpcServer.swift#dispatch has the two catch blocks at lines 415-428 and 429-442, byte-for-byte identical apart from `error` versus `.internalError`. I walked every throw reachable from IpcRequest.swift#decode: `invalid(...)`, `.methodNotFound`, `target()`, `optionalBool()`, `tabTarget()`, `todoOwner()` all throw `IpcRequestDecodeError`; `decodedLaunch` catches both cases of the two-case `LaunchSpecParseError`, the KeyMods site catches the sole case of `KeyModsDecodeError`, and the pane-tape site catches `PaneTapeSyncPolicyError.budgetNotWholeBytes` with a bare `catch` for the other. So the second server branch is genuinely dead today.

**Sharper ideal.** One mechanical cost the finding understates: `throws(IpcRequestDecodeError)` does not propagate through untyped-throwing helpers, so roughly fifteen private helpers in IpcRequest.swift must gain the same typed signature (or be wrapped) before `decode` compiles. Still small, but it is a file-wide edit rather than a one-line signature change.

##### IPC-6. Collapse CLIResolvedTarget into CLIConnectionTarget

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 6 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `cli/main.swift#CLIResolvedTarget`, `lib/DanTermProtocol/Sources/DanTermProtocol/CLIParser.swift#CLIConnectionTarget`

**Problem.** Two enums with identical cases and identical payloads exist side by side, plus a private converter between them. The distinction they claim to draw -- "before" versus "after" ambient socket resolution -- is already carried by the optionality of the parsed value (`CLIInvocation.target` is `CLIConnectionTarget?`, and `selectConnectionTarget` returns a non-optional).

**Evidence.** CLIParser.swift declares `public enum CLIConnectionTarget { case unixSocket(path: String); case tcp(host: String, port: UInt16) }`; cli/main.swift#CLIResolvedTarget declares `enum CLIResolvedTarget: Equatable { case unixSocket(path: String); case tcp(host: String, port: UInt16) }` and `private extension CLIResolvedTarget { init(_ target: CLIConnectionTarget) { switch target { case .unixSocket(let path): self = .unixSocket(path: path); case .tcp(let host, let port): self = .tcp(host: host, port: port) } } }`.

**Ideal fix.** Delete `CLIResolvedTarget` and have `selectConnectionTarget` return a non-optional `CLIConnectionTarget`. `openSession` switches over the one type.

**By construction.** The class of bug where the two enums drift -- one gains a transport case the other lacks, or the converter maps a payload wrong -- stops existing, because there is one type and no conversion.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** The existing target-selection behavior tests must stay green: `quit` without `--socket`/`--tcp` is refused, `DANTERM_SOCK` is used when no explicit target is given, and `DANTERM` set without `DANTERM_SOCK` reports "DanTerm is not running". Run the CLI test target and scripts/tests/danterm-cli_test.sh.

**Risk.** `CLIConnectionTarget` is public in DanTermProtocol while `CLIResolvedTarget` is CLI-local; reusing the public type means the CLI's resolved value is expressible by other clients. That is harmless here -- it is the same shape either way.

**Vetted.** CLIParser.swift line 34 declares `public enum CLIConnectionTarget { case unixSocket(path: String); case tcp(host: String, port: UInt16) }`; cli/main.swift line 505 declares `CLIResolvedTarget` with the identical two cases and identical payloads, and line 540 holds the private converting initializer exactly as quoted. `selectConnectionTarget` already returns non-optional, and the two conversion call sites (lines 526, 529) are the only uses of the converter. Nothing else distinguishes the types.

#### Area: Persistence, recovery, support layer (`PERSIST`)

_Scope: Persistence, recovery, and the portable side-effect layer (lib/DanTermCore Persistence/CheckpointCapture/RecoveryCheckpointPolicy/AgentSession/TabTodo + all of lib/DanTermSupport/Sources/DanTermSupport)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** The pure halves are in good shape: `RecoveryCheckpointPolicy` is a tight, self-consistent state machine (I traced every edge and found no reachable stuck state), `CheckpointCapture` already makes snapshot/scrollback pairing structural, `ControlSocketListener` and `TailnetListener` own their descriptors carefully, and `AgentSession` validation is sound. The weak spots cluster in three places: `RecoveryStore` (the whole session-lock contract is decided by a decode that can fail silently, and each path helper defaults its own directory independently), the snapshot codec's hand-enumerated re-builds, and layer placement in the pane-tape files. I did not audit `CLIPathInstaller`, `FontAvailability`, `TailnetBindAddress`, or the whois/HTTP parsing in `TailnetWhoisResolver` beyond a scan for swallowed failures, and I stayed out of `app/AppRuntime`'s checkpoint scheduling, which another auditor owns.
