<a id="runtime-3"></a>

##### RUNTIME-3. Stop opening nested modal run loops from inside an open send frame

`correctness` &middot; impact 3, confidence 4 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/AppRuntimePorts.swift#live`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#presentConfigError`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#dispatchInFrame`, `app/AppDelegate.swift#applicationDidFinishLaunching`

**Problem.** `AppRuntimePorts.live`'s `presentAlert` runs `NSAlert.runModal()`, and it is reached from inside the command loop: `perform(.saveDanTermConfig)` catches a write failure and calls `presentConfigError` -> `ports.presentAlert`. `runModal` spins a nested run loop while `dispatchInFrame` is still iterating the command array a completed `update()` produced. During that loop the app's local NSEvent monitor and main-queue-delivered IPC requests can both call `send()`, which runs `update(&model, ...)` and a full `reconcile()` re-entrantly; the outer loop then resumes performing commands computed against a model version that no longer exists. The launch-time restore prompt has the same shape: `applicationDidFinishLaunching` calls `alert.runModal()` after `AppRuntime.init` has already started the IPC server, so a client request can mutate the model during the prompt and then be silently discarded by `commitRestoreSession`.

**Evidence.** `AppRuntimePorts.live` defines `presentAlert: { title, message in let alert = NSAlert(); ...; alert.runModal() }`. `AppRuntime.perform` case `.saveDanTermConfig` does `do { try configStore.save(config) } catch { presentConfigError(error) }`, and the whole `perform` loop runs inside `outbox.withFrame { dispatchInFrame(msg) }`. `AppRuntimeIpcDispatch.serve`, built in `makeIpcDispatch`, is `@MainActor` and is awaited from `IpcServer`'s connection task (`await runtimeDispatch.serve(...)`), so it lands on the main queue, which drains under the modal panel run-loop mode. The launch prompt is `let response = alert.runModal()` in `applicationDidFinishLaunching`, before `bootstrapFromValidatedRestore`.

**Ideal fix.** No command arm may block the main actor. Turn user-visible alerts into the model-projected shape the quit confirmation already uses: `update()` puts the message in a model slot, a reconcile pass shows a non-modal panel, and the button press comes back as a Msg. Where a real sheet is wanted, `presentAlert` becomes `beginSheetModal(for:completionHandler:)`, which never nests a run loop. Do the same for the restore prompt: project it from a launch model slot and let the choice arrive as a Msg, so bootstrap does not block the loop it has already started serving.

**By construction.** With no nested run loop reachable from `perform`, a second `update()` cannot begin while the first one's commands are still being performed; "commands executed against a stale model" and "a reconcile pass running inside another pass" stop being expressible from the alert paths.

**Cheaper fallback.** If the launch prompt must stay modal, start the IPC server only after the prompt resolves, so no request can be accepted against a model that is about to be replaced. This is a trade-off: it leaves the in-frame `saveDanTermConfig` alert unfixed.

**Verification.** App test: install a fake `presentAlert` port that calls `runtime.send(...)` with a model-mutating Msg before returning, drive a `saveDanTermConfig` failure, and assert the final model reflects both the config save and the injected message. After the ideal fix, assert the failure produces the alert model slot and that no port call happens inside `perform`.

**Risk.** Non-modal alerts change user-visible behavior: a failure the user currently must dismiss becomes dismissible later or ignorable. The projected panel must still be prominent enough that a config write failure is not missed.

**Vetted.** Every quote is exact: `AppRuntimePorts.live` ends `presentAlert` with `alert.runModal()`, the `.saveDanTermConfig` arm calls `presentConfigError(error)` from inside the `perform` loop that `outbox.withFrame` brackets, and `AppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching` runs `let response = alert.runModal()` after `AppRuntime.init` has already constructed and started `IpcServer` with a `@MainActor` `serve` closure that calls `self.send(message)`. Two things temper the alarm. First, `ReconcileOutbox.withFrame` counts frames, so a re-entrant send accumulates into the open frame rather than draining nested -- the report-ordering half of the hazard is already structurally handled; what remains is the outer `perform` loop finishing against a replaced model. Second, the codebase already re-enters `update()` from inside a command arm on purpose: the `.createSession` arm calls `send(.sessionCreationFailed(...))` when the backend refuses. So "a nested update during perform" is not by itself the unthinkable state the finding implies. The concrete, un-hypothetical part is the launch prompt: an IPC request served during `runModal` mutates a model that `commitRestoreSession` then discards wholesale. Two more modal sites the section misses: `ports.presentAlert("Import Failed", ...)` in `importState` and the export-failure alert, both reached from save/open-panel completions rather than from an open frame.

**Correction.** The mechanism is verified at the code level but not ablated (no probe showed a main-queue IPC request or a local NSEvent monitor callback actually running inside `runModal` here), and one of the two cited sites -- a config *write failure* -- is rare. Score it as the launch-prompt/IPC-race hazard it concretely is: impact 3, confidence 4. Also add the `importState` alert to Files; it is the same shape.

**Sharper ideal.** The stated ideal is right. Worth naming explicitly that the cheaper fallback (start the IPC server only after the launch prompt resolves) is not merely a fallback -- it removes the only *demonstrated* discard-a-client-mutation window, and it is a few lines. Keep it as a first step even if the projected-panel work follows.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 13 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `app/AppRuntimePorts.swift#AppRuntimePorts` declares `var presentAlert: @MainActor (_ title: String, _ message: String) -> Void`, and `AppRuntimePorts.live(terminalBackend:notificationAuthorizationPolicy:)` implements it as an `NSAlert` finished with `alert.runModal()`. Four production call sites reach it: `AppRuntime.swift#presentConfigError` (private, called from the `.saveDanTermConfig` perform arm, from `reloadDanTermConfig`, from `openDanTermConfig`, and from `presentPendingConfigError`), `AppRuntime.swift#showImportError` (from `importState(from:)`), and the export-failure alert captured as a local `let presentAlert = ports.presentAlert` inside the `.exportState` arm. The command loop is `AppRuntime.swift#dispatch` -> `outbox.withFrame { dispatchInFrame(msg) }`, and `dispatchInFrame` runs `let commands = update(&model, msg)` then `for command in commands { perform(command) }` then `reconcile()`. Only the `.saveDanTermConfig` path puts a `runModal` inside that loop; import and export both arrive from panel completions. The launch prompt is a separate `NSAlert` built inline in `app/AppDelegate.swift#applicationDidFinishLaunching` and finished with `let response = alert.runModal()`, reached after `AppRuntime.init` has already constructed `IpcServer` and kicked off `Task { await server?.start() }`, whose `serve` closure (`AppRuntime.swift#makeIpcDispatch`) is `@MainActor` and calls `self.send(message)`.

**Change sites.**

- `app/AppDelegate.swift#applicationDidFinishLaunching` -- The cheap, demonstrated half: do not let the IPC server accept while the restore prompt is up. Either resolve the prompt before `AppRuntime.init` starts the server, or split server start out of `init` into an explicit `runtime.startIpcServer()` the delegate calls after bootstrap. The ideal half: replace the inline NSAlert with a launch model slot projected into a panel, and let Restore / Start Fresh arrive as Msgs.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#init` -- If the server start moves out, `startsApplicationServices` stops meaning "and start IPC now". Check `stopIpcServer`, `ipcSocketPath`, and `AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle.arm(.ipcServer)` still pair correctly.
- `app/AppRuntimePorts.swift#AppRuntimePorts` -- Either delete `presentAlert` (ideal: alerts become a model slot) or change it to a completion-taking sheet port. If it survives, `live` must use `beginSheetModal(for:completionHandler:)`, which needs a window -- the ports struct has none today, so the signature gains a window or the port moves onto the runtime.
- `app/AppRuntimePorts.swift#live` -- Replace `alert.runModal()`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#presentConfigError` -- Becomes `send(.configErrorReported(message:))` (or equivalent) so the message lands in a model slot instead of blocking. Note this makes the `.saveDanTermConfig` arm's already-present re-entrant `send(.fontFamilyResolved(...))` the second send in the same arm -- fine, but the ordering of the two matters for the resulting model.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#perform (case .saveDanTermConfig)` -- The catch arm stops calling a blocking port.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#showImportError` -- Same treatment -- the section's Vetted note adds this site, and the Files list should carry it.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#perform (case .exportState)` -- The captured `presentAlert` in the writer completion becomes the same Msg. Its comment ("this modal cannot open inside the panel's completion") documents why it is currently safe and must be rewritten or deleted.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#reloadDanTermConfig, app/AppRuntime.swift#openDanTermConfig, app/AppRuntime.swift#presentPendingConfigError` -- Three more `presentConfigError` callers that follow whatever shape it takes.
- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Model.swift#AppModel` -- Ideal fix only: add the alert slot (message + title, or a small enum), ephemeral, beside `pendingConfirmation`.
- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Msg.swift#Msg + Update.swift#update` -- Ideal fix only: the report Msg and the dismiss Msg, plus their arms.
- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift + app/Reconcile.swift#reconcile` -- Ideal fix only: a `desiredAlert(in:) -> AlertPanelProjection?`, a `ReconcilerCaches` field, and a pass on the `reconcileConfirmation` template (which already creates `ConfirmationPanel` inside the pass).
- `app-tests/AppRuntimeCommandTestSupport.swift#RecordingAppRuntimePorts` -- `alerts: [(title: String, message: String)]` and the `presentAlert` closure follow whatever the port becomes; if the port is deleted, so are they, and tests read the model slot instead.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- app-tests/AppRuntimeIpcCommandTests.swift -- "input rejection re-enters update and writes the pending reply" -- pins that a command arm may legitimately re-enter `update()` before `perform` returns; the fix must not outlaw that
- app-tests/AppRuntimePendingIpcShutdownTests.swift -- whole suite -- pins IPC connection lifetime across shutdown, which the server-start move touches
- app-tests/IpcServerOwnershipTests.swift and app-tests/IpcServerRemoteTests.swift -- whole suites -- pin server construction and ownership; moving start out of `init` runs straight through them
- app-tests/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycleTests.swift -- whole suite -- the `.ipcServer` token arm/cancel pairing

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- app-tests/AppRuntimeIpcCommandTests.swift -- "config save failure alerts and completes font resolution before return" -- asserts `ports.alerts.count == 1`, `alerts.first?.title == "DanTerm Config Error"`, and the message text. Under the ideal fix there is no port call at all; the assertions move to the model's alert slot. This is the one test that will ambush the work.
- app-tests/AppRuntimeCommandTestSupport.swift -- `RecordingAppRuntimePorts.value` -- not a test, but every suite constructs it, so a changed or deleted `presentAlert` field breaks compilation across app-tests at once
- app-tests/AppRuntimeAmbientCommandTests.swift -- the `.exportState` test around `runtime.perform(.exportState(snapshot))` -- check whether it exercises the failure completion; if it does, the alert assertion moves the same way

**Write this test first.** Suite: DanTermAppTests, app-tests/AppRuntimeIpcCommandTests.swift (beside the existing config-failure test). Name: "a config write failure does not let a port call re-enter the send frame". Scenario: build `RecordingAppRuntimePorts` whose `presentAlert` closure calls `runtime.send(.createTabInSelectedGroup())` before returning (the finding's own suggested probe), give the runtime an unwritable `DanTermConfigStore`, then `runtime.send(.preferencesSaved)` (or whichever Msg emits `.saveDanTermConfig`) rather than calling `perform` directly, so the failure happens inside a real frame. Assert the port was never called -- `ports.alerts.isEmpty` -- and that the model carries the failure message in its alert slot. Why it fails today: the `.saveDanTermConfig` arm calls `presentConfigError` -> `ports.presentAlert` synchronously from inside `dispatchInFrame`'s perform loop, so `ports.alerts` has one entry and no model slot exists. Note honestly what this test does and does not prove: it demonstrates that a port call happens inside the open frame, which is the structural claim; it does not reproduce an actual `runModal`-nested IPC mutation, and the audit's own Correction says that half was never ablated. If the plan takes only the cheap first step (start IPC after the launch prompt), then that step is a pure ordering change with no new failing test available in app-tests -- say so and let app-tests/IpcServerOwnershipTests.swift stand as the characterization suite.

**Blockers and surprises.** Several things make this harder than the section admits. First, the demonstrated hazard and the stated ideal are different pieces of work: the launch-prompt/IPC race is in AppDelegate and is fixed by moving server start; the in-frame alert is in AppRuntime and is fixed by projecting alerts. They share nothing but a rationale, and the audit's own Sharper ideal says to do the ordering fix first regardless. Plan them as two commits. Second, `AppRuntimePorts` has no window reference, so a `beginSheetModal` port cannot be written without changing the port's signature or moving alert presentation onto the runtime -- worth knowing before choosing the sheet route. Third, the codebase deliberately re-enters `update()` from inside a command arm (the `.createSession` arm sends `.sessionCreationFailed`, and the `.saveDanTermConfig` arm itself sends `.fontFamilyResolved` after the alert), and `ReconcileOutbox.withFrame` counts frames so a re-entrant send accumulates rather than draining nested. So "no nested update during perform" is not the invariant to write down; "no command arm blocks the main actor" is. Fourth, the finding's Files list is incomplete: `importState`'s alert and the `.exportState` writer-completion alert are the same shape and the Vetted note adds them. Fifth, `scripts/reducer-command-discard-lint.sh` requires every production `update()` result to be consumed, which constrains how a new report Msg is threaded. Sixth, a non-modal config-write-failure alert is a user-visible behavior change the section flags as a risk and no test can settle -- it needs the user's assent.

**Readiness: needs-decision.** Two calls for the user. (1) Scope: take the cheap, demonstrated fix (start the IPC server only after the launch prompt resolves) alone, or also lift alerts into a model-projected panel? The audit recommends the ordering fix as a first step either way. (2) If alerts get projected: a config write failure stops being modal, so a user could miss it. The user has to say that is acceptable, or say what prominence the projected panel needs.

</details>

##### RUNTIME-4. Give each armed timer one owner instead of a handle field plus a token field

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `app/AppRuntime.swift#shutdown`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#scheduleLightCheckpointIfNeeded`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#applyRecoveryAction`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#cancelCoalescedReconcile`, `app/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle.swift#AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle`

**Problem.** Five scheduled owners are each stored as two fields written in lockstep: `lightCheckpointTimer`/`lightCheckpointTimerToken`, `enrichedCheckpointTimer`/`enrichedCheckpointTimerToken`, `coalescedReconcileTimer`/`coalescedReconcileTimerToken`, `switcherEventMonitor`/`switcherEventMonitorToken`, and `ipcServer`/`ipcServerToken`. Nothing ties a pair together, so the nil-ing is hand-written at eight sites, and the scheduling guard reads only the handle (`guard lightCheckpointTimer == nil`) while cancellation goes through the token. An edit that retires one half leaves either a live timer with no census entry or a census entry whose handle is already gone.

**Evidence.** `shutdown()` ends with ten lines of `switcherEventMonitor = nil; switcherEventMonitorToken = nil; lightCheckpointTimer = nil; lightCheckpointTimerToken = nil; ...` -- pure bookkeeping after `schedulingLifecycle.shutdown()` has already fired every cancel closure. `scheduleLightCheckpointIfNeeded` guards on `lightCheckpointTimer == nil`, while `cancelCoalescedReconcile`, `flushPendingCheckpoint`, `prepareRecoveryForApplicationExit`, and the `.terminate` command arm each clear token then handle by hand. The runtime already knows the right shape: `RosterSubscriber` and `PaneTapeFollowTransport` bundle their connection with their `AppRuntimeSchedulingToken`.

**Ideal fix.** Introduce one small `@MainActor` value that owns a scheduled source and its census token together -- `ScheduledTimer` with `arm(after:handler:)`, `cancel()`, and `isArmed`, built on `AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle`. Each of the five sites becomes a single optional field of that type; `cancel()` retires both halves, `isArmed` answers the scheduling guard, and `shutdown()` loses its nil-ing block because the census already retired the owners.

**By construction.** A live `DispatchSourceTimer` with no census entry, and a census entry whose handle has already been dropped, both stop being representable: handle and token are created and destroyed by the same call, so no caller can leave an intermediate state behind.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- a roughly forty-line type and mechanical replacement at the eight sites.

**Verification.** app-tests/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycleTests.swift style: send a coalescing Msg, assert `captureOwnerCensus()[.timer] == 1`; send a non-coalescing Msg, assert the census returns to zero and that a later coalescing Msg arms again -- the guard and the census must agree after every transition.

**Risk.** The enriched-checkpoint timer is rearmed from inside its own event handler via `applyRecoveryAction`; the new type must allow re-arming from within a handler that has just consumed its own token, or the recovery policy stops rescheduling.

**Vetted.** All five field pairs exist as declared (`lightCheckpointTimer`/Token, `enrichedCheckpointTimer`/Token, `coalescedReconcileTimer`/Token, `switcherEventMonitor`/Token, `ipcServer`/Token). `shutdown()` ends with exactly the ten-line nil-ing block after `schedulingLifecycle.shutdown()` has already run every cancel closure. `scheduleLightCheckpointIfNeeded` and `scheduleCoalescedReconcile` both guard on the handle (`guard lightCheckpointTimer == nil`) while cancellation goes through the token, and each event handler hand-clears both halves inside `schedulingLifecycle.run(token)`. The stated risk is real and I confirmed the shape: `applyRecoveryAction` rearms the enriched timer from inside the handler that just consumed its own token (`applyRecoveryAction(recoveryPolicy.deadlineReached(at:))` called within `schedulingLifecycle.run(token)`), so the new type must permit arm-from-within-handler.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 14 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `app/AppRuntime.swift#AppRuntime` is a `@MainActor class` holding five hand-paired fields: `private var switcherEventMonitor: Any?` / `switcherEventMonitorToken: AppRuntimeSchedulingToken?`, `lightCheckpointTimer: DispatchSourceTimer?` / `lightCheckpointTimerToken`, `enrichedCheckpointTimer: DispatchSourceTimer?` / `enrichedCheckpointTimerToken`, `coalescedReconcileTimer: DispatchSourceTimer?` / `coalescedReconcileTimerToken`, and `ipcServer: IpcServer?` / `ipcServerToken`. The census is `app/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle.swift#AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle`, whose surface is `arm(_ category: AppRuntimeSchedulingCategory, cancel: @escaping () -> Void) -> AppRuntimeSchedulingToken?`, `run(_ token:action:) -> Bool` (removes then invokes), `cancel(_ token: AppRuntimeSchedulingToken?)` (removes then invokes the stored cancel), `shutdown()`, and `captureOwnerCensus() -> [AppRuntimeSchedulingCategory: Int]`. Note the five pairs are not all timers: two of them wrap an `NSEvent` monitor and an `IpcServer`, so a `ScheduledTimer` type alone covers three of five and the ideal is closer to one generic census-owning box parameterized on the concrete handle plus its retire closure. Nothing has moved since the finding was written -- every quoted line is present verbatim.

**Change sites.**

- `app/AppRuntime.swift#AppRuntime (field block, the `switcherEventMonitor` through `ipcServerToken` declarations)` -- Replace the ten fields with five single fields of the new census-owning box type. Keep the existing comments that explain the two checkpoint tiers and the coalescing window.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#init (the `startsApplicationServices` block that builds `IpcServer` and does `self.ipcServer = server; self.ipcServerToken = schedulingLifecycle.arm(.ipcServer) { server.stop() }`)` -- Arm the ipcServer owner through the box in one call. The `.deferredCallback` `startToken` beside it is a separate one-shot and does not move.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#installSwitcherEventMonitor` -- `switcherEventMonitor = monitor; switcherEventMonitorToken = schedulingLifecycle.arm(.eventMonitor) { NSEvent.removeMonitor(monitor) }` collapses into one box `arm`. The box must accept category `.eventMonitor`, so it cannot hardcode `.timer`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#dispatchInFrame` -- `coalescedSweepPending: coalescedReconcileTimer != nil` becomes `coalescedReconcileTimer.isArmed`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#stopIpcServer` -- `schedulingLifecycle.cancel(ipcServerToken); ipcServerToken = nil; ipcServer = nil` becomes one `cancel()` on the box.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#shutdown` -- Delete the ten-line nil-ing block that runs after `schedulingLifecycle.shutdown()`. Confirm the box tolerates being read after the census has already fired its cancel closures (the handles are dropped when the runtime is).
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#perform (the `.terminate` command arm)` -- Replace the six hand-written lines cancelling the light and enriched checkpoint timers with two `cancel()` calls.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#scheduleLightCheckpointIfNeeded` -- `guard lightCheckpointTimer == nil` becomes `guard !lightCheckpointTimer.isArmed`; the build/arm/resume dance and the two-line self-clear inside `schedulingLifecycle.run(token)` move into the box's `arm(after:handler:)`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#scheduleCoalescedReconcile` -- Same shape as the light checkpoint: guard on `isArmed`, arm through the box.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#cancelCoalescedReconcile` -- Three lines become one `cancel()`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#flushPendingCheckpoint` -- Three lines become one `cancel()` before `performLightCheckpoint(async: false)`.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#prepareRecoveryForApplicationExit` -- Three lines become one `cancel()` on the enriched timer.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#applyRecoveryAction` -- The `.schedule(let deadline)` case must cancel-then-arm through the box, and the `.cancel` case becomes one `cancel()`. This is the arm-from-inside-the-handler site: the handler runs inside `schedulingLifecycle.run(token)`, which has already removed the token, then calls back into `applyRecoveryAction` which arms a fresh one. The box's `arm` must not assume it is starting from a clean slot.
- `app/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle.swift (new type, or a new sibling file)` -- Add the census-owning box. If it lands in a new app/ file, that file must be added to the explicit compile list in `test-ui.sh` (the UI harness names every app/ source, and `AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycle.swift` is already on it).

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- app-tests/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycleTests.swift -- shutdownEmptiesEveryOwnerCategory ("shutdown empties every owner category and makes captured callbacks inert") -- the one direct test of the census contract; it must stay green untouched
- app-tests/AppRuntimeAmbientCommandTests.swift -- the primary-history-mutation test that asserts `captureOwnerCensus()[.timer] == 1` after `fixture.session.onPrimaryHistoryMutation?()` and `== nil` after `runtime.perform(.terminate)` -- this is the enriched-timer arm/retire pair and is the closest thing to a characterization test for RUNTIME-4
- app-tests/AppRuntimeSessionCommandTests.swift -- the four `captureOwnerCensus()[.debouncer]` and `[.subscription]` assertions (search-needle debounce arm/retire, bootstrap replacement, absent pane) -- these prove the box did not change census accounting for owners it does not touch
- app-tests/AppRuntimeRosterPushTests.swift -- the `[.subscription]` before/after assertions around `ipcConnectionClosed`
- app-tests/AppRuntimePendingIpcShutdownTests.swift and app-tests/IpcServerOwnershipTests.swift -- the ipcServer owner's teardown behavior through `stopIpcServer` and `shutdown`
- app-tests/AppRuntimeDeallocationTests.swift -- proves the runtime still deallocates; a box holding a strong `DispatchSourceTimer` plus a closure is exactly the shape that can introduce a retain cycle

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- (none) -- no test reads any of the ten fields. They are all `private`, and grep over app-tests, tests-ui and ios found zero references to `lightCheckpointTimer`, `enrichedCheckpointTimer`, `coalescedReconcileTimer`, `switcherEventMonitor`, `ipcServer`, or any of their tokens outside app/AppRuntime.swift. Every existing test observes this code only through `captureOwnerCensus()`, which the refactor preserves. Nothing will stop compiling.

**Write this test first.** There is no behavior change here, so do not invent a failing test. This is a pure refactor and the characterization test is app-tests/AppRuntimeAmbientCommandTests.swift, the test asserting `runtime.schedulingLifecycle.captureOwnerCensus()[.timer] == 1` after `fixture.session.onPrimaryHistoryMutation?()` and `== nil` after `runtime.perform(.terminate)` -- it pins arm and retire of the enriched checkpoint timer through the only public window onto ownership. If you want the audit's suggested coalescing-Msg census test, write it as a new test in app-tests/AppRuntimeSchedulingLifecycleTests.swift named "a coalescing message arms one timer and a non-coalescing one retires it": send `.sessionBell(sessionId:)` (a coalescing Msg per `Msg.swift#coalescesReconcile`) through `runtime.send`, then a non-coalescing Msg, and assert the `.timer` count returns to zero and a later coalescing Msg arms again. Be honest that this test passes against today's tree -- it is a new safety net for the refactor, not a red test. Beware: `dispatchInFrame` also calls `scheduleLightCheckpointIfNeeded` at the end of every frame, so `[.timer]` can legitimately be 2, not 1; assert on a delta or drive `flushPendingCheckpoint` first rather than on a bare count.

**Blockers and surprises.** Four things. First, the finding's `ScheduledTimer` name is too narrow: two of the five pairs are not timers (`NSEvent` local monitor retired with `NSEvent.removeMonitor`, and `IpcServer` retired with `stop()`), so the box has to be generic over the handle and take both the census category and a retire closure -- or the plan accepts covering only the three real timers and leaves the other two pairs alone, which weakens the by-construction claim. Say which up front. Second, the re-arm-from-inside-the-handler path is real and confirmed: `applyRecoveryAction`'s `.schedule` case is reached from inside `schedulingLifecycle.run(token)` in the enriched timer's own event handler, which has already consumed that token, so `arm` must work on a box whose token was retired by someone else. Third, `shutdown()`'s ten-line block runs *after* `schedulingLifecycle.shutdown()` has already fired every cancel closure, so a naive box `cancel()` in its place would double-cancel; the correct replacement is to delete the block, not translate it. Fourth, `arm` returns an *optional* token -- it returns nil once the lifecycle is in the shutdown state -- and all four current arm sites handle that by cancelling the freshly built timer and returning; the box must preserve that fail-closed behavior or a post-shutdown arm leaks a live timer. No ADR constrains this; `docs/design/2026-06-09-appkit-lifetime-safety.md` is the relevant reading for the event-monitor half.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

##### RUNTIME-5. Derive the previously visible tab from the reconcile cache, not from `isHidden`

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 4 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 3 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/Reconcile.swift#reconcileContainers`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#containerOpsStrandVisible`

**Problem.** `reconcileContainers` decides whether an in-flight pane drag must be cancelled by asking AppKit which container is currently unhidden, rather than by remembering what the previous pass applied. The reconciler's contract is that each pass diffs against a cache holding the last value it applied; here it reads the view tree back, so the decision depends on a fact the pass is about to overwrite, and on arbitrary dictionary iteration order when more than one container is momentarily unhidden (a freshly built `SplitContainerView` is unhidden until its `setVisible` op runs).

**Evidence.** `let previouslyVisibleTabId = tabContainers.first(where: { !$0.value.isHidden })?.key`, passed to `containerOpsStrandVisible(ops:previouslyVisibleTabId:)` and `containerOpsEditVisibleTree(ops:previouslyVisibleTabId:)` to decide `cancelPaneDrag()`. `ContainerShape` in ModelOperations.swift deliberately excludes visibility and `computeContainerOps` takes `selectedTabId` as a separate side input, so `caches.containerShape` alone cannot answer the question -- but nothing stops the cache bag from carrying the selection that produced it.

**Ideal fix.** Store the applied selection next to the applied shapes: add `var visibleTabId: TabId?` to `ReconcilerCaches`, pass `caches.visibleTabId` into the two stranding predicates, and set it to `model.selectedTabId` at the end of the pass alongside `caches.containerShape = new`. `ReconcilerCaches()` re-init on teardown resets it for free, matching every other cache field.

**By construction.** The reconciler can no longer read its own output back out of AppKit: the only source for "what did the last pass show" is the cache, so a view whose `isHidden` was changed by anything other than this pass cannot influence the drag-cancel decision.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- one field and two line edits.

**Verification.** UI test (tests-ui/SplitContainerViewTests.swift or PaneWrapperViewTests.swift): with two tabs and an in-flight pane drag, select the other tab and assert the drag overlay is torn down; repeat with the selected tab's tree edited (a split) instead. Both must hold when a second container has been built but not yet hidden in the same pass.

**Risk.** The first pass after a teardown has a nil cached selection where the view scan previously found a container, so a drag started before a restore would no longer be cancelled by the first sweep -- but `tearDownCurrentSession` already calls `cancelPaneDrag()` directly, so this is covered.

**Vetted.** The line is exact: `let previouslyVisibleTabId = tabContainers.first(where: { !$0.value.isHidden })?.key`, feeding `containerOpsStrandVisible` and `containerOpsEditVisibleTree` to decide `cancelPaneDrag()`. But I grepped every `isHidden` write in app/: `Reconcile.swift#reconcileContainers` (`container.isHidden = !visible`) is the *only* writer of a container's hidden flag, and `computeContainerOps` today emits `.setVisible` for every tab on every pass, so each completed pass leaves exactly one unhidden container. The scan also runs before any op is applied. So the stated failure -- arbitrary dictionary order when more than one container is momentarily unhidden -- cannot happen as the code stands; the freshly-built-container window the finding describes exists only *inside* the op loop, after the scan. What survives is the structural objection alone: the reconciler reads its own output back out of AppKit.

**Correction.** Drop the dictionary-order failure claim -- `Reconcile.reconcileContainers` is the only writer of container `isHidden`, and each pass ends with exactly one unhidden container, so the scan is currently unambiguous. The finding is a purity/coupling cleanup, not a latent ordering bug. It becomes a real bug risk only once RECON-1 makes `.setVisible` conditional: a newly built background container is unhidden by default, so if the diffed emission skips it, two containers really can be unhidden at scan time. Score it as the small cleanup it is (impact 2), and land it with RECON-1.

**Sharper ideal.** If RECON-1 lands first, the extra `ReconcilerCaches.visibleTabId` field is redundant: `caches.containerShape[tabId]?.isVisible` already records what the last pass applied. Adding a parallel field beside the shape cache would reintroduce the two-writers-for-one-truth shape this very finding objects to.

**Do after.** [RECON-1](#recon-1)

**Conflicts with.** [RECON-1](#recon-1)

<a id="runtime-6"></a>

##### RUNTIME-6. Move the pane-tape follow broker out of AppRuntime into its own owner

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 3 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `app/AppRuntime.swift#beginPaneTapeFollow`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#finishPaneTapeFollowStart`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#deliverPaneTapeFollowBatch`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#retirePaneTapeFollowTransport`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#tearDownSession`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#shutdown`

**Problem.** `AppRuntime` is 2155 lines holding at least six unrelated jobs: the Elm dispatch frame, the Command interpreter, the IPC request registry, the pane-tape follow streaming broker, checkpoint scheduling, and restore staging. The tape broker alone is roughly 330 lines, nine private methods, two private tables, and one private struct, and its invariants (retire a transport with `run` not `cancel`; a sibling stream on the same socket must keep its notice) are enforced only by comments on runtime fields every other part of the runtime can also reach. Its lifecycle leaks into unrelated methods as well.

**Evidence.** `private var paneTapeFollowSubscriptions`, `private var paneTapeFollowTransports`, `private struct PaneTapeFollowTransport`, plus `streamFinitePaneTape`, `beginPaneTapeFollow`, `finishPaneTapeFollowStart`, `paneTapeFollowEventsAvailable`, `fetchPaneTapeFollow`, `deliverPaneTapeFollowBatch`, `failPaneTapeFollow`, `dropPaneTapeFollow`, `endPaneTapeFollowers`, `writePaneTapeFollowEnd`, and `retirePaneTapeFollowTransport` all live on `AppRuntime`. `shutdown()` contains `for subscriptionId in paneTapeFollowSubscriptions.removeAll() { retirePaneTapeFollowTransport(subscriptionId)?.close() }`, and `tearDownSession(_:)` opens with `endPaneTapeFollowers(for: paneId)`.

**Ideal fix.** Extract a `@MainActor final class PaneTapeFollowBroker` owning both tables, taking the scheduling lifecycle and a session-lookup closure at init, and exposing four entry points: `begin(reqId:paneId:...)`, `paneClosed(_:)`, `connectionClosed(_:)`, and `shutdown()`. `AppRuntime` keeps one field and forwards, so the `.streamPaneTape` arm, `tearDownSession`, `ipcConnectionClosed`, and `shutdown()` each become a one-line call. Follow on by extracting the checkpoint scheduler (`RecoveryCheckpointPolicy`, the two timers, the two capture helpers) the same way.

**By construction.** The transports table stops being reachable from unrelated runtime code, so "another method retired a transport without its notice registration" and "a sibling stream's census token was cancelled" become impossible to write outside one small type whose only exit is `retire`. The broker's shutdown obligation becomes a single visible call rather than a loop buried in `AppRuntime.shutdown()`.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the extraction is mechanical because the broker's state is already private and reached only through these methods.

**Verification.** Existing behavior must hold: app-tests/PaneTapeFollowEncodingTests.swift plus a census test -- open two follow streams on one connection, close one pane, assert the surviving stream still receives batches and that `captureOwnerCensus()[.subscription]` drops by exactly one; then close the connection and assert the census returns to its baseline.

**Risk.** The broker must arm its tokens on the runtime's own lifecycle; if the extraction gives it a separate one, a stream could stay armed after `AppRuntime.shutdown()`. The census test above is what catches that.

**Vetted.** Verified the inventory: `paneTapeFollowSubscriptions`, `paneTapeFollowTransports`, and `private struct PaneTapeFollowTransport` are all `AppRuntime` state, and the eleven named methods plus `streamFinitePaneTape` are all private methods on it. `shutdown()` contains the `for subscriptionId in paneTapeFollowSubscriptions.removeAll() { retirePaneTapeFollowTransport(subscriptionId)?.close() }` loop, `tearDownSession` opens with `endPaneTapeFollowers(for: paneId)`, and `ipcConnectionClosed` walks `paneTapeFollowSubscriptions.connectionClosed(connectionId)`. AppRuntime.swift is 2155 lines as stated. The `retire with run, not cancel` invariant is documented on `PaneTapeFollowTransport.shutdownToken` exactly as the finding says, and today nothing but convention keeps a sibling stream's token from being cancelled by unrelated runtime code.

#### Area: Pane views and geometry (`PANE`)

_Scope: Pane presentation: terminal view, pane host, and pane geometry interaction_

**The auditor's read on the area.** The presentation core of this area is in good shape: `SwiftTerminalSessionView.synchronizePresentation` is a genuinely single geometry/scale detector with the display-scaling invariant stated where it binds, `SplitContainerView` applies the pure `paneLayout` and nothing else, and `PaneDividerView` reports gestures without owning a ratio. The weak seam is everything the model-owned-geometry lift did not reach: pane drag-and-drop still hit-tests live AppKit wrapper frames, and the pane wrapper still keeps its own copies of zoom/splits facts. I did not audit the terminal engine packages under `lib/`, `AppRuntime` beyond the two pane-drag/lookup entry points the area's files call, or the sidebar.

<a id="pane-1"></a>

##### PANE-1. Resolve the pane drop target from the model layout, not from live wrapper frames

`structural` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#PaneDragCoordinator.updateDrag`, `app/PaneWrapperView.swift#ToolbarDragHandleView.mouseDragged`, `app/SplitContainerView.swift#SplitContainerView.reconcilePanes`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#AppRuntime.startPaneDrag`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/PaneLayout.swift#paneLayout`

**Problem.** Pane drag-and-drop is the one pane-geometry consumer that still derives its geometry from AppKit views instead of the model. `PaneDragCoordinator` hit-tests `wrapper.convert(wrapper.bounds, to: nil)` for each candidate pane, and nothing in that path knows which panes the model says are hidden. Under zoom the pure layout returns a frame only for the zoomed pane and puts every sibling in `hiddenPaneIds`, so the siblings keep the frames they had before the zoom -- stale rectangles that still tile the whole container. A drag started while a pane is zoomed therefore highlights and drops onto invisible panes.

**Evidence.** `paneLayout(in:tree:zoomedPaneId:)` returns `PaneLayout(paneFrames: [zoomedPaneId: bounds], dividers: [:], hiddenPaneIds: paneIds.subtracting([zoomedPaneId]))`, and `SplitContainerView.reconcilePanes` only calls `setFrameIfNeeded` `if let rect = layout.paneFrames[paneId]` -- so a hidden wrapper is merely `isHidden = true` with its pre-zoom frame intact. `AppRuntime.startPaneDrag` builds `provider = { findPaneWrapper(for: $0)?.convert(wrapper.bounds, to: nil) }`, which resolves through `paneHost(for:)?.wrapper` and never consults hiddenness, and `PaneDragCoordinator.updateDrag` accepts the first pane where `frame.contains(locationInWindow)`. The comment in `ToolbarDragHandleView.mouseDragged` states the opposite premise the flat container invalidated: "In-tab split/swap targets aren't mounted while zoomed, so those drops stay inert (PaneDragCoordinator skips nil frames)."

**Ideal fix.** Make drop-target resolution a projection of the same `PaneLayout` the container applied. Add a pure core function -- `paneDropTarget(at point: PaneLayoutRect-space point, layout: PaneLayout, excluding source: PaneId) -> PaneDrop?` -- that walks `layout.paneFrames` (which by definition excludes hidden panes) and calls the existing `resolveDropZone`. `PaneDragCoordinator` then holds the layout and a container-to-window transform instead of a frame provider, and stores one `currentDrop: PaneDrop?` in place of the parallel `currentTarget` / `currentIntent` optionals.

**By construction.** A drop onto a pane the model does not display becomes unrepresentable: the only rectangles the resolver can see are the ones the pure layout produced for visible panes, and "a target with no intent" (or an intent with no target) stops being expressible once both live in one optional value.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the frame provider but have it return nil for any pane in the container's hidden set, and have `SplitContainerView` publish that set. This removes the zoom bug without removing the second geometry source, so the next zoom-like presentation state reopens the class.

**Verification.** UI-harness test: build a two-pane tab, zoom one pane, start a pane drag from the zoomed pane's toolbar, drive `updatePaneDrag` to a point inside the zoomed pane's rectangle, and assert `currentPaneDrop()` is nil rather than naming the hidden sibling. Pure-core test: `paneDropTarget` over a zoomed layout returns only the zoomed pane for every point in bounds.

**Risk.** The coordinate transform must be got right once (container space to window space) instead of per-wrapper; a mistake would shift every highlight, which the harness test above catches directly.

**Vetted.** Every quoted line is in the tree and says what the finding claims. `PaneLayout.swift#paneLayout` returns `paneFrames: [zoomedPaneId: bounds]` with `hiddenPaneIds: paneIds.subtracting([zoomedPaneId])`; `SplitContainerView.reconcilePanes` sets `isHidden` for hidden panes but only calls `setFrameIfNeeded` inside `if let rect = layout.paneFrames[paneId]`, so a hidden wrapper keeps its full pre-zoom tiling frame. `AppRuntime.startPaneDrag` builds the provider as `wrapper.convert(wrapper.bounds, to: nil)` via `findPaneWrapper` -> `paneHost(for:)?.wrapper`, which resolves a host for every live pane regardless of hiddenness, and `PaneDragCoordinator.updateDrag` takes the first pane whose frame contains the point and `break`s -- so a stale sibling frame can win before the zoomed pane's. The comment in `ToolbarDragHandleView.mouseDragged` ("In-tab split/swap targets aren't mounted while zoomed, so those drops stay inert") states a premise the flat container invalidated: the wrappers are mounted, just hidden. I also confirmed the drag is cancelled when the visible tree is edited mid-drag (`Reconcile.swift#reconcileContainers` -> `containerOpsEditVisibleTree`), so the reachable path is exactly the one the finding names: a drag started while a pane is already zoomed.

**Conflicts with.** [PANE-2](#pane-2), [LOOKUP-4](#lookup-4), [RECON-1](#recon-1)

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 10 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#PaneDragCoordinator` is a `@MainActor class` holding `let sourcePaneId: PaneId`, `let overlayView: PaneDragOverlayView`, `private(set) var currentTarget: PaneId?`, `private(set) var currentIntent: PaneDropIntent?`, `private let paneFrameProvider: (PaneId) -> NSRect?`, and `private let allTargetPaneIds: [PaneId]`. `updateDrag(locationInWindow:)` loops `allTargetPaneIds`, takes the first pane whose provided window-space frame contains the point, `break`s, and runs the pure `resolveDropZone(cursorInPane:paneSize:)` on the local offset. `AppRuntime.startPaneDrag(paneId:)` builds the provider as `{ [weak self] in self?.findPaneWrapper(for: $0)?.convert(wrapper.bounds, to: nil) }` and the target list as `allPaneIds(tab.paneTree.root).filter { $0 != paneId }` -- neither consults hiddenness. The pure layout is `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/PaneLayout.swift#paneLayout(in:tree:zoomedPaneId:metrics:) -> PaneLayout`, whose zoom branch returns `paneFrames: [zoomedPaneId: bounds]` with `hiddenPaneIds: paneIds.subtracting([zoomedPaneId])`; `app/SplitContainerView.swift#reconcilePanes` sets `isHidden` for those panes but only calls `setFrameIfNeeded` inside `if let rect = layout.paneFrames[paneId]`, so a hidden wrapper keeps its whole pre-zoom frame. `resolveDropZone` lives in lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DropZone.swift over `DropZonePoint` / `DropZoneSize`.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DropZone.swift (or a new file beside PaneLayout.swift)` -- Add the pure resolver the finding names -- something like `func paneDropTarget(at point: PaneLayoutPoint, layout: PaneLayout, excluding source: PaneId) -> PaneDrop?` -- walking `layout.paneFrames` only, and delegating the in-pane zone decision to the existing `resolveDropZone`. Needs a `PaneLayoutPoint` (PaneLayout.swift has `PaneLayoutRect` but no point type) and a `PaneDrop` value pairing target + intent.
- `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/PaneLayout.swift#PaneLayoutRect` -- May need a `contains(_:)` helper; today the struct exposes only minX/minY/maxX/maxY.
- `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#PaneDragCoordinator` -- Replace `paneFrameProvider` + `allTargetPaneIds` with the layout plus a container-to-window transform, and collapse `currentTarget`/`currentIntent` into one `currentDrop: PaneDrop?`. `updateDrag` converts the window point into layout space once, calls the pure resolver, and drives the overlay from the layout rect.
- `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#currentDrop` -- `func currentDrop() -> (source: PaneId, target: PaneId, intent: PaneDropIntent)?` can stay as the public shape so PaneWrapperView is unchanged, or become `PaneDrop?` -- if it changes, `PaneWrapperView` and the harness shim follow.
- `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#teardown` -- Clears one optional instead of two.
- `app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift#highlightRect(for:in:)` -- Now takes a layout rect converted to overlay space rather than a window-space NSRect from a wrapper.
- `app/AppRuntime.swift#startPaneDrag` -- Stop building the frame provider and target list. Compute the layout the container applied -- the same `paneLayout(in:tree:zoomedPaneId:)` call `SplitContainerView.applyModelLayout` makes -- and hand it plus the container's coordinate origin to the coordinator. Getting at the container's layout without recomputing it may mean exposing it from `SplitContainerView`.
- `app/SplitContainerView.swift#applyModelLayout / #reconcilePanes` -- Only if the coordinator reads the container's already-computed layout rather than recomputing: the container would need to publish its last applied `PaneLayout`. Recomputing is also legitimate and keeps the container untouched -- name the choice in the plan.
- `app/PaneWrapperView.swift#ToolbarDragHandleView.mouseDragged` -- The comment "In-tab split/swap targets aren't mounted while zoomed, so those drops stay inert (PaneDragCoordinator skips nil frames)" states a premise the flat container invalidated. Rewrite it to say the resolver sees only visible panes; the guard logic itself (`hasSplits || totalTabCount > 1`) does not change.
- `tests-ui/SidebarViewTestShim.swift#AppRuntime.currentPaneDrop` -- Only if the return type changes -- the shim declares `func currentPaneDrop() -> (source: PaneId, target: PaneId, intent: PaneDropIntent)? { nil }` and must keep matching what PaneWrapperView calls.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/DropZoneTests.swift -- all 14 tests (testDropZoneLeft, ...Right, ...Bottom, ...Top, ...Center, ...ExactCenter, ...CornerCloserToTop, ...CornerCloserToLeft, ...CornerEquidistantHorizontalWins, ...BoundaryIsEdge, ...ZeroWidth, ...ZeroHeight, ...CursorOutside, ...CursorOutsideRight) -- the in-pane zone rule is unchanged and the new resolver must keep delegating to it
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/PaneLayoutTests.swift -- whole suite -- pins the layout the resolver now reads, including the zoom branch
- tests-ui/SplitContainerViewTests.swift -- "nested zoom fills the container and unzoom restores every pane" and "hidden and visible containers use identical geometry" -- pin the hidden-wrapper behavior that creates the bug

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- Nothing. There is no test anywhere that constructs a PaneDragCoordinator, calls updateDrag, or asserts on currentPaneDrop -- I grepped the whole tree for `PaneDragCoordinator` and `paneFrameProvider` and the only hits are production code, the harness shim's inert stubs, and old plan files. That is the important fact about this work: the drop-target path is entirely uncovered today, so the change starts by writing coverage rather than by adapting it.

**Write this test first.** Suite: DanTermCoreTests, lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/DropZoneTests.swift (or a new PaneDropTargetTests.swift beside it). Name: "a zoomed layout offers no drop target outside the zoomed pane". Scenario: build a two-leaf horizontal split tree, call `paneLayout(in: bounds, tree: tree, zoomedPaneId: paneB)`, then ask `paneDropTarget(at:layout:excluding:)` for a point in the left half of `bounds` -- the rectangle the hidden pane A occupied before the zoom. Assert the answer names pane B (the only pane in `paneFrames`), never pane A, for every point inside bounds; and with `excluding: paneB` the answer is nil. Why it fails today: `paneDropTarget` does not exist, and the behavior it encodes is the opposite of what ships -- `PaneDragCoordinator.updateDrag` asks `findPaneWrapper(for: paneA)?.convert(bounds, to: nil)`, which returns pane A's stale pre-zoom frame because `reconcilePanes` only hides the wrapper and never reframes it, so pane A wins the containment test and `break`s before pane B is considered.

**Blockers and surprises.** Nothing hidden, but four things worth knowing. (1) The audit proposes a UI-harness test as the second verification; test-ui.sh does not compile app/PaneDragCoordinator.swift, and the harness `AppRuntime` shim's `startPaneDrag`/`updatePaneDrag`/`currentPaneDrop` are deliberately inert stubs. Driving the drag from the harness therefore means promoting PaneDragCoordinator.swift into test-ui.sh's compile list and testing the coordinator directly, not through the runtime -- the harness ADR (docs/design/2026-08-06-ui-harness-whole-module-substitution.md) calls that promotion the price of the seam. The pure-core test above needs none of that. (2) The coordinate transform is the one place a mistake shifts every highlight: today each wrapper converts its own bounds, so per-pane errors cancel; a single container-to-window transform does not. (3) `Reconcile.swift#reconcileContainers` already cancels an in-flight drag when the visible tree is edited (`containerOpsEditVisibleTree` -> `cancelPaneDrag`), so the reachable bug is exactly the narrow one the finding names: a drag started while a pane is already zoomed. (4) The section lists conflicts with PANE-2 (retype `leafViews` as `[PaneId: PaneWrapperView]`), LOOKUP-4 (stop materializing `allPaneIds`), and RECON-1 (diff container visibility). None of them blocks this; PANE-1 removes a `findPaneWrapper` consumer and LOOKUP-4 removes an `allPaneIds(...)` call site in `startPaneDrag`, so whichever lands second gets a smaller diff.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

<a id="pane-2"></a>

##### PANE-2. Type the container's leaf cache as the wrapper it needs, so a missing wrapper is retried, not cached

`correctness` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/SplitContainerView.swift#SplitContainerView.reconcilePanes`, `app/AppRuntime.swift#AppRuntime.buildAndInsertContainer`

**Problem.** When the wrapper lookup fails, the container substitutes a bare placeholder view and stores it permanently under that pane id. Every later layout pass finds the placeholder in `leafViews`, so it never asks for the real wrapper again: the pane is a blank rectangle for the rest of the tab's life, with no error and no path back. The lookup is a weak-self closure into `AppRuntime`, so "nil" is a transient condition, not a permanent fact about the pane.

**Evidence.** `reconcilePanes` does `view = wrapperLookup(paneId) ?? NSView()` and then `leafViews[paneId] = view`, keyed `[PaneId: NSView]`; on the next pass `if let existing = leafViews[paneId] { view = existing }` short-circuits the lookup. The lookup itself is `{ [weak self] paneId in self?.paneHost(for: paneId)?.wrapper }` from `buildAndInsertContainer`.

**Ideal fix.** Declare `leafViews` as `[PaneId: PaneWrapperView]` and skip a pane whose wrapper is absent -- no placeholder, no cache entry. The next layout pass (the container already re-runs `applyModelLayout` from `layout()`) resolves it as soon as the wrapper exists.

**By construction.** The container can no longer hold a view that is not a pane's wrapper, so "a pane permanently showing a placeholder" stops being a state the cache can represent.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** UI-harness test: build a container whose lookup returns nil for one pane, force a layout pass, then make the wrapper available and force another pass; assert the pane's `PaneWrapperView` is a subview of the container and occupies the model's frame.

**Risk.** None beyond the type change; the divider path is untouched.

**Vetted.** The evidence is exact: `reconcilePanes` does `view = wrapperLookup(paneId) ?? NSView()` then `leafViews[paneId] = view` over a `[PaneId: NSView]` cache, and the next pass short-circuits on `if let existing = leafViews[paneId]`. But I could not reach the nil branch in production. `AppRuntime.perform(.createSession)` installs the host before the sweep returns, `commitRestoreSession` assigns `paneHosts = staged.hosts` before `sweepAndDispatchFollowUps()`, and the one failure path -- `send(.sessionCreationFailed)` -- resolves in `Update.swift` by removing the whole containing tab, which prunes the leafViews entry. So the "blank rectangle for the rest of the tab's life" is a latent trap in the cache's type, not an observed defect. The fix is still tiny and removes an unrepresentable state, so it stays; the impact drops to 2 because no user-reachable failure was demonstrated.

**Correction.** The failure is latent, not live: every production path installs the pane host before the container reconciles, and the one creation-failure path removes the tab. The finding should say the type permits a permanently-cached placeholder, not that a pane becomes a blank rectangle today.

**Conflicts with.** [PANE-1](#pane-1), [LOOKUP-4](#lookup-4), [RECON-1](#recon-1)

<a id="pane-3"></a>

##### PANE-3. Record which button a press forwarded, replacing the two ad-hoc pairing booleans

`correctness` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.mouseDown`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.rightMouseUp`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.forwardPointerDown`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.forwardPointerUp`

**Problem.** Press/release pairing is encoded in two independent booleans that each cover one button. `rightButtonForwarded` exists precisely because an unpaired press or release latches the engine's button owner -- the code says so -- but the left and middle buttons have no equivalent, and `forwardPointerDown` can silently drop a press (`guard ... let cell = normalizedCell(for: event)`) that `forwardPointerUp` will still answer with a release once geometry exists. `controlClickIsActive` is a third piece of the same fact: which button the current press is being reported as.

**Evidence.** `rightMouseDown` sets `rightButtonForwarded = true` before forwarding and `rightMouseUp` does `guard rightButtonForwarded else { return }`, with the comment "an unpaired press would latch the engine's button owner and swallow the next right-click". `mouseDown` instead does `controlClickIsActive = event.modifierFlags.contains(.control); forwardPointerDown(event, button: controlClickIsActive ? .right : .left)` and `mouseUp` forwards unconditionally on the same boolean. Both `forwardPointerDown` and `forwardPointerUp` open with `guard isTornDown == false, let cell = normalizedCell(for: event) else { return }`, and `normalizedCell` returns nil whenever `displayedCellSize` or `currentDimensions` is nil.

**Ideal fix.** Hold one `forwardedButton: TerminalMouseButton?` (or a small set, if simultaneous buttons matter) written only by `forwardPointerDown` when the press actually reached the controller, and read by `forwardPointerUp` to decide both whether to send a release and which button to name. `controlClickIsActive` and `rightButtonForwarded` both disappear into it.

**By construction.** A release for a button whose press was never forwarded -- and a release naming a different button than its press -- stops being expressible, because the release reads the button out of the record the press wrote.

**Cheaper fallback.** Add the same explicit guard to the left and middle paths. Cheaper, but it keeps three booleans whose combinations include states the gesture cannot be in.

**Verification.** UI-harness test against the session view with a scripted controller: synthesize a press while the view has no resolved geometry, then give it geometry and synthesize the matching release; assert no pointer-up reached the controller. A second case: control-press, release Control, release the mouse; assert down and up both name the right button.

**Risk.** Must keep the existing behavior that a control-click still reports focus even when its press is dropped -- `mouseDown` emits `.clickedToFocus` ungated today, and that must stay ungated.

**Vetted.** All four quotes verified in `SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift`: `rightMouseDown` sets `rightButtonForwarded = true` before forwarding with the latching comment on the stored property; `mouseDown` sets `controlClickIsActive` and forwards, `mouseUp` forwards unconditionally on it; both `forwardPointerDown` and `forwardPointerUp` open with `guard isTornDown == false, let cell = normalizedCell(for: event)`, and `normalizedCell(at:)` returns nil when `displayedCellSize` or `currentDimensions` is nil. The unpaired-release window is therefore real but narrow: it needs a press taken before the pane has any resolved geometry (or while torn down) followed by a release after geometry arrives. `controlClickIsActive` is not a bug -- it correctly keeps the release naming the button the press named when Control is let go mid-click -- so the finding's framing of it as "a third piece of the same fact" is fair but carries no defect of its own. Impact drops to 2: a first-frame click is the only reachable trigger.

**Sharper ideal.** A single `forwardedButton: TerminalMouseButton?` would regress simultaneous buttons: AppKit can deliver `mouseDown` (left) then `rightMouseDown` before `mouseUp`, and one optional lets the right press overwrite the left record so the left release names the wrong button or is dropped. The ideal is a per-physical-button record -- e.g. a small dictionary or set keyed by the AppKit button that stores the reported `TerminalMouseButton` -- written only when `forwardPointerDown` actually reached the controller. That subsumes `controlClickIsActive` (the reported button for the left physical button) and `rightButtonForwarded` (presence of a record for the right one) without collapsing distinct buttons into one slot.

**Conflicts with.** [INTERACT-2](#interact-2)

<a id="pane-4"></a>

##### PANE-4. Give the pane toolbar one projection argument instead of thirteen optional parameters and two model mirrors

`api-shape` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/PaneWrapperView.swift#PaneWrapperView.updateToolbar`, `app/PaneWrapperView.swift#PaneWrapperView.makePaneMenu`, `app/Reconcile.swift#AppRuntime.reconcilePaneChrome`

**Problem.** The single production caller already holds one projection value and unpacks it into thirteen arguments, three of which are `Bool?` meaning "leave whatever you had". The wrapper then stores `isZoomed` and `hasSplits` as its own copies of model facts and builds the context menu from them, so the menu's zoom title and enablement come from a second source of truth rather than from the model the same menu reads for cwd and agent id. Adding a field to the projection does not force the call site to pass it, so a new toolbar fact can be silently dropped.

**Evidence.** `func updateToolbar(label:progress:isRemote:remoteLabel:agentLabel:chipTooltip:chipKind:unreadAlertCount:totalTodoCount:uncompletedTodoCount:isZoomed:hasSplits:isGridClaimed:)` with defaults for all but `label`; `reconcilePaneChrome` calls it passing exactly `render.label ... render.isGridClaimed` from one `desiredPaneToolbar` value. Inside, `if let isZoomed { self.isZoomed = isZoomed; ... }` and `if let hasSplits { self.hasSplits = hasSplits }`, and `makePaneMenu` uses them: `let zoom = wrapperItem(isZoomed ? "Unzoom Pane" : "Zoom Pane", ...); zoom.isEnabled = hasSplits || isZoomed` -- while three lines above, the same method reads `runtime?.model.pane(paneId)?.session?.cwd` straight from the model.

**Ideal fix.** Take the projection whole: `func apply(_ render: PaneToolbarRender)`. Store that one value as the wrapper's rendered state, and have `makePaneMenu` read zoom and splits from it (or from the model, as the cwd and agent items already do) instead of from separate stored booleans. Tests construct a `PaneToolbarRender` rather than relying on parameter defaults.

**By construction.** A wrapper whose menu disagrees with the toolbar it is showing, and a call site that forgets a newly added toolbar fact, both become unexpressible: there is one value, and the compiler requires all of it.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the parameter list but make `isZoomed`/`hasSplits`/`isGridClaimed` non-optional, so "told nothing" stops being a state. This removes the stale-mirror risk without removing the drift risk when a field is added.

**Verification.** UI-harness test: apply a projection with `isZoomed: true, hasSplits: true`, open the pane menu, and assert the item reads "Unzoom Pane" and is enabled; apply the unzoomed projection and assert it reads "Zoom Pane". Existing `PaneWrapperViewTests` cases for the grid-claim button must keep passing after being rewritten to pass a whole projection.

**Risk.** Touches every UI-harness call site that relies on defaults; those rewrites are mechanical.

**Vetted.** Signature confirmed verbatim at `PaneWrapperView.updateToolbar` -- thirteen parameters, all but `label` defaulted, with `isZoomed`/`hasSplits`/`isGridClaimed` as `Bool?`. `Reconcile.swift#reconcilePaneChrome` unpacks exactly one `PaneToolbarRender` into all thirteen, and `PaneToolbarRender` declares `isZoomed`/`hasSplits` as non-optional `Bool`. The mirrors are real (`if let isZoomed { self.isZoomed = isZoomed }`, `makePaneMenu` reading `isZoomed`/`hasSplits` three lines from a live `runtime?.model.pane(paneId)` read). But the stale-mirror risk is not live: the diffed apply always passes both values, so the mirrors cannot lag the projection today; the optionality exists only for the four `tests-ui/PaneWrapperViewTests.swift` call sites. This is a clean api-shape finding with no reachable defect, so impact drops to 2.

**Correction.** The mirrors cannot go stale in production -- `reconcilePaneChrome` always supplies both fields from one `PaneToolbarRender`, and the fields are non-optional there. The live problem is only the drift risk when a field is added to the projection and the call site is not forced to pass it.

<a id="pane-5"></a>

##### PANE-5. Collapse the four duplicated fire-and-forget input methods into one completion-taking path

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.sendInputKey`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.sendText`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.sendInputText`, `app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#SwiftTerminalSessionView.sendInputWheel`, `app/TerminalSession.swift#TerminalSession`

**Problem.** Every pane input verb exists twice -- once fire-and-forget, once with a completion -- giving four verbs, eight protocol requirements, eight implementations in the session view, four default implementations, and a matching pair in each shim. The two forms of a verb must stay behaviorally identical by hand, and they already differ in one place: the unmappable-key rejection is expressed in the completion form and expressed as a silent `return` in the other, while the protocol's default extension answers `.delivered` for an input the fire-and-forget form may have dropped.

**Evidence.** In the session view: `func sendInputKey(_ key: KeyName, modifiers: KeyMods) { guard let key = Self.terminalKey(for: key) else { return } ... }` beside `func sendInputKey(_:modifiers:onCompletion:) { guard let key = ... else { ... onCompletion(.rejected) ... } ... }`; the same doubling for `sendText`, `sendInputText`, `sendInputWheel`. `TerminalSession`'s extension defines each completion form as `sendX(...); DispatchQueue.main.async { MainActor.assumeIsolated { onCompletion(.delivered) } }` -- a report that cannot know whether the call it wrapped delivered anything.

**Ideal fix.** One requirement per verb, with an optional completion: `func sendInputKey(_ key: KeyName, modifiers: KeyMods, onCompletion: (@MainActor @Sendable (TerminalInputSubmissionResult) -> Void)?)`. Better still, one requirement total -- `func send(_ input: PaneInput, onCompletion: ...)` over a `PaneInput` enum with `.text`, `.paste`, `.key`, `.wheel` cases -- so a new input kind adds one enum case rather than two protocol requirements, two implementations, and one default.

**By construction.** Two forms of one verb cannot disagree about what they reject, and no default implementation can claim `.delivered` for a submission it did not observe, because there is only one submission path to observe.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the four verbs but delete the fire-and-forget requirements, letting callers pass an ignoring completion. Halves the surface without introducing the input value type.

**Verification.** Existing IPC-level behavior tests for `input`/`text` submission results must pass unchanged; add one asserting that an unmappable key name reports `.rejected` on every entry point that reports at all.

**Risk.** Touches the `TerminalSession` protocol and both UI-harness shims; the compiler enumerates every site, and no observable IPC behavior changes.

**Vetted.** Verified the full doubling: `TerminalSession` declares four fire-and-forget requirements and four completion requirements; `SwiftTerminalSessionView` implements all eight; the protocol extension supplies four defaults that call the fire-and-forget form and then report `.delivered`. The `sendInputKey` asymmetry is exactly as quoted -- silent `return` on an unmappable key in one form, `onCompletion(.rejected)` in the other. One mitigation the finding omits: the extension carries a comment saying these defaults exist only for a session with no terminal behind it (the UI-test shim), and a live pane always overrides them, so the `.delivered` lie is confined to test shims and never reaches an IPC caller against a real pane. The only non-test conformer is `tests-ui/SidebarViewTestShim.swift`. That makes this a pure surface-reduction finding, so impact drops to 2; effort stays medium (protocol, view, shim, and the app-tests support file).

**Correction.** The `.delivered` default is annotated as shim-only ("A live terminal pane always overrides them with a real tape"), so no production submission is misreported. The defect is duplication and the hand-maintained agreement between the two forms, not a wrong IPC result.

#### Area: Window chrome and auxiliary UI (`CHROME`)

_Scope: Window chrome and auxiliary UI (sidebar, TODO/alerts popovers, preferences, confirmation, theme browser, chips, chrome bar)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** Most of this area is in good shape: the chip stack (ChipArtwork/ChipRenderer/ChipView), SingleLineLabel, SidebarCellViews, SidebarReconcileDriver, and SidebarView's rename slot are careful, well-owned code with their invariants written down. The weak spots are all at boundaries where a typed fact is flattened before it crosses: the two TODO popover controllers share an abstract base Swift cannot check, ConfirmationPanel re-derives which answer it is sending from a button's visibility, sidebar menu items carry bare UUIDs, and PreferencesPanel addresses grid rows by literal index. I did not audit TerminalPaneView/PaneWrapper or Reconcile.swift/AppRuntime.swift themselves (other owners), citing them only as call sites; I also did not review layout constants or visual design.

<a id="chrome-1"></a>

##### CHROME-1. Replace the fatalError-based TODO popover base class with one controller parameterized by a scope value

`structural` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 1 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/TodoPopoverControllerBase.swift#TodoPopoverControllerBase`, `app/TodoPopoverView.swift#TodoPopoverViewController`, `app/TabTodoPopoverView.swift#TabTodoPopoverViewController`

**Problem.** TodoPopoverControllerBase emulates an abstract class with about twenty members whose bodies are `fatalError("subclass must override")`. Swift cannot check that emulation: an added member, or a third TODO scope, compiles and traps at runtime instead of failing to build. The two concrete subclasses then re-implement the same algorithm twice -- projection apply with first-responder capture and restore, selection preservation across every mutating Msg, list key handling, and the Cmd-key equivalent table -- differing only in the row type, the edit-target type, and the TodoOwner they send to. That duplication has already drifted.

**Evidence.** TodoPopoverControllerBase declares `composeDraft`, `clearComposeDraft()`, `isEditing`, `applyStoredProjection()`, `saveEditThenReturnToList()`, `addTodoAndStayInCompose()`, `cancelEditAndReturnToList()`, `enterEditForSelectedRow()`, `focusListFromInput()`, `closePopoverFromList()`, `handleListKeyDown(_:)`, `performTodoKeyEquivalent(with:)`, `syncModeVisibility()`, `parentTodoPopover`, `shortcutHelpScope`, `clearCompleted()`, `headerTitle`, `tableColumnIdentifier`, `registerDragTypes(on:)`, `numberOfRows(in:)` -- every one a `fatalError` override point. `TodoPopoverViewController.apply(_:)` and `TabTodoPopoverViewController.apply(_:)` are the same sequence (capture five first-responder booleans, save the edit draft, swap the projection, reconcile the edit target, reload, restore selection, `restoreFirstResponder(...)`). Drift is already visible: `TodoPopoverViewController.selectNearestSelectableRow(near:focus:)` searches backwards only (`delta: -1`) while the tab version searches forward then backward; `TodoPopoverViewController.cancelEditAndReturnToList()` calls `makeFirstResponder(tableView)` even when `selectTodo(id:)` returned false, while `TabTodoPopoverViewController.cancelEditAndReturnToList()` falls back to `focusListFromInput()`. The split leaks outward too: `AppRuntime.closeTodoShortcutHelpPopover()` casts the same content view controller twice, once per subclass, to call a method that lives on the base.

**Ideal fix.** Keep one non-generic `TodoPopoverViewController` (so @objc actions and delegate methods stay legal) and move everything scope-specific into a `TodoPopoverScope` protocol value the controller holds: it vends rows as a uniform row description (optional item, isSelectable, isHeader, an opaque edit-target token), answers headerTitle / composePlaceholder / shortcutHelpScope / drag type, and builds the Msgs (add, edit, toggle, delete, reorder, move, clearCompleted, closePopover) for a target. Pane and tab become two conforming values, not two subclasses; apply, focus restore, selection preservation, list-key routing, and Cmd-key handling exist once. Reconcile's two-case applyTodoPopover switch and AppRuntime's double cast collapse to one call.

**By construction.** "A TODO popover forgot to override a required member" and "the pane and tab popovers behave differently in a case nobody meant them to differ" both stop being expressible: there is one implementation of the algorithm and no unimplemented member to forget. A future third scope becomes a value, not a class that can silently trap.

**Cheaper fallback.** If a scope value proves awkward for the tab's grouped drag/drop, keep the subclass split but delete every fatalError member that has a sane default and make the remaining ones a protocol the concrete class must satisfy, so a missing implementation is a compile error rather than a trap. That leaves the duplicated apply/selection algorithm in place, which is where the drift actually lives.

**Verification.** Extend tests-ui/TodoPopoverViewTests.swift and tests-ui/TabTodoPopoverViewTests.swift with the same behavioral scenarios run against both scopes: delete the selected row and assert the selection lands on a neighbour; cancel an edit whose item was removed and assert focus lands somewhere valid; Cmd-N from list mode focuses compose. Both suites must pass unchanged after the refactor, and today the shared cases expose the two drifts above.

**Risk.** Large, and it touches the most keyboard-sensitive surface in the app; drag/drop and focus restoration are easy to regress. Mitigate by first driving the two existing UI suites to cover the shared behaviors, then refactoring under them.

**Vetted.** Counted 21 `fatalError("subclass must override")` bodies in `TodoPopoverControllerBase` (plus the `init(coder:)` one), covering every member the finding lists. `AppRuntime.closeTodoShortcutHelpPopover` really does cast the same content view controller twice, once per subclass, for a method that lives on the base -- that one is fixable today with a single `as? TodoPopoverControllerBase`. The two drift claims are both in the tree but weaker than stated: `cancelEditAndReturnToList` genuinely diverges (pane calls `makeFirstResponder(tableView)` regardless of whether `selectTodo` succeeded; tab falls back to `focusListFromInput()`), but `selectNearestSelectableRow` differs because the row models differ -- the pane list is flat and uniformly selectable, so a forward search would be a no-op there, while the tab list has headers and sections. Calling that a drift overstates it. Impact drops from 5 to 4: this is the right refactor by the design bar, but no user-visible defect was demonstrated, only one undocumented focus-fallback difference.

**Correction.** `selectNearestSelectableRow` is not drift: the pane rows are flat and all selectable, so a forward pass has nothing to find, while the tab rows carry headers and sections. The genuine divergence is `cancelEditAndReturnToList`'s focus fallback. Also note `closeShortcutHelpPopover` already lives on the base, so `AppRuntime`'s double cast collapses to one line independently of the refactor.

The row description and Msg-builder protocol must be wide enough for all of it.

- tests-ui/TodoPopoverViewTests.swift -- all 22 uiTests, notably "apply mid-edit preserves draft when target still exists", "apply mid-edit exits when target is gone and selects nearest row", "apply preserves compose focus and draft", "apply preserves table focus or falls back to compose when rows empty", "Cmd-Backspace deletes selected row and selects nearest survivor", "Cmd-N while editing saves, clears compose draft, and focuses compose", "Escape in compose focuses list when possible and dismisses empty lists", "shortcut help closes before pane parent disappears"
- tests-ui/TabTodoPopoverViewTests.swift -- all 18 uiTests, notably "apply renders populated tab and pane sections in row order", "shouldSelectRow focuses pane headers and only selects item rows", "pasteboardWriterForRow emits tab and pane drag payloads", "apply mid-edit preserves draft when target still exists", "apply mid-edit exits edit mode when target is gone", "shortcut help closes before tab parent disappears"
