- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests/TodoShortcutCatalogTests.swift and TabTodoTests.swift -- whole suites -- the pure classifier and row builder both controllers already share

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- tests-ui/TodoPopoverViewTests.swift -- its private fixture builder and every test through it -- only for the controller's initializer signature; no assertion should change. If an assertion has to change, that is a behavior regression, not a refactor.
- tests-ui/TabTodoPopoverViewTests.swift -- same

**Write this test first.** This is a pure refactor: no user-visible behavior is meant to change, and I could not find a reachable defect to write a red test against. The one genuine divergence the section names -- pane `cancelEditAndReturnToList` calling `makeFirstResponder(tableView)` even when `selectTodo(id:)` returned false, versus the tab version falling back to `focusListFromInput()` -- is not reachable in production: `TodoPopoverViewController.apply(_:)` already runs `popoverState.reconcileEditTarget { ... }`, which drops edit mode whenever the target leaves the projection, so cancel can never run against a missing target. The pane suite's "apply mid-edit exits when target is gone and selects nearest row" pins exactly that. So: do NOT invent a structural test. The characterization suites are tests-ui/TodoPopoverViewTests.swift and tests-ui/TabTodoPopoverViewTests.swift in full, run before and after with no assertion edited. The one preparatory step the section's Verification asks for is worth doing first and is honest work: cross-port the shared scenarios each suite is missing -- the tab suite has no equivalent of "Cmd-N while editing saves, clears compose draft, and focuses compose", no "Cmd-Backspace deletes selected row and selects nearest survivor", no "Escape in list mode sends toggleTodoPopover", and no compose/table focus-preservation cases. Those additions must pass against today's tree (I read both controllers and expect them to); if one fails, that is the real first failing test and it should be fixed as its own commit before the refactor.

**Blockers and surprises.** The size is the risk and the section already says so, but three specifics sharpen it. (1) The tab controller is nearly twice the pane controller and carries everything hard: grouped rows with headers and per-pane sections, cross-bucket moves (`moveSelectedTodoToAdjacentBucket`), Cmd-Shift-H/L swallowed as key equivalents, a Codable `TabTodoDragPayload` with tab and pane sources, and post-add selection of the newly created tab todo. The scope protocol has to carry all of that or the refactor stalls half-done. (2) `selectNearestSelectableRow` is NOT drift: the pane list is flat and uniformly selectable so a forward search finds nothing, while the tab list has headers -- the audit's Correction says this and the plan should not try to unify them into a single search direction on the theory that one is a bug. (3) The harness constraint: both suites run through test-ui.sh's explicit source list against the fake `AppRuntime` in tests-ui/SidebarViewTestShim.swift, so any new file under app/ must be added to that list, and scripts/tests/test-ui-harness_test.sh is a gate step over the harness itself. One thing is easier than the finding implies: `closeShortcutHelpPopover()` already lives on the base, so `AppRuntime.closeTodoShortcutHelpPopover`'s double cast collapses to one line today, independent of everything else -- a fine first commit.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** No disagreement with the stated ideal -- one controller parameterized by a scope value is the simplest structure in which "a scope forgot to override a member" cannot exist. Two adjustments to how the section frames the work. First, its motivation leans on drift that is not observable: `cancelEditAndReturnToList` genuinely diverges in source, but `apply`'s `reconcileEditTarget` makes the divergent branch unreachable, so this refactor buys structure and future safety, not a bug fix. Plan it and describe it that way. Second, the section's own sequencing is the right one and should be the commit plan: first bring the two UI suites to parity on the shared behaviors (a real, independently valuable commit that passes today), then refactor beneath them.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

##### CHROME-2. Make the confirmation projection carry each button's answer instead of inferring it from button visibility

`correctness` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/ConfirmationPanel.swift#confirm`, `app/ConfirmationPanel.swift#configure`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/Projections.swift#ConfirmationProjection`

**Problem.** The panel decides which Msg the primary button sends by reading its own view state. ConfirmationProjection carries only titles, so "this confirmation has a secondary button" is being used as a stand-in for "this confirmation is a delete-group transaction". Any future confirmation that wants a third choice, or a two-button quit variant, silently answers as a delete-group.

**Evidence.** `configure(_:)` sets `secondaryButton.isHidden = projection.secondaryTitle == nil`. `confirm(_:)` reads that flag back: `if secondaryButton.isHidden { runtime?.send(.confirmConfirmation(id: transactionId)) } else { runtime?.send(.chooseDeleteGroupConfirmation(id: transactionId, moveTabs: true)) }`, and `chooseCloseTabs(_:)` hardcodes `.chooseDeleteGroupConfirmation(id:, moveTabs: false)`. `ConfirmationProjection` in Projections.swift holds exactly id, title, informativeText, commands, confirmTitle, secondaryTitle -- no answer semantics at all.

**Ideal fix.** Give the projection a typed answer per button: a `ConfirmationAnswer` enum (confirm, deleteGroupMovingTabs, deleteGroupClosingTabs, ...) paired with each title, so a button is a (title, answer) pair. The panel's three actions collapse into one `answer(_:)` that sends `.answerConfirmation(id:, answer:)`; the reducer switches on the answer. The panel no longer knows any transaction kind exists.

**By construction.** It becomes impossible for the panel to send an answer that does not belong to the confirmation it is showing, because the only answers it can send are the ones the projection handed it. "Button visibility means transaction kind" ceases to be a rule anyone can break.

**Cheaper fallback.** None -- the ideal fix is small: one enum, one Msg case, and three action bodies become one.

**Verification.** In tests-ui/ConfirmationPanelTests.swift, configure the panel with a quit projection that has a secondary title and assert the primary button dispatches the quit answer, not the delete-group one. That test fails today.

**Risk.** Low. One projection field, one reducer switch, and the existing panel tests cover the current two flows.

**Vetted.** Every quote is exact. `ConfirmationPanel.configure` sets `secondaryButton.isHidden = projection.secondaryTitle == nil`; `confirm(_:)` branches on `secondaryButton.isHidden` to choose between `.confirmConfirmation` and `.chooseDeleteGroupConfirmation(moveTabs: true)`; `chooseCloseTabs` hardcodes `moveTabs: false`. `ConfirmationProjection` in Projections.swift carries only id/title/informativeText/commands/confirmTitle/secondaryTitle. I read every arm of `desiredConfirmation` and confirmed only the delete-group arm sets `secondaryTitle` -- .app, .pane, .tab, .tabs all pass nil. So the implicit rule holds today and there is no live bug; the defect is that the panel infers a transaction kind from its own view state. Impact drops to 3 (latent, one small fix), confidence 5.

**Do after.** [MODEL-2](#model-2)

<a id="chrome-3"></a>

##### CHROME-3. Carry typed ids in sidebar menu items instead of bare UUIDs

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/SidebarView.swift#contextMenu`, `app/SidebarView.swift#contextNewTab`, `app/SidebarView.swift#contextRenameTab`, `app/SidebarView.swift#contextRenameGroup`

**Problem.** AGENTS.md says entity ids are phantom-typed so the compiler rejects passing one where another is expected, but the sidebar's context menus launder them through `NSMenuItem.representedObject` as raw UUID and re-wrap them in the handler. TabId and GroupId are both UUID-backed, so wiring a group menu item to a tab action (or the reverse) compiles, passes AppKit validation, and acts on the wrong entity -- or on nothing -- with no diagnostic. The pairing of an item's action with its payload is enforced only by reading the two lines side by side.

**Evidence.** `contextMenu(forGroupId:)` sets `newTabItem.representedObject = groupId.rawValue`, `renameItem.representedObject = groupId.rawValue`, `deleteItem.representedObject = groupId.rawValue`; `contextMenu(forTabId:clickedRow:)` sets `renameItem.representedObject = tabId.rawValue`. Each handler does `guard let rawId = sender.representedObject as? UUID` and re-types it: `GroupId(rawValue: rawId)` in `contextNewTab`, `contextRenameGroup`, `contextDeleteGroup`; `TabId(rawValue: rawId)` in `contextRenameTab`. The multi-tab items already do better with `TabIdsBox` and `SetTabColorsInfo`, so the file carries both patterns side by side.

**Ideal fix.** Box one payload type for the whole menu: a `final class SidebarMenuCommand` whose `Intent` enum carries the typed ids (`newTab(GroupId)`, `renameGroup(GroupId)`, `deleteGroup(GroupId)`, `renameTab(TabId)`, `setColors([TabId], TabColor?)`, `clearTitles([TabId])`, ...). Every item points at one `@objc func performSidebarCommand(_:)` that switches exhaustively on the intent and sends the matching Msg. Item construction names the intent, not an action selector plus a loose payload.

**By construction.** A menu item whose payload does not match the action it triggers stops being expressible: there is one action, and the payload is a typed enum case naming both the operation and the id type it needs. Adding a sidebar menu command becomes an exhaustive-switch obligation instead of a hand-matched pair.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the per-action selectors but box each id in a typed wrapper class (GroupIdBox, TabIdBox) so the `as?` in the handler rejects a mismatched payload at runtime. That turns a silent wrong-entity action into a no-op -- better, but still not a compile-time guarantee.

**Verification.** In tests-ui/SidebarContextMenuTests.swift, build the group menu, invoke each item's action against a recording runtime, and assert the dispatched Msg names the clicked group; do the same for the tab menu. After the fix a cross-wired item fails to compile.

**Risk.** Medium. Mechanical, but it touches every context-menu action; the existing menu tests plus per-item dispatch assertions cover it.

**Vetted.** All four launderings verified in `SidebarView.swift`: `newTabItem`/`renameItem`/`deleteItem` in the group menu and `renameItem` in the tab menu all set `representedObject = <id>.rawValue`, and `contextNewTab`, `contextRenameGroup`, `contextDeleteGroup`, `contextRenameTab` each do `as? UUID` and re-wrap with `GroupId(rawValue:)` / `TabId(rawValue:)`. The mixed pattern is real -- the multi-tab items in the same file use `TabIdsBox` and `SetTabColorsInfo`. This does violate the phantom-typed-id rule AGENTS.md states, but there is no live defect: each item's action and payload are set on adjacent lines, and a mis-wiring would have to be introduced by a future edit. Impact drops from 4 to 3. Effort stays medium -- the true ideal (one intent enum for the whole menu) should absorb `TabIdsBox` and `SetTabColorsInfo` too, which is more call sites than the finding's Files list implies.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- tests-ui/SidebarContextMenuTests.swift -- "single group keeps Delete Group disabled after menu update" -- pins that a detached menu with `autoenablesItems = false` keeps a manually disabled item disabled through `menu.update()`; the refactor must not change enablement or item titles
- tests-ui/SidebarContextMenuTests.swift -- "multiple groups keep Delete Group enabled after menu update"
- tests-ui/SidebarContextMenuTests.swift -- "a right-click on a tab marks the clicked row so AppKit outlines it" -- reaches the tab menu through the real `SidebarOutlineView.menu(for:)` and finds the item titled "Rename Tab", so it pins both the routing and the title
- lib/DanTermCore/Tests/DanTermCoreTests -- the `resolveContextTargets` tests behind `contextTargetTabIds` (the Finder/Mail multi-select rule lives in ModelOperations.swift and is untouched)

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- (none will fail to compile) -- the existing UI tests only build menus and read `title` and `isEnabled`; none reads `representedObject`, none names a handler selector, and `SetTabColorsInfo`/`TabIdsBox` are `private` to SidebarView.swift so nothing outside can reference them. Grep over tests-ui and app-tests for `representedObject`, `TabIdsBox` and `SetTabColorsInfo` returns nothing outside app/SidebarView.swift. The list of tests that need updating is genuinely empty; what is missing is coverage, not correctness.

**Write this test first.** Suite: the UI harness, tests-ui/SidebarContextMenuTests.swift (add to the existing `sidebarContextMenuTests()` body). Name: "each group menu item dispatches a message naming the clicked group". Scenario: build the two-group harness via `makeSidebarContextMenuHarness(groupCount: 2)`, assign `sidebar.runtime = AppRuntime()` (the tests-ui shim `AppRuntime` in SidebarViewTestShim.swift records every `send` into `sentMessages`), take `sidebar.contextMenu(forGroupId: model.groups[1].id)`, then for each item call `NSApp.sendAction(item.action!, to: item.target, from: item)`, and assert `runtime.sentMessages` contains `.createTab(inGroupId: model.groups[1].id)` and `.requestDeleteGroup(id: model.groups[1].id)` -- the second group's id, not the first. Write the mirror for the tab menu asserting `.beginSidebarRename(target: .tab(clickedTabId))`. Why it fails today: `makeSidebarContextMenuHarness` never sets `sidebar.runtime`, so `runtime?.send` is a no-op and there is no recorder; the test fails on an empty `sentMessages` until the harness is extended. Once the harness records, the test passes against today's tree as well -- which is the honest situation: CHROME-3 has no live defect (the Vetted note says so), so this test is the regression net that lets the refactor be verified, and the real win is that after the change a cross-wired item stops compiling. Note the rename items dispatch through `DispatchQueue.main.async`, so the two rename assertions need a main-runloop turn before reading `sentMessages`; use the harness's existing pump rather than a sleep.

**Blockers and surprises.** Three things worth knowing. First, the two rename handlers deliberately hop off the menu-tracking runloop turn with `DispatchQueue.main.async` and carry a comment explaining why (AppKit is still tearing the menu down while the reconcile installs a field editor); a single exhaustive switch must preserve that asymmetry, and losing it breaks inline rename in a way no existing test catches. Second, the tests-ui harness compiles app/SidebarView.swift against a *shim* `AppRuntime` (tests-ui/SidebarViewTestShim.swift) rather than the production one, so any new type the menu code references must compile in both worlds -- keep the intent enum free of AppRuntime and of anything in app/ that the harness does not compile. Third, `app/SidebarView.swift` is a marked region for `scripts/reconcile-pass-lint.sh` (`REGION_FILES=("$ROOT/app/SidebarView.swift")`), so read that lint's rules before restructuring the file; the menu code is outside the reconcile region but the lint parses the whole file.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The finding's ideal is right, but its Files list understates the scope, and the Vetted note already says so: a single `Intent` enum that leaves `TabIdsBox` and `SetTabColorsInfo` in place would put three payload conventions in one file instead of two, which is worse than today. The ideal must absorb all nine handlers and both existing box classes, or it is not the simplest structure. Scope it that way in the plan.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

##### CHROME-4. Build the preferences grid from declared rows so warning rows and padding stop being addressed by literal index

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `app/PreferencesPanel.swift#buildUI`

**Problem.** The settings form is one positional `NSGridView(views:)` array, and six statements then reach back into it by literal row number to attach padding and capture the three warning rows. Inserting, removing, or reordering a settings row silently retargets all six: the panel would pad the wrong row and hide the wrong warning, with no compile error and no visible failure until someone opens Settings with a bad font configured. The file already shows awareness of this hazard -- the width loop runs over `0..<grid.numberOfRows` with a comment saying every row is constrained "so reordering or removing a row cannot silently drop it" -- yet the warning rows beside it stay index-addressed.

**Evidence.** After the ten-entry `NSGridView(views:)` literal: `grid.row(at: 5).topPadding = 8`, `grid.row(at: 7).topPadding = 8`, `grid.row(at: 9).topPadding = 4`, `themeWarningRow = grid.row(at: 1)`, `fontFamilyWarningRow = grid.row(at: 3)`, `remoteThemeWarningRow = grid.row(at: 8)`. The indices are correct today (Theme=0, themeWarning=1, Font Family=2, fontFamilyWarning=3, Font Size=4, Clear Alerts=5, copyOnSelect=6, Remote Theme=7, remoteThemeWarning=8, Config file=9) -- correct only by counting.

**Ideal fix.** Describe the form as a list of row descriptors (label, control, optional warning label, optional top padding) and build the grid by appending them with `NSGridView.addRow(with:)`, which returns the NSGridRow it just added. Capture the warning row and apply the padding from that returned object as the row is created, and apply the control-column width constraint in the same pass; no index is ever written down.

**By construction.** "A settings row was reordered and the warning row or padding now points at the wrong row" stops being expressible, because no code names a row position: each row's handle comes from creating that row.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the array literal but look each special row up by identity -- find the row containing a given warning label -- instead of by number. That removes the silent-retarget failure without restructuring the builder, at the cost of a lookup helper.

**Verification.** In tests-ui/PreferencesPanelTests.swift, apply a projection with only `fontFamilyWarning` set and assert the font-family warning label is visible while both other warning labels stay hidden; then add a settings row to the form in the same commit and re-run -- the test must still pass.

**Risk.** Low. Layout-only, and the panel sizes itself from its content, so a mistake shows immediately in the UI harness.

**Vetted.** Verified line-for-line in `PreferencesPanel.buildUI`: the ten-entry `NSGridView(views:)` literal, then `grid.row(at: 5).topPadding = 8`, `grid.row(at: 7).topPadding = 8`, `grid.row(at: 9).topPadding = 4`, `themeWarningRow = grid.row(at: 1)`, `fontFamilyWarningRow = grid.row(at: 3)`, `remoteThemeWarningRow = grid.row(at: 8)`, and the index-free width loop with the comment the finding quotes. The indices match the literal's order as claimed. `NSGridView.addRow(with:)` does return the `NSGridRow`, so the ideal fix is buildable as written. Downscored: the blast radius is one 40-line function that only one person edits, and the failure is visible the first time Settings is opened, so impact 2. Effort is small, not medium -- it is a rewrite of one builder with no callers outside the file.

##### CHROME-5. Extract the theme list (filter, selection, cell vending) shared by the browser and the picker sheet

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 4 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 3 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `app/ThemeBrowserView.swift#searchChanged`, `app/RemoteThemePickerSheet.swift#searchChanged`, `app/ThemeSwatchViews.swift#themeCell`

**Problem.** Two surfaces present the same theme catalog and each keeps its own copy of the list state and the algorithms over it: the name array, the filtered array, the case-insensitive filter, the reselect-after-filter step, the table column setup, and the current-theme row lookup. Only the commit gesture genuinely differs -- the browser applies on selection change, the sheet applies on Select or double-click. The cell body was already factored into `ThemeBrowserCellView.themeCell`, so what remains duplicated is the state machine around it, which is exactly where the two have already diverged.

**Evidence.** `ThemeBrowserView.searchChanged(_:)` and `RemoteThemePickerSheet.searchChanged(_:)` are the same five lines (`trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces).lowercased()`, empty-query reset, `allNames.filter { $0.lowercased().contains(query) }`, `reloadData()`, `selectCurrentThemeRow()`). Both types declare `allNames` / `filteredNames`, both build `NSTableColumn(identifier: "ThemeName")` with `rowHeight = 24` and `intercellSpacing = .zero`, both implement `numberOfRows(in:)` over `filteredNames`, and both implement `selectCurrentThemeRow()` -- with different bodies: the sheet's also drives `selectButton.isEnabled`, the browser's short-circuits on `tableView.selectedRow != idx`. Both `viewFor` bodies call `ThemeBrowserCellView.themeCell` differing only in reuse identifier.

**Ideal fix.** One `ThemeListController` owning allNames, the filter query, the current theme name, and the table's data source and delegate; it exposes `apply(currentThemeName:)`, `filter(_:)`, and an `onActivate: (String) -> Void`. The browser embeds it with activate-on-selection, the sheet with activate-on-commit plus an observer for Select-button enablement. The filter and reselect algorithms then exist once.

**By construction.** "The two theme lists filter or reselect differently" stops being expressible: there is one filter and one selection rule, and a host can only choose what happens when a theme is activated.

**Cheaper fallback.** If embedding a controller inside the sheet's lifecycle is awkward, at minimum move the filter and the current-row lookup into free functions over `[String]` (they are pure) and have both call sites use them, leaving only the AppKit wiring duplicated.

**Verification.** tests-ui/ThemeBrowserViewTests.swift and tests-ui/RemoteThemePickerSheetTests.swift both exist; add the same scenario to each (type a query that excludes the current theme, assert selection state, clear the query, assert the current theme is reselected) and require both suites to pass unchanged after the extraction.

**Risk.** Medium. The sheet's Select-button enablement and the browser's apply-on-selection are genuinely different behaviors that must stay separate; both have UI test coverage.

**Vetted.** The duplication is exactly as quoted: `ThemeBrowserView.searchChanged` and `RemoteThemePickerSheet.searchChanged` are the same five lines, both types hold `allNames`/`filteredNames`, both implement `numberOfRows(in:)` over `filteredNames`, and both `viewFor` bodies call `ThemeBrowserCellView.themeCell` differing only in reuse identifier. But the finding presents the two `selectCurrentThemeRow` bodies as drift, and they are not. The browser applies the theme live from `tableViewSelectionDidChange` (the method carries the comment "Selection-driven preview: fires for both click and keyboard navigation"), so its `guard tableView.selectedRow != idx else { return }` is a re-entrancy guard against re-applying the theme on a programmatic reselect; the sheet has no preview and instead drives `selectButton.isEnabled`. Those bodies differ for reasons. What is actually duplicated is about fifteen lines of pure list state. One is an NSView and the other an NSViewController with different lifecycles, so a shared controller is a lot of indirection for that.

**Correction.** The two `selectCurrentThemeRow` bodies are not divergent copies of one algorithm: the browser's early return exists because selection change applies the theme live (apply-on-selection preview), and the sheet's extra line drives Select-button enablement. The genuinely duplicated code is the filter and the `allNames`/`filteredNames` pair, roughly fifteen lines.

**Sharper ideal.** The finding's stated cheaper fallback is the better first move and should be the recommendation: lift the filter and the current-row lookup into pure free functions over `[String]` and have both call sites use them. A shared `ThemeListController` owning the table's data source and delegate has to reconcile two different activation models (apply-on-selection with a preview re-entrancy guard vs. commit-on-button) inside one type, which reintroduces the branch it was meant to remove.

**Conflicts with.** [RUNTIME-2](#runtime-2)

##### CHROME-6. Give the alerts popover a typed, reusable row cell and stop computing row age at build time

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `app/AlertsPopoverView.swift#makeAlertRow`, `app/AlertsPopoverView.swift#relativeTime`, `app/AlertsPopoverView.swift#apply`

**Problem.** Every alert row is assembled from scratch on every reload -- six subviews and about twenty constraints per row, with no reuse identifier -- which is the one place in this area that ignores the typed-cell pattern the rest of the app uses (SidebarTabCellView, SidebarGroupCellView, TodoRowView, ThemeBrowserCellView). The same ad-hoc construction bakes the relative timestamp into the view at build time, so an open popover's "now" or "5m" labels are frozen until some unrelated model change re-pushes the projection; nothing in the runtime reconciles on a clock tick.

**Evidence.** `makeAlertRow(_:)` returns a bare `NSView` built from an `NSImageView`, two `NSTextField`s, a `SingleLineLabel`, a dot `NSView`, and an `NSBox`, then activates the full constraint set -- and never sets an `identifier`, so `tableView(_:viewFor:)` cannot reuse it. `apply(_:)` ends with an unconditional `tableView.reloadData()`. The time text comes from `relativeTime(alert.createdAt)`, evaluated once inside `makeAlertRow`; `AlertsPopoverProjection` carries `createdAt: Date` per row (Projections.swift) and nothing re-renders on a timer.

**Ideal fix.** Add an `AlertRowCellView` in the SidebarCellViews mould -- it owns its whole view tree once and exposes a single `apply(_ row: AlertRowProjection)` -- and vend it through `makeView(withIdentifier:)`. For the timestamp, project the display string in the core alongside the other row text (the model already owns wall clock through CoreEnv), so a row's age is a projected fact that changes when the projection changes, exactly like the unread flag.

**By construction.** With the age projected, "a row shows a time that no longer matches the model" stops being expressible -- the label is a projected string, not a value computed during view construction. The typed cell also removes the class of bug where a rebuilt row keeps a stale subview because one path forgot to set it.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the view-side `relativeTime` but drive a refresh while the popover is open (recompute the visible rows' time labels on a coarse timer owned by the controller and torn down in `viewWillDisappear`). That fixes the staleness without moving the clock read, at the cost of a timer where a projection would do.

**Verification.** In tests-ui/AlertsPopoverViewTests.swift, apply a projection twice with different row content and assert the row views are the same reused instances carrying the new text; and assert a row's time text equals the value the projection supplies rather than one derived at construction.

**Risk.** Low. The row is presentation-only; the main care is keeping click-to-activate working with reused cells, since it currently rides `tableViewSelectionDidChange` with `selectionHighlightStyle = .none`.

**Vetted.** Evidence confirmed: `makeAlertRow` builds a bare `NSView` with an `NSImageView`, two `NSTextField`s, a `SingleLineLabel`, a dot view, and an `NSBox`, sets no `identifier`, and is called fresh from `tableView(_:viewFor:)`; `apply(_:)` ends with an unconditional `tableView.reloadData()`; `relativeTime(_:)` reads `-date.timeIntervalSinceNow` at construction. But the stated ideal fix does not solve the stated problem. Moving the relative-time string into the projection changes nothing about staleness on its own, because nothing re-runs `desiredAlertsPopover` on a clock -- the reconcile sweep only runs when a Msg lands, exactly as today. Projecting the age is necessary but not sufficient; the tick is the actual missing piece, and the finding files it under the cheaper fallback.

**Correction.** Projecting the age string does not fix the staleness by itself: the reconcile sweep is Msg-driven, so a projected age is recomputed on exactly the same occasions the view-side `relativeTime` is today. The ideal is a coarse tick Msg that runs only while the popover is open (owned by the runtime, torn down with the popover) driving a re-projection, with the age string projected in the core so the view holds no clock. Cell reuse via an `AlertRowCellView` with a reuse identifier is a separate, independent cleanup and should be scored as one.

#### Area: PTY host and session boundary (`PTY`)

_Scope: Process lifecycle and the engine/app session boundary (lib/TerminalPTY, app/TerminalSession.swift, DanTermCore boundary files)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** The lifecycle reducer (PaneProcessLifecycle.swift) and the launch policy are genuinely clean: pure, exhaustively cased, and well covered by LifecycleReducerTests/LaunchPolicyTests. InFlightLaunch and ResizeCoalescer are exemplary -- each is a single ownership rule in its own file with the argument written down. The tests do not re-implement production; the spawner, exit probe, and resource-lifecycle protocols are real injected seams and the suite drives real PTY descriptors through them (scripts/terminal-pty-host-test-seam-lint.sh enforces that). The weight of my findings is in TerminalPTYHost.swift, where several facts are stored twice and two teardown paths hand-enumerate the same source set. I did not audit rendering, the flight recorder's internals, DoctorPermissionProber (self-contained and outside process lifecycle in any meaningful sense), or TerminalHostTools' two standalone executables.

##### PTY-1. Cancel every retained dispatch source from the one registry that already holds them

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#exitBoundElapsed`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#finishTeardown`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#retainUntilCancellation`

**Problem.** The host owns seven dispatch sources (read, write, process, child-exit poll, grace, session poll, exit bound) and two independent teardown paths each hand-enumerate all of them. `exitBoundElapsed` and `finishTeardown` are the same ladder written twice in a different order. A source added later must be remembered in both, and nothing makes that failure visible: a forgotten cancel leaks a live timer or descriptor source past the point the host reports irreversible quiescence, which is exactly the guarantee `whenQuiescent` exists to make.

**Evidence.** `exitBoundElapsed` runs `cancelExitBound(); cancelGrace(); cancelSessionPoll(); cancelProcessSource(); cancelChildExitPoll(); closeMaster()` (closeMaster cancels read and write). `finishTeardown` runs the identical set: `cancelExitBound(); closeMaster(); cancelGrace(); cancelSessionPoll(); cancelProcessSource(); cancelChildExitPoll()`. Meanwhile `retainUntilCancellation(_:descriptorBacked:)` already stores *every* source in `retainedSources[id]`, and `completeTeardownIfPossible` already gates completion on `retainedSources.isEmpty`, so the registry is the authority on what exists but is not the thing the cancel paths iterate.

**Ideal fix.** Make `retainUntilCancellation` the sole place a source is remembered, and store beside each entry what its cancel needs: whether it has been activated (libdispatch requires resume before cancel -- `cancelReadSource` and `cancelProcessSource` both open-code that), and a closure that clears the typed field (`readSource = nil`, etc.). Both teardown paths then become one `cancelAllRetainedSources()` that walks `retainedSources`. Adding an eighth source registers it once and is cancelled by both paths without either being edited.

**By construction.** A teardown path that cancels only some of the host's sources becomes unrepresentable: there is one enumeration of "sources this host owns", and it is the same collection that `completeTeardownIfPossible` waits on, so "registered but not cancelled" and "cancelled but still counted" cannot diverge.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is medium and mechanical; the registry and its id already exist.

**Verification.** The existing resource-census assertions already state the behavior: after `close()` and after `forceExitBoundForTesting()`, `resourceSnapshot().isReleased` must hold (activeSourceCount == 0, hasOpenMaster == false). Add a third source-bearing scenario -- a host torn down while its child-exit poll and session poll are both armed -- and assert `isReleased` on both the ordinary and the forced-quiescence path.

**Risk.** Read and process sources must still be activated before cancellation, and the master close barrier still depends on `descriptorSourceIDs`; both facts must move into the registry entry rather than being dropped.

**Vetted.** Read `TerminalPTYHost.swift#exitBoundElapsed`, `#finishTeardown`, `#retainUntilCancellation`, `#acknowledgeSourceCancellation`, `#completeTeardownIfPossible` and `#closeMaster`. The two ladders really are the same six calls in different order, and all seven sources really do register through `retainUntilCancellation` (seven call sites, matching the seven sources). But the stated failure mode is inverted: `completeTeardownIfPossible` gates `teardownFinished` on `retainedSources.isEmpty`, so a source that is registered and never cancelled cannot slip past quiescence -- it prevents quiescence from ever being reached. The failure is a hang on quit, not a leak past the guarantee.

**Correction.** The duplication is real: `exitBoundElapsed` and `finishTeardown` each hand-enumerate the same six cancel calls (`cancelExitBound`, `cancelGrace`, `cancelSessionPoll`, `cancelProcessSource`, `cancelChildExitPoll`, and `closeMaster`, which cancels the read and write sources) in different orders, while `retainUntilCancellation` already holds every source in `retainedSources`. What a forgotten cancel costs is not a leak past quiescence but the opposite: `completeTeardownIfPossible` requires `retainedSources.isEmpty`, so an unregistered-for-cancellation source wedges the host short of `teardownFinished` forever -- `whenQuiescent` never resolves and the forced path in `exitBoundElapsed` cannot rescue it either, because it enumerates the same stale list. The cost is a quit hang, which is why the enumeration should be the registry.

**Sharper ideal.** The registry walk cannot simply replace both ladders. `closeMaster` does more than cancel two sources -- it sets `descriptorOwnershipSealed`, calls `activateProcessSourceIfNeeded`, `rejectPendingInput(because: .processEnded)`, and `completeMasterCloseIfPossible`, which in the forced path re-enters `performForcedCleanupAfterMasterClose` synchronously. `cancelSessionPoll` also clears `sessionPollStage` and `sessionPollStageSignaled`. So the shape is: each registry entry carries its activation state and a clear-closure (as the finding says), `cancelAllRetainedSources()` replaces the four bare cancels and the two inside `closeMaster`, and `closeMaster` stays as a separate call for its seal/reject/barrier work. Ordering is load-bearing too: `exitBoundElapsed` deliberately calls `closeMaster` last, because that call is what drives the forced cleanup; a mechanical merge that reorders it changes when the kill-and-reap runs.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 22 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `TerminalPTYHost` is a `public actor` in `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift` (2317 lines, one file). It holds seven dispatch sources in seven separately typed optional fields -- `readSource: (any DispatchSourceRead)?`, `writeSource: (any DispatchSourceWrite)?`, `processSource: (any DispatchSourceProcess)?`, `childExitPollSource`, `graceSource`, `sessionPollSource`, `exitBoundSource` (all `(any DispatchSourceTimer)?`) -- plus two activation flags (`readSourceActivated`, `processSourceActivated`) and two extra facts owned by the session poll (`sessionPollStage: TeardownStage?`, `sessionPollStageSignaled: Bool`). Alongside them sits the registry the finding wants to become the authority: `private var retainedSources: [Int: any DispatchSourceProtocol]`, `private var descriptorSourceIDs: Set<Int>`, `private var nextSourceID: Int`, fed by `private func retainUntilCancellation<Source: DispatchSourceProtocol>(_ source: Source, descriptorBacked: Bool)` from exactly seven call sites -- one per source. Cancellation drains through `sourceCancellationHandlerRan(_ id: Int)` -> `acknowledgeSourceCancellation(_ id: Int)`, which removes the id from both collections and then calls `completeMasterCloseIfPossible()` and `completeTeardownIfPossible()`; the latter gates `teardownFinished` on `retainedSources.isEmpty`. Everything the finding quotes is present verbatim and nothing has moved: the last two commits touching the file are `82b6a79d` and `72e587b2`, neither in the teardown region.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#retainUntilCancellation` -- Becomes the single place a source is remembered. Its stored value grows from a bare `any DispatchSourceProtocol` into an entry that also carries whether the source has been activated and a closure that clears the typed field. Callers that today follow the call with `readSource = read` / `readSourceActivated = false` hand that assignment in instead.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#retainedSources` -- Element type changes from `any DispatchSourceProtocol` to a private `RetainedSource` struct (source, activated flag, clear closure). `completeTeardownIfPossible`'s `retainedSources.isEmpty` and `resourceSnapshot`'s `retainedSources.count` keep working unchanged.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#exitBoundElapsed` -- The four bare cancels (`cancelGrace`, `cancelSessionPoll`, `cancelProcessSource`, `cancelChildExitPoll`) collapse into one `cancelAllRetainedSources()`. `cancelExitBound()` folds into the same walk. `closeMaster()` must stay a separate call and must stay LAST -- it is what drives `performForcedCleanupAfterMasterClose` re-entrantly through `completeMasterCloseIfPossible`.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#finishTeardown` -- Same collapse, but note the order here is `cancelExitBound(); closeMaster(); cancelGrace(); ...` -- `closeMaster()` is second, not last, because this path is not the forced one. Landing on `cancelAllRetainedSources()` plus `closeMaster()` changes the relative order of the read/write cancels and the timer cancels; verify that is inert (it is, since each cancel only requests, and the barrier is `descriptorSourceIDs`).
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#closeMaster` -- Stops open-coding `cancelReadSource(); cancelWriteSource()` if the registry walk covers them, but must keep `descriptorOwnershipSealed = true`, `masterCloseRequested = true`, `activateProcessSourceIfNeeded()`, `rejectPendingInput(because: .processEnded)`, and `completeMasterCloseIfPossible()`. Careful: `closeMaster` is also called from `activateIO` and from `finishTeardown`, where it must NOT cancel the timer sources -- so it likely keeps cancelling only the descriptor-backed entries (`descriptorSourceIDs`), not the whole registry.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelReadSource` -- Deletes. Its activate-before-cancel dance moves into the registry entry's activated flag.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelProcessSource` -- Deletes, same reason.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelWriteSource` -- Called from `flushInput` (twice) and `closeMaster`, not only from teardown, so it survives as a targeted single-source cancel that goes through the registry by id rather than through `writeSource?.cancel()`.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelGrace` -- Called from `scheduleGrace` as well as from teardown, so it survives as a targeted cancel. Its body becomes a registry lookup.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelSessionPoll` -- Survives, because it does more than cancel: it also clears `sessionPollStage` and `sessionPollStageSignaled`. Either that clearing rides in the entry's clear-closure or this stays a wrapper the walk calls.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelChildExitPoll` -- Deletes or becomes a registry lookup; it is called only from the two teardown ladders.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#cancelExitBound` -- Called from `armExitBound` (to replace a prior timer) as well as from both teardown paths, so it survives as a targeted cancel.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#activateReadSourceIfNeeded` -- Writes the activation flag into the registry entry instead of `readSourceActivated`.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#activateProcessSourceIfNeeded` -- Same. Note it is called from `closeMaster` as well as `activateIO`, and that call is load-bearing for the close-during-spawn case.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#installSources` -- Registers read (descriptorBacked: true) and process (descriptorBacked: false) with their clear closures and initial activated=false, instead of assigning the two typed fields and two flags.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#installWriteSourceIfNeeded` -- Registers write as descriptorBacked and already-activated (it calls `source.activate()` immediately, unlike read and process).
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#installChildExitPollIfNeeded` -- Registers the timer as activated; its `guard childExitPollSource == nil` idempotence check needs a registry-backed equivalent.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#installSessionPollSourceIfNeeded` -- Same idempotence concern (`guard sessionPollSource == nil`).
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#scheduleGrace` -- Cancels the previous grace timer and registers a new one each time, so the registry gains a fresh id per escalation stage; the old entry must be gone before the new one lands or `retainedSources` grows.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#armExitBound` -- Same replace-on-arm pattern as `scheduleGrace`.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#acknowledgeSourceCancellation` -- Runs the entry's clear closure when it removes the entry, so the typed field is nilled by the same act that drops the registration -- this is where 'registered but not cleared' stops being expressible.
- `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#resourceSnapshot` -- No source change needed (`retainedSources.count`, `descriptorSourceIDs.count`), but re-read it after the refactor: it is the only window the tests have into this machinery.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "shutdown completion waits for every source cancellation acknowledgement" (shutdownCompletionJoinsDispatchSources) -- that quiescence waits for every cancellation handler, observed through `activeSourceCount > 0` while held and `isReleased` after release
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "forced cleanup starts only after descriptor cancellation joins" (forcedShutdownWaitsForDescriptorJoin) -- the forced path's ordering; this is the test that pins `closeMaster` running last in `exitBoundElapsed`
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "close during spawn activates inactive sources before cancellation" (closeDuringSpawnJoinsInactiveSources) -- the activate-before-cancel rule the registry must carry; asserts `descriptorSourceCount == 1` mid-teardown
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "a stalled teardown ladder still quiesces inside the host's own bound" (applicationExitTerminationForcesQuiescenceWithinBound) -- forced quiescence with grace and session poll armed
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "forced cleanup does not resume a result-bearing reducer" -- second `forceExitBoundForTesting()` caller
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "joined descriptor sources cannot touch a reused fd number" (teardownDoesNotTouchReusedDescriptor) -- proves no late callback fires on a recycled fd
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "teardown reaches every job in the owned session without touching a sibling" -- the ordinary ladder end to end
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "rapid create-close and resize-close races release descriptors and owners" -- many hosts, `isReleased` on each
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "application termination remains bounded with stalled input and chatty output" -- three concurrent teardowns under load
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "dispatch-submitted termination releases every pane and signals from its own queue"
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "close racing a prompt spawn converges inside the real host bound"
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift -- "a host on a childless channel lives and quiesces with nothing to reap" -- the no-process-source shape (`installSources` returns early)
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPaneSessionTests/TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests.swift -- "application termination drains the retained registry while main is blocked" -- names the registry directly
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPaneSessionTests/TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests.swift -- "ordinary teardown and app exit release identical registry ownership" -- asserts the two paths agree, which is exactly the invariant this refactor makes structural
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPaneSessionTests/TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests.swift -- "teardown suppresses exit callbacks and releases controller and host"
- lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYExternalTests.swift -- "ssh disconnect tears down its local and remote terminal jobs" and "tmux client loss terminates its isolated server and session"

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- none -- every assertion goes through `resourceSnapshot()`, which keeps its shape. No test names `readSource`, `graceSource`, `retainedSources`, or any cancel helper directly; the private fields are unreachable from the suites.

**Write this test first.** There is no failing test to write. This is a pure refactor: `completeTeardownIfPossible` already gates on `retainedSources.isEmpty`, so today's tree cannot exhibit the failure the registry prevents -- the audit's own Correction says so, and the cost is a future quit hang if someone adds an eighth source and forgets a cancel. Writing a test that a source is registered would assert private structure, which AGENTS.md forbids. The characterization tests are the pair that already state the whole contract from the outside: `lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPaneSessionTests/TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests.swift` -- "ordinary teardown and app exit release identical registry ownership" (asserts both `liveHost` and `closingHost` reach `isReleased`, which is precisely 'the two ladders agree'), and `lib/TerminalPTY/Tests/TerminalPTYHostTests/TerminalPTYHostTests.swift` -- "close during spawn activates inactive sources before cancellation" (the activate-before-cancel rule the registry entry must carry). Run both before touching anything, and treat any change in them as the refactor having changed behavior. The audit's suggested extra scenario -- a host torn down with childExitPoll and sessionPoll both armed, asserting `isReleased` on the ordinary and the forced path -- passes today, so it is a coverage addition, not a first failing test; "a stalled teardown ladder still quiesces inside the host's own bound" already covers the forced half.

**Blockers and surprises.** Four things make this harder than the finding admits. (1) `closeMaster` is not just two cancels: it also sets `descriptorOwnershipSealed`, sets `masterCloseRequested`, calls `activateProcessSourceIfNeeded()`, `rejectPendingInput(because: .processEnded)`, and `completeMasterCloseIfPossible()`, and the last of those re-enters `performForcedCleanupAfterMasterClose()` synchronously on the forced path. It cannot be folded into a registry walk. (2) The two ladders order `closeMaster` differently on purpose -- last in `exitBoundElapsed` (it drives the forced kill-and-reap), second in `finishTeardown` -- so a mechanical merge that unifies the order changes when the kill runs; `forcedShutdownWaitsForDescriptorJoin` is the test that will catch it. (3) The three registry-adjacent facts are not uniform: read and process are installed suspended and activated later, write is installed already activated, and `cancelSessionPoll` clears two extra fields (`sessionPollStage`, `sessionPollStageSignaled`) that are not source state at all. (4) `scripts/terminal-pty-host-test-seam-lint.sh` hard-codes the path `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift` and fails if the file is gone, and it bans a fixed list of test-control seam names from the host -- so splitting the registry out into a new file in the same target is fine, but renaming or removing TerminalPTYHost.swift is not, and no new debug hook may be added there. Easier than admitted: nothing outside the actor reads any of these fields; `resourceSnapshot()` is the only window, it is `internal` (`func`, not `public`), and it keeps its exact shape.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The finding's ideal is right, with the audit's own Sharper ideal correction folded in: `cancelAllRetainedSources()` replaces the four bare timer/process cancels, not `closeMaster`, which stays a separate call for its seal/reject/barrier work and keeps its position in each ladder. One addition worth making explicit in the plan: the entry's clear-closure should be run from `acknowledgeSourceCancellation`, not from the cancel call, because that is the moment the source actually leaves the host -- doing it at cancel time would nil the typed field while `retainedSources` still holds the entry, which re-opens the exact divergence the change exists to close.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

<a id="pty-2"></a>

##### PTY-2. Give TerminalPTYHost its geometry from the launch input instead of storing a second copy

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#start`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#init`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPaneSession/TerminalPaneLaunch.swift#TerminalPaneLaunchConfiguration`

**Problem.** The pane's initial grid is stored twice -- once as `TerminalPTYHost.initialDimensions` (used to build the Terminal) and once inside `LaunchPolicyInput.initialDimensions` (used to size the PTY at spawn). Because they can disagree, `start` has to reconcile them, and the way it does so is to silently rewrite the caller's value to a sentinel 0x0 so the pure reducer will reject it. A caller who passes a valid but different grid gets `.launchFailed(.invalidDimensions)` -- a diagnosis that is simply false about the input it was handed.

**Evidence.** `start(_:)` reads: `guard input.initialDimensions == initialDimensions else { var invalidInput = input; invalidInput.initialDimensions = .init(columns: 0, rows: 0); process(.start(invalidInput)); return }`. `resolveLaunchPlan` then fails on `input.initialDimensions.isValid`. `TerminalPaneLaunchConfiguration` already solved the same problem the right way one layer up -- its `initialDimensions` is a computed property over `launchInput`, with the comment "a second copy could only ever be a launch failure waiting to happen" -- so the host is the last place holding the duplicate.

**Ideal fix.** Move the launch input into `TerminalPTYHost.init`, which needs a grid at construction anyway to build the `Terminal`, and drop the parameter from `start()` (it becomes `start()` with no argument, or the host stores the input and `submitStart()` kicks it). The stored `initialDimensions` then *is* `launchInput.initialDimensions`; the mismatch guard and the 0x0 poisoning both delete.

**By construction.** "A host whose terminal grid and whose child's PTY grid disagree" stops being expressible, and with it the whole class of launch failures that report the wrong reason.

**Cheaper fallback.** If some caller genuinely must build a host before it knows its launch input, keep the two-step construction but make the mismatch a `preconditionFailure` rather than a fabricated `.invalidDimensions` result -- it is a programming error, not a launch failure. Say plainly that this is the trade-off: it keeps the duplicate fact alive.

**Verification.** `TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests` and `TerminalPTYHostTests` both already assert `.launchFailed(.invalidDimensions)` for a 0x0 input; those keep passing because 0x0 is still genuinely invalid. The new behavioral assertion is that a host constructed from a launch input carrying, say, 100x30 starts a child whose `TIOCGWINSZ` reports 100x30 -- readable today through the childless PTY channel fixture, which already inspects the winsize the host installs.

**Risk.** `TerminalPaneSessionController.init(host:launchInput:)` is the package/test constructor that currently lets the two be supplied separately; the tests that use it need reshaping to build the host from the input.

**Vetted.** Confirmed the quote in `TerminalPTYHost.swift#start` verbatim, the `.invalidDimensions` failure at `LaunchPolicy.swift#resolveLaunchPlan`, and the computed `initialDimensions` with its comment in `TerminalPaneLaunch.swift#TerminalPaneLaunchConfiguration`. But every production and test construction path already goes through `TerminalPaneSessionController`, whose four convenience inits all build the host from `configuration.initialDimensions` and pass `configuration.launchInput` -- so the duplicate is already collapsed one layer up and the mismatch branch is unreachable in the tree today. It is dead defensive code around a fact that has a single owner, not a live source of false diagnoses.

**Correction.** The 0x0 poisoning in `start(_:)` is real and is a bad way to state a programming error, but no caller in the tree can reach it: `TerminalPaneSessionController`'s four inits all derive the host's grid and the launch input from the same `TerminalPaneLaunchConfiguration`, whose `initialDimensions` is already a computed projection of `launchInput`. This is a dead branch that fabricates a launch diagnosis, not a live wrong-diagnosis bug. Also note the finding's verification claim is wrong: if the launch input moves into `init`, a 0x0 input can no longer produce `.launchFailed(.invalidDimensions)` at all, because `Terminal(columns: 0, rows: 0)` returns nil and `init` throws `TerminalPTYHostError.invalidDimensions` first. The existing `TerminalPTYHostTests` and `TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests` assertions on `.launchFailed(.invalidDimensions)` therefore have to be restated as construction failures, which is most of the effort in this change.

**Sharper ideal.** Moving the launch input into `init` is right, but the honest statement of what it buys is 'delete a dead branch and a fabricated failure reason', not 'stop a class of misdiagnosed launches'. The cheaper fallback the finding names (turn the mismatch into `preconditionFailure`) is a one-line change that removes the fabricated diagnosis and keeps every existing test shape; the ideal additionally removes the duplicate field, at the cost of reshaping the 0x0 tests.

<a id="pty-3"></a>

##### PTY-3. Record every applied transition on the flight tape and delete the five parallel capture buffers

`simplification` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 2 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#applyOutput`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#execute`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#applyResize`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPaneSession/TerminalPaneSession.swift#neutralEvents`

**Problem.** The host runs two recorders over the same event vocabulary. The always-on `flightTape` records `.feed`, `.write`, and `.resize`. Behind the `captureTransitions` flag, five more buffers record overlapping slices of the same stream -- `appliedTransitions`, `capturedOutput`, `capturedInputWrites`, `capturedReplyWrites`, `capturedSubmittedTransitions` -- updated at eight separate `if captureTransitions` sites scattered through the shipping input, output, resize and pointer paths. `capturedOutput` is a concatenation of `appliedTransitions`' `.feed` payloads; `capturedInputWrites` is `capturedSubmittedTransitions` filtered to `.input`. A new transition kind has to be threaded into whichever subset of the six a future reader happens to consult, and nothing forces them to agree.

**Evidence.** `TerminalPTYAppliedTransition` has cases feed/input/paste/focus/mouse/resize/scrollByRows/scrollToTopRow/scrollToBottom. `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent` -- what the flight tape already stores -- has exactly those plus `.write` and `.checkpoint`, and `TerminalPaneSessionController.neutralEvents(_:)` is a pure 1:1 translation between the two. In `applyOutput` the two recorders sit four lines apart: `flightTape.record(.feed(bytes))` at the top, then `if captureTransitions { capturedOutput.append(contentsOf: bytes); appliedTransitions.append(.feed(bytes)) }` at the bottom. `applyResize` does the same with `flightTape.record(.resize(...))` and `appliedTransitions.append(.resize(grid))`.

**Ideal fix.** Record the remaining transition kinds (`.input`, `.paste`, `.focus`, `.mouse`, `.viewport`) on `flightTape` at the same points that record them into `appliedTransitions` today, and make `captureTransitions` select an unbounded recorder configuration rather than a second set of buffers -- the `flightTapeConfiguration` knob already exists and the test suite already uses it to control retention. `TerminalPTYAppliedTransition`, the five buffers, the eight branch sites, the four test-only accessors, and `neutralEvents(_:)` all delete; the characterization recording is built from a tape capture.

**By construction.** Two logs of the same pane's transitions cannot disagree about order or content, because there is one log. A transition kind added to the vocabulary is recorded in one place or in none.

**Cheaper fallback.** If unbounded tape retention proves too costly for the characterization app build, keep one ordered `[NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent]` log behind the flag and derive `outputBytes`, `inputWrites`, `replyWrites`, and `submittedTransitions` from it as computed projections. That still collapses five stores into one; it just keeps two recorders instead of one.

**Verification.** `TerminalPTYHostTests` already asserts recording equality by building a `NeutralTerminalRecording` from `host.transitions()` and comparing whole values after replay; keep those assertions and source the events from the tape capture instead. Add one behavioral test that a key press, a paste, a pointer drag, and a resize all appear in `flightRecordingCapture()` in the order the owner applied them.

**Risk.** The two recorders observe at different points -- the tape records `.write` after the bytes cross the descriptor and split at submission boundaries, while `capturedInputWrites` records at command emission before nonblocking IO splits them. Tests that assert pre-split write shapes need restating against post-split spans, or the tape needs both events.

**Vetted.** Verified all five buffers (`capturedOutput`, `appliedTransitions`, `capturedSubmittedTransitions`, `capturedInputWrites`, `capturedReplyWrites`) at TerminalPTYHost.swift lines 364-371, and the eight `if captureTransitions` sites in `#applyOutput`, `#applyResize`, `#applyKey`, `#applyPaste`, `#applyFocus`, `#applyWheel`/pointer, `#applyViewportNavigation`, and `#execute(.writeInput)`. `neutralEvents(_:)` in TerminalPaneSession.swift is the 1:1 translation the finding describes. Two corrections to scope rather than to substance: `captureTransitions` is false in production except when a recording directory is set (`app/SwiftTerminalBackend.swift`), so this is test-and-recording support, not shipping cost -- impact 4 was too high. And the surface is much larger than the finding implies: roughly forty assertion sites across `TerminalPTYHostTests` and `TerminalPaneSessionControllerTests` read `inputWrites()`, `replyWrites()`, `submittedTransitions()`, `outputBytes()`, and `transitions()`.

**Correction.** Keep the finding as written, with two scope corrections. First, `captureTransitions` is off in production (`app/SwiftTerminalBackend.swift` enables it only when a recording directory is configured), so the six-recorder duplication is a test-support and characterization-recording cost, not a shipping one. Second, the Risk section understates one loss: `inputWrites()` is documented as 'the reducer-emitted writes before nonblocking partial IO splits them', and the flight tape records `.write` only after the bytes cross the descriptor, split at submission boundaries. There is no projection of the tape that recovers the pre-split shape, so either the tape gains a submission-time event or roughly a dozen assertions change meaning.

**Do after.** [XPORT-1](#xport-1)
