##### PTY-4. Read the PTY through one loop instead of one per drain reason

`simplification` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#readReady`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#drainCommittedOutput`

**Problem.** The host reads the master descriptor with two hand-written loops that differ only in what bounds them. Each allocates its own 16 KiB buffer, each open-codes the EINTR retry, each decides independently what counts as end of output. The EOF rules already differ -- `readReady` treats `result == 0` and `errno == EIO` as the end-of-output edge, while `drainCommittedOutput` treats any non-EINTR error including EIO as a plain `break` -- and a future fix to one loop's error handling has no reason to reach the other.

**Evidence.** `readReady` loops `while bytesReadThisTurn < turnLimit` over `Darwin.read(masterFD, ...)`, handling `result > 0`, `result == 0 || errno == EIO`, and `errno == EINTR`. `drainCommittedOutput` loops `while remaining > 0` over the same call with the same `buffer.withUnsafeMutableBytes` shape, handling `result > 0`, `errno == EINTR`, and `else { break }`. Both feed the reducer with `process(.output(Array(buffer.prefix(result))))`.

**Ideal fix.** One private `readChunks(upTo:)` that owns the buffer, the EINTR retry, and the EOF classification, and returns why it stopped (`.limitReached`, `.wouldBlock`, `.endOfOutput`). `readReady` calls it with the turn limit and cancels the read source on `.endOfOutput`; `drainCommittedOutput` calls it with the FIONREAD count and reports `.outputEOF` unconditionally, as it does today.

**By construction.** "Two read paths that disagree about what EIO means" stops being expressible: there is one classification of a read result and both callers consume it.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** The existing childless-channel tests cover both edges behaviorally: closing the child end must produce `.rejected(.writeFailed(EIO))` for a queued submission and drive the descriptor source count to zero, and a child that exits with output still in the buffer must have that output present in the final snapshot (`__FRAGMENTED_DONE__` case). Both must keep passing unchanged.

**Risk.** Low. The one behavioral decision to make explicit is whether `drainCommittedOutput` should adopt `readReady`'s EIO-is-EOF rule; it reports `.outputEOF` on that path anyway, so the observable result is the same.

**Vetted.** Read `#readReady` and `#drainCommittedOutput` in full. Both quotes are exact. The EOF divergence is real: `readReady` treats `result == 0 || (result < 0 && errno == EIO)` as the end-of-output edge and cancels the read source, while `drainCommittedOutput` falls into a bare `else { break }` for any non-EINTR error including EIO. Both allocate their own zero-filled 16 KiB `[UInt8]` and both call `process(.output(Array(buffer.prefix(result))))`. The behavioural equivalence argument holds -- `drainCommittedOutput` reports `.outputEOF` unconditionally on exit -- so unifying them is observably neutral.

**Do after.** [XPORT-1](#xport-1)

<a id="pty-5"></a>

##### PTY-5. Dedupe grid submissions on the applied fact, not on an optimistic mirror in the controller

`correctness` &middot; impact 2, confidence 4 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPaneSession/TerminalPaneSession.swift#setGridDimensions`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#applyResize`

**Problem.** `TerminalPaneSessionController.lastSubmittedGrid` is a main-actor mirror of "the grid the engine is running at", but it is advanced at submission time while the authority -- `applyResize` on the owner queue -- is free to decline. When it declines, the mirror is permanently wrong and the dedupe guard then swallows every later attempt to submit that same grid, so the pane can never recover the geometry it believes it already has.

**Evidence.** `setGridDimensions` does `guard isTornDown == false, submission != lastSubmittedGrid else { return }` then `lastSubmittedGrid = submission; host.resize(submission)`. `applyResize` opens with `guard descriptorOwnershipSealed == false, masterFD >= 0 else { return }` and then `guard ioctl(masterFD, TIOCSWINSZ, &size) == 0 else { return }` -- three ways to return before `terminal.resize` and before `flightTape.record(.resize(...))`. Nothing reports the refusal back, so the controller keeps `lastSubmittedGrid` at a grid the terminal never adopted.

**Ideal fix.** Delete `lastSubmittedGrid`. The host already knows the applied geometry fact whole -- it is what `flightTape.record(.resize(columns:rows:pinned:))` states -- so make `applyResize` the deduping authority: it compares the submission against the last *applied* grid-and-pinnedness and does nothing when they match. Submission-rate control is not what this guard buys anyway; `ResizeCoalescer` already collapses a drag into as many reflows as the owner can afford.

**By construction.** "The pane believes it submitted a grid the engine never applied" becomes unrepresentable, because the only record of what has been submitted is the record of what was applied.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the controller-side guard but set `lastSubmittedGrid` only from a value the host reports back as applied (it can ride the update signal alongside `primaryHistoryGeneration`). This is a trade-off: it keeps a mirror alive and only shortens the window in which it is wrong.

**Verification.** Behavioral test through the existing childless PTY channel: submit a grid while the child end is closed (so `applyResize` returns early), then reopen and submit the same grid again, and assert the terminal's reported columns/rows change. Today the second submission is swallowed and the assertion fails.

**Risk.** Moving the dedupe onto the owner queue means every submission crosses the queue, which is a change in submission traffic during a drag; `ResizeCoalescer` already bounds the work that traffic causes, but the change should be measured against the drag workload before it lands.

**Vetted.** Confirmed both quotes: `#setGridDimensions` guards on `submission != lastSubmittedGrid` and advances the mirror before `host.resize`, and `#applyResize` has the three early returns. But I then read `PaneProcessLifecycle.swift#handleSpawning`, which already covers the reachable window: a `.resize` arriving while spawning is stored as `context.pendingGrid` and replayed as a `.resize` command on `.spawnSucceeded`, so a grid submitted before `masterFD` is set is not lost. The remaining early returns are `descriptorOwnershipSealed` (set one-way in `closeMaster`, i.e. teardown has begun, which the controller's own `isTornDown` guard also covers) and a failed `TIOCSWINSZ` on a live master, which means the pty is already gone. The finding's verification scenario -- close the child end, submit, reopen, submit the same grid -- is not constructible: closing the slave does not seal descriptor ownership or make `ioctl(TIOCSWINSZ)` on the master fail, and sealing is never undone.

**Correction.** The mirror is real but the correctness claim does not survive. The one window where the authority could decline a grid the controller had already recorded -- a resize submitted before the spawn returns and `masterFD` is set -- is closed by construction in the reducer: `PaneProcessLifecycle.swift#handleSpawning` parks a `.resize` as `pendingGrid` and re-emits it on `.spawnSucceeded`. The other two returns in `applyResize` (`descriptorOwnershipSealed`, failed `TIOCSWINSZ`) only fire once the pty is being torn down or is already gone, when a stale mirror costs nothing and `isTornDown` guards the controller anyway. Reclassify from `correctness` to `structural`: what is left is a second copy of 'the grid the engine is running at' living on the main actor, kept correct only because a third place (the reducer's `pendingGrid`) covers the gap. That is worth collapsing onto the applied fact, but it is a tidiness argument, not a recoverable-geometry bug, and no test can be written today that fails on the current code.

<a id="pty-6"></a>

##### PTY-6. Give viewport navigation its own three-case type instead of a nine-case enum guarded by preconditionFailure

`api-shape` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 6 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#applyViewportNavigation`, `lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/TerminalPTYHost/TerminalPTYHost.swift#TerminalPTYAppliedTransition`

**Problem.** `applyViewportNavigation` takes the full nine-case `TerminalPTYAppliedTransition` but accepts only three of them, and enforces that at runtime with a `preconditionFailure` -- a crash in a shipping pane, reachable from any future call site that passes the wrong case. The parameter type is documenting a contract the compiler could enforce instead.

**Evidence.** The function's switch ends with `case .feed, .input, .paste, .focus, .mouse, .resize: preconditionFailure("applyViewportNavigation takes only .scrollByRows, .scrollToTopRow, .scrollToBottom")`. It is called with a literal case at five sites (`send`, `applyKey`, `applyPaste`, `scroll(byRows:)`, `scroll(toTopRow:)`, `scrollToBottom`, `applyWheel`, and the test interaction switch), so the wide type buys nothing at any of them.

**Ideal fix.** Declare a three-case `ViewportNavigation { case byRows(Int); case toTopRow(Int); case toBottom }`, take that as the parameter, and map it to a `TerminalPTYAppliedTransition` only where the transition is appended for capture. The `preconditionFailure` and its six dead cases delete.

**By construction.** Passing a non-navigation transition to the navigation path stops compiling, so the crash it currently guards against cannot be written.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** Existing behavior must not move: `TerminalPTYHostTests` already asserts that a scroll that changes the projection appears in `transitions()` as `.scrollByRows(-1)` and that a key press snaps the viewport to the bottom before writing. Both keep passing unchanged.

**Risk.** None beyond mechanical churn; `NeutralTerminalViewportNavigation` in TerminalCoreRecording already has this exact shape, so the mapping in `neutralEvents(_:)` gets shorter rather than longer.

**Vetted.** Read `#applyViewportNavigation` -- the `preconditionFailure` and its six dead cases are exactly as quoted, and the parameter is the full nine-case `TerminalPTYAppliedTransition`. All call sites pass a literal case (`scroll(byRows:)`, `scroll(toTopRow:)`, `scrollToBottom`, the pre-write snap in `submitInput`/`sendKey`, `applyWheel`, and the test interaction switch at line 1239), so the crash is unreachable today; 'reachable from any future call site' is aspirational, which is why impact 2 is the right number. The fix is mechanical and `NeutralTerminalViewportNavigation` really does already have the three-case shape.

**Conflicts with.** [PTY-3](#pty-3)

#### Area: iOS client (`IOS`)

_Scope: The iOS client (ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources, ios/DanTermMobileApp)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** This is the cleanest area I have audited in this repo: the pure kit really does hold every session decision, the shell really does hold only effects, and the recent keyboard work is finished properly -- `MobileContentBox` is keyboard-absent by construction and `MobileSurfacePlacement` is the single presentation offset that the drawn layer, the scroll chrome, and hit-testing all read, so no grid, claim, or frame-store allocation can see the keyboard. The findings below are about facts that still have two owners (pinnedness, the connection identity), one gesture the reconnect policy drops, one hand-maintained integer table, and vocabulary that only tests reach. I did not audit the render-execution or TerminalCore packages the surface links against, `PaneReplica`'s event-application arithmetic beyond its pinnedness bit, or the checkpoint digest/plist envelope.

<a id="ios-1"></a>

##### IOS-1. Let the replica report pinnedness instead of re-decoding tape JSON in the session model

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#pinnedStatement`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#noteRecordPinnedness`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplica.swift#applyEvent`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionEvent.swift#MobileSessionEvent`

**Problem.** One wire fact -- whether the pane's grid is a pinned override -- is decoded twice by two unrelated decoders. `PaneReplica` decodes it properly, through `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent`, and holds it in `heldPinned`. `MobileSessionModel` decodes it again by hand, sniffing the raw JSON object of an event record for a `"type" == "resize"` string and a `"pinned"` boolean, and uses that second reading to decide whether a standing claim was released externally. The two readings agree only by coincidence of two independently written literals.

**Evidence.** `MobileSessionModel.pinnedStatement(in:)` contains `guard event.event["type"]?.asString == "resize" else { return nil }` and then `if case .bool(let pinned)? = event.event["pinned"] { return pinned }; return false`. The same record shape is decoded in `NeutralTerminalRecording.swift` under `case "resize"` as `.resize(columns:rows:pinned: try values.decodeIfPresent(Bool.self, forKey: .pinned) ?? false)`, and `PaneReplica.applyEvent` stores the result in `heldPinned`, which is what `PaneReplica.pinned` and therefore `MobileSurfaceFacts.pinned` already expose to the model. So the model reaches the same bit by two paths: through `surface.pinned` (used by `claimControl`) and through its own string-matching sniff (used by `noteRecordPinnedness`).

**Ideal fix.** Delete `pinnedStatement` and `noteRecordPinnedness`'s decoding. Make `MobileSessionEvent.recordApplied` carry the replica's post-apply state -- `case recordApplied(PaneTapeRecord, pinned: Bool?)` -- filled in by the shell from `surfaceView.pinned` right after `surfaceView.apply(record)` succeeds. The model then ends a confirmed standing claim when that reported bit is `false`. Ordering is preserved: the shell dispatches `.recordApplied` inside the same drain turn as the frame that produced it, strictly before any later frame event, which is exactly the response-versus-record ordering the current comment relies on. The model keeps one reader of pinnedness and no knowledge of the tape's JSON keys.

**By construction.** A tape record whose pinnedness the model reads differently from the replica that applied it becomes unspellable: the model has no access to the record's raw fields at all, so a rename of the `pinned` key or the `resize` type name is a compile error in one decoder rather than a silent `false` in a second one.

**Cheaper fallback.** If carrying the bit on the event is unwanted, have `PaneReplica` expose a `static func pinnedStatement(in: PaneTapeRecord) -> Bool?` built on `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent`, so there is still exactly one decoder even though two callers ask it. This keeps the duplicate call site but removes the duplicate parser.

**Verification.** A behavioral test in `MobileSessionModelTests`: drive a claim, confirm it with its success response, then feed a resize event record whose pinnedness is stated only through the recording schema (including one with the key absent) and assert that a following rotation emits no renewal resize -- and that a record stating `pinned: true` still renews. Run `swift test --package-path ios/DanTermMobileKit`.

**Risk.** The claim-release timing is subtle and already well tested; the fix must keep `.recordApplied` dispatched only when `apply` did not throw, so a rejected record still cannot end the claim.

**Vetted.** Both readers are where the finding says. `MobileSessionModel#pinnedStatement` really contains `guard event.event["type"]?.asString == "resize"` and the `.bool(let pinned)?` sniff, and `PaneReplica#applyEvent` really re-decodes the same record through `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent` and stores the bit in `heldPinned`. But the duplicate parse is only the `.event` case: `pinnedStatement`'s other two arms read `start.pinned` and `sync.pinned`, which are already typed fields of the client's record and are not duplicated anywhere. More importantly the stated ideal fix does not preserve behavior. `PaneReplica#applyStart` never writes `start.pinned` into `heldPinned`, and `PaneReplica#pinned` answers nil whenever the replica is not exact, so a `.recordApplied(record, pinned:)` filled from `surfaceView.pinned` would report a stale or absent bit exactly on the start record the model reads today. Impact drops to 3: this is a two-decoder-for-one-key hazard in one private eight-line function inside one module, not a live defect.

**Correction.** The duplicated decoder is the `.event` arm alone -- `.start` and `.sync` read typed fields of `PaneTapeStartRecord`/`PaneTapeStateSynchronization` and have no second reader. The finding should say: one wire fact (the resize event's `pinned` key) is parsed by hand in `MobileSessionModel#pinnedStatement` and properly in `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent`, so a rename of the key or the `resize` type name silently degrades the model's reading to `false` instead of failing to compile.

**Sharper ideal.** Make `PaneReplica` the single owner of the bit rather than making the event carry a post-apply snapshot: read the statement from the replica, as a `static func pinnedStatement(in: PaneTapeRecord) -> Bool?` built on the typed event (the finding's own fallback) or as a reported post-apply bit. This has no precondition in `applyStart`. An earlier version of this paragraph also required `applyStart` to store `start.pinned` in `heldPinned`; that restated MOBILE-6's wrong premise -- `start.pinned` is the bit at the record's own initial geometry, which on a resume is the recorder's birth grid and not the grid at the cursor -- and it is struck. The event-carried variant as written loses two behaviors the current code has: a `.start` record's pinnedness, and any statement made while the replica is not exact (`pinned` is nil there by design, documented on `PaneReplica#pinned`, so a claim that the tape says is released would stop being released behind a gap).

**Conflicts with.** [MOBILE-3](#mobile-3), [IOS-3](#ios-3)

<a id="ios-2"></a>

##### IOS-2. Make an authorized attempt carry its target so a Go tap can never be dropped against a stale one

`correctness` &middot; impact 3, confidence 4 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#handle`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#startAttempt`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#connect`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift#oneAttemptAtATime`

**Problem.** The episode's target and the target the in-flight attempt actually dialed are owned separately and can disagree. `MobileConnectTarget.setTarget` retargets the episode on every Go gesture, but `MobileReconnectPolicy.handle(.userRequestedConnect)` answers `.rest` whenever an attempt is already in flight, so the model starts nothing and never tears the old attempt down. A user who taps Go, waits during a slow dial, edits the host, and taps Go again gets: the new host stored and remembered, no new attempt, and -- if the first dial eventually succeeds -- a connection to the host they just replaced, while the status line still reads the old target's wording. The same seam has a second face: `startAttempt` guards `guard let target = connectTarget.established else { return [] }`, so the policy can latch `attemptInFlight = true` for an attempt that was never started and whose outcome nothing will ever report; every later signal then answers `.rest`, including `userRequestedConnect`, which is a permanently unrecoverable session.

**Evidence.** `MobileReconnectPolicy.handle` under `case .userRequestedConnect` sets `remainingDelays`/`standing` and then `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }`. `MobileSessionModel.connect(to:env:)` returns `[.storeTarget(host:port:)] + reconnect(.userRequestedConnect, env:)`, with no `.disconnect` of its own -- the teardown lives only in `startAttempt`, which `.rest` never reaches. `ReconnectPolicyTests.oneAttemptAtATime` pins this as intended, justified by "two concurrent attempts would race over the same stored resume cursor" -- but `startAttempt` already begins with `[.flushCheckpoint(...), .disconnect]` and the shell bumps `connectionGeneration`, so a gesture-started attempt replaces rather than races.

**Ideal fix.** Move the episode target into the decision: `MobileReconnectPolicy.MobileReconnectDecision.attemptNow(MobileServerTarget)`, with the policy taking the target on `.userRequestedConnect` and reusing it for automatic attempts. `userRequestedConnect` then always returns `attemptNow` -- it is the manual remedy, and the model's existing `.disconnect` fences whatever was in flight -- and `startAttempt` takes a non-optional target from the decision, so its `guard ... else { return [] }` disappears.

**By construction.** "The policy authorized an attempt but no attempt ran" and "the in-flight attempt is dialing a target the model has already replaced" both stop being expressible: an authorization is a value that carries the target it authorizes, and there is no way to hold one without starting the attempt it names.

**Cheaper fallback.** Leave the policy alone and have `MobileSessionModel.connect` compare the newly resolved target against `connectTarget.established` before calling `reconnect`, emitting an explicit teardown plus a fresh attempt when it changed. This fixes the user-visible wrong-host case but leaves `attemptInFlight` able to latch on an attempt that was never started.

**Verification.** In `MobileSessionModelTests`, drive `.connectRequested` for host A, do not answer the attempt, then `.connectRequested` for host B, and assert the effects contain `.disconnect` followed by `.connect(target B)`. Replace `ReconnectPolicyTests.oneAttemptAtATime`'s gesture expectation with `attemptNow` carrying the target. Run `swift test --package-path ios/DanTermMobileKit`.

**Risk.** The rewritten test currently encodes the opposite contract, so the change must be argued in the plan rather than slipped in; and the shell must keep fencing the old attempt's callback (it already does, via `connectionGeneration`) or a late `.connected` from the abandoned dial would resurface.

**Vetted.** The first half is real and I confirmed every quote. `MobileReconnectPolicy#handle` under `.userRequestedConnect` resets the budget and standing, then `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }`; `MobileSessionModel#connect` returns `[.storeTarget] + reconnect(.userRequestedConnect)` with no teardown of its own, and `MobileConnectTarget#setTarget` has already overwritten `established`. So a second Go tap during a slow dial stores and remembers the new host, starts nothing, and lets the old dial land. `ReconnectPolicyTests#oneAttemptAtATime` does pin the gesture at `.rest`. The second half is wrong: `startAttempt`'s `guard let target = connectTarget.established else { return [] }` is unreachable. `established` is never set back to nil, `.userRequestedConnect` reaches `attemptNow` only through `setTarget`/`reuseTarget` gestures that require a resolved target, and `automaticDecision` only fires from a `.waiting` standing that only a failed or backgrounded attempt can create. So there is no path that latches `attemptInFlight` on an attempt that never started, and no "permanently unrecoverable session". The user-visible case is also recoverable: after the stale dial connects, `attemptInFlight` clears and a third Go tap works.

**Correction.** Drop the second face. The live defect is one: a Go gesture that arrives while an attempt is in flight retargets the episode without replacing the attempt, so the phone can finish connecting to the host the user just replaced while the status line names the new one. `startAttempt`'s optional-target guard is dead code that the ideal fix happens to delete, not a second hazard.

**Sharper ideal.** The stated ideal (a `MobileReconnectDecision.attemptNow(MobileServerTarget)` that carries what it authorizes) is right and also removes the dead guard. Worth naming in the plan: the shell already fences the abandoned dial -- `MobileSessionController#disconnect` bumps `connectionGeneration` and `MobileSessionController#connect` checks it in the attempt callback -- so the "two concurrent attempts race over the resume cursor" justification in `oneAttemptAtATime` does not apply to a gesture-started attempt, which replaces rather than overlaps.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 11 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** Three types in `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/`. `public struct MobileReconnectPolicy: Equatable, Sendable` has one entry point, `public mutating func handle(_ event: MobileReconnectEvent, at now: TimeInterval) -> MobileReconnectDecision`, over `public enum MobileReconnectDecision { case attemptNow; case wait(until: TimeInterval); case rest }`. Its `.userRequestedConnect` arm clears `connectedAt`, restores `remainingDelays = schedule.delays[...]`, sets `standing = .clear`, then `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }` before `attemptInFlight = true; return .attemptNow`. `MobileSessionModel` (same directory) holds `private var connectTarget = MobileConnectTarget()` and `private var reconnectPolicy = MobileReconnectPolicy()`. `private mutating func connect(to draft: MobileTargetDraft, env:) -> [MobileSessionEffect]` calls `connectTarget.setTarget(from: draft)` -- which overwrites `established` before the policy is ever consulted -- and on `.connect(target)` returns `[.storeTarget(host:port:)] + reconnect(.userRequestedConnect, env: env)`, with no teardown of its own. `private mutating func reconnect(_:env:)` maps `.attemptNow` to `[.cancelRetryTimer] + startAttempt() + [.redraw]`, and `private mutating func startAttempt() -> [MobileSessionEffect]` opens `guard let target = connectTarget.established else { return [] }` then returns `[.flushCheckpoint(...), .disconnect] + [.connect(target)]`. `MobileConnectTarget` owns `public private(set) var established: MobileServerTarget?`, set only by `setTarget(from:)` and read by `reuseTarget()`. Every quote in the finding is exact.

**Change sites.**

- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#MobileReconnectDecision` -- `case attemptNow` becomes `case attemptNow(MobileServerTarget)`. This is a public enum in the kit; every `== .attemptNow` comparison in the suite stops compiling.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#MobileReconnectEvent` -- `case userRequestedConnect` becomes `case userRequestedConnect(MobileServerTarget)` -- the gesture is the only thing that knows the target, and it always has one (both model call sites come from a `.connect(target)` gesture result).
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#handle` -- Stores the episode target on `.userRequestedConnect` and returns `.attemptNow(target)` unconditionally -- deleting `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }`, which is the actual defect. `attemptInFlight = true` is then a set, not a guard.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#automaticDecision` -- Returns `.attemptNow(episodeTarget)`. This is where the totality question bites: the policy needs a stored target and the type must make 'authorized with nothing to dial' unspellable. See blockers.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#MobileReconnectPolicy` -- Gains a stored episode target field. It is `Equatable, Sendable`; `MobileServerTarget` is both, so no conformance work.

- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#startAttempt` -- Takes a non-optional `MobileServerTarget`; `guard let target = connectTarget.established else { return [] }` deletes. Its doc comment ('The policy only says `attemptNow` inside an episode a gesture started') has to be rewritten, because it is the justification for the guard being removed.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#connect` -- Passes the resolved target into the event: `reconnect(.userRequestedConnect(target), env: env)`.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#handle` -- The `.paneSelected` arm's `case .connect:` currently discards the target; it must bind it (`case .connect(let target)`) and pass it into `.userRequestedConnect(target)`. The other five `reconnect(...)` call sites (`.appForegrounded`, `.appBackgrounded`, `.networkPathChanged`, `.clockFired`, `.attemptConnected`, `.attemptFailed`) are unchanged.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileConnectTarget.swift#MobileConnectTarget` -- Only if the policy becomes the episode-target owner: `established` and `reuseTarget()` would then be a second copy of the same fact, and the type shrinks to a draft validator. This is the ripple to decide before starting -- see blockers.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift` -- 35 occurrences of `attemptNow` and every `.userRequestedConnect` become the associated-value forms. Mechanical, but it is most of the file's assertions.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift -- "Delays grow across an episode and the budget is finite" (boundedAutomaticPhase) -- the episode budget
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift -- "A user gesture restores the whole budget from a rested state" (gestureRestoresTheBudget)

- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/MobileSessionModelTests.swift -- "Backgrounding saves the position, drops the connection, and owes a reconnect"
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/StatusLineTests.swift -- the recovery-phase wording tests, unchanged by this

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift -- "At most one attempt runs at a time" (oneAttemptAtATime) -- its line `#expect(policy.handle(.userRequestedConnect, at: 104) == .rest)` encodes exactly the contract being reversed, and must become `== .attemptNow(target)`. Its 'Why it exists' preamble ('two concurrent attempts would race over the same stored resume cursor') has to be rewritten too: the shell fences the abandoned dial via `MobileSessionController#connect`'s `connectionGeneration` check, and `startAttempt` already emits `.disconnect` first, so a gesture-started attempt replaces rather than overlaps. The automatic-signal lines in the same test (appForegrounded / networkPathChanged / clockFired answering `.rest`) stay -- only the gesture line flips.
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ReconnectPolicyTests.swift -- every other test in the file, mechanically: 35 `attemptNow` occurrences and every `.userRequestedConnect` gain associated values.
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/ConnectTargetTests.swift -- only if `MobileConnectTarget` loses `established`/`reuseTarget()` to the policy; all three tests are written against those two members.

**Write this test first.** Suite: `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/MobileSessionModelTests.swift`. Name: "A second Go tap replaces the attempt still dialing the old host". Scenario, using the file's private `Session` harness: `var session = Session()`, drive `handle(.connectRequested(MobileTargetDraft(host: "old.tailnet", port: "7420")))` and confirm the effects contain `.connect(MobileServerTarget(host: "old.tailnet", port: 7420))`; do NOT dispatch `.attemptSucceeded` or `.connectionEnded`, so the attempt stays in flight; then drive `handle(.connectRequested(MobileTargetDraft(host: "new.tailnet", port: 7420)))`. Assertion: the second call's effects contain `.disconnect` and then `.connect(MobileServerTarget(host: "new.tailnet", port: 7420))`, in that order. It fails against today's tree because `MobileReconnectPolicy.handle`'s `.userRequestedConnect` arm hits `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }`, so `reconnect` returns `[.cancelRetryTimer, .redraw]`, `startAttempt()` is never called, and the effects contain neither `.disconnect` nor any `.connect` -- only `.storeTarget(host: "new.tailnet", port: "7420")`, which is the finding's whole point: the new host is stored and remembered while the old dial is left to land. Write this before touching `ReconnectPolicyTests.oneAttemptAtATime`, because it is the behavioral statement that justifies reversing that test's expectation.

**Blockers and surprises.** One design question the finding does not name, and it should be settled in the plan rather than discovered mid-change. If `MobileReconnectDecision.attemptNow` carries a target, the policy has to hold one, and `automaticDecision` can be reached from a `.waiting` standing without the type proving a target exists -- so a naive `episodeTarget: MobileServerTarget?` plus `guard let` just moves the dead guard from `startAttempt` into the policy and buys nothing. Two ways out: fold the target into the `Standing` cases that can authorize an attempt (`.waiting` and `.gaveUp` both follow an attempt, so both can carry it), or leave the target with the model and fix only the `.rest` return -- see the disagreement below. Second: if the policy owns the episode target, `MobileConnectTarget.established` and `reuseTarget()` become a second copy of the same fact, and `ConnectTargetTests` is written entirely against those two members. Decide whether `MobileConnectTarget` shrinks to a draft validator in this change or stays as is. Easier than admitted: the shell already fences the abandoned dial -- `MobileSessionController#disconnect` bumps `connectionGeneration` and the attempt callback in `MobileSessionController#connect` checks it before adopting a `.connected` result -- so the abandoned dial cannot resurface, and `startAttempt` already leads with `.flushCheckpoint` and `.disconnect`. Also confirmed dead, as the audit says: `startAttempt`'s optional-target guard is unreachable today (`established` is never set back to nil), so it is code the change deletes, not a second live hazard.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** Worth stating plainly in the plan: making the decision carry its target does not by itself fix the reported defect. The user-visible bug -- a Go tap dropped against a stale attempt -- is fixed by deleting `guard attemptInFlight == false else { return .rest }` from the `.userRequestedConnect` arm, and nothing else. The target-carrying decision is what makes 'authorized but nothing started' unspellable, which is the structural half, and it also deletes the dead guard in `startAttempt`. Both are worth doing, but the plan should order them: the guard deletion is the behavior change the first failing test pins, and the decision reshape is the by-construction change that follows it. Presenting the reshape as the fix would hide that the whole behavioral delta is one deleted guard.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

<a id="ios-3"></a>

##### IOS-3. Give the model one connection identity instead of four optionals a nil response id can match

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#receive`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#endConnection`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift#MobileSessionModel`

**Problem.** What the model knows about the live connection is spread over four independent optionals -- `tapeRequestId`, `serverVersion`, `standingClaim`, and `status.connection` -- kept in step only by everyone remembering to call `endConnection()`. Combinations such as "subscribed but no tape request id" or "a standing claim with no connection" are representable. One of them has a sharp edge: `receive` decides whether a response belongs to the tape subscription with `response.id == tapeRequestId`, comparing two `JSONValue?`s, so a response carrying no id at all (`JsonRpcResponse.id` is optional, and JSON-RPC uses a null id for a request the server could not parse) matches whenever `tapeRequestId` is nil and is treated as the subscription's refusal, ending the connection with the wrong cause. The file already knows this hazard -- it guards against exactly it for the claim -- but does not apply the same care to the subscription.

**Evidence.** `MobileSessionModel.receive` contains `guard response.id == tapeRequestId else { ... }` twice, on the error and the success path, with `private var tapeRequestId: JSONValue?`. Immediately above, the claim path is written defensively with the comment "`pending` is unwrapped first so a confirmed claim (pending nil) can never match a response that carries no id" and the code `if let pending = standingClaim?.pendingRequestId, pending == response.id`. `endConnection()` is the only thing that keeps the four fields consistent, resetting `status.noteStream(nil)`, `status.noteRequestOutcome(nil)`, `tapeRequestId`, `serverVersion`, and `standingClaim` by hand.

**Ideal fix.** Replace the four fields with one `private var connection: Connection` enum: `case none`, `case establishing`, `case handshaken(serverVersion: String)`, `case subscribed(tapeRequestId: JSONValue, claim: StandingClaim?)`. The tape request id is then non-optional exactly where it exists, so `response.id == tapeRequestId` becomes a comparison against a real value and a nil-id response cannot match it; `endConnection()` collapses to `connection = .none`, and a claim outliving its connection stops being expressible.

**By construction.** "A response with no id was read as the tape subscription's", "a standing claim survives its connection", and "a subscribed connection with no subscription id" all become unspellable, because each fact only exists inside the case that owns it.

**Cheaper fallback.** Unwrap before comparing -- `if let tapeRequestId, response.id == tapeRequestId` -- mirroring the claim guard. One line, closes the nil-matching hole, leaves the four-optional bookkeeping and the hand-written reset in place.

**Verification.** In `MobileSessionModelTests`, feed a `JsonRpcResponse(id: nil, error: ...)` frame on a connection whose subscription id is not nil and assert the connection does not end and only the request-outcome part of the status moves; then assert an error response carrying the real subscription id does end it. Run `swift test --package-path ios/DanTermMobileKit`.

**Risk.** The four fields are read from several branches, so the refactor touches most of `receive`, `end`, and `paneAttached`; the existing model tests are behavioral and should carry it without edits.

**Vetted.** The four optionals and the hand-written `endConnection()` reset are exactly as quoted, as is the asymmetry between the defensive claim guard (`if let pending = standingClaim?.pendingRequestId, pending == response.id`) and the bare `guard response.id == tapeRequestId`. `JsonRpcResponse#id` is indeed `JSONValue?`. But the sharp edge is not reachable. `tapeRequestId` is nil only between `endConnection()` and `.paneAttached`, and every `endConnection()` call site returns a `.disconnect` effect whose handler `MobileSessionController#disconnect` bumps `connectionGeneration` and cancels the runner, so no frame from the torn-down connection reaches `receive` afterwards. The one other window -- `.attemptSucceeded` to `.paneAttached` -- is closed inside a single `MobileSessionController#drain` turn, because `perform(.attachPane)` dispatches `.paneAttached` synchronously into the same drain loop, so no socket frame can interleave. So no nil-id response can be read as the subscription's refusal today.

**Correction.** The nil-matching hole is latent, not live: there is no reachable state in which a frame arrives while `tapeRequestId` is nil, because every reset of it is paired with a `.disconnect` that fences the runner, and the attach window is closed inside one synchronous drain. What remains is the structural claim -- four independently reset optionals kept in step only by everyone remembering to call `endConnection()`, with combinations like "a standing claim with no connection" representable -- which is worth doing on its own terms but is not a correctness fix. Impact drops from 3 to 2 and the finding should be reclassified as `structural` hygiene, not a defect.

**Sharper ideal.** The `Connection` enum is still the right shape. Note that the cheaper fallback (`if let tapeRequestId, response.id == tapeRequestId`) buys nothing today, since the state it guards against is unreachable, so it should not be presented as the pragmatic alternative.

**Conflicts with.** [IOS-1](#ios-1)

##### IOS-4. Build the accessory key row from the key enum instead of matching two hand-numbered tag tables

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#terminalAccessoryEntries`, `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#accessoryTapped`, `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#configureViews`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileInputMapper.swift#MobileAccessoryKey`

**Problem.** Which key a button sends is carried by a bare integer written twice, in two separately maintained lists that nothing checks against each other: a `TerminalAccessoryEntry` table with literal tags 0 through 9, and a `MobileAccessoryKey(tag:)` switch mapping those same literals back. The Ctrl button -- the one with behavior, since it holds the latch highlight -- is found by the third copy of the same number, `entry.tag == 1`. Adding, removing, or reordering a key means editing three places, and a mismatch compiles cleanly and silently sends the wrong key to the Mac.

**Evidence.** `terminalAccessoryEntries` is a literal array of `TerminalAccessoryEntry(title: "Esc", systemImage: nil, tag: 0)` through `tag: 9`; `private extension MobileAccessoryKey { init?(tag: Int) }` switches `case 0: self = .escape` ... `case 9: self = .slash`; `configureViews` picks the latch button with `if entry.tag == 1 { controlButton = button }`; and `accessoryTapped` recovers the key with `guard let key = MobileAccessoryKey(tag: sender.tag)`, whose `default: return nil` silently swallows an unmapped tag.

**Ideal fix.** Make the row one table of `(key: MobileAccessoryKey, title: String, systemImage: String?)`, and give each button a `UIAction` that captures its own `key` and calls `onAccessoryKey`. The tag, the `init?(tag:)` extension, and the failable recovery all disappear; `controlButton` is found by `entry.key == .control`. Make `MobileAccessoryKey` `CaseIterable` in the kit and derive the table with an exhaustive `switch` over the key for its title and image, so a new key added to the enum fails to compile until the row is told how to draw it.

**By construction.** "A button whose tag names a different key than the row intended" and "a key added to `MobileAccessoryKey` that the bar silently cannot send" both stop being expressible: the button holds the key value itself, and the presentation table is an exhaustive switch over the enum.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the two tables but store the key on the button through the table rather than through `tag`, e.g. a `[ObjectIdentifier: MobileAccessoryKey]` the bar owns. This removes the numeric coupling without making the key set exhaustive.

**Verification.** Behavioral, through the existing smoke path rather than a unit test the app package cannot host: extend `MobileSmokeInputScript` / `scripts/ios-app.sh`'s driven probe to tap each accessory key and assert the pane received the corresponding input, so a tag/key mismatch fails the run rather than a reading.

**Risk.** None beyond the usual UIKit target/action rewrite; the bar holds no session fact, so nothing else observes the change.

**Vetted.** Every quote is present in `TerminalBottomBarView.swift`: `terminalAccessoryEntries` is a literal array with tags 0 through 9, `private extension MobileAccessoryKey { init?(tag: Int) }` maps the same literals back with a silent `default: return nil`, `configureViews` picks the latch button with `if entry.tag == 1 { controlButton = button }`, and `accessoryTapped` recovers the key from `sender.tag`. `MobileAccessoryKey` in `MobileInputMapper.swift` has exactly the ten cases in the same order, and `MobileInputMapper#accessory` switches exhaustively over it. The three tables really are hand-numbered against each other with nothing checking them. Scores stand; the fix is one file and touches no session fact.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 7 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift` holds a `@MainActor final class TerminalBottomBarView: UIView` with `var onAccessoryKey: ((MobileAccessoryKey) -> Void)?` and `private weak var controlButton: UIButton?`. At file scope below it sits `private struct TerminalAccessoryEntry { let title: String; let systemImage: String?; let tag: Int }` and `private let terminalAccessoryEntries = [...]`, a literal array of ten entries tagged 0 through 9. `configureViews()` loops that array, calls `makeKeyButton(_ entry:) -> UIButton` (which sets `button.tag = entry.tag` and wires `#selector(accessoryTapped(_:))` via `addTarget`), and picks the latch button with `if entry.tag == 1 { controlButton = button }`. `@objc private func accessoryTapped(_ sender: UIButton)` recovers the key with `guard let key = MobileAccessoryKey(tag: sender.tag) else { return }`, against a `private extension MobileAccessoryKey { init?(tag: Int) }` at the foot of the same file whose `default: return nil` swallows any unmapped tag. `public enum MobileAccessoryKey: Equatable, Sendable` in `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileInputMapper.swift` has the ten cases in the same order and is switched exhaustively by `MobileInputMapper.accessory(_:) -> MobileInputAction?`. Every quote in the finding is present; the file's last touch was `82b6a79d`, in the keyboard-lift region, not here.

**Change sites.**

- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#TerminalAccessoryEntry` -- Field `tag: Int` is replaced by `key: MobileAccessoryKey`.
- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#terminalAccessoryEntries` -- Stops being a literal array of ten tagged entries and becomes a derivation over `MobileAccessoryKey.allCases` with an exhaustive `switch key` supplying title and systemImage -- so a case added to the enum fails to compile here until the row is told how to draw it.
- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#makeKeyButton` -- Drops `button.tag = entry.tag` and the `addTarget(_:action:for:)` wiring; instead builds the button with a `UIAction` that captures `entry.key` and calls `self?.onAccessoryKey?(key)`. Watch the retain cycle -- the closure must not strongly capture the view.
- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#configureViews` -- `if entry.tag == 1 { controlButton = button }` becomes `if entry.key == .control { controlButton = button }`.
- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#accessoryTapped` -- Deletes entirely, along with its `@objc` attribute and the `#selector` reference.
- `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalBottomBarView.swift#MobileAccessoryKey` -- The `private extension MobileAccessoryKey { init?(tag: Int) }` at the foot of the file deletes entirely.
- `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileInputMapper.swift#MobileAccessoryKey` -- Gains `CaseIterable`. It is a public enum in a library target, so this widens the kit's public API; there are no external consumers, but say so in the plan. The declaration doc comment ('Names every key in the step-0 phone accessory row') should say the order is the row order, since the row now derives its layout from `allCases`.

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/InputMappingTests.swift -- the `cases: [(MobileAccessoryKey, MobileInputAction, MobileInputAction)]` table test -- pins what each key sends, latched and unlatched. This is the safety net for the enum side.
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/MobileSessionModelTests.swift -- "An armed Ctrl latch chords the next input, clears, and redraws the projection" and "With the latch off every input category keeps today's intent and redraw behavior" -- pin the latch behavior the Ctrl button drives

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- none -- `ios/DanTermMobileApp` is an executable package with no test target (stated in the header of ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSmokeInputScript.swift), so no test compiles against `TerminalAccessoryEntry`, the tag table, or `init?(tag:)`. Adding `CaseIterable` cannot break an existing kit test either.

**Write this test first.** There is no unit test to write against the app package -- it has no test target, which is the whole reason `MobileSmokeInputScript` exists in the kit. Two honest options, and the plan should pick one. (a) Treat the bar rewrite as a pure refactor with no new test, and name `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/InputMappingTests.swift`'s accessory table test as the characterization test -- it pins what every key must send, so a tag/key mismatch introduced by the rewrite would still send the wrong bytes, and only the smoke run would catch it. (b) Take the finding's Verification seriously and write a failing kit test first, in `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/SmokeInputScriptTests.swift`, named something like "The smoke probe presses every accessory key": assert that `MobileSmokeInputScript.steps(for: "echo hi")` contains one `.accessoryKey(key)` step for each `MobileAccessoryKey.allCases`. It fails to compile today for two reasons -- `MobileSmokeInputStep` has only `insertText`/`deleteBackward`/`paste`, and `MobileAccessoryKey` is not `CaseIterable` -- and a compile failure for exactly the missing vocabulary is a legitimate red. Option (b) is the one that makes a tag/key mismatch fail a run rather than a reading, and it forces the `CaseIterable` half of the ideal.

**Blockers and surprises.** One surprise, and it bounds option (b) above. The smoke probe is delivered by `ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/MobileSessionController.swift#perform` with `case .driveSmokeInput(let steps): inputView.drive(steps)` -- it goes through `TerminalInputView`, the keyboard responder, not through the bottom bar. Driving an accessory key from the probe therefore needs the controller to route that step to the bar (or the root view controller to hold both), which is real work beyond the one-file rewrite the finding scopes. Decide that before starting. Otherwise: `scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh` cross-compiles every target of every iOS-pinned package including test targets, so both packages get rebuilt for the device triple -- nothing in this change is host-bound, so it is a gate step to run, not a constraint. The bar's header comment ('What does not belong here: any session fact') stays true -- the key enum is input vocabulary, not a session fact -- and `setControlLatched(_:)` continues to render the latch from the projection, so no state moves into the view.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** No disagreement. The finding's ideal is correct as written, and adding `CaseIterable` plus an exhaustive presentation switch is what makes 'a key the bar silently cannot send' unrepresentable. The cheaper fallback it names (an `[ObjectIdentifier: MobileAccessoryKey]` side table) is strictly worse than a `UIAction` capturing its own key and should not be carried into the plan.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

##### IOS-5. Delete the session vocabulary only tests can reach

`simplification` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 6 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileConnectionState.swift#MobileConnectionState`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileReconnectPolicy.swift#MobileReconnectEvent`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileResumePolicy.swift#resumeCheckpoint`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileDeadlineTimer.swift#isPending`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplicaCheckpoint.swift#PaneReplicaCheckpointStore`

**Problem.** Five public entry points are produced or called by nothing but their own tests, and two of them carry doc comments describing callers that no longer exist. Because they are tested, they read as live contracts: a future reader extending the reconnect or resume story will reason about states the app can never enter, and the `MobileDeadlineTimer.isPending` comment actively points at a scheduling pattern the model replaced with its own `checkpointDeadlineIsArmed` flag.

**Evidence.** `MobileConnectionState.listingPanes` appears only in `MobileStatus`'s two switches and `StatusLineTests`; nothing calls `status.noteConnection(.listingPanes, ...)`. `MobileReconnectEvent.userCancelled` is handled in `MobileReconnectPolicy.handle` and asserted in `ReconnectPolicyTests` but is never dispatched -- the model has no cancel gesture. `MobileResumePolicy.resumeCheckpoint(stored:)` is used only by `ResumePolicyTests`; production asks `trustsStoredPosition` instead and the shell does the `? load : nil` itself. `MobileDeadlineTimer.isPending` is referenced only in `DeadlineTimerTests`, while its comment says "Callers that schedule one flush per dirty period use it to leave a pending deadline alone". `PaneReplicaCheckpointStore.remove()` has no caller at all.

**Ideal fix.** Delete all five, with the assertions that only exercised them, and let the compiler prove nothing else wanted them. If a cancel gesture or a pane-listing status is wanted, add it with the code that produces it.

**By construction.** n/a

**Cheaper fallback.** None -- the ideal fix is small.

**Verification.** `swift test --package-path ios/DanTermMobileKit` and `./scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh` after the deletions; the remaining suites must pass untouched, which is what shows nothing behavioral was carried by these symbols.

**Risk.** `userCancelled` may be a placeholder for a planned disconnect gesture; if so it should be raised with the user rather than deleted quietly, since the surrounding policy comments treat cancel as part of the design.

**Vetted.** I grepped the whole of ios/ (sources and tests) for each of the five. `MobileConnectionState.listingPanes` appears only in `MobileStatus`'s two switches and `StatusLineTests`. `MobileReconnectEvent.userCancelled` appears only in `MobileReconnectPolicy#handle` and one line of `ReconnectPolicyTests`. `MobileResumePolicy#resumeCheckpoint` appears only in `ResumePolicyTests` (seven assertions), and production really does ask `trustsStoredPosition` while `MobileSessionController#perform(.attachPane)` does the `? load : nil` itself. `MobileDeadlineTimer#isPending` appears only in `DeadlineTimerTests`, and its doc comment does describe a scheduling pattern the model replaced with `checkpointDeadlineIsArmed`. `PaneReplicaCheckpointStore#remove()` has no caller anywhere. All five confirmed dead.

**Sharper ideal.** Split the deletion. Four are unambiguous. `userCancelled` is not just an unused case: `handle` gives it a full branch that sets `Standing.manual`, and the policy's prose treats cancel as part of the design, so deleting it removes a designed behavior rather than dead vocabulary. Raise that one with the user and delete the other four now. Deleting `resumeCheckpoint` also means rewriting `ResumePolicyTests` onto `trustsStoredPosition` rather than just dropping assertions -- those seven expectations are the only coverage of the trust rules.

#### Area: Build, gate, CI, docs (`BUILD`)

_Scope: Build, gate, CI, and the documentation contract_

**The auditor's read on the area.** This area is unusually well engineered: the bundle layout is generated from a Swift declaration rather than restated in YAML, the ADR index is machine-checked against the notes it lists, and two of the biggest hand-copied inventories (Swift test-estate coverage, manifest ownership) already have dedicated lints with their own self-tests. The remaining weaknesses are all the same shape -- an inventory that lives in prose or in a step string with no generator or executable check behind it. I did not audit Swift sources, the benchmark harness internals, or docs/research/.

##### BUILD-1. Declare each source target's purity profile once, and make the gate enumerate targets

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 6 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `scripts/run-test-suite.sh#STEPS`, `scripts/core-purity-lint.sh`, `scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py`

**Problem.** Which purity policy applies to which module is written nowhere except eleven hand-typed lines of the gate's step array. A target nobody remembers to add a line for is silently unlinted forever, and no check says so -- exactly the gap scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py was written to close for test estates, left open for purity. The hand-maintained nature already shows: three of the eleven lines are strict subsets of another line and do nothing.

**Evidence.** STEPS contains both `./scripts/core-purity-lint.sh --allow-imports DequeModule lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore` and `./scripts/core-purity-lint.sh lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore`. Reading scripts/core-purity-lint.sh, the first runs the import allowlist, then the Cocoa/AppKit rule, then (PROFILE defaults to `pure`) the token denylist -- a strict superset of the second, which runs only the last two. The same duplication exists for lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalRenderPlanning (`--allow-imports TerminalCore` plus a bare invocation) and lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/PaneProcessLifecycle (`--forbid-imports` plus a bare invocation). Meanwhile `ls lib/*/Sources/*/ ios/*/Sources/*/` lists 34 first-party source directories; only 8 distinct ones are named by any purity step. TerminalRenderExecution, TerminalSpriteGeometry, TerminalCoreRecording, TerminalPaneSession, and ios/DanTermMobileApp are among the unlinted ones.

**Ideal fix.** Move the policy next to what it describes: give every first-party source target a declared purity policy (a table keyed by target path, or a marker in the owning Package.swift read as text the way scripts/manifest_targets.py already reads targets), including an explicit `unrestricted` for host-bound ones. Replace the eleven step lines with one gate step that enumerates every declared target under lib/*/Sources/* and ios/*/Sources/*, applies the declared policy, and fails when a target has no declaration -- the same 'checking nothing is a failure' posture gate-test-coverage-lint.py and ios-portability-gate.sh already take.

**By construction.** A first-party source target with no purity policy becomes unrepresentable: adding a new module under lib/ or ios/ fails the gate until someone states what it may import and do. Two lint lanes over the same directory also become unrepresentable, since the enumeration visits each target once.

**Cheaper fallback.** Delete the three redundant bare invocations and add a small lint asserting every source directory appears in exactly one purity step. Removes the duplication and the silent skip, but the policy still lives in the gate rather than with the module.

**Verification.** Add a throwaway target lib/TerminalCore/Sources/ScratchTarget containing `import AppKit` and run `just test`; it must fail naming the target as having no declared purity policy. Then declare it `pure` and confirm the failure changes to the Cocoa-import violation. Separately, delete the three redundant STEPS lines and confirm the gate still fails when `import Darwin` is added to lib/TerminalPTY/Sources/PaneProcessLifecycle.

**Risk.** Enumerating targets means some currently-unlinted module gets a policy for the first time and may fail; each needs a deliberate `unrestricted` or a real cleanup. That is the point of the change, but it makes the first commit larger than the mechanism alone.

**Vetted.** Every quoted fact is in the tree. scripts/run-test-suite.sh#STEPS carries eleven core-purity-lint invocations, and reading scripts/core-purity-lint.sh confirms three of them are strict subsets of a sibling line: the bare TerminalCore, bare TerminalRenderPlanning, and bare PaneProcessLifecycle runs each re-do the Cocoa rule plus the pure token denylist that the `--allow-imports` / `--forbid-imports` line beside them already runs. `ls lib/*/Sources/*/ ios/*/Sources/*/` gives exactly 34 directories and only 8 distinct ones are named. But the finding's headline gap is narrower than 34-minus-8: lib/TerminalCore, lib/DanTermProtocol, lib/DanTermClient, ios/DanTermMobileKit and ios/DanTermMobileApp all declare `.iOS(` and scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh cross-compiles each pinned package whole (`--build-tests`, no target list), so the Cocoa/AppKit/SwiftUI half of the purity rule is already enforced structurally for TerminalRenderExecution, TerminalSpriteGeometry, TerminalCoreRecording, every TerminalCore benchmark target, and ios/DanTermMobileApp. docs/design/2026-05-28-pure-core-support-split.md also states outright that the lint is a heuristic regression guard and the structural proof is the package graph.

**Correction.** The gap is not "26 source targets are unlinted". For the iOS-pinned packages (lib/TerminalCore, lib/DanTermProtocol, lib/DanTermClient, ios/*), scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh already cross-compiles every declared target and so already rejects a Cocoa/AppKit/SwiftUI import there. What no check covers is (a) the pure profile's token denylist and import allowlist for targets that ought to be pure but are named by no step -- TerminalRenderExecution, TerminalSpriteGeometry, TerminalCoreRecording -- and (b) the host-bound packages lib/TerminalPTY and lib/TerminalHostTools, whose targets are unlinted and unpinned, so nothing states what they may do. The real defect the finding proves cleanly is that the policy is a hand-typed list with no completeness check, and its hand-maintained nature already shows in three no-op lines. Keep that as the argument; drop the 34-vs-8 framing, which credits the change with coverage the iOS gate already provides.

**Sharper ideal.** The ideal is unchanged in shape -- a declared purity policy per target, one enumerating gate step, an undeclared target is a failure -- but the declaration should be read from the owning Package.swift by scripts/manifest_targets.py, which already parses target declarations, rather than a new side table keyed by path. A side table is a second inventory of the same targets and reintroduces exactly the drift the finding is about.

**Do after.** [BUILD-5](#build-5)

##### BUILD-2. Make an orphaned gate self-test fail the gate instead of silently never running

`tooling` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 6 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `scripts/run-test-suite.sh#STEPS`, `scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py#gate_steps`, `scripts/tests/terminal_benchmark_state_test.py`

**Problem.** scripts/tests/ holds 68 self-tests, and whether one runs depends entirely on somebody having typed its path into the STEPS array. Nothing checks the two against each other. gate-test-coverage-lint.py solves precisely this for Swift packages -- the manifest is the claim, the step list is the fulfilment -- and the equivalent claim for a shell/python self-test (its existence on disk) has no such check.

**Evidence.** Diffing the `scripts/tests/` paths named inside the STEPS array against the files on disk yields two files present in the tree but absent from STEPS: danterm-cli_test.sh (deliberately opt-in via the justfile's `test-cli` recipe, which needs a GUI) and terminal_benchmark_state_test.py. The latter runs only because scripts/tests/terminal-benchmark-harness_test.sh happens to invoke `python3 "$ROOT/scripts/tests/terminal_benchmark_state_test.py"` inside its body. Neither situation is declared anywhere, so the invariant holds by coincidence rather than by check.

**Ideal fix.** Extend the lint that already parses STEPS as text (gate-test-coverage-lint.py#gate_steps) to require that every scripts/tests/*_test.{sh,py} is reachable from STEPS -- named directly, or named by a wrapper the gate runs, using the one-level-of-indirection rule the lint already implements -- or carries an explicit in-file opt-out line stating why (`# gate: opt-out -- requires a GUI, run via just test-cli`). A file that is neither reachable nor opted out fails the gate.

**By construction.** A self-test that exists but never runs becomes unrepresentable: the file's presence is itself the claim, and the gate refuses to pass until the claim is fulfilled by a step or explicitly withdrawn in the file.

**Cheaper fallback.** A plain glob-versus-STEPS diff with a hardcoded exemption list inside the lint. Cheaper, but the reason for an exemption then lives away from the test it exempts, which is the same drift in a new place.

**Verification.** Add scripts/tests/orphan_test.sh that exits 0, run `just test`, and confirm the gate fails naming the orphan. Add the opt-out marker line and confirm it passes. Add a STEPS entry instead and confirm it also passes.

**Risk.** The indirection follower must handle a test invoked from inside another test's body (the terminal_benchmark_state_test.py case) or that file becomes a false positive on day one. Over-permissive following could also mark a test 'covered' by a mention in a comment; the existing lint's token-level parsing is the guard against that.

**Vetted.** Diffing scripts/tests/*_test.{sh,py} against the names appearing in scripts/run-test-suite.sh#STEPS reproduces exactly the two orphans claimed: danterm-cli_test.sh (reachable only through the justfile's `test-cli` recipe, commented as needing GUI access and jq) and terminal_benchmark_state_test.py, which runs only because scripts/tests/terminal-benchmark-harness_test.sh line-invokes `python3 "$ROOT/scripts/tests/terminal_benchmark_state_test.py"` inside its body. scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py#gate_steps does parse STEPS as text and already implements one level of indirection (tokenize_script/lanes_in), so the extension the finding proposes fits the existing mechanism. One number is off: there are 67 `*_test.{sh,py}` files, not 68.

##### BUILD-3. Put every gate scratch tree under one root so `just clean` cannot miss one

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 6 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `justfile#clean`, `scripts/tests/just-clean_test.sh`, `scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh`, `scripts/ios-app.sh`, `.gitignore`

**Problem.** `just clean` claims to need no inventory, but it is an inventory -- four literal directory names -- and it is already incomplete. Build trees the gate creates survive `just clean`, and the test written to prevent exactly this cannot see them, because it derives its expectations from only one of the several files that choose scratch paths.

**Evidence.** justfile#clean prunes `-name .spm-build -o -name .build -o -name .build-gate -o -name .build-app-tests`, under a comment claiming 'Scratch trees are matched by name, not listed, so a gate step that picks a new --scratch-path is cleaned without a second list to keep in step.' But scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh builds into `--scratch-path "$package/.build-ios-gate"` and scripts/ios-app.sh writes `OUT="$ROOT/.build-ios-app/$TARGET"`; neither name is in the prune list. scripts/tests/just-clean_test.sh builds its SCRATCH_PATHS list by grepping `--scratch-path` out of scripts/run-test-suite.sh only, so the iOS gate's path is invisible to it. .gitignore is a third copy of the same inventory and carries `.build-ios-*/` -- so the tree is known to exist and known to be build output, and only the cleaner does not know.

**Ideal fix.** Give the gate one scratch root: every step that names a scratch path names <repo>/.build-gate/<slug> (distinct subdirectories still satisfy the 'no shared build directory' rule the STEPS header states), and `just clean` removes .build, .spm-build, and .build-gate. Three fixed names, no per-step list, and a new step's scratch tree is inside the cleaned root by construction.

**By construction.** A gate build tree that `just clean` does not remove becomes unrepresentable, because there is nowhere for a scratch tree to live except inside a directory clean already deletes.

**Cheaper fallback.** Have scripts/tests/just-clean_test.sh derive its path list from every script that names a --scratch-path or a .build-* output directory, not just run-test-suite.sh, and add the two missing names to the justfile. Restores the check but leaves three copies of the inventory in place.

**Verification.** Run `just test` on a clean checkout, then `just clean`, then assert `find . -maxdepth 3 -type d -name '.build*' -not -path './references/*'` prints nothing. Pin that as the assertion in scripts/tests/just-clean_test.sh instead of the derived path list.

**Risk.** Moving lib/TerminalCore/.build-gate and ios/DanTermMobileKit/.build-gate to a shared root invalidates those warm incremental trees once, so the first gate run after the change is cold. scripts/type-check-budget-gate.sh parses --scratch-path from its wrapped command and must keep working with the new location.

**Vetted.** justfile#clean prunes only `.spm-build`, `.build`, `.build-gate`, `.build-app-tests`. scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh builds into `--scratch-path "$package/.build-ios-gate"` for every iOS-pinned package (five of them today) and scripts/ios-app.sh sets `OUT="$ROOT/.build-ios-app/$TARGET"`; neither name is pruned. scripts/tests/just-clean_test.sh does build SCRATCH_PATHS by grepping `--scratch-path` out of scripts/run-test-suite.sh alone, so it cannot see the iOS gate's path, and .gitignore line 19 carries `.build-ios-*/` -- three inventories, one of them wrong. scripts/type-check-budget-gate.sh parses --scratch-path positionally from the wrapped command and is indifferent to the location, so the stated migration risk is small. One caveat for the rewritten assertion: just-clean_test.sh deliberately pins that `.build-not-a-tree` survives, so the proposed `find -name '.build*'` check must keep that negative case.
