##### BUILD-4. Lint the Swift file-header rule AGENTS.md states, which is already violated nine times

`tooling` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 6 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `AGENTS.md`, `app/AlertsPopoverView.swift`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/TodoInputCommand.swift`, `lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DragDropInput.swift`, `scripts/run-test-suite.sh#STEPS`

**Problem.** AGENTS.md states a mechanically checkable rule and gives a concrete reason it matters -- `///` on line 1 silently attaches to the next declaration rather than documenting the file -- but nothing enforces it. The rule has drifted, and it drifted into exactly the failure mode it warns about. This repo already runs sixteen lints for rules of this kind; the file-header rule is the one left as prose.

**Evidence.** AGENTS.md, Code Style: 'Every `.swift` file opens with a `//` block on line 1, above the imports -- not Xcode's `//  FileName.swift` banner, and not `///` (Swift has no file-level doc comment, so `///` would silently attach to the next declaration).' Scanning the 600 tracked .swift files under app/, lib/, and ios/ finds nine first lines that break it: eight begin with `///` (app/AlertsPopoverView.swift, app/TodoShortcutHelpView.swift, app/TodoRowView.swift, app/TodoToolbarButton.swift, app/TabTodoPopoverView.swift, lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/TodoInputCommand.swift, TodoPopoverState.swift, TodoShortcutCatalog.swift), and lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DragDropInput.swift opens with `import Foundation` and no header at all.

**Ideal fix.** Add scripts/swift-file-header-lint.sh with a scripts/tests/swift-file-header-lint_test.sh self-test in the house style, wire it into STEPS, and fix the nine files. The check is three conditions on line 1: it starts with `//`, it does not start with `///`, and it is not a bare `// <Filename>.swift` banner.

**By construction.** A .swift file whose leading `///` silently becomes documentation for the first declaration below it becomes unrepresentable in the tree, because the gate rejects it on the commit that introduces it.

**Cheaper fallback.** none -- the ideal fix is small. The rule is already written; only the enforcement is missing.

**Verification.** Add a scratch .swift file whose first line is `/// something` and run `just test`; the gate must fail naming the file. Change it to `// something` and confirm the gate passes. Run the lint over the tree at HEAD and confirm it reports exactly the nine files above before they are fixed.

**Risk.** Low. The only judgement call is whether the eight `///` headers should become `//` headers verbatim or be rewritten as real file headers plus a declaration doc; a mechanical `///`-to-`//` change would satisfy the lint while leaving the type without the `///` comment AGENTS.md separately requires.

**Vetted.** The AGENTS.md quote is verbatim, and scanning the 600 tracked .swift files under app/, lib/, ios/ reproduces exactly nine violations -- the same eight `///` openers plus lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DragDropInput.swift, which opens on `import Foundation`. But I opened all eight `///` files and in every one the block is followed by a blank line before `import Cocoa` / `import Foundation` / the first declaration (TodoShortcutCatalog.swift, the closest case, still has a blank line before `enum TodoShortcutScope`). A blank line detaches a Swift doc comment, so none of the nine has actually landed in the failure mode AGENTS.md warns about; they are style drift, not silent misattached documentation.

**Correction.** The rule is violated nine times and a lint is cheap and correct, but the finding's claim that "it drifted into exactly the failure mode it warns about" is not true of any of the nine files: each `///` block is separated from the next declaration by a blank line, so nothing silently became that declaration's documentation. State the value plainly -- an AGENTS.md rule that is mechanically checkable and unchecked, in a tree that already runs sixteen lints of this kind -- rather than claiming live damage. That drops the impact to housekeeping.

<a id="build-5"></a>

##### BUILD-5. Give the three manifest-discovery lists one owner so a new package root cannot be skipped

`structural` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 1 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py#MANIFEST_GLOBS`, `scripts/manifest-ownership-lint.py#MANIFEST_GLOBS`, `scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh#MANIFESTS`, `scripts/manifest_targets.py`

**Problem.** Three separate checks each carry a private copy of 'where first-party packages live'. Each guards against an empty result, so a wholesale move is caught -- but adding a package root none of the three globs matches is caught by none of them, and each check keeps reporting success over a smaller tree than it claims to police.

**Evidence.** scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py has `MANIFEST_GLOBS = ("Package.swift", "lib/*/Package.swift", "ios/*/Package.swift")`; scripts/manifest-ownership-lint.py has the identical tuple with an identical comment; scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh has `MANIFESTS=(Package.swift lib/*/Package.swift ios/*/Package.swift)`. All three fail only when the list resolves to nothing -- e.g. gate-test-coverage-lint's 'no first-party manifest found, so this check is checking nothing'. A package added at, say, tools/Foo/Package.swift would have no ownership check, no test-estate coverage check, and no iOS-pin check, while all three lints keep printing a pass.

**Ideal fix.** Declare the package roots once -- scripts/manifest_targets.py is already the shared reader for two of the three -- and have it expose both a Python API and a `--list` mode the shell gate consumes. Then add the assertion the current 'empty means failure' guard cannot make: every tracked Package.swift outside references/ must be matched by the declared roots, so a manifest in an undeclared location fails the gate rather than being ignored.

**By construction.** A first-party Package.swift that no gate check ever looks at becomes unrepresentable: every tracked manifest is either matched by the declared roots or fails the gate.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep three copies but add a single check that `git ls-files '*Package.swift'` (minus references/) equals the declared set. Drift can still happen, but it can no longer be silent.

**Verification.** Create tools/Scratch/Package.swift declaring a target and a test target, run `just test`, and confirm the gate fails saying the manifest sits outside the declared package roots. Move it to lib/Scratch/ and confirm the failure becomes the real coverage complaint (no gate lane runs its tests) instead.

**Risk.** scripts/terminal-headless-draw-compare.py writes a synthetic Package.swift into a temporary tree; the new completeness assertion must read tracked files only, or that scratch manifest becomes a spurious failure.

**Vetted.** All three copies are exactly as quoted: scripts/gate-test-coverage-lint.py and scripts/manifest-ownership-lint.py both carry `MANIFEST_GLOBS = ("Package.swift", "lib/*/Package.swift", "ios/*/Package.swift")` under an identical comment, and scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh carries `MANIFESTS=(Package.swift lib/*/Package.swift ios/*/Package.swift)`; all three fail only on an empty resolution. The stated ideal fix, however, is wrong as written: `git ls-files '*Package.swift'` returns three tracked manifests outside the declared roots today -- docs/research/35-ios-remote-client/{ios-render-spike,t4-spike,t9-checkpoint}/Package.swift -- so "every tracked Package.swift outside references/ must be matched" fails on the current tree. ios-portability-gate.sh already states the policy the assertion needs: `references/` and `docs/` hold external and throwaway trees. Second wrinkle: each of the three checks re-roots itself through a test seam (GATE_TEST_COVERAGE_LINT_ROOT, MANIFEST_OWNERSHIP_LINT_ROOT, IOS_PORTABILITY_GATE_ROOT) onto a fixture tree that is not a git checkout, so a git-backed completeness assertion cannot live inside them.

**Correction.** The completeness assertion must exclude docs/ as well as references/ -- three tracked spike manifests live under docs/research/35-ios-remote-client/ and are deliberately not first-party packages, a policy scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh already states in its MANIFESTS comment. And because all three consumers re-root onto a non-git fixture tree under their test seams, the git-backed assertion belongs in one place (scripts/manifest_targets.py's `--list`/API owner, checked as its own gate step against the real repo root), not replicated inside the three re-rootable lints. The realistic exposure is also small: no first-party package has ever been added outside lib/ or ios/, so this buys a guard against a move nobody has made rather than fixing a live hole.

**Sharper ideal.** Have scripts/manifest_targets.py own the package roots and expose both a Python API and `--list` for the shell gate, exactly as the finding says, but put the "no tracked manifest outside the declared roots" assertion in a single gate step that reads `git ls-files` at the real repo root, with docs/ and references/ excluded by the same declaration. Pushing the assertion into all three lints would either break their fixture seams or force each to special-case them.

### Cost findings

#### Area: Terminal feed hot loop (`FEED`)

_Scope: Terminal.feed hot loop: per-byte and per-cell ingestion cost (Terminal.swift print/scroll/erase, TerminalInputStream, EscapeAbsorber, UTF8Decoder, TerminalScalars, GraphemeBreak)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** This path has clearly been worked over: the ASCII-run granularity, the packed two-stage Unicode table, the word-based damage bitset, the interned style pen, the inline CSI parameter storage, and the carried-forward damage snapshot are all deliberate and documented, and I found nothing wrong with any of them. The remaining cost is concentrated in three representations that were never lifted: rows as a flat `[GridCell]`-of-`[GridRow]` reached by a two-level CoW subscript per cell, the viewport as a fixed array that must physically shift on every scroll, and tab stops as a `Set<Int>` over a dense bounded column domain. I did not audit `LogicalLineStore.admit` / scrollback retention, the frame planner, or the render path -- other auditors own those, and I stopped at `history.admit` even though the scroll path calls straight into it.

<a id="feed-1"></a>

##### FEED-1. Represent the viewport as a rotating row ring so a scroll advances a head index instead of moving every row

`data-modeling` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 2 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift`

**Problem.** `ScreenState.rows` is a flat `[GridRow]` whose physical index is its viewport row, so scrolling by one row must physically move every surviving row. `Terminal.moveInPlace` runs one `screen.rows[destination] = screen.rows[source]` per row in the region, each a `GridRow` copy that retains the source's `cells` buffer and releases the destination's; the vacated row is then a freshly allocated 179-cell array from `makeBlankRow`, and the evicted prefix is copied into a throwaway `Array` just to be iterated once. This runs once per line feed that reaches the bottom of the region. Two of the four committed `terminal-feed` corpora hit it on essentially every record: `scrollback-stream` is 25,000 `\n`-terminated lines against the full 0..<66 region (65 row moves + one 5,728-byte row allocation + one 1-element `Array` allocation each), and `incremental-screen-updates` is 100,000 repeats that each end with `ESC[23;1H...\n` inside the `ESC[2;23r` region, putting the cursor on `region.upperBound - 1` and scrolling 22 rows every iteration.

**Evidence.** `Terminal.moveInPlace`: `if delta > 0 { for destination in range.reversed() { body(destination, source(for: destination)) } } else { for destination in range { body(destination, source(for: destination)) } }`, whose body in `Terminal.moveAndFillRows` is `if let source { let moved = screen.rows[source]; screen.rows[destination] = moved } else { screen.rows[destination] = makeBlankRow(columns: columnCount, styleId: styleId) }`. `Terminal.makeBlankRow` is `GridRow(cells: (0..<columns).map { _ in GridCell(styleId: styleId) })` -- one allocation plus one closure call per column. `Terminal.moveAndFillRows` also does `appendToScrollback(Array(screen.rows[range.lowerBound..<(range.lowerBound + amount)]))`, with the comment "It must be materialized rather than passed as a slice of `rows`: `appendToScrollback` is mutating".

**Ideal fix.** Give `ScreenState` a `firstRowSlot` head index over a fixed-size row store and reach rows through one `slot(for:)` translation, so a scroll whose region is the whole viewport is a head advance plus blanking exactly `amount` recycled rows in place -- O(amount * columns) cell writes, zero row moves, zero allocation. `DequeModule` is already a declared dependency of `TerminalCore` and `TerminalSearch` already uses `Deque`, so a `Deque<GridRow>` with `removeFirst()`/`append()` is the off-the-shelf spelling if the recycling is dropped; the hand-rolled head index is what additionally lets the evicted row's `[GridCell]` buffer be blanked and reused rather than freed and reallocated. Sub-region scrolls (`ESC[2;23r`) still shift, but only within the region, which is what they already do.

**By construction.** A viewport row's identity stops being its storage slot, so "scroll" stops being expressible as a bulk permutation of storage at all -- and with it the whole class of bugs where a shift and the damage recorded for it disagree about which rows moved.

**Cheaper fallback.** Leave the array but kill the two per-scroll allocations: admit the evicted rows one at a time from a local copy (`let row = screen.rows[i]; history.admit(row)`) instead of materializing an `Array`, and build the blank row with `Array(repeating:count:)` rather than `map`. That removes the allocations and the per-column closure but keeps the O(region) row moves.

**Measurement.** `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed`. The number that must move is `feedDurationNanoseconds`; the corpus contains 25,000 full-region scrolls and 100,000 sub-region scrolls, so this is the workload's own dominant structure and not a corner of it. `just terminal-memory-probe --payload scrollback-plain --vmmap` is the secondary read: removing the per-scroll blank-row allocation should show up in allocator churn, not in the exact census, which is unchanged by construction.

**Regression risk.** Every row lookup gains one add and one conditional subtract. That is charged per row access, and the print path already hoists the row (`printBulkASCII` reads `screen.cursor.row` once per run), but `screen.rows[row].cells[...]` appears 95 times in `Terminal.swift` and any site that indexes rows inside a per-cell loop would pay it per cell. Finding 2's row-scoped mutable view is the prerequisite that keeps that from happening. The workloads that would show a regression are `retained-browse` and `content-churn`, which walk rows without scrolling.

**Verification.** `TerminalScrollbackTests` and `TerminalEditingTests` already pin IL/DL/scroll-region behavior against overlapping moves with distinct per-position content, per the `moveInPlace` doc comment; those must pass unchanged. Add a behavioral test that a full-region scroll followed by a sub-region scroll followed by a resize projects the same `viewportText` and the same `drainDamage()` value as the array implementation for a scripted byte stream.

**Risk.** Largest change here by far. `screen.rows` is also read by resize/reflow, state synchronization, and the projections, all of which currently assume slot == row.

**Vetted.** Every code quote is exact: `Terminal.moveInPlace`, the `moveAndFillRows` body with `screen.rows[destination] = makeBlankRow(...)`, the `Array(screen.rows[...])` materialization and its comment, and `makeBlankRow` as `GridRow(cells: (0..<columns).map { _ in GridCell(styleId: styleId) })`. The frequency claims check out against the committed corpus (`benchmarks/fixtures/terminal-app.json`): `scrollback-stream` is `repeat: 25000` of a `\n`-terminated template, and `incremental-screen-updates` is `repeat: 100000` of a template that sets `ESC[2;23r` once and then ends each cycle with `ESC[23;1H...\n`, i.e. the cursor sits on the last row of a 22-row region every iteration. `TerminalWiredHistoryAttributionProbe` independently transcribes the 25,000-line stimulus at 179x66, so the 5,728-byte blank row is right at 32 bytes/cell. I dropped impact from 5 to 4 only because the finding double-counts with ROW-5, which proposes the same structural change from the other side.

**Correction.** This is the same change as ROW-5 ("Recycle the vacated row's cell buffer on scroll"), written from the parser side. They must be merged before either is planned, or the work is done twice: ROW-5's ideal (one contiguous `rows * columns` cell buffer plus a ring base) is strictly stronger than FEED-1's (`Deque<GridRow>` or a head index over `[GridRow]`), and ROW-5's cheaper fallback is FEED-1's cheaper fallback. Merge under ROW-5's flat-buffer ideal and keep FEED-1's corpus evidence, which is the better-verified half.

**Do after.** [FEED-2](#feed-2)

**Conflicts with.** [ROW-5](#row-5) (pruned), [ROW-2](#row-2), [PARSE-2](#parse-2)

**Absorbs.** [ROW-5](#row-5) was pruned in favour of this finding; the [Pruned](#pruned) entry says which of its points to carry over.

<a id="feed-2"></a>

##### FEED-2. Reach a row's cells once per run, not once per cell, on the bulk ASCII write and scan loops

`perf-hot-path` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 1 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift`

**Problem.** `writeNarrowCells` stores each cell through `screen.rows[row].cells[column + offset]`, and `printBulkASCII`'s pre-scan reads each cell's kind through `screen.rows[row].cells[column + count]`. Both are two-level array accesses inside a per-cell loop, so the write loop re-proves uniqueness of the `rows` array and of the `cells` array on every single cell. This is the innermost loop of the hot path: the ASCII-run granularity exists precisely to make everything else per-run, and this is the one thing left that is still per-cell. `scrollback-stream` alone writes roughly 1.5 million cells through it, and `styled-screen-redraw` writes a full 179x66 screen 3,500 times.

**Evidence.** `Terminal.writeNarrowCells`: `for offset in 0..<count { screen.rows[row].cells[column + offset] = GridCell(scalars: .single(scalar(offset)), kind: .narrow, styleId: styleId, hyperlinkId: hyperlinkId, contentIdentity: baseIdentity + ContentIdentity(offset)) }`. The repo already names this exact cost and already fixed it for erase -- `Terminal.eraseCells` carries the comment "whose two nested array subscripts cost a COW uniqueness check on the row array and another on the cell array for every single cell erased" and writes through `screen.rows[row].cells.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer { cells in for column in lower..<upper { cells[column] = blank } }`.

**Ideal fix.** Make "a mutable view of one row's cells" a real thing the grid vends -- `withRowCells(row:_:)` -- and route every per-cell loop through it, so the row is resolved and proved unique once per run and the two-level subscript is not expressible inside a cell loop at all. `writeNarrowCells` already takes everything it needs (`styleId`, `hyperlinkId`, the `scalar` supplier) before the loop and touches no other part of `self` inside it, and the pre-scan is a pure read, so both convert directly. This also becomes the single seam the row-ring in finding 1 has to teach, instead of 95 open-coded subscripts.

**By construction.** A per-cell loop can no longer be written that re-resolves the row, because the loop body only has the cell buffer in scope.

**Cheaper fallback.** Apply `withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` inline at `writeNarrowCells` and hoist a borrowed row for the scan loop, copying the `eraseCells` pattern verbatim without introducing the shared accessor.

**Measurement.** `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed`, reading `feedDurationNanoseconds`. If it comes back `inconclusive`, escalate to `just benchmark-confirm baseline=HEAD`. `just benchmark-feed-sample` is the diagnostic that would show the uniqueness-check frames disappearing from the `writeNarrowCells` stack before deciding.

**Regression risk.** None identified for the write loop: it is strictly fewer checks over the same stores, and it introduces no cache, mirror, or side table. The one hazard is correctness, not speed -- the closure must not touch `self` -- and `printBulkASCII` already guarantees `screen.rows[row].cells.count == columnCount` and `column + count <= columnCount` before calling.

**Verification.** `TerminalASCIIRunTests` already pins that a run produces exactly the token stream one `.print` per byte would; it must pass unchanged. Add nothing new -- the point of the change is that observable behavior is identical, and a test that could tell the two apart would be structure-sensitive.

**Risk.** Unsafe buffer access, so an off-by-one becomes memory corruption rather than a trap. Mitigated by the existing bounds guarantees at the single call site and by the identical precedent in `eraseCells`.

**Vetted.** Both quotes are exact. `Terminal.writeNarrowCells` stores through `screen.rows[row].cells[column + offset]` inside `for offset in 0..<count`, `Terminal.printBulkASCII`'s pre-scan reads `screen.rows[row].cells[column + count].kind` per cell, and `Terminal.eraseCells` carries the cited comment verbatim and already uses `screen.rows[row].cells.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer`. I checked both `writeNarrowCells` call sites: the supplied closures are `{ Unicode.Scalar(bytes[start + $0]) }` and `{ _ in scalar }`, neither of which touches `self`, so the exclusivity hazard the finding names is currently satisfied at both sites. Bounds are guaranteed by `printBulkASCII`'s `screen.rows[row].cells.count == columnCount` and `available = min(limit - start, columnCount - column)` guards. What is wrong is one frequency claim.

**Correction.** `styled-screen-redraw` does not write a full 179x66 screen 3,500 times. Its committed template (`benchmarks/fixtures/terminal-app.json`) is a two-line frame -- `ESC[H` plus two ~60-character styled rows each ended with `ESC[K` -- described as 80x24, so it writes on the order of 400,000 cells across the whole workload, not 41 million. The load-bearing evidence is `scrollback-stream`'s ~1.4 million cells (25,000 lines x ~55 characters), which does hold. Impact drops to 3 accordingly; the change is still strictly fewer uniqueness checks over the same stores, and it is the seam the row-ring work has to teach instead of 95 open-coded subscripts.

**Conflicts with.** [ROW-4](#row-4), [ROW-2](#row-2)

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 7 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** There is no separate grid type: `Terminal` (public, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift`) holds `private var screen: ScreenState`, `private struct ScreenState` holds `var rows: [GridRow]`, and `struct GridRow` holds `var cells: [GridCell]`. The write loop is `private mutating func writeNarrowCells(row: Int, column: Int, count: Int, baseIdentity: ContentIdentity, breakClass: GraphemeBreakClass, scalar: (Int) -> Unicode.Scalar)`; it reads `currentStyleId()` and `hyperlinkPen` before the loop, then does `for offset in 0..<count { screen.rows[row].cells[column + offset] = GridCell(...) }`, and after the loop sets `clusterContext`, `marginErased`, `screen.cursor.column` and `screen.isPendingWrap`. The pre-scan is inside `private mutating func printBulkASCII(_ bytes: UnsafeBufferPointer<UInt8>, from start: Int, limit: Int) -> Int`: `while count < available { let kind = screen.rows[row].cells[column + count].kind; guard kind == .narrow || kind == .padding else { break }; count += 1 }`. The precedent the finding cites is `mutating func eraseCells(row: Int, columns: Range<Int>)`, which already uses `screen.rows[row].cells.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer { cells in for column in lower..<upper { cells[column] = blank } }` under the quoted copy-on-write comment. `writeNarrowCells` has exactly two callers, `printBulkASCII` (closure `{ Unicode.Scalar(bytes[start + $0]) }`) and `printNarrow(_:breakClass:)` (closure `{ _ in scalar }`); neither closure touches `self`. All of `currentStyleId()`, `invalidateInspection`, `clearPreviousSpacer` and `rememberOpenCluster` are mutating and already run outside the loops.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#writeNarrowCells` -- Replace the `for offset in 0..<count` body's two-level subscript with a single resolution of the row's cell buffer -- either `screen.rows[row].cells.withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` inline (the `eraseCells` pattern) or the new shared accessor. Everything after the loop stays where it is.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#printBulkASCII` -- Hoist the pre-scan's row read out of the loop -- `screen.rows[row].cells.withUnsafeBufferPointer` around the `while count < available` walk, or the read half of the accessor. The existing guards `screen.rows[row].cells.count == columnCount` and `available = min(limit - start, columnCount - column)` already bound it.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#Terminal (new member) or Terminal.ScreenState (new member)` -- The accessor itself if the ideal fix is taken: `withRowCells(row:_:)` handing a mutable cell buffer to a non-escaping closure. Placing it on `Terminal` as a `mutating` method is the stronger form -- the closure then cannot touch any part of `self`, which is exactly the by-construction property the finding claims. Placing it on `ScreenState` is looser (the closure could still reach other terminal state) but composes better with callers that need a sibling field. This is the one shape decision in the change.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#eraseCells` -- Optional. Convert its existing inline `withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` to the shared accessor so there is one seam rather than two spellings, and move its copy-on-write comment onto the accessor's doc comment.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#clearPromptCells` -- Optional, same class of loop: `for column in 0..<columnCount { screen.rows[row].cells[column] = GridCell(styleId: styleId) }`. Converts cleanly -- nothing in the body touches self.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#repairHorizontalMove` -- Optional. Its second loop, `for column in invalidColumns { screen.rows[row].cells[column] = GridCell(styleId: replacementStyleId) }`, converts cleanly. Its first loop already binds `let cells = screen.rows[row].cells` and is fine.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#moveAndFillCells` -- Optional and the hard one: its per-cell work is inside a closure passed to `Self.moveInPlace(_:by:amount:)`, and that closure reads `styleId` from an enclosing local while writing through `screen.rows[row].cells`. Converting it means nesting the accessor outside `moveInPlace`, not inside. Leave it out unless the agent is deliberately taking the full accessor sweep.

_How this list was built: I grepped `screen.rows[` in Terminal.swift and read all 95 hits to separate per-cell loops from single-cell accesses, then grepped `writeNarrowCells`, `printBulkASCII`, `eraseCells` and `withUnsafeMutableBufferPointer` across `lib/TerminalCore/Sources`. I read both `writeNarrowCells` call sites in full and checked that their closures and the surrounding mutating helpers keep every `self` access outside the loop. I read the whole of `TerminalASCIIRunTests.swift` to inventory the safety net. The change-site list is complete for the two hot sites and for every remaining per-cell loop in Terminal.swift; I did not search outside TerminalCore, but both functions are private so nothing else can reach them. I ran no test and no benchmark._

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalASCIIRunTests.swift -- runsAreChunkInvariant (parameterized over 13 scenarios x 7 chunk sizes) -- the whole safety net: it replays each byte stream at chunk sizes 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 64 and requires byte-identical terminals, so the bulk path and the per-character path must agree on screen text, cursor, viewport cells and scrollback row count

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- None. `writeNarrowCells` and `printBulkASCII` are both private to `Terminal`, no test names them, and no test asserts on the shape of a row write. Nothing stops compiling.

**Write this test first.** There is no first failing test. FEED-2 is a pure refactor: the same `GridCell` values are stored in the same order at the same columns, with fewer copy-on-write uniqueness checks proved along the way. A test that could tell the two apart would have to observe the uniqueness checks, which is structure, not behavior -- and the finding says so itself under Verification ("Add nothing new"). The characterization test is `runsAreChunkInvariant` in lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalASCIIRunTests.swift: it replays 13 named byte streams at 7 chunkings and requires byte-identical terminals, so it exercises the write loop at count 1 and at count 64 across every cut rule, including the wide-cell overwrite, both DECAWM states, insert mode, prepend clusters, the scroll region, the alternate screen, and styled and hyperlinked runs. Run it before the change to confirm it is green and after to confirm nothing moved. The proof that the change is worth keeping is the benchmark the finding names (`just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed`, reading `feedDurationNanoseconds`), not a test.

**Blockers and surprises.** Nothing blocks it, and two things make it easier than the finding suggests. Both `writeNarrowCells` call sites already satisfy the exclusivity requirement: the supplied closures are `{ Unicode.Scalar(bytes[start + $0]) }` over a caller-owned `UnsafeBufferPointer` and `{ _ in scalar }` over a local, and every mutating helper the function needs (`currentStyleId()`, `hyperlinkPen`, `clusterContext`, the cursor writes) already sits outside the loop. And the precedent is in the same file with its rationale already written down, so the change reads as consistency rather than novelty. Two things to watch. `writeNarrowCells` calls `scalar(count - 1)` again after the loop to compute `retainedUTF8ByteCount`; that call must stay outside the buffer scope, or the closure runs while the row's storage is borrowed. And the scope decision above matters -- decide how far the accessor sweep goes before starting, because `moveAndFillCells` resists conversion while the other loops do not. Two other findings sit on the same code: ROW-4 removes `clearCellAndPair`'s redundant store on the `printNarrow` path, and ROW-2 changes `GridCell`'s shape. Neither blocks FEED-2 and FEED-2 blocks neither, but doing FEED-2 first gives ROW-4 a cleaner seam to land on. No public API in `lib/` moves -- `GridRow` and `ScreenState` are internal to TerminalCore, and both functions are private. No `@inlinable` is involved, so the cross-module value-dispatch ADR does not bind.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** Partly. The finding's stated ideal -- one `withRowCells(row:_:)` that every per-cell loop routes through -- is right for the two hot sites and for `eraseCells`, `clearPromptCells` and `repairHorizontalMove`'s repair loop. But the sentence "the single seam the row-ring has to teach, instead of 95 open-coded subscripts" oversells it: of the 95 `screen.rows[...]` occurrences in Terminal.swift, the large majority are single-cell reads and single-field row writes (`isSoftWrapped`, `semanticPrompt`, `marginErased`) that a buffer accessor cannot absorb without making them worse. The honest ideal is narrower and still holds by construction: one accessor that owns every loop over a row's cells, with the single-cell sites left alone. Write that into the plan so the next reader does not measure the change against a claim it was never going to meet.

<a id="feed-3"></a>

##### FEED-3. Store tab stops as a column bitset instead of a Set<Int>, so HT is a word scan rather than an allocation

`data-modeling` &middot; impact 2, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift`

**Problem.** `tabStops` is a `Set<Int>` over a dense bounded domain (columns `0..<columnCount`), and every ordered query over it is expressed as a filter that materializes a new collection. Handling one HT byte allocates a whole new `Set<Int>` -- `Set.filter` returns a `Set`, so it rehashes every retained stop -- and then scans it for a minimum. At the default 179 columns that is 22 stops rehashed into a fresh hash table per tab character. `moveCursorAcrossTabStops` (CHT/CBT) is worse: an array allocation plus a sort per sequence. The domain is bounded, dense, and ordered; the representation is unordered, sparse, and heap-allocated.

**Evidence.** `Terminal.execute`, case 0x09: `screen.cursor.column = tabStops.filter { $0 > screen.cursor.column }.min() ?? columnCount - 1`. `Terminal.moveCursorAcrossTabStops`: `let candidates = tabStops.filter { forward ? $0 > screen.cursor.column : $0 < screen.cursor.column }.sorted(by: forward ? (<) : (>))`. Declared as `private var tabStops: Set<Int>`, seeded by `Set(stride(from: 0, to: columns, by: 8))`.

**Ideal fix.** Represent tab stops as a bitset over columns -- one `[UInt64]` of `(columnCount + 63) / 64` words, or `BitCollections.BitSet` (AGENTS.md says to prefer swift-collections over hand-rolling a bitset; only `DequeModule` is currently a declared product dependency, so this adds one). "Next stop after column c" becomes mask-off-the-low-bits plus `trailingZeroBitCount` across at most three words at 179 columns, with no allocation and no hashing; "previous stop" is the symmetric `leadingZeroBitCount` scan; `resizeTabStops` becomes a truncate-and-fill instead of `Set(tabStops.filter { $0 < newColumnCount })`; and `appendControlState`'s `tabStops.sorted()` becomes an in-order word walk with the sort deleted.

**By construction.** Answering an ordered query by materializing a filtered copy stops being possible, because the representation is already ordered. The `sorted()` in `appendControlState` and both `filter`s disappear rather than getting faster.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the `Set` for membership but maintain the ordered column list alongside it. Rejected: that is exactly the hand-maintained mirror this audit is told to avoid, and it must be invalidated on TBC/TBC-all/HTS/resize -- four sites, each a chance to desynchronize.

**Measurement.** No existing instrument can see this, and I want to be plain about that: none of the four committed `terminal-feed` corpora contains a single HT byte (I checked `benchmarks/fixtures/terminal-app.json` for `\t`; it is absent), so `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed` would correctly report `equivalent`. Deciding it would mean either adding a tab-bearing segment to the committed corpus -- which redefines the workload and forces recalibration before directional claims resume -- or a one-off `Terminal.feed` timing in a test process, which the measurement rules do not treat as decision-bearing. Report it as an unmeasured structural win, not a measured speedup. The workloads that would contain it in real use are tab-emitting output: `git diff`, `make`, and `cat` of tab-indented source.

**Regression risk.** Memory grows by a few words per terminal (three `UInt64`s at 179 columns) against a `Set<Int>` holding 22 boxed-in-a-hash-table entries, so it is a reduction, not a cost. No path gets slower: every current operation is a hash lookup or a full-set materialization, and both are strictly more work than a word test. `just terminal-memory-probe` will not see it -- it is fixed per-terminal state, not per-cell.

**Verification.** `TerminalEditingTests`-style behavioral coverage of HT at the last stop, HT with all stops cleared (`ESC[3g`), HTS at the current column, CHT/CBT with counts past the end, and a resize that both grows and shrinks the column count -- all asserted through `Terminal.feed` and the resulting cursor column, never through the stop representation.

**Risk.** Low. The one behavior to preserve exactly is what happens when no stop lies ahead (`?? columnCount - 1`) and when the stop set is empty.

**Vetted.** All three quotes are exact: `Terminal.execute` case 0x09 is `tabStops.filter { $0 > screen.cursor.column }.min() ?? columnCount - 1`, `Terminal.moveCursorAcrossTabStops` is the `filter`-then-`sorted` form, `tabStops` is `private var tabStops: Set<Int>` seeded by `defaultTabStops(columns:)` = `Set(stride(from: 0, to: columns, by: 8))`, and `appendControlState` iterates `tabStops.sorted()`. I also confirmed only `DequeModule` is a declared product of the swift-collections dependency in `lib/TerminalCore/Package.swift`, so `BitCollections` would be a new product. I dropped impact to 2 on the finding's own honest measurement note, which I verified: none of the templated corpora contains a tab byte, so this is an unmeasured structural win that AGENTS.md's measurement rules forbid claiming as a speedup. It still stands on the simplification: two `filter`s, one `sorted()` and one `Set(...)` rebuild all disappear.

**Conflicts with.** [PARSE-6](#parse-6)

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 11 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `private var tabStops: Set<Int>` on `Terminal`, initialized in `init` from `private static func defaultTabStops(columns: Int) -> Set<Int> { Set(stride(from: 0, to: columns, by: 8)) }`. Six sites touch it: `execute(_:)` case 0x09 does `screen.cursor.column = tabStops.filter { $0 > screen.cursor.column }.min() ?? columnCount - 1`; `moveCursorAcrossTabStops(amount:forward:)` does `tabStops.filter { ... }.sorted(by: forward ? (<) : (>))` and indexes the result; `dispatchEscape` HTS does `tabStops.insert(screen.cursor.column)`; `clearTabStop(_:)` does `remove` for TBC 0 and `removeAll(keepingCapacity: true)` for TBC 3; `resizeTabStops(from:to:)` rebuilds with `Set(tabStops.filter { $0 < newColumnCount })` then inserts new multiples of 8, and is called once from `resize`; `resetControlState()` reassigns the defaults. The state-sync encoder `appendControlState(for:to:)` emits `ESC[3g` then walks `tabStops.sorted()`, emitting a cursor position and `ESC H` per stop. `Terminal`'s `Equatable` conformance is synthesized, so the representation participates in terminal equality directly. Every quote in the finding is exact.

**Change sites.**

- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#tabStops` -- Declaration changes from `Set<Int>` to the bitset representation. Give the new type a `///` comment stating the invariant that bits at or above `columnCount` are always clear -- synthesized `Terminal` equality compares the words directly, so a stray high bit makes two behaviorally identical terminals unequal.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#defaultTabStops` -- Returns the bitset instead of a `Set`; still every eighth column from 0.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift (Terminal.init)` -- The `tabStops = Self.defaultTabStops(columns: columns)` line keeps its shape; only the type changes.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#execute case 0x09` -- The `filter { $0 > column }.min() ?? columnCount - 1` becomes mask-off-the-low-bits plus `trailingZeroBitCount` across the words at and after the cursor. The `?? columnCount - 1` fallback and the `if screen.cursor.column != previousColumn { clusterContext = nil }` tail must both survive verbatim.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#moveCursorAcrossTabStops` -- The `filter`-then-`sorted` becomes a forward or backward word walk that takes the nth stop, with the existing fallbacks (`columnCount - 1` forward, `0` backward) preserved. It keeps calling `movePositionedCursor`.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#dispatchEscape (HTS, ESC H)` -- `tabStops.insert(screen.cursor.column)` becomes a bit set.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#clearTabStop` -- TBC 0 clears one bit; TBC 3 zeroes every word. The arity guard and the `clearPendingMotionState()` tail are unchanged.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#resizeTabStops` -- Becomes truncate-and-fill: resize the word array, clear every bit at or above the new column count (this is the high-bit invariant site), then set the new multiples of 8 above the old count. Called only from `resize`.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#resetControlState` -- Same line, new type.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#appendControlState` -- `for column in tabStops.sorted()` becomes an in-order word walk; the `sorted()` disappears rather than getting faster. The emitted byte sequence must be identical.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Package.swift` -- Only if `BitCollections.BitSet` is chosen: add `.product(name: "BitCollections", package: "swift-collections")` to the TerminalCore target. swift-collections is already a package dependency at exact 1.6.0, but BitCollections is not currently a declared product anywhere in the repo.

_How this list was built: Grepped `tabStops` and `tabStop` across lib/ and app/: eleven production references, all in Terminal.swift and all listed above, and zero references in any test file outside `TerminalTabStopTests` -- which drives everything through `feed` and `geometry.cursor`, never through the representation. So nothing stops compiling. Grepped `BitCollections` and `import BitCollections` across lib/ and app/ sources and every `Package.swift`: no declared product, confirming the finding. Also grepped every JSON fixture for tab bytes to find the fixture-level coverage. I am confident this list is complete._

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- tabStopDispatch -- HTS at 3 and 5, TBC 0, TBC 3, and the empty-set clamp to column 11
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- tabClampsWithDefaultStopsPresent -- the defaults-present clamp; its preamble explicitly says it exists to catch an implementation that computes defaults arithmetically instead of storing them, which is close enough to a bitset rewrite to be the sharpest guard in the suite
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- tabStopsAcrossResize -- grow to 20, shrink to 10, grow to 20 again, asserting that shrunken stops are gone and only newly introduced columns get defaults; this is the truncate-and-fill contract and the high-bit invariant's real test
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- cursorTabMovement -- eight CHT/CBT fixtures including counts past both ends
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- tabStopsAffectEquality -- synthesized `Terminal` equality over the new representation; this is the test that catches a stray high bit
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalTabStopTests.swift -- tabAtLastColumnIsBitIdentical, tabClearNormalizationAndSideState, cursorTabClearsPendingState -- the side-state and no-op rules
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalFixtureTests.swift -- replayFixtures over libvterm/state-tabstops.json, which combines HTS, TBC 0, TBC 3, a stop at column 50, RIS, and a resize from 80 to 100 columns in one recording, replayed under every chunk split

**Write this test first.** There is no new failing test: this is a pure representation change with no observable behavior difference. The characterization tests are `TerminalTabStopTests#tabStopsAcrossResize` (the shrink-then-grow sequence, which is the only place the truncate-and-fill rule is observable and the only place a leftover high bit would show up as a wrong cursor column) and `TerminalFixtureTests#replayFixtures` over libvterm/state-tabstops.json (the same rules replayed across every chunk split, plus RIS and a resize). Do not write a test that reaches at the bitset -- the existing suite already asserts every rule through `feed` and `geometry.cursor`, which is exactly the structure-insensitive form AGENTS.md asks for. The finding's Verification list (HT at the last stop, HT with all stops cleared, HTS at the current column, CHT/CBT past the end, grow and shrink resize) is already covered item for item by the tests above; check that off rather than re-adding it.

**Blockers and surprises.** Nothing blocks it, and the test coverage is unusually good -- `TerminalTabStopTests` alone pins every rule behaviorally, and no test or helper reaches into `tabStops`. Four things to know. First, `Terminal`'s `Equatable` is synthesized, so the bitset's spare high bits become part of terminal identity; `tabStopsAcrossResize` and `tabStopsAffectEquality` will catch a leak, but the invariant belongs in a comment on the declaration, not just in the resize function. Second, `lib/TerminalCore/Package.swift` compiles with `-warn-long-function-bodies=500` enforced by `scripts/type-check-budget-gate.sh`; a word-walk written as a chained lazy expression can breach it, so write the scans as plain loops. Third, choosing `BitCollections.BitSet` adds a product to the TerminalCore target, which puts docs/design/2026-08-17-package-owns-its-targets.md in scope; a hand-rolled `[UInt64]` avoids that but runs against AGENTS.md's standing preference for swift-collections over hand-rolled bitsets. That is the one thing a human may want to weigh, though either choice is defensible and the finding names both. Fourth, and worth writing into the plan verbatim: the audit's own Measurement paragraph establishes that no committed corpus contains a tab byte, so `just benchmark-quick` will correctly report `equivalent`. Report this as an unmeasured structural win. Claiming a speedup here would breach agent-docs/measurement-discipline.md.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** No disagreement. The domain is bounded, dense and ordered and the representation is not, so the bitset is the structure in which "answer an ordered query by materializing a filtered copy" cannot be written. The finding is also honest about what it cannot measure, which is the right call and should be carried into the plan.
