So `TerminalSurfaceView.apply`, `ensureSurfaces`, `layoutSubviews`, and the metrics refresh have no automated cover before or after. That changes how the work should start -- the kit half can be TDD'd, the view half can only be reasoned about and then exercised on a device.

**Write this test first.** This is a pure refactor with no behavior change, so there is no new failing test to write first; a test counting `TerminalRenderMetrics` constructions would be asserting the mechanism, not behavior. The characterization tests are `ContentBoxTests.contentBoxClaimAndDrawAgree` (the claimed grid and the drawn surface agree inside one content box, at both handset display scales) together with `ObserveSurfaceTests.observeSurfaceStaysInsideTheView` and `observeSurfaceKeepsNativeScaleWhenItFits`. Those three pin the exact values the metrics-ownership move must not change: port them to the new signatures without touching an assertion, and a passing run is the proof. One genuinely new behavioral test is worth adding once the API exists, but as a guard rather than a first failing test -- build a surface at displayScale 3, refresh the held metrics at displayScale 2 for the same box extent, and assert the resolved cell pixel dimensions differ. That pins the stale-metrics regression the finding names as its only risk, and it cannot be written today because there is no held value to go stale.

**Blockers and surprises.** Two real ones and one caution. (1) `MobileObserveSurface.init` cannot become pure arithmetic. Its fitted branch builds `TerminalRenderMetrics(displayScale: scale, fontSize:)` at a scale `fittedRenderScale` derives from columns and rows, so a remote resize genuinely changes it and it cannot be precomputed where displayScale moves. What makes today expensive is that the *unchanged* case rebuilds it too, which the hoisted guard fixes. Say this in the plan, because a planner reading only the Sharper ideal will drop the hoist. (2) `MobileContentBox`'s file comment states the constraint the refactor must not break: both readings of the drawable region -- the grid a claim names and the pixels a surface draws -- must come from one value. Putting metrics on the box costs the box its cheapness and makes its `Equatable` compare a whole `TerminalFontSet`; a sibling value pairing box and metrics keeps the single-reading property without that. Caution: `scripts/ios-portability-gate.sh` cross-compiles every target of every iOS-pinned package (tests included) and `scripts/core-purity-lint.sh --profile portable` runs over the kit's sources, so a new kit type must stay free of host-bound API. Nothing found suggests it would not.

**The preparer's read on the ideal fix.** The finding's stated ideal has two halves and the second is wrong for this tree, which the audit's own 'Sharper ideal' already concedes: routing a typed `.resize` transition out of the record stream to move `ensureSurfaces` off the per-record path buys nothing once metrics are owned elsewhere, and it would push stream decoding into the view. Drop that half. What the Sharper ideal understates is that hoisting the idempotence check is not optional polish -- it is load-bearing, because the fitted-scale metrics genuinely depend on the grid and so cannot be resolved purely at the layout edge. The ideal is: metrics owned where displayScale and fontSize move, AND the existing geometry comparison hoisted above the construction. Neither alone is sufficient.

<a id="mobile-2"></a>

##### MOBILE-2. Feed the drained damage into the frame stores instead of re-rendering the whole grid every tick

`structural` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 2 &middot; rescored

**Files.** `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalSurfaceView.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobilePresentationPolicy.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplica.swift`

**Problem.** `PaneReplica.drainPresentation()` returns `(terminal, damage)` and the display tick throws the damage away: it plans with the free function `planFrame(for:presentation:)`, which passes `damage: .full`, and rasterizes with `renderFull`. So every published frame on the phone replans every row and repaints every pixel of the grid, whatever moved -- once per display-link tick for as long as output keeps arriving. The information needed to do better is already computed by the engine and already returned by the replica; it is discarded one line later. `TerminalRenderExecution` already ships `TerminalFrameSwapchain`, which owns exactly this triple-buffer discipline, accumulates per-buffer stale damage, and calls `store.apply(plan:damage:)` with `renderFull` only as its fallback. `MobilePresentationPolicy` reimplements the buffer rotation without the damage, so the phone -- the device with the least CPU and a battery -- is the one client doing full-frame work.

**Evidence.** TerminalSurfaceView.displayTick: `guard let frame = replica.drainPresentation() else { ... }` then `let plan = planFrame(for: frame.terminal, presentation: RenderPresentation(...))` and `stores[surfaceId].renderFull(plan)` -- `frame.damage` is never read. MobilePresentationPolicy's whole damage model is `private var hasDamage = false` with `public mutating func noteDamage() { hasDamage = true }`. Compare TerminalFrameSwapchain.render: `let incremental = buffer.isCurrent && buffer.store.apply(plan: plan, damage: buffer.staleDamage)` / `if incremental == false { buffer.store.renderFull(plan) }`.

**Ideal fix.** Delete the parallel implementation: have `TerminalSurfaceView` own a `TerminalFrameSwapchain` over its three stores and publish `(plan, damage)` into it, so per-buffer stale-damage composition and the incremental/full decision live in the one place that already gets them right. Where the phone genuinely needs its own policy (it publishes on a display link rather than on a draw callback), change `MobilePresentationPolicy`'s `hasDamage: Bool` to an accumulated `TerminalDamage` and thread it through `didRender`, so the type can no longer represent "something changed" without saying what.

**By construction.** Once the policy carries `TerminalDamage` instead of a Bool, "we know something changed but not what" stops being a representable state, and a full repaint becomes an explicit `.full` value rather than the silent default.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the policy as is but pass the drained damage straight to `stores[surfaceId].apply(plan:damage:)`, falling back to `renderFull` on refusal. This is wrong for a rotating buffer -- a store that missed several publishes needs the union of the damage since it was last current, which is precisely what the swapchain's per-buffer `staleDamage` exists for -- so it must union damage per store rather than trusting the latest value.

**Measurement.** No existing instrument reaches iOS. `just benchmark-headless-draw` measures exactly this operation (`drawRenderFrame` on an already-clipped plan) but only for macOS TerminalCore arms, so it can bound the win in principle and cannot decide the iOS change. What would decide it: a device Time Profiler capture under an `incremental-mixed`-shaped stimulus (a TUI touching a few rows of a settled screen in the observed pane), reading main-thread self time in `drawRenderFrame` per published frame; that number must fall while the published-frame count holds. The workload shape matters -- on a full-screen content flood, damage is every row and the correct outcome is no change at all.

**Regression risk.** `TerminalFrameBackingStore.apply` does erase-span and ink-reach work that `renderFull` skips, so on frames whose damage really is the whole grid the incremental path can cost more before refusing; the swapchain already guards this with `damage.isFull` and `damagedRowCount == plan.rows`, and any hand-rolled version must too. A full-screen flood in the observed pane is the workload that would show a regression.

**Verification.** Pixel-equality: apply a recorded record stream twice, once forcing `renderFull` on every frame and once through the damage path, and assert the surfaces' bytes are identical at each publish. That is a behavioral assertion on the drawn result and is insensitive to how the buffers are rotated.

**Risk.** The store's incremental path is the subtlest code in the render layer (translation stale strips, ink-reach ledger); adopting it on iOS means the phone inherits any bug there, which today only the Mac exercises.

**Vetted.** Confirmed in full. `TerminalSurfaceView#displayTick` binds `frame.damage` and never reads it, calls the free `planFrame(for:presentation:)` -- which is hardcoded to `.plan(reusing: nil, damage: .full)` in `RenderFramePlanner.swift`, so every row is replanned as well as repainted -- and then `stores[surfaceId].renderFull(plan)`. `MobilePresentationPolicy`'s entire damage model really is `private var hasDamage = false`. `TerminalFrameSwapchain#render` really is `let incremental = buffer.isCurrent && buffer.store.apply(plan: plan, damage: buffer.staleDamage)` with `renderFull` as fallback, and `publish` composes per-buffer `staleDamage` and installs the whole-frame barrier. Raising effort from medium to large: adopting the swapchain deletes `MobilePresentationPolicy` and its `PresentationPolicyTests`, and the two do not have the same shape -- the swapchain renders synchronously inside `publish` and returns the store to attach, while the phone deliberately splits render and publish across display-link ticks with a `retryPublish` state. Reconciling the phone's tick pacing with the swapchain's publish-driven pacing is the bulk of the work, and the pixel-equality verification the finding asks for has no iOS harness today.

**Do after.** [MOBILE-1](#mobile-1)

##### MOBILE-3. Decode each tape event once into a typed value instead of re-encoding and re-decoding it per record

`data-modeling` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplica.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift`

**Problem.** `PaneTapeEventRecord.event` is left as an untyped `JSONValue`, so every consumer re-parses it in its own way, once per record -- i.e. once per PTY chunk the Mac forwards. `PaneReplica.applyEvent` allocates a fresh `JSONEncoder`, serializes the already-parsed JSON tree back to `Data` (base64-re-encoding the whole feed payload), allocates a fresh `JSONDecoder`, and parses it again into `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent` -- whose own decoder additionally builds a `Set<String>` of every key for validation. That is a third and fourth full traversal of bytes that were already parsed on the reader thread, and it runs on the main actor. Separately, `MobileSessionModel.pinnedStatement` reaches into the same `JSONValue` with string subscripts to answer "is this a resize, and what does it say about pinnedness" -- a question the typed event answers directly.

**Evidence.** PaneReplica.applyEvent: `let data = try JSONEncoder().encode(record.event)` / `guard let event = try? JSONDecoder().decode(NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.self, from: data) else { throw PaneReplicaError.invalidEvent }`. MobileSessionModel.pinnedStatement: `guard event.event["type"]?.asString == "resize" else { return nil }` / `if case .bool(let pinned)? = event.event["pinned"] { return pinned }`. NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.init(from:) opens with `let keys = Set(dynamicValues.allKeys.map(\.stringValue))`.

**Ideal fix.** Decode once at the edge where a record enters the phone's model and carry the typed value from there. `MobileSessionModel.receive` already calls `decodePaneTapeRecord`; have it produce a mobile-side record whose event case holds a decoded `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent` (the kit already links `TerminalCoreRecording`), and let both `pinnedStatement` and `PaneReplica.applyEvent` switch on that value. The `.applyRecord` effect then carries a typed record, and no JSON tree survives past the decode point. Backwards compatibility is not a constraint here, so the record type itself can change shape.

**By construction.** A record whose event is typed cannot be parsed a second time -- there is no JSON left to parse -- so "two consumers disagree about what this event said" and "the same bytes were walked three times" both stop being representable.

**Cheaper fallback.** If the typed record cannot cross the effect boundary yet, at minimum hold one `JSONEncoder`/`JSONDecoder` pair for the replica's lifetime instead of constructing both per record. That removes two allocations per record and none of the two redundant traversals, so it is strictly the lesser fix and should be recorded as such.

**Measurement.** No existing instrument sees this path. What would decide it: a benchmark-shaped test in ios/DanTermMobileKit that applies N recorded `.event` records (feed payloads of a realistic chunk size) into a `PaneReplica` and reports elapsed time per record, with the record count emitted beside the aggregate so a zero cannot be confused with an unmeasured run. Wall time there is diagnostic only and must not become a pass/fail threshold; the deciding number is the same stimulus profiled on device, where `JSONEncoder`/`JSONDecoder` frames must vanish from the main thread.

**Regression risk.** None identified: the change removes work and adds no store. The one thing to watch is that the current round trip also acts as a validator -- `PaneReplicaError.invalidEvent` is thrown when the re-decode fails -- so the typed decode must keep raising the same refusal rather than silently accepting a malformed event.

**Verification.** PaneReplicaTests already pin the exactness and gap-detection semantics per event kind, including refusal of a malformed event; those tests must pass unchanged, since they assert replica state and cursor advance rather than how the event was decoded.

**Risk.** The typed record has to cross the DanTermMobileKit effect boundary, which today deliberately keeps DanTermClient's record type engine-free; the mobile-side record must be a new type rather than a change to the shared reader, or the client library gains an engine dependency it does not want.

**Vetted.** `PaneReplica#applyEvent` really is `let data = try JSONEncoder().encode(record.event)` followed by `JSONDecoder().decode(NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.self, from: data)`, per record, on the main actor, with the feed payload's base64 re-materialized in both directions. The boundary the Risk section names is real and documented at the source: `PaneTapeEventRecord#event` carries the comment "left as JSON so this module does not depend on the terminal engine. A client that links the recording types decodes it further", so the typed record must be a mobile-side type and cannot be a change to `DanTermClient`'s reader. The kit already imports `TerminalCoreRecording` in `PaneReplica.swift`, so the decode can move to `MobileSessionModel#receive` without a new dependency. Worth flagging for the plan: WIRE-2 is the producer-side mirror of exactly this round trip (`app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#paneTapeFollowEventJSON`), and the two should be designed against one typed-event boundary rather than separately, since both argue about whether a tape record may hold a `JSONValue` at all.

<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 14 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

Two consumers then re-parse it per record on the main actor. `PaneReplica.applyEvent(_ record: PaneTapeEventRecord) throws` (ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplica.swift) does `let data = try JSONEncoder().encode(record.event)` then `guard let event = try? JSONDecoder().decode(NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.self, from: data) else { throw PaneReplicaError.invalidEvent }`, switches on the typed event, and passes it to `private func advancedCursor(from:record:event:) -> PaneTapeCursor?`. `MobileSessionModel.pinnedStatement(in record: PaneTapeRecord) -> Bool?` reaches into the same tree with `event.event["type"]?.asString == "resize"` and `if case .bool(let pinned)? = event.event["pinned"]`. - ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/PaneReplicaTests.swift -- the private `eventRecord` helper only; every test using it keeps its assertions verbatim. Worth saying so the implementer does not go hunting for more.
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/PaneReplicaCheckpointTests.swift -- the private `checkpointEvent` helper, same shape
- ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/MobileSessionModelTests.swift -- the `case .attachPane, .applyRecord, ...` pattern in the effect-classifying helper binds nothing so it still compiles, but recheck it after the type change
- Correction to the finding: it claims PaneReplicaTests pins 'refusal of a malformed event'. It does not. I grepped the whole ios tree for `invalidEvent` and the only hits are the declaration and the throw site in PaneReplica.swift. That refusal has no test today, which is exactly the behavior this change relocates -- so the first failing test below is also the first test this error has ever had.

**Write this test first.** Suite: `MobileSessionModelTests` in ios/DanTermMobileKit/Tests/DanTermMobileKitTests/MobileSessionModelTests.swift. Name: "A tape event the engine cannot decode ends the stream at the decode point". Scenario: build a session attached to a pane with a live tape subscription (the file's existing private `tapeResizeNotification` helper shows the exact frame shape), then deliver a `.frameReceived(.notification(method: Methods.paneTapeEvent, ...))` whose `record.event` object is well-formed JSON but not a decodable recording event -- for example `.object(["type": .string("feed")])` with no `base64` key, which `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.init(from:)` rejects through its key validation. Assertion: the returned effects contain no `.applyRecord`, and the model ends the connection the way `.replicaRejectedRecord` does today (a `.deviceSetup` failure carrying the "Replica rejected the stream" detail). Why it fails against today's tree: `decodePaneTapeRecord` never looks inside `event`, so `receive` returns `[.applyRecord(record)]`; the refusal only happens later inside `PaneReplica.applyEvent` on the app side, which a pure-model test never reaches. Today the test sees an `.applyRecord` effect and no end, and both assertions fail for the right reason -- nothing decodes the event at the edge yet. The test also survives the refactor untouched, which is what makes it the right one to write first: it states where refusal happens in terms of the model's observable effects, not in terms of who calls JSONDecoder.

**Blockers and surprises.** Three. (1) The layering constraint is real and documented at the source: `PaneTapeEventRecord.event` carries the comment 'left as JSON so this module does not depend on the terminal engine. A client that links the recording types decodes it further.' So the typed record must be a new mobile-side type and `DanTermClient` must not change -- `PaneTapeRecordReaderTests` is the suite pinning that. (2) A decision the plan must make explicitly rather than by accident: today a malformed or future-unknown event kills the connection late (replica throws -> controller catches -> `.replicaRejectedRecord` -> end). Moving the decode to `receive` moves that refusal earlier, and the tempting alternative -- treat an undecodable event as unknown-but-fine and skip it -- would be a real behavior change, because `NeutralTerminalRecordingEvent.init(from:)` rejects unknown `type` values and unknown keys outright, so a future recorder event kind ends the phone's connection today. Preserve that unless the user says otherwise, and decide what still raises `replicaRejectedRecord` afterwards. (3) WIRE-2 is the producer-side mirror of the same round trip (`app/SwiftTerminalSessionView.swift#paneTapeFollowEventJSON` encodes then decodes the same event). The two argue about one question -- whether a tape record may hold a `JSONValue` at all -- and should be designed against one typed-event boundary. MOBILE-3 does not depend on WIRE-2 landing and can go first; just do not invent a second, incompatible mobile event spelling that WIRE-2 then has to reconcile. Minor: `scripts/core-purity-lint.sh --profile portable` runs over the kit's sources, so the new type must stay portable.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

</details>

##### MOBILE-4. Signal replica state and surface geometry only when they change, not once per applied record

`perf-occupancy` &middot; impact 4, confidence 5 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalSurfaceView.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/MobileSessionController.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/ConnectionStatusPillView.swift`

**Problem.** `TerminalSurfaceView.apply` fires `didChangeReplicaState?(replica.state)` after every record, whether or not the state moved -- it is named as a change notification but behaves as a value notification. The controller's handler then does two things per record: it dispatches `.replicaStateChanged`, which in the model returns `[.redraw]` for the steady `.exact` case, and it calls `surfaceDidLayout()`. So each record composes a fresh `MobileSessionProjection` (including `MobileStatus.line`'s `parts.joined(separator: " - ")` string build), writes `statusLabel.text` and `titleLabel.text` -- UIKit does not compare, so an identical string still invalidates intrinsic content size and schedules layout -- scans the pane list for the selected pane's title, and drives `scrollChrome.refresh()`, which writes `frame`, `contentSize`, and `contentOffset` on a UIScrollView and re-enters `scrollViewDidScroll`. All of that is per PTY chunk, on the main actor, for a screen whose pixels are published on the display link and not by any of it.

**Evidence.** TerminalSurfaceView.apply: `try replica.apply(record)` / `didChangeReplicaState?(replica.state)` -- unguarded. MobileSessionController.start: `surfaceView.didChangeReplicaState = { [weak self] state in guard let self else { return }; dispatch(.replicaStateChanged(state)); surfaceDidLayout() }`. MobileSessionModel: `case .replicaStateChanged(let state): status.noteStream(state)` ... `case .exact: resumePolicy.replicaBecameExact(); return [.redraw]`. ConnectionStatusPillView.show: `statusLabel.text = status` (unguarded, while the neighbouring `titleLabel.isHidden` write is explicitly guarded with the comment "Written only on a change").

**Ideal fix.** Make the callback mean what it is named: hold the previously reported state in the surface view and call `didChangeReplicaState` only on a transition. Then split the two reasons `surfaceDidLayout` runs -- a layout pass changes the offered grid, an applied record does not -- so a record no longer reports surface facts at all; `MobileSessionModel.handle(.surfaceChanged)` already guards `facts != surface`, so the geometry half self-corrects once the surface stops volunteering unchanged facts. The scroll chrome's reconciliation is the one part that legitimately follows the engine's viewport, so drive `scrollChrome.refresh()` from the display tick that publishes a frame rather than from record application, which is also the moment the drawn window actually moved.

**By construction.** A callback that only fires on a transition makes "the UI was rebuilt because output arrived" unrepresentable; the redraw path can then only be entered by an actual session change.

**Cheaper fallback.** Guard the label writes in `ConnectionStatusPillView.show` and make `MobileSessionModel` return no `.redraw` when the projection is unchanged. That suppresses the UIKit half while leaving the per-record projection composition and scroll-chrome writes in place, and it puts the change detection in the wrong layer.

**Measurement.** No existing instrument sees this. What would decide it: a device Time Profiler capture during a sustained flood in the observed pane, reading main-thread time in `MobileStatus.line`, `UILabel.setText`, and `UIScrollView` layout, each of which must fall to the rate of real state changes rather than the rate of records. A cheaper structural check that is decisive on its own: count `.redraw` effects produced by a fixed record stream in a MobileSessionModelTests scenario -- it must be a small constant, not one per record.

**Regression risk.** A missed transition would leave the status line or the scroll indicator stale, which is a correctness regression rather than a speed one; the workload that shows it is a gap or stream end arriving between two ordinary records. Nothing here can make the steady state slower.

**Verification.** MobileSessionModelTests covering the state-change sequence (awaitingSynchronization -> exact -> gap -> exact) must still produce a redraw on each real transition, and MobileScrollTests must still reconcile the chrome after a remote viewport record. Both assert observable outputs of the pure model, so they survive the callback change.

**Risk.** The scroll chrome's reconciliation currently rides the record path, so moving it to the display tick changes when the indicator catches up with a remote viewport record; MobileScrollDriver's idle-reconciliation rules must be re-read before the move.

**Vetted.** Every quote checks out. `TerminalSurfaceView#apply` fires `didChangeReplicaState?(replica.state)` unguarded on every record; `MobileSessionController#start` wires that closure to `dispatch(.replicaStateChanged(state))` followed by `surfaceDidLayout()`; `MobileSessionModel` returns `[.redraw]` for the steady `.exact` case; `surfaceDidLayout` calls `scrollChrome.refresh()` and dispatches `.surfaceChanged` built from `surfaceView.nativeGrid` -- which is itself a full `TerminalRenderMetrics` construction, so this path is also one third of MOBILE-1's per-record font work. `ConnectionStatusPillView#show` writes `statusLabel.text` and `titleLabel.text` unguarded right beside the explicitly guarded `titleLabel.isHidden` with its "Written only on a change" comment. Raising confidence from 4 to 5. Effort stays small for the transition guard, which is the part that removes most of the work; moving `scrollChrome.refresh()` onto the display tick is the part that needs `MobileScrollDriver`'s idle rules re-read first.

<a id="mobile-5"></a>

##### MOBILE-5. Own the replica off the main actor and hand the main actor frames instead of records

`structural` &middot; impact 3, confidence 2 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 3 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/MobileSessionController.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileConnectionRunner.swift`, `/Users/dan/Code/danterm/ios/DanTermMobileApp/Sources/DanTermMobileApp/TerminalSurfaceView.swift`

**Problem.** Every frame the reader thread pulls off the socket is hopped to the main queue individually (`deliveryQueue` targets `.main`), and everything downstream of it runs on the main actor: `decodePaneTapeRecord`'s JSON walk, the model's event drain, the replica's decode, `Terminal.feed` (parsing and grid mutation for the entire remote stream), damage accumulation, and the geometry and redraw work the other findings describe. The phone therefore parses the Mac's whole output on the thread that also runs touch handling, scrolling physics, keyboard animation, and the display link. Nothing forces this: `PaneReplica` is a `Sendable` value over a pure engine, and the only main-actor consumer is the display tick, which needs a plan and a damage set -- not a record.

**Evidence.** MobileConnectionRunner.init: `self.deliveryQueue = DispatchQueue(label: "com.danneu.danterm.mobile-connection-delivery", target: deliveryQueue)` with `deliveryQueue: DispatchQueue = .main` and the comment "The main queue is the default so UIKit can consume events without a second asynchronous hop"; `enqueue` performs one `deliveryQueue.async` per frame. MobileSessionController: `@MainActor final class MobileSessionController`, `case .applyRecord(let record): try surfaceView.apply(record)`. TerminalSurfaceView is `@MainActor` and owns `private var replica = PaneReplica()`.

**Ideal fix.** Give the replica its own actor (or keep it on the reader thread behind the existing serialized delivery queue) and let it consume records where they arrive. The main actor then receives only what it must: replica-state transitions, and at display-link cadence a published `(RenderFramePlan, TerminalDamage)` pair -- which is also the shape finding 2 wants. Local scroll and input stay ordered by going through the same actor, and `checkpointSource()` stops copying a live main-actor value.

**By construction.** With the replica behind its own actor, a record cannot reach the main actor at all, so "the phone parses the remote stream on the UI thread" stops being expressible; the main-actor surface can only be handed a plan.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the replica on the main actor but batch: drain all records available in one main-queue hop instead of one hop per record, so the queue drain amortizes and the intervening UIKit work happens once per batch rather than once per record. That reduces hop and redraw overhead without moving `Terminal.feed` off the main thread, which is the dominant term under a flood.

**Measurement.** No existing instrument sees this, and the ladder's own warning applies in spirit: moving work off the critical path onto another core reads as neutral to any CPU-total metric, so process CPU is the wrong number here. What would decide it: a device Time Profiler capture under a sustained flood, reading main-thread on-CPU share (which must fall) together with a scroll-gesture responsiveness measure taken during the same flood -- hitch or frame-drop count while dragging the scroll chrome. If neither can be captured, this finding is honestly unmeasurable today and should be treated as an occupancy argument, not a benchmarked win.

**Regression risk.** Ordering is the risk: local viewport scrolls, claim renewals, and checkpoint snapshots currently interleave with record application in one serialized main-actor drain, and an actor hop can reorder them, which would show up as a viewport that jumps or a claim renewed against a stale grid. Throughput could also fall slightly if the hand-off per published frame is more expensive than the per-record hop it replaces, which a low-output interactive session would show.

**Verification.** The kit's existing pure tests (MobileSessionModelTests, PaneReplicaTests, MobileScrollTests) still pin the ordering semantics because the model stays pure and synchronous; add a behavioral test that a local scroll issued between two records lands at the same viewport row as it does today, which is the invariant the hop threatens.

**Risk.** Largest change of the five, and the one whose failure mode is a subtle ordering bug rather than a visible break; worth doing only after findings 1, 2, and 4 remove the per-record work that makes the main actor hot in the first place.

**Vetted.** The factual claims are exact: `MobileConnectionRunner#init` targets `deliveryQueue: DispatchQueue = .main` with the quoted comment and does one `deliveryQueue.async` per frame in `enqueue`, `MobileSessionController` is `@MainActor` and performs `.applyRecord` by calling `surfaceView.apply(record)`, and `TerminalSurfaceView` is `@MainActor` and owns `private var replica = PaneReplica()`. But the claim that "nothing forces this" is wrong, and the recent keyboard work made it more wrong. Four main-actor paths read the replica synchronously and cannot await: `layoutSubviews` reads `anchorSlackPixels` -> `replica.cursorAnchorRow` to position the drawn layer, `scrollFacts` reads `replica.terminal?.scrollProjection` for the scroll chrome, `gridCell(at:)` answers a live gesture, and `isAlternateScreenActive` gates local scrolling. An actor-owned replica turns each of those into an async read from a synchronous UIKit callback, so the design must include a main-actor-held snapshot of those facts that the actor republishes -- which is real design work the finding does not name, and which weakens its "by construction" claim, since the snapshot is a second copy of replica state that can go stale.

**Correction.** The problem statement stands: the phone parses the Mac's whole output stream on the thread that also runs touch handling, scroll physics, keyboard animation, and the display link. The ideal fix is under-specified. Moving `PaneReplica` behind an actor is not sufficient on its own, because `TerminalSurfaceView.layoutSubviews`, `scrollFacts`, `gridCell(at:)`, and `isAlternateScreenActive` all read the replica synchronously from the main actor and cannot await. The fix has to define what the actor publishes to the main actor -- at minimum the cursor anchor row, the scroll projection, the alternate-screen bit, and the drawn geometry -- alongside the `(RenderFramePlan, TerminalDamage)` pair, and accept that those published facts lag the actor by one hop. Confidence drops to 2 because the shape of that boundary decides whether the change is worth making at all.

**Sharper ideal.** Reconsider the cheaper fallback as the leading candidate rather than the lesser one. Batching the drain -- one main-queue hop per available batch of frames instead of one per frame -- combined with MOBILE-1, MOBILE-3, and MOBILE-4 removes nearly all the per-record main-actor work except `Terminal.feed` itself, with none of the snapshot-staleness design. The actor move should be reserved for the case where a profile shows `Terminal.feed` alone dominating the main thread, which the finding honestly admits nothing in this repo can measure today.

**Do after.** [MOBILE-1](#mobile-1), [MOBILE-2](#mobile-2), [MOBILE-4](#mobile-4)

<a id="mobile-6"></a>

##### MOBILE-6. Store the start record's stated pinnedness in the replica instead of keeping the checkpoint's

`correctness` &middot; impact 4, confidence 4 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 2 &middot; found by the vetting pass

**Files.** `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/PaneReplica.swift`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileSessionModel.swift`, `ios/DanTermMobileKit/Sources/DanTermMobileKit/MobileClaimControl.swift`

**Problem.** A pane tape's opening contract states whether the pane's grid is a pinned override, and the replica drops that statement. `PaneReplica.applyStart` sets `state = .exact` on a matching resumed cursor without touching `heldPinned`, so after a resume the replica keeps whatever bit the stored checkpoint carried -- possibly from a previous session, minutes or days earlier. `PaneReplica.pinned` is what `MobileSurfaceFacts.pinned` and therefore `MobileClaimControl` read, and `MobileClaimControl` offers Release only when `pinned == true`. So a pane whose override another client dropped while the phone was away offers Release until the next resize event or sync transfer, and a pane that gained an override offers Claim when it should offer Release. The model reads the true bit from `start.pinned` on the same record (in `pinnedStatement`), so the two readings of one record disagree by construction.

**Evidence.** `PaneReplica.applyStart` in full: after `guard terminal != nil else { state = .gap(.detected); return }` it does only `cursor = startCursor; state = .exact` -- `heldPinned` is not assigned on any path through it, while `replace(with:)` assigns `heldPinned = synchronization.pinned` and `init(checkpoint:for:)` assigns `heldPinned = checkpoint.pinned`. `MobileSessionModel.pinnedStatement` reads the same record's `start.pinned` directly, and `MobileClaimControl.init` sets `release = pinned == true ? .paneResize(pane: pane, resize: .fit) : nil` from `surface.pinned`, which is `PaneReplica.pinned`.

**Ideal fix.** Assign `heldPinned = start.pinned` on the path in `applyStart` that reaches `state = .exact`. The start record is the producer's statement of the pane's pinnedness at the cursor the subscription resumes from, so it is the authority there, exactly as `synchronization.pinned` is in `replace(with:)`. This also makes `PaneReplica` the single owner of the bit, which is what IOS-1's ideal fix needs in order to be safe.

**By construction.** With every path that sets `state = .exact` also stating pinnedness from the record that made it exact, "the replica is exact and its pinnedness bit came from a different position than its cursor" stops being representable.

**Cheaper fallback.** None; the fix is one assignment.

**Verification.** A behavioral test in `PaneReplicaTests`: build a replica from a checkpoint whose `pinned` is true, apply a start record at the checkpoint's cursor whose `pinned` is false, and assert `replica.pinned == false`; and the mirror case. Then a `MobileSessionModelTests` case asserting the projection's claim control offers Claim rather than Release after that resume. Run `swift test --package-path ios/DanTermMobileKit`.

**Risk.** Low. The only behavior that changes is the bit's value immediately after a resumed start; nothing else reads `heldPinned` before the next event. Worth confirming with the user that the start record's pinnedness is meant to be authoritative on resume rather than deliberately deferred to the first resize event -- nothing in the code says it is deliberate, but nothing says it is an oversight either.

**Resolved by docs.** The finding's premise is wrong and its fix would be a regression: on a `--from-cursor` resume the producer states the recorder's **birth** geometry beside the client's own cursor, so `start.pinned` is the bit at sequence zero rather than at the cursor, and a replica that adopted it would replace a correct checkpoint bit with the birth bit -- a phone that claimed a pane, checkpointed, and resumed would offer Claim on a pane it still holds until the next resize, which may never come. Keeping the checkpoint's bit and letting events and syncs move it is the intended behavior; it was only ever recorded in a commit message, which is why two auditors misread it. Closed by stating the contract at `PaneTapeStartRecord`'s geometry fields, `PaneReplica#applyStart`, `PaneTapeStreamState`'s resume branch, and the pane-tape geometry section of `integrations/danterm/SKILL.md`, and by pinning both halves with behavioral tests in `PaneReplicaTests` and `PaneTapeStreamStateTests`.

#### Area: Unicode tables and lookups (`UNI`)

_Scope: Generated Unicode property tables and the lookups over them (UnicodeProperties.generated.swift, CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift/.swift, GraphemeBreak.swift, TerminalScalars.swift, scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py)_

**The auditor's read on the area.** The packed two-stage trie is already the right shape -- `GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables.record(for:)` is two dependent loads for any scalar, with no linear or binary search anywhere on the width/grapheme path, and no table is built at startup from a search structure. What ASCII costs there is worth stating plainly: nothing, on the dominant path. `TerminalInputStream.nextAction` emits `.printASCIIRun` and `Terminal.printBulkASCII` stamps the whole run through `writeNarrowCells` without consulting the table at all, so a printable-ASCII byte pays zero table lookups; only ASCII that `printBulkASCII` declines (pending wrap, insert mode, an open prepend cluster, a wide/spacer cell in the way, a content-identity wrap) falls into `Terminal.print` and pays the same two loads a supplementary-plane scalar pays. Adding a Latin-1 direct-index fast path in front of `record(for:)` would therefore be a cache-shaped answer to a problem the run granularity already solved, and I am not proposing one. The findings below are where the *representation* is still doing avoidable work: a record vocabulary of 29 values stored in 16 bits, a bulk-print predicate expressed as a byte range instead of the table property it actually is, UAX #29 pair rules expressed as array-literal set membership, and canonical-caseless tables whose "this scalar is unaffected" answer costs a binary search and a heap allocation. I did not look at UTF8Decoder, EscapeAbsorber, sprite classification, or the render-side consumers of `TerminalScalars` -- other auditors own those.

<a id="uni-1"></a>

##### UNI-1. Store the packed scalar record as a palette index over 29 decoded entries, not a 16-bit bitfield

`data-modeling` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 1 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/UnicodeProperties.generated.swift`, `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py`

**Problem.** `GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables.stageTwo` holds 31,488 `UInt16` entries (62,976 bytes) and `stageOne` holds 4,352 `UInt16` entries (8,704 bytes), 71,680 bytes total. I reconstructed the full 0x110000-entry record array from the committed tables: the whole table contains exactly **29 distinct record values**, and the largest stage-one block index is **122**. So stage one is a `UInt16` array whose values all fit a byte, and stage two is a `UInt16` array drawing on a 29-value vocabulary. On top of the size, every call to `terminalUnicodeClassification` -- once per non-ASCII printed scalar, and once per ASCII character `printBulkASCII` declines -- re-derives the four fields from bits (`record & 0b11`, three shifted mask tests, `record >> 5`) and runs two failable `rawValue` initializers guarded by `preconditionFailure`, because the bitfield can represent a width of 3 and a grapheme class of 31 that no generated entry ever holds.

**Evidence.** `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#packed_two_stage_tables`: `block_size = 1 << 8` (hardcoded, never searched) and `if len(block_indexes) > 0x10000: raise RuntimeError("packed Unicode table exceeds UInt16 stage-one indexes")` -- the generator guards a 65,536-block ceiling while actually emitting 123 blocks. `UnicodeProperties.generated.swift#GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables`: `static let stageOne: [UInt16]`, `static let stageTwo: [UInt16]`, and `static func record(for value: UInt32) -> UInt16 { let block = Int(stageOne[Int(value >> 8)]); return stageTwo[(block << 8) | Int(value & 0xFF)] }`. `UnicodeProperties.generated.swift#terminalUnicodeClassification`: `guard let width = TerminalCellWidth(rawValue: UInt8(record & 0b11)) else { preconditionFailure("Generated cell width is invalid") }` and `guard let result = GraphemeBreakClass(rawValue: UInt8(record >> 5)) else { preconditionFailure("Generated grapheme class is invalid") }`. Reconstructed counts: 29 distinct stage-two values, max value 545, max stage-one value 122.

**Ideal fix.** Have the generator emit the record vocabulary as what it is: a `static let palette: [TerminalUnicodeClassification]` of 29 fully-formed entries, `stageTwo` as `[UInt8]` palette indices, and `stageOne` as `[UInt8]` block indices. `record(for:)` becomes `palette[Int(stageTwo[(block << 8) | Int(value & 0xFF)])]` -- a load of an already-decoded value. Also let the generator search the block shift instead of fixing it at 8; I computed the packed sizes across shifts 5-11 on the committed data, and shift 7 with a palette is the minimum at 32,186 bytes (8,704 + 23,424 + 58) against 35,898 at shift 8 and 71,680 today.

**By construction.** A cell width of 3 and a grapheme-break class of 31 stop being representable, so the two `preconditionFailure` arms in the hottest lookup in the engine cease to exist rather than being merely unreached, and the four bit-mask extractions per scalar disappear with them. The bit layout also stops being a contract restated in two places (the generator's `records = [1 | (grapheme_classes[value] << 5) ...]` and the Swift decoder's masks) and becomes a single generated palette literal.

**Cheaper fallback.** If the extra palette indirection is unwanted, take the free half: `stageOne` as `[UInt8]` (max value 122) and keep stage two `UInt16`. That alone is 67,328 bytes and needs no change to the decode.

**Measurement.** `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed` -- `feedDurationNanoseconds` is the number that must move, and per the A/A table a difference under 0.9 points is not a difference. Be honest about what that instrument can see: the `unicode-wrapping` corpus is one of four streams in the workload and its own non-ASCII share is roughly 13 scalars per ~145-character line, so the per-scalar decode saving is diluted and `equivalent` is a plausible honest outcome. The size half is directly measurable and not on the ladder at all: `size -m` on the built `TerminalCore` object, or `nm -S` on the two table symbols, must show ~71,680 bytes of `__const`/`__data` fall to ~32-36 KB. `just terminal-memory-probe` cannot see it -- it reports `Terminal.memoryCensus`, which measures grid state, not static module data.

**Regression risk.** The palette adds a third dependent load to a chain that is currently two. The palette is 29 entries, so it occupies a couple of cache lines and stays resident under any sustained feed, but a workload that touches the table sparsely between long gaps could pay a miss the bitfield form does not. That risk is the reason `terminal-feed` must be run rather than reasoned about, and it is the argument for the fallback if the run comes back `slower`. No mirror, cache, or hand-maintained side table is introduced -- the palette is generated output, regenerated by the same script from the same pinned data files.

**Verification.** `UnicodeWidthTests` and `GraphemeBreakTests` already check the table against the committed `reference_grapheme_properties` and `GraphemeBreakTest.txt` ranges for every scalar, and `TerminalASCIIRunTests` checks that every scalar in 0x20...0x7E is narrow and `.other`. Those are exhaustive over the codespace and structure-insensitive: they assert what the lookup returns, not how it is packed, so a correct repacking keeps them green and an incorrect one fails on a named scalar.

**Risk.** Regenerating the file requires the pinned Unicode data files; the header records their sha256 so a regeneration from different inputs is detectable. Low.

**Vetted.** I parsed the committed tables out of `UnicodeProperties.generated.swift` and reproduced every number: `stageOne` 4,352 entries with max value 122, `stageTwo` 31,488 entries with max value 545 and exactly 29 distinct values, 71,680 bytes total. `record(for:)`, the two `preconditionFailure` guards, and the generator's hardcoded `block_size = 1 << 8` with its 0x10000 ceiling check are all as quoted. Impact drops one because the certain half is static size (~71 KB to ~32-36 KB) while the per-scalar decode saving is, by the finding's own honest measurement note, likely to read `equivalent` on `terminal-feed`; the palette also adds a third dependent load.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 9 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/UnicodeProperties.generated.swift` is emitted whole by `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#production_source` as one Python f-string. It declares `enum TerminalCellWidth: UInt8` (zero/narrow/wide), `struct TerminalUnicodeProperties: Equatable, Sendable` (cellWidth plus three emoji bools), `struct TerminalUnicodeClassification` (properties plus graphemeBreakClass, with NO protocol conformances), the thin wrappers `terminalUnicodeProperties(for:)` and `graphemeBreakClass(for:)`, the decoder `terminalUnicodeClassification(for scalar: Unicode.Scalar) -> TerminalUnicodeClassification`, and `private enum GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables` holding `static let stageOne: [UInt16]` (4,352 entries), `static let stageTwo: [UInt16]` (31,488 entries) and `static func record(for value: UInt32) -> UInt16 { let block = Int(stageOne[Int(value >> 8)]); return stageTwo[(block << 8) | Int(value & 0xFF)] }`. The decoder does five bit extractions and two failable rawValue inits guarded by preconditionFailure. On the generator side, `packed_two_stage_tables(...)` builds `records = [1 | (grapheme_classes[value] << 5) for value in range(MAX_SCALAR + 1)]`, overwrites the low two bits for wide and zero-width ranges, ORs in bits 2/3/4 for the three emoji properties, then dedupes 256-scalar blocks with a hardcoded `block_size = 1 << 8`. Nothing has moved since the finding was written.

**Change sites.**

- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#packed_two_stage_tables` -- Stop packing a bitfield. Build a per-scalar tuple (width, isExtendedPictographic, isEmojiModifier, isEmojiVariationBase, graphemeClass), intern it into an ordered palette dict (expect 29 entries), and dedupe blocks of palette indices. Make block_size a searched parameter rather than a constant if the shift search is in scope. Return (stage_one, stage_two, palette) -- a three-tuple, so the call site in main changes too.
- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#production_source` -- Emit `static let palette: [TerminalUnicodeClassification]` as 29 literal initializers, stageOne and stageTwo as [UInt8], and a record(for:) returning the decoded value: `palette[Int(stageTwo[(block << SHIFT) | Int(value & MASK)])]`. Delete both preconditionFailure arms and the five bit extractions from the emitted terminalUnicodeClassification, which becomes a one-line forward. Its Python signature must accept the third argument.
- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#main` -- Unpack the third return value from packed_two_stage_tables and pass it to production_source.
- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#integer_array` -- Reused for both stages; it already takes values_per_line, so at most a formatting tweak for byte-wide values.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/UnicodeProperties.generated.swift` -- Regenerated wholesale. Never hand-edit -- the header says so and the sha256 line is the audit trail.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/UnicodeProperties.generated.swift#TerminalUnicodeClassification` -- Must gain `: Sendable` (and probably Equatable). It has no conformances today, and the package builds in .swiftLanguageMode(.v6), so a `static let palette: [TerminalUnicodeClassification]` of a non-Sendable element type will not compile. This is an emitted-text edit inside production_source.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift#print` -- Calls terminalUnicodeClassification(for: scalar) and reads .properties / .graphemeBreakClass. Signature unchanged, so no edit expected -- listed so the next agent knows this is the hot caller.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/GraphemeBreak.swift#shouldBreak` -- Reaches the table twice per pair via graphemeBreakClass(for:). No edit expected; the second hot caller.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift (emoji-variation-base guard)` -- Calls terminalUnicodeProperties(for: baseScalar).isEmojiVariationBase. No edit expected.

_How this list was built: I grepped app/, lib/, and scripts/ (excluding .build) for terminalUnicodeClassification, terminalUnicodeProperties, graphemeBreakClass(for, TerminalCellWidth, TerminalUnicodeClassification, stageOne, stageTwo, and record(for to establish the full consumer set, and read packed_two_stage_tables, production_source, and main in the generator end to end. The consumer set is small and closed because the table enum is private, so I am confident the list is complete. I did not build or run the generator._

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/UnicodeWidthTests.swift -- "generated policy matches every Unicode 17.0 scalar" -- walks all 1,112,064 scalars against the independently generated unicodeReferenceRanges and pins width, Extended_Pictographic and Emoji_Modifier; exhaustive and structure-insensitive, so a mispacked palette fails it on a named scalar
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/GraphemeBreakTests.swift -- "generated grapheme properties match every Unicode 17.0 scalar" -- the same exhaustive walk for the folded break class and isEmojiVariationBase, asserting a classified count of exactly 1,112,064
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/GraphemeBreakTests.swift -- "pairwise segmenter matches every Unicode 17.0 grapheme boundary" -- replays the committed GraphemeBreakTest.txt corpus through the segmenter, exercising the table via its real consumer
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/UnicodeWidthTests.swift -- "width policy handles narrow, wide, zero-width, and property overlaps" and "Extended_Pictographic is independent from scalar width" -- named-scalar spot checks
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/UnicodeWidthTests.swift -- "Unicode tables are pinned to version 17.0.0" -- asserts terminalUnicodeVersion, so it fails loudly if the file is regenerated against different inputs
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalASCIIRunTests.swift -- "every printable ASCII scalar is narrow and breaks as .other" -- re-reads the table for 0x20...0x7E; the precondition printBulkASCII relies on
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalASCIIRunTests.swift -- "Prepend is the only class an ASCII scalar does not break from" and "an ASCII scalar still joins an open prepend cluster" -- the other two table-derived preconditions of the bulk-print path

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- None. Every test reaches the table only through terminalUnicodeProperties(for:), graphemeBreakClass(for:), or terminalUnicodeClassification(for:), and asserts the returned values. GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables is private, so no test can name stageOne, stageTwo, or record(for:). I grepped the whole tree for all three entry points and for the two table symbols to confirm this.

**Write this test first.** There is no new failing test. UNI-1 is a pure repacking: the same classification comes back for every one of the 1,112,064 scalars, and the only behavior that disappears -- the two preconditionFailure arms -- was unreachable, so it cannot be asserted. The characterization tests that guard the change are `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/UnicodeWidthTests.swift -- "generated policy matches every Unicode 17.0 scalar"` and `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/GraphemeBreakTests.swift -- "generated grapheme properties match every Unicode 17.0 scalar"`. Together they compare the production table against an independently generated reference across the entire codespace for all five fields, and they already run in the gate. Do not invent a test asserting that stage one is [UInt8] or that the palette holds 29 entries -- that is the structure assertion AGENTS.md forbids, and a future Unicode revision could legitimately change the count. If a deciding number is wanted for the size half of the claim, `nm -S` on the two table symbols of the built TerminalCore object is the measurement, reported once in the commit message rather than frozen in a test.

**Blockers and surprises.** Four things worth knowing, one of them a real gate. (1) Regenerating needs the pinned Unicode data. scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#verified_data downloads ten files from unicode.org unless --data-dir points at an already-downloaded copy, and checks each against a committed sha256. There is no justfile recipe for it and nothing in scripts/run-test-suite.sh regenerates or diff-checks the output, so the gate cannot tell you the file is stale. Plan for network access or a local data dir. (2) main() writes SIX artifacts from one run, not one: the production file, UnicodeReference.generated.swift, GraphemeReference.generated.swift, GraphemeBreakCorpus.generated.swift, CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift, plus the two conformance corpora under Tests/TerminalCoreTests/Fixtures/unicode/. Only the production file should change; the other five must come back byte-identical, and a diff on them means the input data drifted. That is the cheapest correctness check available before running any test. (3) Swift 6 language mode is on for this target and TerminalUnicodeClassification carries no conformances today, so a static let palette of it will not compile without adding Sendable. Easy, but it stops the first build if unnoticed. (4) The audit's own honest note stands: the per-scalar decode saving will likely read `equivalent` on terminal-feed, so the claimable win is the static size drop from ~71,680 bytes to ~32-36 KB. Report it that way rather than hunting a feed verdict the instrument cannot produce. Two things easier than they read: nothing outside the generated file can name the tables (GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables is private), and UNI-1 has no upstream dependency -- UNI-2 and UNI-4 are the ones that say 'do after UNI-1', not the reverse.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.
