<a id="uni-2"></a>

##### UNI-2. Derive the bulk-print run predicate from the scalar record instead of from a printable-ASCII byte range

`perf-hot-path` &middot; impact 4, confidence 4 &middot; effort large &middot; wave 2 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalInputStream.swift`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Terminal.swift`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/UnicodeProperties.generated.swift`

**Problem.** The run granularity that makes plain text cheap is keyed on a byte property -- `byte >= 0x20 && byte <= 0x7E` -- rather than on the grid property it stands for. So a scalar the generated table classifies as identical to ASCII 'A' still arrives as a separate `.print(scalar)` action and pays, per cell: one table lookup and decode, the whole `appendToOpenClusterIfJoined` attempt (two `indices.contains` bounds checks, two cell-kind reads, a `graphemeBreak` call, a `scalars.first` read), `invalidateInspection`, `currentStyleId()`, a one-cell `writeNarrowCells`, and `rememberOpenCluster()` reading the cell back and copying its `TerminalScalars`. I checked the committed table directly: U+2500 (box drawing), U+2588 (block element), U+2801 (braille), U+0410 (Cyrillic), U+03B1 (Greek) and U+00E9 all carry record value `1` -- byte-identical to the record for `A` -- and 921,871 scalars in the codespace carry that exact record. Those are precisely the character sets a real TUI paints, so on a full-screen btop or ncurses frame essentially every cell takes the per-character path that ASCII was explicitly lifted out of.

**Evidence.** `TerminalInputStream.swift#isPrintableASCII`: `byte >= 0x20 && byte <= 0x7E`, and `TerminalInputStream.swift#nextAction`: `if absorber.isGround, decoder.isIdle, Self.isPrintableASCII(byte) { let start = index; repeat { index += 1 } while index < bytes.count && Self.isPrintableASCII(bytes[index]); return .printASCIIRun(start..<index) }` -- every other scalar falls through to `default: return .print(scalar)`. `Terminal.swift#printBulkASCII` states the precondition it is really relying on: "every scalar in 0x20...0x7E is narrow and grapheme-break-`.other` in the generated table, so no character of a run can be wide or be joined by the next one; and Prepend is the only class an `.other` scalar does not break from". That is a statement about records, not about bytes.

**Ideal fix.** Let the generated record carry the predicate. With the palette from finding 1, a `isBulkPrintable` field on the 29 palette entries costs zero extra table bytes and is derived by the generator from the same width and class data (`width == .narrow && class == .other && !isExtendedPictographic && !isEmojiModifier && !isEmojiVariationBase`). Then `nextAction` extends the run across decoded scalars carrying that flag rather than across bytes in 0x20...0x7E, and `printBulkASCII` keeps its existing cut rules unchanged. `writeNarrowCells` already takes a `scalar: (Int) -> Unicode.Scalar` supplier, so the write side needs no new shape -- only a supplier that walks decoded scalars in order rather than indexing bytes.

**By construction.** The duplicated statement of "which characters can be stamped in bulk" collapses. Today it exists three times -- as a byte range in `isPrintableASCII`, as a prose invariant in `printBulkASCII`'s doc comment, and as an assertion in `TerminalASCIIRunTests` that re-reads the table to confirm the range still holds. After the lift the table is the only statement, and a future Unicode revision that moved a character out of the bulk-safe set would change the run, not silently invalidate a comment.

**Cheaper fallback.** Keep the byte-range parser run as-is and add a second, narrower run only for the two-byte and three-byte UTF-8 ranges that are wholly bulk-printable (Latin-1 supplement through Greek/Cyrillic, and U+2500-U+259F). That recovers box drawing and blocks without touching the decoder's structure, but it re-introduces exactly the hardcoded range list this finding is about, so it is a worse representation and should be named as such if chosen.

**Measurement.** `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed`, watching `feedDurationNanoseconds`. State the limitation up front rather than after the run: the `unicode-wrapping` corpus is Spanish written without accents, CJK (wide -- excluded by the predicate), combining marks and emoji (excluded), so it contains almost no narrow non-ASCII *runs* and terminal-feed will most likely read `equivalent`. The workload that contains this cost is `synchronized-frames` (95 captured btop frames, ~95% drain, box drawing and braille throughout) -- and per `research/23/D4` it carries no frozen rule and issues no verdict. So this win is largely **unmeasurable by the calibrated ladder**; the honest instruments are a descriptive `synchronized-frames` collection and `just benchmark-trace synchronized-frames template="Time Profiler"` showing the share of `Terminal.print`/`appendToOpenClusterIfJoined` fall. If the change is wanted as a decision, a new terminal-feed corpus of box-drawing frames is the prerequisite, not an optional extra.

**Regression risk.** The parser gets a per-scalar table load inside its run loop where it currently has a byte comparison, so a stream of scalars that are *not* bulk-printable pays a lookup the byte test did not. Since those scalars go on to `Terminal.print`, which does the same lookup, the fix is to carry the already-decoded classification into the action rather than look it up twice -- if that carry is not done, mixed emoji/CJK text gets slower and `terminal-feed` on `unicode-wrapping` is exactly the arm that would show it. No cache or mirror.

**Verification.** `TerminalASCIIRunTests` already pins the contract that a run must be indistinguishable from one `.print` per character, and `TerminalInputStream`'s token tests state the stream that way. Extending the run must keep those green, plus new cases feeding a box-drawing row, a Cyrillic row, and a row that mixes bulk-printable scalars with a combining mark and with a wide scalar, asserting the resulting grid equals the grid produced by feeding the same bytes one at a time. Chunk-invariance (feed the same bytes split at every offset, expect the same grid) is the structure-insensitive form of that test and it is what catches a run that crosses a boundary it should have cut.

**Risk.** Highest-effort item here and it touches the decoder/reducer seam, which is where chunk-invariance lives. Medium-high; the chunk-split test above is the thing that makes it safe.

**Vetted.** `isPrintableASCII`, the run loop in `nextAction`, and `printBulkASCII`'s doc comment stating the record-level precondition are all verbatim. I evaluated the committed tables directly: U+0041, U+00E9, U+03B1, U+0410, U+2500, U+2588 and U+2801 all carry record value 1, and exactly 921,871 scalars in the codespace carry it -- the finding's counts are exact. One gap the plan must settle: `.printASCIIRun` hands back a byte range and `printBulkASCII` indexes bytes, so a scalar-keyed run needs either a second sequential UTF-8 decode at write time or a scratch scalar buffer, and `nextAction`'s doc comment explicitly refuses to materialize a token array (`research/33/F9`). The sequential re-decode is the version that keeps that rule; say which one is chosen.

**Do after.** [UNI-1](#uni-1)

<a id="uni-3"></a>

##### UNI-3. Generate the UAX #29 pair verdicts as a class table instead of array-literal set membership

`perf-hot-path` &middot; impact 2, confidence 4 &middot; effort small &middot; wave 4 &middot; rewritten

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/GraphemeBreak.swift`, `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py`

**Problem.** `GraphemeBreakState.shouldBreak` runs once per non-ASCII printed scalar (from `Terminal.appendToOpenClusterIfJoined`) and once per ASCII character `printBulkASCII` declines. It decides the Hangul rules by building four `Array` literals and calling `contains` on each -- an O(n) scan over a freshly constructed array, at a point in the cascade every scalar passes through, for rules that fire only on Hangul. `GraphemeBreakClass` has 19 cases, so each of those sets is a 19-bit value; representing them as arrays turns a single mask-and-test into an allocation-shaped construct that depends on the optimizer's willingness to stack-promote and unroll it. The whole cascade is ~15 sequential branches plus a `normalize` switch, evaluated per scalar, to answer a question whose inputs are two 19-valued enums.

**Evidence.** `GraphemeBreak.swift#shouldBreak`: `if previous == .l && [.l, .v, .lv, .lvt].contains(current) { return false }`, `if [.lv, .v].contains(previous) && [.v, .t].contains(current) { return false }`, `if [.lvt, .t].contains(previous) && current == .t { return false }`. These sit above the far more common GB9/GB9a/GB11 paths, so ordinary combining-mark and emoji text pays all three before reaching the rule that decides it.

**Ideal fix.** Have the generator emit a 19x19 pair table of three-state verdicts -- `break`, `noBreak`, `consultState` -- keyed by (previous, current), 361 bytes. `shouldBreak` becomes one load and a switch, with the stateful machinery (GB9c indic, GB11 pictographic, GB12/13 regional indicator) reached only for the pairs the table marks `consultState`. All of GB3-GB9b, which is where ordinary text lands, is answered by that single load. As a strictly smaller version of the same idea, the class sets become `UInt32` bitmask constants tested with `mask & (1 << rawValue)`, which is by construction allocation-free.

**By construction.** A set of grapheme classes stops being an `Array` that must be built, scanned, and hopefully optimized away, and becomes a value whose membership test cannot allocate. With the full pair table, the rule text also stops being a hand-transcribed cascade whose order is load-bearing -- the ordering constraint that makes `if previous.isControl || current.isControl` have to sit above the Hangul rules disappears into a generated table.

**Cheaper fallback.** Replace only the four array literals with `UInt32` bitmask constants and leave the cascade's shape alone. That removes the array construction with a two-line change and no new generated artifact, but it leaves the branch chain and the duplicated rule statement in place.

**Measurement.** `just benchmark-quick baseline=HEAD workload=terminal-feed` -- `feedDurationNanoseconds`, distrust anything under 0.9 points. Unlike finding 2, the workload genuinely contains this cost: `unicode-wrapping` puts a combining mark (`café` as e + U+0301) and a four-scalar emoji ZWJ sequence on every one of its 9,000 lines, and every one of those scalars traverses `shouldBreak`. If the win is real this is the cell that should show it. `just benchmark-feed-sample` is the diagnostic to run first, since it isolates `Terminal.feed` headlessly and will say whether `shouldBreak` appears at all before a paired run is spent on it.

**Regression risk.** A 361-byte pair table is one to six cache lines and is touched on the same path as the scalar trie, so it competes with it for L1 -- negligible against the 70 KB the trie itself occupies today, and smaller still after finding 1. The real risk is behavioral, not performance: the cascade's rule ordering encodes GB precedence, and a table generated from a wrong precedence reading is wrong on pairs no ordinary text produces. That is what makes the exhaustive test below non-negotiable rather than nice to have.

**Verification.** `GraphemeBreakTests` already replays the committed `GraphemeBreakTest.txt` corpus (its sha256 is pinned in the generated header), which is the exhaustive conformance suite for exactly these rules and is entirely structure-insensitive -- it feeds scalar sequences and asserts boundary positions. A pair table that gets any precedence wrong fails it on a named case. No new test shape is needed; the existing corpus is the proof.

**Risk.** Medium. The rules are subtle and stateful, but the conformance corpus is exhaustive and already wired up.

**Vetted.** The three quoted lines are verbatim in `GraphemeBreak.swift#shouldBreak`, and `shouldBreak` does run once per printed scalar with an open cluster (`Terminal.appendToOpenClusterIfJoined`) and once per search-query scalar pair. But this is the same finding as FEED-5, on the same three lines of the same file, and FEED-5 states the better ideal. I also read the whole cascade against the proposed pair table: `normalize` mutates state before any rule runs, and the GB9c/GB11/GB12 arms both read and write state, so a pair table would have to mark a large share of pairs `consultState` and still guarantee the state each `break` verdict leaves behind -- it does not remove the cascade, it adds a generated artifact in front of it.

**Correction.** Merge into FEED-5 and use its vetted ideal: rewrite the four array literals as `==` chains, matching the five class predicates already written that way. Drop the 19x19 pair table: it is a larger structure, not a simpler one, it introduces a hand-transcribed precedence reading as a new failure mode, and the stateful rules still have to run. A `UInt32` bitmask also adds new vocabulary and would achieve uniformity only by rewriting five correct predicates, with no expected generated-code difference for these 2-4-element sets. Also correct the count -- `shouldBreak` has three set-shaped rules holding four array literals, not five.

**Sharper ideal.** The `==` chains are the ideal here: they remove the collection-shaped expression and make this file consistent without adding a mask representation. The pair table addresses a different, unmeasured problem (branch count) and should be raised separately if a profile ever shows the cascade rather than the array literals.

**Conflicts with.** [FEED-5](#feed-5)

<a id="uni-4"></a>

##### UNI-4. Let the canonical-caseless tables answer "this scalar is unaffected" without a binary search or an allocation

`perf-hot-path` &middot; impact 3, confidence 5 &middot; effort medium &middot; wave 4 &middot; confirmed

**Files.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift`, `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift`

**Problem.** Every non-ASCII grapheme the search scan touches goes through `canonicalCaselessKey`, which runs `canonicalDecomposition` twice with a `flatMap(fullCaseFold)` between them. For a scalar that has neither a canonical decomposition nor a case fold -- the overwhelming majority, and every CJK ideograph, box-drawing character and braille pattern -- that costs three `exactIndex` binary searches (~11 dependent, cache-scattered probes each over the 8,324-byte `decompositionScalars` and the 6,340-byte `foldScalars`) purely to return "absent", plus a fresh single-element heap array from `fullCaseFold` per scalar, plus the `result` array, the `.map` array, and the second pass's copies. `canonicallyOrder` adds a fourth binary search per scalar through `canonicalCombiningClass` over 403 ranges whenever a decomposition produced more than one scalar. This is the only place in my area where a search still stands where a table would answer, and it is per-cell over the scanned region, per search keystroke.

**Evidence.** `CanonicalCaseless.swift#exactIndex`: `while lower < upper { let middle = lower + (upper - lower) / 2; if sortedValues[middle] < value { lower = middle + 1 } else { upper = middle } }` over `GeneratedCanonicalCaselessTables.decompositionScalars` (2,081 `UInt32`) and `foldScalars` (1,585 `UInt32`). `CanonicalCaseless.swift#fullCaseFold`: `guard let index = exactIndex(...) else { return [scalar] }` -- the unmapped case, which is the common one, allocates an array to hold one scalar. `CanonicalCaseless.swift#canonicalCombiningClass` is a third hand-written binary search over three parallel arrays (`combiningClassLowerBounds`, `combiningClassUpperBounds`, `combiningClassValues`, 403 entries each). `TerminalSearch.swift#searchGraphemeKey` reaches all of it: `let key = canonicalCaselessKey(for: scalars)`, guarded only by an ASCII fast path (`scalar.value < 0x80`).

**Ideal fix.** Two changes, both representational. First, give the scalar record two more states -- `hasCanonicalDecomposition`, `hasCaseFold` -- either as fields on the palette from finding 1 or as a small parallel two-stage trie generated by the same script; then "unaffected" is answered by the same constant-time trie the width path already uses, and the binary searches run only for the scalars that actually have mappings. Second, make `fullCaseFold` return `TerminalScalars` instead of `[Unicode.Scalar]`: fold outputs are one to three scalars, `TerminalScalars` already exists in this module precisely to keep the one-scalar case off the heap, and the identity case then allocates nothing at all.

**By construction.** "This scalar is unchanged by NFD and by full case folding" stops being a conclusion reached by failing three searches and becomes a property read from the table -- and returning `TerminalScalars` makes the identity fold structurally incapable of touching the heap, rather than merely usually cheap.

**Cheaper fallback.** Emit the minimum mapped scalar for each table (`0xC0` for decomposition, `0x41` for folding) and early-return below it. That is a single comparison and it covers all of ASCII and most of Latin-1, but it is a threshold that must be kept in step with regenerated data by hand, which is a weaker guarantee than a generated bit.

**Measurement.** No instrument on the ladder can see this, and I want to say that plainly rather than name a workload that would report `equivalent` by construction: none of the six calibrated workloads runs a search, and `terminal-feed` never calls `canonicalCaselessKey` at all. `Instrument.searchDistanceWork` and `Instrument.searchIndexMaintenance` count content units inspected, not work per unit, so they will not move either. Deciding this needs an instrument that does not exist -- a headless search microbenchmark over a CJK-heavy retained scrollback, paired the way `benchmark-headless-draw` is paired. Until that exists, the claimable part is the allocation count, which is countable by reading the code: one array per scalar from `fullCaseFold` plus four per grapheme from the two decomposition passes, all of which the ideal fix removes for unmapped scalars.

**Regression risk.** Two extra bits on the record widen nothing if they ride the palette (finding 1), and widen the record's bit budget from 10 to 12 -- still inside a `UInt16` -- if they do not. A separate parallel trie would add a second table to keep in cache on the search path only, which is not the feed path, so it cannot regress `terminal-feed`. Changing `fullCaseFold`'s return type touches only two call sites, both in this file. None identified beyond that; I looked for a feed-path caller of these functions and there is none.

**Verification.** `CanonicalCaselessTests` already checks `canonicalDecomposition` and `fullCaseFold` against the committed reference derived from `UnicodeData.txt` and `CaseFolding.txt`, and `TerminalSearchTests` checks match results through `canonicalCaselessKey` end to end. Both assert returned values, not internal shape, so a correct short-circuit keeps them green. The specific case worth adding is a scalar that folds to itself but *does* decompose, and one that decomposes to itself but *does* fold, so a single conflated "unaffected" bit cannot pass.

**Risk.** Low. The change is confined to two files plus a generator field, and the conformance tests are already exhaustive over the mapped scalars.

**Vetted.** `exactIndex`, `fullCaseFold`'s `return [scalar]` unmapped path, and the third hand-written binary search in `canonicalCombiningClass` are all verbatim. `canonicallyOrder` already guards `values.count > 1`, so the fourth search is correctly described as conditional. The reach is confirmed: `TerminalSearch.searchGraphemeKey(for: TerminalScalars)` short-circuits only single ASCII scalars and otherwise falls through to `canonicalCaselessKey`, and `Search.init(query:)` builds the index over all closed history, so a CJK-heavy scrollback pays this per cell per query.

**Sharper ideal.** Two refinements. First, the allocation count is one higher than stated: `searchGraphemeKey(for: TerminalScalars)` calls `Array(scalars)` before `canonicalCaselessKey`, so the ideal shape takes the borrowed scalars rather than an array. Second, prefer a small generated "affected by NFD / affected by full fold" table of its own over adding the two bits to the width/grapheme record: this is a search-only property, and hanging it on the feed path's palette grows that palette's vocabulary and couples two paths that share no caller. Returning `TerminalScalars` from `fullCaseFold` is the part that is unambiguously right and can land alone.

<details>
<summary><b>Starter kit</b> -- current shape, 16 change sites, the tests, and the first failing test</summary>

**Current shape.** `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift` is a 120-line file of five internal free functions and one private one: `func canonicalDecomposition(of scalars: [Unicode.Scalar]) -> [Unicode.Scalar]`, `func fullCaseFold(of scalar: Unicode.Scalar) -> [Unicode.Scalar]`, `func canonicalCaselessKey(for scalars: [Unicode.Scalar]) -> [Unicode.Scalar]`, plus private `appendCanonicalDecomposition(of:to:)`, `canonicallyOrder(_:)`, `canonicalCombiningClass(of:)` and `exactIndex(of:in:)`. `canonicalCaselessKey` is literally `canonicalDecomposition -> flatMap(fullCaseFold) -> canonicalDecomposition`, so an unmapped scalar pays two `exactIndex` decomposition probes, one `exactIndex` fold probe, and a one-element `[scalar]` from `fullCaseFold`, all to return itself. The tables live in `CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift` as nine flat parallel arrays under `enum GeneratedCanonicalCaselessTables` (2,081 `decompositionScalars`, 1,585 `foldScalars`, 403 combining-class ranges), emitted by `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#canonical_caseless_source`. The reach is `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift`: `Terminal.Search.searchGraphemeKey(for scalars: TerminalScalars) -> SearchGraphemeKey` short-circuits only a single sub-0x80 scalar and otherwise does `searchGraphemeKey(for: Array(scalars))`, which calls `canonicalCaselessKey`. Its two hot callers are the closed-record index build (inside `history.forEachClosedRecordCell`) and the live-projection scan (inside `stream.forEachRow`). Nothing has moved: the last touch to CanonicalCaseless.swift is `edd3eeb0 refactor(terminal): emit canonical caseless tables as flat typed literals`.

**Change sites.**

- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#canonical_caseless_source` -- Emit the new affectedness table. Two bits per scalar -- 'has a canonical decomposition (Hangul range included)' and 'has a full case fold' -- built from the `decompositions` and `case_folding` dicts it already receives, so no new UCD file is needed.
- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#packed_two_stage_tables` -- The existing 256-entry-block, dedup-by-block trie builder for the width/grapheme records. Either generalize it to take a records list, or add a sibling that reuses the same block loop. Most blocks in the new table are all-zero, so stage two should collapse to a handful of blocks.
- `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#main (the write step)` -- Only if the new table lands in its own generated file rather than inside `CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift`; the path list is the block that already names `canonical_caseless` at the bottom of main.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift#GeneratedCanonicalCaselessTables` -- Gains the stage-one/stage-two arrays plus a `static func record(for value: UInt32) -> UInt8` reader shaped exactly like `GeneratedPackedUnicodeTables.record(for:)` (`stageTwo[(Int(stageOne[Int(value >> 8)]) << 8) | Int(value & 0xFF)]`). Regenerated file -- do not hand-edit; the header says so.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift#fullCaseFold` -- Return `TerminalScalars` instead of `[Unicode.Scalar]`, and guard on the fold bit before `exactIndex`. The unmapped path becomes `TerminalScalars(scalar)`, which is `.single` inline storage and touches no heap. Note the honest limit: a genuine two- or three-scalar fold still hits `.spill`, because `TerminalScalars` is inline only for 0 and 1 scalars.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift#appendCanonicalDecomposition` -- Check the decomposition bit before the `exactIndex` probe; on a clear bit, `result.append(value)` and return. Keep the Hangul algorithmic branch first, or let the generator set the bit across the Hangul syllable range and keep the branch as the mapping.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift#canonicalCaselessKey` -- The shape change. Today it always builds three arrays. With the two bits it can answer 'no scalar here is affected' up front and return the input unchanged, and its `decomposed.flatMap(fullCaseFold)` must be rewritten as a loop appending each `TerminalScalars` result, since `flatMap` over the new return type would re-introduce the arrays. Signature should take borrowed scalars rather than `[Unicode.Scalar]` -- the audit's Sharper ideal note that `searchGraphemeKey` calls `Array(scalars)` first is correct and that allocation is the one the ideal shape removes.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift#canonicalDecomposition` -- Signature follows `canonicalCaselessKey`'s to accept the borrowed form; the body is unchanged apart from the early-out inside `appendCanonicalDecomposition`.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/CanonicalCaseless.swift#canonicallyOrder and #canonicalCombiningClass` -- No change required. `canonicallyOrder` already guards `values.count > 1`, so its combining-class searches only run when a decomposition actually produced multiple scalars -- which after the early-out is exactly the affected scalars. Leave them alone; a third generated bit here is a separate, unmeasured idea.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift#Search.searchGraphemeKey(for: TerminalScalars)` -- Drop `Array(scalars)` and call the borrowed-scalar `canonicalCaselessKey` directly. This is the per-cell allocation the Sharper ideal names.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/TerminalSearch.swift#Search.searchGraphemeKey(for: [Unicode.Scalar])` -- The query-side sibling, called from `searchGraphemeKeys(for query: String)`. Signature adapts to whatever borrowed form the key function takes; behavior unchanged.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/NeedleWindow.swift#SearchGraphemeKey` -- Optional and out of scope unless you want it: `case scalars([Unicode.Scalar])` could become `case scalars(TerminalScalars)` so a multi-scalar key never round-trips through an array. That ripples into `NeedleWindow.Unit` equality and the `TerminalSearchTests` oracle, so treat it as a follow-on, not part of this change.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift#officialCaseFoldingCorpusMatches` -- `#expect(fullCaseFold(of: scalar) == expected)` where `expected` is `[Unicode.Scalar]`. Stops compiling when the return type changes -- wrap as `TerminalScalars(expected)` or compare `Array(fullCaseFold(of: scalar))`.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift#canonicalCaselessKeyOrder` -- Three `canonicalCaselessKey(for:) == [Unicode.Scalar]` comparisons; adapt to the new argument and return types.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift#officialNormalizationCorpusMatches` -- Its inner `check` helper calls `canonicalDecomposition(of: input)` with `[Unicode.Scalar]` and compares against `[Unicode.Scalar]`. Mechanical, but it is the 20,034-line sweep, so keep the comparison allocation-free enough that the suite does not slow down noticeably.
- `lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalSearchTests.swift#independentSearchMatchRanges` -- Two `canonicalCaselessKey(for: Array(...))` calls feeding `SearchOracleGrapheme.key: [Unicode.Scalar]`. The oracle must keep producing the same keys; adapt the argument and the field type together.

_How this list was built: I grepped app/, lib/, scripts/, tests-ui/, docs/ and agent-docs/ for `canonicalCaselessKey`, `fullCaseFold`, `canonicalDecomposition`, `CanonicalCaseless`, `GeneratedCanonicalCaselessTables`, `searchGraphemeKey`, `SearchGraphemeKey` and `generate-terminal-unicode-tables`, and opened every hit. The symbol surface here is genuinely small -- five internal functions, one generated enum, two private call sites in TerminalSearch.swift, three test files -- so I believe the list is complete. I also read `TerminalScalars.swift`'s storage cases and `UnicodeProperties.generated.swift`'s `record(for:)` reader to confirm the trie shape the new table should copy, and `packed_two_stage_tables` in the generator to confirm the builder is reusable. I did not build or run anything._

**Tests that must keep passing.** These are the safety net.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- officialNormalizationCorpusMatches -- the whole pinned Unicode 17.0 NFD corpus, 20,034 lines and 100,170 relations, checking c1/c2/c3 against c3 and c4/c5 against c5. This is the characterization test for the decomposition half and it is exhaustive over every mapped scalar
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- officialCaseFoldingCorpusMatches -- every C and F mapping in the pinned CaseFolding.txt. The characterization test for the fold half
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- canonicalCaselessKeyOrder -- the D145 pipeline end to end on precomposed uppercase N-tilde
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalSearchTests.swift -- the whole suite, in particular every case routed through independentSearchMatchRanges, which recomputes matches from an independent oracle built on canonicalCaselessKey; if the short-circuit ever disagrees with the tables these fail on real search results rather than on a unit boundary

**Tests that will need updating.** Expect these; they assert the thing being changed.

- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- officialCaseFoldingCorpusMatches -- compares `fullCaseFold(of:)` against `[Unicode.Scalar]`; stops compiling the moment the return type becomes TerminalScalars. This is the compile break that lands first
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- canonicalCaselessKeyOrder -- three equality comparisons against `[Unicode.Scalar]` literals built by its private `scalars(_:)` helper
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/CanonicalCaselessTests.swift -- officialNormalizationCorpusMatches -- its private `check(_:equals:relation:line:)` helper takes and compares `[Unicode.Scalar]`, so it moves with `canonicalDecomposition`'s signature
- lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/TerminalSearchTests.swift -- independentSearchMatchRanges and the private SearchOracleGrapheme struct -- both hold `[Unicode.Scalar]` keys produced by canonicalCaselessKey

**Write this test first.** This is not a pure refactor -- there is a real behavioral claim available and it should be the first test, because the corpus tests cannot fail for the reason this change exists. Suite `CanonicalCaselessTests`. Name: "an unaffected scalar is keyed without probing either mapping table". Add one `Instrument` case in lib/TerminalCore/Sources/TerminalCore/Instruments.swift -- `case canonicalCaselessTableProbe`, documented as 'scalars that fell through to a binary search over the decomposition or fold tables, so the search key path can assert that a scalar with neither mapping is answered from the table' -- and record it once per `canonicalCaselessKey` call with the number of scalars that fell through, following the `recordCellMaterialization` convention of one task-local lookup per call rather than per cell. The test feeds a handful of scalars that have neither a canonical decomposition nor a case fold -- a CJK ideograph such as U+6F22, a box-drawing character U+2500, a braille pattern U+2800 -- and asserts `Instrument.canonicalCaselessTableProbe.measure { _ = canonicalCaselessKey(for: ...) } == 0`. It fails today with a nonzero count, because `appendCanonicalDecomposition` runs `exactIndex` over `decompositionScalars` for every scalar on both NFD passes and `fullCaseFold` runs one over `foldScalars`, all three returning absent. It asserts work done, not structure: any representation that answers 'unaffected' from a table passes. Two guard tests belong in the same commit, and they pass both before and after -- one scalar that folds to itself but does decompose (U+00C0 LATIN CAPITAL A WITH GRAVE folds to U+00E0 and decomposes, so use U+0134 or check the tables), and one that decomposes to itself but does fold (U+0130 or a Cyrillic capital) -- so that a single conflated 'unaffected' bit cannot pass. If the user rejects a new instrument on the search path, then the change is a pure refactor and the characterization test is `CanonicalCaselessTests.officialNormalizationCorpusMatches` plus `officialCaseFoldingCorpusMatches`; do not invent a structural test in its place.

**Blockers and surprises.** Three, all manageable, plus one honest limit.

The generator needs the network. `scripts/generate-terminal-unicode-tables.py#verified_data` fetches all nine UCD files from unicode.org and sha256-checks them, with `--data-dir` as the only offline path. Only two of the nine are in the tree (`CaseFolding-17.0.0.txt` and `NormalizationTest-17.0.0.txt` under lib/TerminalCore/Tests/TerminalCoreTests/Fixtures/unicode/, which are renamed copies the same script writes). Regenerating `CanonicalCaseless.generated.swift` therefore needs either network access or the seven missing files staged in a directory. Plan for that before the work starts. A workaround worth knowing: the affectedness bits are derivable from data already committed -- `decompositionScalars` is exactly the scalar set with canonical decompositions and `foldScalars` exactly the fold set -- so a table built from those plus the Hangul range is provably identical to one built from UnicodeData.txt, if network access turns out to be the obstacle.

The finding's Ideal-fix paragraph proposes hanging the two bits on 'the palette from finding 1' (the packed width/grapheme record). Its own Sharper-ideal paragraph then reverses that and prefers a standalone table, on the grounds that affectedness is a search-only property and the width record is the feed path's. Follow the Sharper ideal: it removes any dependency on that other finding, so UNI-4 has no ordering constraint on anything.

`TerminalScalars` is inline only for the empty and single-scalar cases -- `Storage` is `.empty` / `.single` / `.spill([Unicode.Scalar])`. So changing `fullCaseFold`'s return type removes the heap for the identity fold and every one-to-one fold, which is the overwhelming majority, but a genuine one-to-three fold still allocates. Say that plainly in the commit rather than claiming the allocation is gone.

Nothing else bites. `fullCaseFold`, `canonicalDecomposition` and `canonicalCaselessKey` are all internal to TerminalCore, so no `lib/` public API ripples; `TerminalScalars` is public but unchanged. No design doc constrains this file -- I grepped docs/ and agent-docs/ for the three function names and the table enum and found nothing outside the audit itself. The two hot call sites are both inside `Terminal.Search`, both `private static`, and both already hand over a `TerminalScalars`.

**Readiness: ready.** An agent can start on this from the above.

## Pruned

Findings the vetting pass took out of the plan. They keep their ids and their
sections above so a link never dangles; this is the index and the reason.

- [DRAW-2](#draw-2) -- Give RenderFramePlan row-indexed run ranges so drawing a row set is an index, not a filter of every run
  Duplicate of FRAME-1 with the weaker ideal. Its two distinct contributions are worth folding into FRAME-1 rather than kept as a separate item: (a) with a row-indexed plan `clipFramePlan` is deleted outright and `drawRenderFrame` takes a row set, so the notion of a "clipped plan" -- a value that reads as a complete frame but is not one -- stops existing; (b) `RenderFramePlan` is public and `Equatable`, so equality after the change must compare logical run sequences and not storage layout. DRAW-2's claim that `clipFramePlan`'s fast path "silently assumes" row-sorted runs is not quite right: the fast path tests `rows.damagedRowCount == plan.rows` against one row-0-anchored span, which is whole-viewport coverage regardless of run order, so nothing is being assumed there.
- [FRAME-2](#frame-2) -- Recompute ink reach only for the damaged rows instead of the whole plan on every incremental apply
  Duplicate of DRAW-1 over the same code, with a weaker ideal fix. Fold its one distinct contribution into DRAW-1: FRAME-2 names the ledger lineage argument precisely -- the store's `rowReaches` is already translated with the pixels on a shift and `staleDamage` names every row that changed since this buffer last presented, so the ledger is current for every undamaged row by contract, and that is what makes any narrowed recompute correct. FRAME-2 also slightly misstates the consumption: `newReaches` is not read only at the damaged indices. `renderApplyShape`'s plan-set loop reads `newReaches` at every row within one row of an erase span, so a narrowed recompute must still supply correct values for those neighbors -- which the ledger does.
- [FRAME-5](#frame-5) -- Derive each swapchain buffer's missed damage from its presented generation instead of mirroring damage into every buffer
  The cure is worse than the disease. The cost being removed is three `formUnion` calls per publish at depth 3 -- the finding itself reports it as undecidable on the ladder. The replacement is an ordered publish log, a trimming policy at the oldest presented generation, a fall-back-to-full rule when a buffer outruns the log, and a fold at acquisition that the finding's own Regression risk admits can be slower than today's incremental union and can grow unbounded while a buffer stays cold. That is strictly more machinery guarding a hazard that is already unrepresentable. Note also that shift composition is order-dependent and `formUnion` escalates to `.full` on a region mismatch, so the fold would have to replay publishes in order per buffer -- reproducing exactly the work it defers, not removing it. If anything here is worth keeping it is the observation that `isCurrent`, `lastPresented` and `latestWholeFrameDamageGeneration` are three spellings of "how far behind is this buffer"; that is a naming and documentation remark, not a restructure.
- [RECON-3](#recon-3) -- Normalize terminal-reported text once at ingress so DisplayLine is stored, not recomputed every sweep
  The stated ideal fix breaks a deliberate, documented contract in lib/DanTermCore/Sources/DanTermCore/DisplayLine.swift#DisplayLine (raw stays verbatim for IPC targeting and checkpoint reproduction; the type is deliberately non-Codable). Strip that out and what remains -- avoid re-normalizing text that is already clean -- is already written up as LOOKUP-3 (impact 4, small), at the same call sites, with a fix that keeps the contract and adds no stored state. Two findings for one line of work, one of which fights a design doc-grade comment, is worse than one. Track it under LOOKUP-3.
- [ROW-1](#row-1) -- Delete PackedRetainedRow's store and readers; keep only the shared C1 cell-word constants
  Duplicate of STORE-2, already marked dropped in the audit file. Carry ROW-1's one distinct sentence -- that this is deliberately unmeasurable, so `benchmark-quick` must read `equivalent` and the census must be byte-identical -- into STORE-2's measurement note, and delete the rest.
- [ROW-5](#row-5) -- Recycle the vacated row's cell buffer on scroll instead of allocating a fresh one per line
  Subsumed by FEED-1, which quotes the same `moveAndFillRows`/`makeBlankRow` code, proposes the same ring-base ideal, and covers the two costs ROW-5 omits (the per-row `GridRow` moves and the throwaway `Array` for `appendToScrollback`). Keeping both means two plans against the same twenty lines. Carry into FEED-1: ROW-5's measurement line that `just terminal-memory-probe --payload scrollback-plain --json` must show `rowStorageAllocationCount` fall to one per live screen, and the correction that the per-cell blank initialization survives the fix.
- [WIRE-4](#wire-4) -- Detect persisted-state divergence without re-projecting the whole model on every message
  LOOKUP-1 and LOOKUP-2 already cover this ground and cover it better. LOOKUP-1 states the same problem with the same evidence and proposes the fix that actually removes it (split `AppModel` into a stored `persisted` half so divergence is a comparison of a value the model already holds, with `Array.==` short-circuiting on identical buffer storage). LOOKUP-2 is exactly WIRE-4's stated ideal fix -- typed ids in the snapshot DTOs -- scoped as its own finding. WIRE-4's own combination is internally inconsistent: its title promises "without re-projecting the whole model on every message" while its ideal fix keeps projecting the whole model every message and only shrinks the constant factor (no `uuidString`, cheaper compare). Fold it into LOOKUP-1 + LOOKUP-2 and drop the id. One caveat worth carrying into LOOKUP-2: the snapshot ids are optional on purpose -- Model.swift#validateAndBuildDetailed mints fresh ids for id-less hand-authored init-file entries and `compactMap`s away a todo with a bad id -- so typed ids must keep the optionality and will convert a malformed todo id from "skip that todo" into a whole-file decode failure.
